News.title: Inflation and government borrowing highest for a year ahead of next week's Budget
News.content:
UK inflation and government borrowing both hit their highest in a year on Wednesday, adding to the pressure on Chancellor John Healey ahead of his first Budget in a week.

The pace of UK price rises accelerated to 3.5% in the year to September, pushed up by sharp increases in petrol and diesel prices.

The inflation figures came as UK government borrowing jumped to nearly Â£25bn in September, which means borrowing for the financial year to date is running Â£6bn above official forecasts.

Healey has promised a Budget which will keep to Labour's commitment not to hike the three main taxes - income tax, National Insurance and VAT - while sticking to the party's fiscal rules.

Inflation, the rate at which prices are rising, jumped from 3.1% in the year to August to 3.5% in the year to September. It is the highest inflation has been since October 2025, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

The cost of filling up a vehicle has soared in recent months as conflicts in the Middle East and Europe continue to squeeze global oil supplies.

The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran after US and Israeli attacks has severely disrupted a major global supply line for crude oil, while oil refining capacity has been hampered globally by Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other's infrastructure after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Petrol prices in September were the highest since August 2022, the ONS said, while diesel also rocketed.

The average price of petrol rose by 8.2p per litre to 169.5p per litre between August and September, while diesel rose to 192.5p per litre.

Motor fuel prices overall rose by 29.8% in the period covered by the figures.

ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said September's "notable" increase meant inflation was at its highest rate in almost a year.

As well as fuel prices, the increase was driven by rising prices for airfares, computer games and live events, Fitzner said.

September's inflation figure is also important because it suggests how benefits will increase next April.

It means the state pension will most likely rise by 3.9%, in line with average wage rises from May to July, due to the triple lock.

The inflation figure for September also dictates how other benefits will rise in April. By law, benefits such as personal independence payment (PIP) and carer's allowance must rise in line with September's consumer price index (CPI) measure of inflation.

News.title: Lawyer caught by BBC offering to make illegal-worker fine go away
News.content:
A solicitor has been secretly filmed by the BBC explaining how he could make a Â£45,000 illegal-working fine go away.

Mohammad Alias Yousaf - also known as Alias - made the claim to an undercover reporter, who was posing as a mini-mart owner facing a fine for employing an illegal worker.

The Bradford-based solicitor told his potential client he could avoid paying the fine, if he could find someone overseas prepared to declare themselves the owner of the mini-mart.

Alias has denied ever providing such advice to anyone, or giving false information to the Home Office.

At least Â£150m is currently owed to the government in uncollected illegal-working fines, according to Home Office figures obtained by the BBC.

In response to our investigation, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced a review of the way such fines are issued and collected.

In a statement, she said she wanted to thank the BBC "for exposing those who undermine our rules".

Many business owners do not take the fines seriously, a law enforcement official has told us anonymously.

She told us she had seen immigration fine notices, "some worth Â£40,000, stuffed in a box" on a mini-mart counter.

When she had asked a member of staff if the business owners intended to pay, she said she had been told: "'It's got nothing to do with me.'"

News.title: Huge crowds watch attempt to save shark stranded in South Korean canal
News.content:
Huge crowds have flocked to a canal in South Korea to watch a stranded shark.

The 9ft 10in (3m) shark, nicknamed Bukangi, was first spotted in the waterway last month in the south-eastern city of Busan.

Now a third attempt has been made to rescue the female using nets to guide her back to the open sea.

It is thought the shark may have been drawn to the canal by unusually warm water and plenty of fish.

The BBC's Seoul correspondent Jake Kwon goes to Busan to follow the latest attempt to rescue Bukangi.

Video editor: Marina Costa

News.title: Zelensky says intelligence sharing 'works now' as US envoy to meet Putin in Russia
News.content:
Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who also took part in the talks in Oslo alongside the Norwegian prime minister, said "genuine progress" had been made on proposals to achieve peace but gave no details, and warned that patience would be needed.

Witkoff was not present at their joint press conference with Zelensky after the talks, nor was President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner who had attended via video link.

A US official later said the meeting had been "very productive and constructive" and that there was a "strong alignment at the working level" between the US, Ukraine and Europe on "next steps".

Relations between Ukraine and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that President Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".

Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has also sought to blame Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.

Speaking after the news conference in Oslo, Trump again told reporters at the White House he wanted Kyiv to "make a deal".

He said Russia would like to "get it done" and it was "time for Ukraine to end this war".

Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

Russian drone attacks have continued this week. Ukrainian officials said at least 10 people were killed on Tuesday - four in Kyiv and the capital region, another four in the eastern Donetsk region, and two in the central city of Dnipro.

Another attack overnight on Wednesday killed two more people near Kharkiv, the country's second-largest city.

News.title: Woman given cancer diagnosis by hospital employee who accessed her records
News.content:
A woman was told she had cancer by a hospital employee who accessed her record days before she was due to receive test results from her consultant.

Pippa Boardman, from Lostwithiel in Cornwall, said she had lost her dignity and privacy through the data breach at the Royal Cornwall Hospital in Truro. She said she did not receive an apology from the hospital until it was contacted by the BBC.

The trust said it was "truly sorry" and "appropriate action had been taken".

It added: "While we cannot disclose the details of individual employment matters, we want to reassure Ms Boardman that we have treated this extremely seriously."

Boardman, who is now recovering well from cancer, said her personal information was accessed by a man she vaguely knew who worked at the hospital.

She said: "I got a phone call at home from somebody I know through the sport that I play.

"This man said to me 'Pippa, I don't want you to worry, but you've got cancer'.

"I just couldn't really believe it".

Two days later Boardman was told by her consultant she did have breast cancer.

Nine months on, she said her strong recovery did not undo the damage done by the experience, adding: "I lost my dignity and I've lost my privacy."

Along with Boardman's case there have also been other recent NHS data breaches, described by Health Secretary Yvette Cooper as a disgrace.

News.title: Amber warning issued as Storm Austen threatens UK with strong winds and heavy rain
News.content:
The Met Office has issued an amber weather warning for strong winds as Storm Austen is forecast to sweep across parts of the UK.

The warning - the second-highest tier that the Met Office issues - is valid for Cornwall and parts of west Devon from 03:00 until 10:00 BST on Friday.

Wind gusts of up to 80mph (130km/h) are expected around exposed coasts, with 60-70mph gusts elsewhere.

Flying debris could lead to injuries or a danger to life, with the risk of power cuts and damage to buildings.

A broader yellow Met Office wind warning covers large swathes of southern England and south Wales with some travel disruption possible.

Southern and eastern Scotland is also covered by a Met Office yellow warning - this one for heavy rain which could bring the risk of flooding.

News.title: The Aberfan disaster through the eyes of those who survived, 60 years on
News.content:
"Once I got down into the village, the people were standing all over the pavements with bewildered looks on their faces.

"But then of course, as the day went on, then we realised the extent of this tragedy, and we just stood around talking and holding hands and just waiting and wondering.

"I think the real effect of it came during the night, when mainly fathers had to go in to identify their children and that was the worst part of all.

"And I went in with quite a number of the fathers.

"I well remember one fellow I went in with, and we went around the pews where the children were laid out with blankets over them, and then eventually we lifted the blanket and there was his son.

"And of course, he burst into tears, and I followed. And we just stood there crying.

"To me, it was a ministry of tears.

"In the Bethania vestry, nurses and St John's Ambulance people had to wash down these little bodies and then lay them out.

"That must have been the hardest part of all."

News.title: Giant tunnel proposed to clean up Windermere's sewage problem
News.content:
A Â£3.6bn proposal to stop sewage being discharged into Windermere, England's largest lake, has been unveiled.

The plans, which are backed by the local water company United Utilities and clean water campaigners, would see a tunnel up to 12 miles (19km) long built to transport sewage away from the lake.

At the moment both raw sewage and treated effluent are discharged into Windermere and campaigners say that is why parts of the lake have been turning green each summer, so-called algal blooming.

It is now up to the government to decide if the plan can be further developed, and if the Â£3.6bn price-tag is acceptable.

The Lake District is a Unesco World Heritage site and attracts close to 18m visitors each year.

Windermere is at its heart, with the lake holding around 300bn litres of water. That is so big that it can take 9 months for water entering one end to reach the other.

News.title: Man charged after three Jewish women assaulted
News.content:
A 33-year-old man has been charged after three Jewish women were assaulted in Hackney, east London.

Police were called to Clapton Common at about 13:40 BST on Monday following reports that a man had been detained by Shomrim, a Jewish neighbourhood watch group, after assaulting the women.

The victims suffered minor injuries. The Metropolitan Police said it was treating the incident as a hate crime.

Abdisamad Siad, of Pilgrims Way, Islington, has been charged with three counts of assault by beating. He is due to appear at Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court later.

CCTV posted online by Shomrim appears to show a man running up to a woman before pausing briefly and then punching her twice.

The group said on X that it had already been called because another "visibly Jewish" woman had reported being punched in the face on Clapton Common on Monday.

The Met Police said it had increased its patrols in the local area since the incident.

The force said it was also working with Jewish community leaders to provide "further reassurance" to those living nearby.

Siad has also been charged with grievous bodily harm with intent over an unrelated attack on a woman, who is believed to be known to him, in the Islington area on 16 October.

News.title: Tighter rules planned to protect people from cosmetic surgery that goes badly wrong
News.content:
Only properly trained professionals will be allowed to offer high-risk cosmetic procedures like liquid Brazilian butt lifts (BBLs), vampire facials and chemical peels, under long-awaited government plans for England in 2027.

The government said it wanted to "drive cosmetic cowboys out of the market" and shield people from treatments "that can go badly wrong".

Currently, there are no restrictions over who can carry out these 'no scalpel' procedures, which can harm or kill if not performed safely.

Under the new rules, high-risk procedures for under-18s will also be banned, and rogue providers will face new criminal offences and fixed fines of up to Â£4,000.

News.title: Teenager arrested aged 16 jailed after terror conviction
News.content:
A teenager who was 16 when he was arrested at Heathrow Airport has been jailed after being convicted of providing cyber-security support to groups including al-Qaeda.

Yusuf Shah, from Ilford, was also found to have downloaded documents including instructions on how to make explosives and how to use different types of weapons.

Analysis of Shah's phone found that he had accessed an online magazine published by al-Qaeda that contained information on how to carry out acts of terrorism, and had engaged in chat groups where he offered technical help.

Cdr Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said the case should act as a "warning to parents and carers to be aware of what their children are doing online".

Shah, who was stopped at Heathrow Airport in London under schedule 7 of the Terrorism Act in January 2024, was convicted at Kingston Crown Court and sentenced to four years and two months in prison.

Cdr Flanagan said the police investigation found Shah was being drawn into extremist material and ideologies "when he was only 13 or 14 years old".

She added: "This is reflective of a growing trend of young people being radicalised and accessing extremely dangerous and violent terrorist ideologies and material online."

Shah, who is now 18, had downloaded documents providing instructions on the use of different types of weapons, the Metropolitan Police said.

He had also engaged in chat groups that supported terrorist groups, on the messaging app Telegram.

At one point, the teenager advised members of the group on how to use an untraceable cryptocurrency to make a donation to al-Qaeda.

In March 2024, Shah was approached by an individual on the Telegram app to help produce a guide to cyber-security for Tehrik-e-Taliban (TTP), a terror group. The individual said a senior official within TTP had asked him for this.

Shah produced and sent the individual a document he titled "A Guide on Cybersecurity" that provided detailed information and instruction on cyber-security and the use of cryptocurrency.

He had been convicted of three counts of collecting terrorist materials, one count of entering or becoming concerned in an arrangement to make funds available for terrorism, and one count of providing instruction intended for use in terrorist activities.

Flanagan said: "Even at the age of just 16, Shah had enough knowledge of the online world to be able to provide practical advice to terrorist groups on how to make anonymous cryptocurrency payments."

She added: "I would implore you to have conversations, to be inquisitive about what your children are doing online."

News.title: King praises Strait of Hormuz peace efforts at glittering banquet
News.content:
The US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran in February, killing the country's supreme leader and sparking the ongoing Iran war.

The Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most vital shipping lanes, has been effectively closed since then.

King Charles, Queen Camilla, Prince William and Catherine and Princess Anne were among the royals on duty at Windsor for the state visit.

It was the first state banquet for Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was seated next to the Omani academic and novelist, Jokha Alharthi.

It was a table laden with elaborate candelabra and polished decorations, with five glasses per setting, and even the surface of the salt had an imprint of the cypher of King Charles.

The hot summer meant a bumper crop of pomegranates in the Windsor Castle gardens, and the fruits were placed on the table alongside the floral decorations.

The King's speech, delivered to 160 guests in English with some quotes in Arabic, expressed his approval that his son Prince William had worked on an expedition project alongside the Sultan's son.

"There can be few happier symbols of success than a living relationship being passed from one generation to the next," said the King.

News.title: Two men re-arrested on suspicion of assisting Iran intelligence after RAF Fairford incident
News.content:
Two men have been re-arrested after an incident near RAF Fairford last month, counter-terrorism police have said.

A 24-year-old UK national, and a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national, are being held on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service under Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023, with police saying the investigation relates to Iran.

Police had been alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the US airbase in Gloucestershire in the early hours of 27 September - a major incident was subsequently declared and dozens of homes evacuated.

Seven men in total have been arrested as part of the counter-terror police investigation.

Gloucestershire Police said it had received a call about "three suspicious vehicles" travelling towards RAF Fairford at 00:45 BST on 27 September.

A bomb disposal team was deployed to the village to examine a number of vehicles.

Petrol was found in three vans near the airbase and five men were arrested.

They had been initially arrested on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act and then further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act.

Police later said they did not find "improvised explosive devices".

The re-arrests announced on Tuesday relate to a 24-year-old man who was initially arrested on 27 September near the base and a 25-year-old who was arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts days later on 1 October in the borough of Westminster.

The other five men - who also include a 22-year-old British national arrested in Westminster on 6 October - remain on police bail.

The head of National Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said: "This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement.

"Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it."

The officer added that national security investigations can take time to progress due to their sensitive nature.

"Our specialist teams have been working tirelessly to interrogate the many lines of enquiry involved in this hugely complex investigation," he said.

Days after the incident, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC there were "strong indications" Iran had played a part in the incident.

He did not provide further details at the time.

Iran has previously denied any involvement.

RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for Fairford to be used for defensive strikes against Iran.

In the week after the incident, it emerged that the US had pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America.

US President Donald Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base without giving specific details.

Vice-President JD Vance said it was done out of an "abundance of caution".

News.title: Audit regulator looking into Manchester City accounting
News.content:
The UK audit regulator has confirmed it is leading inquiries into accounting irregularities at Manchester City.

The Financial Reporting Council confirmed in a letter to the House of Commons business select committee it had taken over "regulatory consideration" of the case from the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales on 30 September.

No formal investigation has started, but the FRC is making inquiries into the case.

It comes after Manchester City were found guilty by an independent commission of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, including by artificially inflating the club's financial position by more than Â£900m. City are appealing the verdict.

The FRC has greater resources, and greater powers, to apply sanctions if it does find evidence of violations. It routinely oversees accounting standards at bigger institutions such as listed public companies, but not football clubs.

The FRC can look into the conduct of BDO, Manchester City's auditors, to ask whether the audit was in line with the rules.

It can also apply sanctions to individuals such as directors or employees of the Etihad club, if they are members of professional accountancy bodies.

BDO is the UK's fifth-biggest accounting firm, but claims to be a market leader in football, advising more Premier League and Championship clubs than any other firm.

The independent commission which looked into Manchester City found that the club gave a "misleading impression" of the scheme used to disguise the origin of shareholder funds injected into the club to its auditors, who were "unaware" of the scheme.

Manchester City have said they will appeal against the commission's decision, arguing that it contains "material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe".

Liam Byrne, chair of the business select committee, called for greater powers for the FRC to look into similar cases.

He wrote on X: "The regulator's letter exposes gaps in its ability to compel evidence from the club and pursue directors who fall outside its disciplinary rules.

"This raises serious questions about the powers available to hold companies and directors to account.

"The government has a responsibility to explain why reforms to close these gaps were abandoned - and what will now be done to strengthen accountability."

BDO declined to comment.

News.title: BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra broadcast channels to close
News.content:
BBC Three, which is aimed at young audiences and launched hits such as Fleabag, Normal People and Gavin & Stacey, previously moved online in 2016, but was reinstated as a TV channel in 2022.

BBC Scotland launched as a channel in 2019, broadcasting a variety of Scottish programming including news, sport, documentaries and entertainment.

However, some of the shows that air on the two networks, such as Two Doors Down on BBC Scotland and Sort Your Life Out on BBC Three, are repeats of episodes originally broadcast on other more mainstream BBC channels.

Both networks currently only broadcast TV programming in the evenings, although BBC Scotland simulcasts BBC Radio Scotland during the rest of the day.

The BBC said that the network's nightly programme Reporting Scotland: News at Seven will not move to BBC iPlayer and will cease when the linear channel closes.

Audiences will continue to be served by BBC Scotland's wider news offering, including Reporting Scotland, The Sunday Show, Radio Scotland Breakfast, Debate Night and Scotcast, the corporation said.

While Radio 4 Extra does air some original programming, its schedule is predominantly made up of archive content, much of which is available on BBC Sounds.

Sir Peter Bazalgette, former chairman of ITV and production company Endemol, told BBC News: "This is a modest and pretty well-judged package.

"The essence of it is it protects the spending on content, it really cuts money in the distribution of programmes, and it really had to happen because the BBC has lost 30% of its revenue in 10 years."

But entertainment trade union Equity said Tuesday's announcement "does not signal a thriving BBC, and we are concerned about the UK's preeminent public service broadcaster's ability to meet its duties to the fullest".

Affected staff were told about the changes on Tuesday, although the proposed closure of BBC Scotland and BBC Three had been reported by some media outlets in recent weeks.

The BBC is aiming to cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - almost one in 10 - in an attempt to save Â£500m over two years as it faces "significant financial pressures".

Around 550 job closures have already been announced in news, while more than 30 job cuts have so far been announced for BBC Sport.

The newly appointed director of BBC News, Rachel Jupp, announced on Tuesday that a further Â£5.5m of savings were being proposed, which would represent the closure of around 100 roles.

Meanwhile, several high-profile BBC TV series have been cancelled altogether in recent weeks.

RuPaul's Drag Race UK, Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live at the Apollo, Football Focus, Ski Sunday and Radio 4âs The World Tonight and You & Yours are among the programmes the BBC has dropped so far.

News.title: UK weather: ‘Danger to life’ warning issued by Met Office as Storm Austen set to bring 80mph winds
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

An amber wind warning has been issued for parts of south-west England, where heavy rain and severe gusts of up to 80mph are predicted.

Storm Austen, marking the season’s first named storm, is anticipated to cause travel chaos and potential damage towards the tail end of the week.

In effect from 3am until 10am on Friday, the amber alert applies to Cornwall, Devon, Plymouth and the Isles of Scilly. Gusts between 60mph and 70mph are predicted across these areas, peaking at 80mph in exposed spots.

Heavy downpours may also develop, though winds are expected to ease gradually as the rest of Friday unfolds.

The weather service warned of likely power cuts and building damage, alongside a ‘danger to life’ warning along sea fronts and coastal roads due to large waves and thrown beach debris.

A broader yellow weather warning covers parts of Wales, Herefordshire in the West Midlands, and the South West and South East from midnight to 2pm on Friday.

open image in gallery Storm Austen, marking the season’s first named storm, is anticipated to cause travel chaos and potential damage towards the tail end of the week ( PA )

Strong winds will sweep across southern regions of England and Wales from Thursday night, bringing speeds of 50 to 60mph, with exposed locations reaching 70mph or higher.

A yellow warning for rain has been issued in parts of Scotland between 6am on Friday and 3am on Saturday.

Met Office deputy chief forecaster Chris Bulmer said: “Storm Austen is expected to bring a spell of impactful weather to parts of the UK from Thursday night and through Friday.

“While there remains some uncertainty in the exact track of the storm, there is increasing confidence in the potential for disruptive winds across parts of southwest England, which is why an Amber warning has been issued.

“Winds gusts could potentially reach 60-70 mph for a time, and these strong winds will be combined with spells of heavy rain.

“People in affected areas should keep up to date with the latest forecast and warnings as the event develops.”

open image in gallery The amber warning is in place between 3am and 10am on Friday for Cornwall, Devon, the Isles of Scilly and Plymouth, where gusts of 60 to 70 mph will develop with some exposed areas expecting 80 mph. ( Met Office )

The Met Office said the weather is expected to remain unsettled through the weekend and into next week while low pressure is likely to bring strong winds to northern parts of the UK on Saturday and Sunday.

Ross Macleod, RNLI water safety manager, has asked people not to take “unnecessary risks” when visiting the coast.

He said: “If you plan to visit the coast or a waterside location, we urge you stay a safe distance from the water as conditions could knock you off your feet or wash you into the sea.”

The Met Office storm year runs from September to August, with each 12-month period having its own alphabetical list of names that are used to label successive storms.

This year’s list begins with Austen and continues with Boelo, Chloe, Dano and Evelyn, ending at W with Wende.

News.title: Women’s Aid calls out Big Brother over controversial scenes that ‘risk presenting abuse as entertainment’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Big Brother is at the centre of controversy over housemate Omar’s behaviour, which has prompted Women’s Aid to share a statement.

Viewers have been contacting the charity after Monday’s episode (19 October) due to Omar’s response when Rhianna called time on their relationship.

“You’ve really f***ed me off by saying what you said,” he told Rhianna, and during a later moment, while she was chatting to other housemates, he said into her ear: “Do me a favour. I know you’re upset, but don’t talk about me.”

open image in gallery ‘Big Brother’ viewers left feeling uncomfortable over Omar’s treatment of Rhianna ( ITV )

Later, when Rhianna tried to cover her head in her hands, Omar told her: “Look at me – don’t look away from me.” Big Brother called Rhianna to the Diary Room to separate the pair. After the scenes aired, many concerned viewers flooded X and Instagram with messages urging ITV to remove Omar from the house.

Women’s Aid said that Big Brother is “risking presenting abuse as a form of entertainment” by giving a platform to “worrying” behaviours.

Veronica Oakeshott, the charity’s head of external affairs, said: “The nature of abuse means that it often begins with ‘red flag’ coercive and controlling behaviours like isolating you from friends or repeatedly putting you down, before escalating into other forms of abuse.

“Coercive control creates invisible chains and a sense of fear that impacts every element of a survivor’s life.”

She continued: “It’s worrying to see behaviours like this being given a platform in popular media like Big Brother. We’ve been contacted by many viewers who have expressed concern.

open image in gallery 'Big Brother' viewers are urging Omar to be removed from house ( ITV )

“Not only does Big Brother risk minimising survivors’ experiences, it also risks presenting abuse as a form of entertainment. We must do better to call out and reject abuse as soon as we see it, so women and children can learn the signs and themselves feel confident in speaking up and seeking safety.

“Producers should understand their responsibility to keep contestants emotionally and physically safe. The women in these programmes are real people and need real support.”

The Independent has contacted ITV for comment. But ahead of Women’s Aid’s statement, a spokesperson said: “All Housemates receive Respect and Inclusion training and an extensive briefing from the Big Brother Senior team to prepare them for living in the House and to set out Big Brother’s expectations for appropriate behaviour and language.

“Housemates are monitored 24 hours a day and any instances of inappropriate behaviour are responded to appropriately. Welfare and safeguarding are prioritised throughout the production, with a dedicated welfare team available to support Housemates before, during and after their time in the House.”

After one encounter with Omar, Rhianna tearfully told another housemate: “I don’t know what’s wrong with Omar, but it’s literally making me feel like I’ve constantly been doing something wrong.

“If he’s just in a mood or something, fine. But like it’s just making me feel like I’m going crazy.”

Big Brother was rebooted by ITV in 2023, and this year’s edition – the fourth – has been the most successful yet.

According to ITV, the series has amassed 202m streams on ITVX. Following its success, the channel has commissioned a reunion episode, which will bring back all the housemates after the finale airs on 6 November.

News.title: Halfords sales jump after warm weather boosts summer trading
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Halfords has revealed a surge in sales for the past half-year after a boost from warm summer weather.

The retail firm reported stronger trading across both its motoring and cycling businesses.

Nevertheless, shares in the company slumped after it indicated that investment plans will weigh on profitability in the second half of the financial year.

The Redditch-based business, which runs 367 Halfords stores, two performance cycling stores and 497 consumer garages, said it saw positive momentum in the six months to October 2.

open image in gallery Halfords runs autocentres alongside its retail stores (Matt Alexander Media Assignments/PA) ( PA Archive )

It said group like-for-like increased 7.1% for the half-year, compared with the same period a year earlier.

This included 7.7% growth across its retail operations, with a 7.3% increase in its motoring arm and an 8.3% rise in cycling sales.

Meanwhile, the group’s autocentres business reported a 6.1% sales increase.

Halfords said its first-half growth was supported by the firm’s strategy and positive demand for “seasonal categories” during the summer.

In August, Halfords improved its profit outlook on the back of strong sales for products such as bikes, camping and air conditioning services during the unusually warm weather.

The company said it is still on track to deliver an underlying pre-tax profit of between £55 million and £65 million for the current financial year.

Henry Birch, chief executive of the business, said: “The business continued to perform positively through the first half as we benefited from good execution against our strategic priorities and strong sales of seasonal categories through the warm summer weather.

“We move into the second half with confidence and look forward to sharing more detail on our progress at our interim results announcement later next month.”

Shares in Halfords were 8.3% lower on Wednesday morning.

News.title: Putin says Russia has freed US citizen, 74, jailed since 2022
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Russian president Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday that Moscow has agreed to free the imprisoned US citizen Stephen Hubbard following a plea from US president Donald Trump.

Mr Hubbard, 74, had been held in Russian custody since April 2022 and was serving a nearly seven-year prison sentence in a penal colony for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine, charges he denies.

Putin told US special envoy Steve Witkoff that the former schoolteacher was at the St Petersburg Pulkovo airport and waiting to fly back to the US with him. Witkoff thanked him for the goodwill gesture.

The US envoy flew into Russia's second city on Wednesday morning to review new ideas on ending the war in Europe, with allies anxious that president Trump appears to be turning away from Kyiv while firming up relations with Moscow.

open image in gallery Hubbard was accused of serving as a mercenary for Ukraine against Russia in the course of a military conflict ( Reuters )

Trump told reporters at the White House on Tuesday that he had spoken to Putin about Hubbard, who had been declared wrongfully detained by the State Department.

“Just stick with me,” he said. “I don't want to talk about it, but everybody has been after Hubbard for a long time, long before I got here. And just remember that question for a couple of days from now, okay? Because I do things that nobody else can do.”

“Watch what happens. We have been focused on Hubbard.”

Following a closed trial, a Moscow court convicted Hubbard of being a mercenary in October 2024 and sentenced him to six years and 10 months in prison.

open image in gallery Vladimir Putin, US special envoy Steve Witkoff and other officials attend a meeting at the Constantine Palace on Wednesday ( Reuters )

Prosecutors said Hubbard had joined a Ukrainian territorial defence unit, received training, weapons and ammunition, and was promised $1,000 a month. Russian state media said he had pleaded guilty to the charges he faced.

Family questioned the reported confession, however, saying Hubbard held pro-Russian views and was unlikely to have taken up arms in his seventies.

Martin De Luca, his US-based lawyer, told Reuters in June 2025 that Hubbard had told him the charges against him were false and that he was not in any combat or military unit. He cited Hubbard as telling him Russian soldiers had simply grabbed him from his house.

Putin decided to release him this week on ‘humanitarian grounds’, according to Russian news agency TASS.

open image in gallery Vladimir Putin, pictured in Moscow on Monday, met with Witkoff and suggested new deals with the US ( Reuters )

Speaking at the White House on Tuesday, Trump also took the opportunity to pile more pressure onto Ukraine to cut a deal with Russia to end the four-year conflict.

“Ukraine has to want to settle this war,” he said, suggesting Moscow has the upper hand in the fight as “Russia is a big machine; they just keep grinding forward.”

Ties with Kyiv have been dented by Trump’s October 9 announcement that he would lift sanctions on Moscow to allow for diesel exports in a bid to help lower prices in the US ahead of the November midterm elections.

Since the announcement, Ukraine has complained of disruption to some intelligence sharing and to its use of the Starshield military satellite system, though Zelensky said that a meeting with Witkoff in Oslo on Tuesday had reached an agreement to resolve the issues.

open image in gallery Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev, right, greets U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday ( AP )

Despite the apparently cordial nature of the Oslo summit, Trump remains frustrated with Zelensky, whom he has repeatedly rebuked and suggested needs to be replaced.

Putin, who has shown few signs of compromising on his central war aims, said on Wednesday that Russia would be open to restoring full economic ties with the US, in a sign of the deepening relationship with Trump.

He also suggested Russia could supply fertilisers in a larger amount the US.

Witkoff said he hoped that Putin would at least consider the resumption of trilateral talks with Washington and Kyiv, after the last round in Geneva in February came to nothing.

He said the talks this week in Oslo had been productive and that there was a basis for a ceasefire, according to Russian media.

Who is Stephen Hubbard?

Hubbard was placed in custody in 2022 after Russia captured Izyum, the city in Ukraine where he was living with his Ukrainian partner.

Local journalists have not been able to independently establish the circumstances of his capture, but his sister Patricia Hubbard Fox said she recognised her brother from a YouTube video.

open image in gallery Hubbard spent four years in Russian detention ( Reuters )

The clip, which was recorded in an unknown location, appeared to show Mr Hubbard being questioned about his views on Putin and the war. Another video showed him with his hands bound, being struck with a sandal.

Fox said in 2024 that Hubbard was living off his pension and had few connections with local people – but the siblings haven’t spoken since September 2021.

Why was Stephen Hubbard imprisoned?

A Moscow court convicted Hubbard of being a mercenary during a closed trial in October 2024. He was sentenced to six years and 10 months in prison.

Prosecutors said Hubbard had joined a Ukrainian territorial defence unit, received training, weapons and ammunition, and was promised 1,000 US Dollars (around £747.83) a month.

open image in gallery Hubbard's legal team found out in April 2025 that he was being held in a facility in the Mordovia region, east of Moscow ( AFP/Getty )

State-owned media reported that Hubbard had pleaded guilty to the charges, but Fox argued that he held pro-Russian views and was unlikely to have taken up arms given his age.

Hubbard’s legal team argued that the charges were false and that soldiers had grabbed him from his home.

The US government under the Biden administration designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained. But The State Department has said Russia refused to grant US officials consular access.

The New York Times reported in February 2025 that Hubbard had been moved ​through at least five Russian detention centres before ‌his trial.

News.title: French supermarket chain suffers €1.6 billion hit after riots and looting
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

French supermarket chain Carrefour has seen more than £1bn wiped off the company valuation overnight after riots and looting caused damage worth “tens of millions of euros” across stores.

Curfews have been imposed in cities across France this week after days of destruction and fires being set, aimed at showcasing anger around the cost of living crisis and poor conditions at schools.

In a call with journalists on Tuesday night, the supermarket’s finance ‌chief Matthieu Malige said stores had needed to spend extra on security and in some cases completely shut down, with consumer confidence across the country also impacted.

The result has been a massive drop in share price once markets opened on Wednesday, with the stock down 14 per cent by mid-morning - equivalent to losing €1.62bn (£1.36bn) in market capitalisation - or total company value - overnight.

“The direct costs add up to ⁠several tens of millions of euros of stolen or destroyed merchandise, damaged stores, damaged equipment, and then there are ​also the ​stores we were forced ​to close,” said Mr Malige.

“In the weeks to come we will continue to be impacted as some stores have to close earlier due to curfews, and more broadly we think we're in a new ‌situation marked by deep uncertainty for ​our customers.”

Up to 50 stores were directly hit by the riots, he added, in what CEO Alexandre Bompard said was an “unprecedented situation”, but Carrefour did not clarify exactly how many of the supermarkets would be closed.

That would suggest around 1 per cent of the total stores were affected so far but the company have cut their financial guidance of profits expected for the year ahead.

In part, therefore, management’s slowdown comments can be attributed to the riots in France - but also there remains a wider concern around business operations in other countries.

Garry White, chief investment commentator at Raymond James, suggested the supermarket executives had seized something of an opportunity to roll multiple out-of-sight issues into one very visible one.

“Never let a good crisis go to waste. The cynics amongst us may impertinently suggest that today’s profit warning from Carrefour is a case of its management doing just that,” he said.

“The French supermarket group has warned that the current riots and looting will have a major impact on operating income by between €80m and €200m. This is also a good opportunity to ‘kitchen sink’ a significant sales slowdown caused by other factors.

“Beyond the riots, Carrefour is facing several challenges and the company has also flagged weaker consumption trends in its domestic market, while analysts have pointed to sluggish sales volumes in other key regions, including Spain and Brazil. Some of these slowdowns – such as those caused by the rioting will be one-off events. Many others may be structural and could have a permanent impact on future earnings, expectations of which drive a company’s market valuation.”

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG, added the firm and the wider French stock markets have both suffered as a result of social instability - with potentially more ahead.

“It's no surprise to see this from Carrefour and helps everyone to understand why the CAC40 has done so badly in recent months. French assets have the risk of serious instability hanging over them, which only adds to the gloom around the stock, itself a dismal performer over the last 25 years,” he said. “April's elections mean there is a serious risk of further social disruption early next year, if not before. Any improvement in performance needs to be set against that possibility.”

The CAC40, France’s primary index, is up about 0.6 per cent on Wednesday.

The stock was further hit by Morgan Stanley downgrading its investor guidance on the firm from “overweight” - or buy, in other words - to an effective hold rating, while JPMorgan also cut their estimated price target for the shares.

News.title: Ebola has spread from Congo to 4 other countries. A look at where things stand
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Ebola disease from the fast-moving outbreak in Congo has now spread to four other countries, including two where it's active. It has spread farther across Africa than any previous Ebola outbreak, reaching three regions.

Nigeria on Tuesday became the latest country affected by the outbreak, which was first declared in eastern Congo in mid-May. Caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus for which there’s no approved vaccine or drug, the outbreak has killed at least 4,600 of the 9,500 people infected in Congo.

The World Health Organization has said it is the fastest-growing outbreak of Ebola in history. In Africa, it's been recorded in the central, western and eastern regions.

A recurring problem in the spread in Africa is what appears to be lax surveillance efforts as most of the first cases were confirmed long after people started showing symptoms or after traveling.

Here is where things stand in other countries affected by this Ebola outbreak:

The patient in Nigeria had returned from Uganda

Nigeria confirmed an Ebola infection in its capital, Abuja, in a woman who arrived from Uganda about two weeks ago.

The woman began showing symptoms on Oct. 7 and was admitted to a private hospital in Abuja on Oct. 11, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola.

It is still unclear when she arrived in Nigeria. Health Minister Muhammad Pate said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient and were “doing everything possible to contain this case.”

Uganda reported 20 cases; none are active

Uganda confirmed an Ebola outbreak on the same day as neighboring Congo after detecting the infection in a man traveling from Congo.

The first cases in Uganda were Congolese patients who crossed the border to seek treatment for an unknown illness before it was known they had Ebola, according to health authorities.

The Uganda outbreak was declared over by WHO on Aug. 27, after 20 confirmed cases, including 15 patients from Congo. Eighteen people recovered and two died. More than 800 contacts were identified and monitored, and the country said Tuesday that it has no new cases.

Kenya's first patient traveled from Congo via Uganda

Kenya announced its first Ebola case on Oct. 6, involving a man who traveled from Congo via Uganda before arriving in the capital, Nairobi, on Oct. 3.

He tested positive for Ebola on Oct. 5 and died the same day.

Ebola cases in Kenya have increased to nine, including four relatives of the first patient and four health workers.

Authorities have also identified 135 contacts linked to the nine patients, with 134 in quarantine. Kenya's Health Ministry said there was still no evidence of transmission beyond known contacts of the first patient.

France is the only non-African country to record a case

France in June confirmed a positive case of Ebola in a doctor traveling back from Congo, making it the first and only country outside Africa to have recorded a case in this outbreak.

The individual returned from a humanitarian mission in one of the virus transmission zones in Congo and was taken into care at a specialized facility in France. The person recovered and was discharged on July 4, according to WHO.

News.title: Marco Rubio heads to world’s biggest oil refinery as US scrambles to reshape global energy trade
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Secretary of State Marco Rubio is visiting an unexpected location during his trip to India, heading on Wednesday to a small coastal city in the western state of Gujarat that houses the world's largest oil-refining hub.

The city, Jamnagar, hosts a massive complex run by Reliance Industries, led by billionaire Mukesh Ambani. The stop underscores the growing prominence of energy investments in Washington and New Delhi's relationship, as the United States searches for buyers of Venezuelan oil.

The American government is encouraging India to shift away from Russian fuel imports while simultaneously seeking outlets for increased Venezuelan petroleum output.

open image in gallery Secretary of State Marco Rubio looks on as he speaks with members of the media at the Taj Mahal Palace hotel in Mumbai, India, October 21 ( Reuters )

In Mumbai on Tuesday, Rubio described India as a "refining superpower" capable of processing heavy crude. He noted plans to discuss Venezuelan oil processing with Reliance, adding, "They have the capability to refine heavy crude. They’ve done so in the past, and I think as more and more Venezuelan oil comes online, it’s something they can do."

The Jamnagar facility boasts a processing capacity of roughly 1.4 million barrels daily, turning crude into fuels like diesel and gasoline, as well as raw materials for plastics and synthetic fibers.

Its advanced engineering and vast size make it crucial during geopolitical turmoil, such as conflicts involving Iran and Yemen that threaten key maritime lanes like the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz.

To address these global stability risks, Rubio emphasized that large-scale refining operations help nations navigate energy security challenges.

open image in gallery Tanker "Bald Man" at the Port of Fujairah, as the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran limits marine traffic in the Strait of Hormuz ( Reuters )

"Energy is related to national security. You know, countries fight wars over energy, as an example. Economies collapse over lack of energy. So we’re going to go see a company that has a tremendous amount of refining capability, so it makes all the sense in the world to talk to them about it," he stated.

While Venezuelan crude cannot single-handedly fix wider supply shocks, expanded production offers an immediate buffer.

The visit also highlights the global standing of Reliance Industries and its chairman, Mukesh Ambani, who is scheduled to meet with Rubio. The private conglomerate holds vast investments across retail, telecom, petrochemicals, traditional oil and gas, and green energy.

Reliance is also supporting energy initiatives inside the United States, backing a planned $300 billion refinery initiative in Brownsville, Texas, which U.S. President Donald Trump unveiled in March.

Beyond its industrial significance, Jamnagar gained international fame in March 2024 when Ambani’s youngest son, Anant Ambani, held lavish pre-wedding celebrations with Radhika Merchant there. The festivities brought together prominent politicians, celebrities, and international corporate leaders, highlighting the family’s wealth.

Subsequent elaborate family events have further established Jamnagar and its central refinery as the corporate empire's crown jewel, converting the industrial hub into a prominent international display of Reliance Industries' reach.

News.title: Rio Ngumoha dazzles on coming-of-age night in Europe
News.content:
Iraola made major changes at half-time, substituting Araújo and playing without a conventional right-back for the second half. It was brave and changed the momentum of the game, pushing his team higher up the pitch in what looked like a man-to-man marking arrangement. It enabled Iraola’s players to deny Villarreal the space and possession they had enjoyed in the first half when they had taken a two-goal lead – chiefly because of the mistakes of the home team. However much that was destabilising for Liverpool, by half-time they were level.

“They are so good on the ball,” Iraola said of Villarreal afterwards. Indeed, Villarreal’s manager Iñigo Pérez, a former Athletic team-mate of the Liverpool manager, was a coach whom Iraola sought to appoint at Bournemouth. “People probably don’t rate them [Villarreal],” Iraola said, “but after Barça they are probably the best in La Liga. They have 61 per cent of possession. Probably they have not had the results they deserve. If you are not really aggressive, you are not going to get the ball.

“We didn’t take as much risk. We were struggling because it is not a team that you can just press a bit. Either you go all the way or you will struggle without the ball.” Once Liverpool had done so, he said, his team had “won a lot of duels”. He was right in that respect. With the space squeezed, it was the power of Liverpool’s midfield that was telling.

Virgil van Dijk gave the first goal to Villarreal’s small No 9 Georges Mikautadze who had looked up to that point like he was hopelessly mismatched against the Liverpool captain and Jérémy Jacquet. Van Dijk’s misjudged header back to Alisson let in the striker, who did well to gather the ball and then hit it early. The second Villarreal goal at the midpoint of the first half was a mistake from Kostas Tsimikas, who failed to step up and played both Mikautadze and Cardona onside from Nathan Saliba’s ball. Either might have tucked it in but it was the left-back Cardona who took it on.

News.title: Inflation jumps in run-up to Healey’s maiden Budget
News.content:
Inflation has jumped to its highest level in almost a year, underlining the challenges facing John Healey, the Chancellor, ahead of his first Budget next week.

The consumer prices index climbed from 3.1pc in August to 3.5pc in September, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

Inflation was ahead of the 3.4pc predicted by economists and is now at its highest level since October 2025.

The sharp rise was driven by soaring fuel costs as a result of the Iran war. The ONS said average petrol prices rose by 8.2p a litre in September and diesel by 10.7p. Both reached levels not seen since 2022, in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Suren Thiru, chief economist at the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, said: “Rising inflation is turning the Budget into a perilous high-wire act for the Chancellor, increasing pressure for cost-of-living support while pushing up government borrowing costs, which is shrinking fiscal headroom and narrowing his policy options.”

Britain spent more money on debt interest last month than in any September on record, official figures show.

The UK’s debt servicing costs rose to £10.9bn in September, the highest total for the month since at least 1997, according to the ONS.

This burden helped to push national debt above £3 trillion for the first time.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said the unhappy milestone and the rise in inflation “show Labour has lost control of the economy”.

Public sector net debt has soared by 50pc since it first exceeded £2tn in June 2020.

Mr Healey insisted the British economy still had “momentum” and pointed to Wednesday morning’s approval of new drilling for gas in the North Sea as evidence of this.

He said: “We know that price rises from conflicts in the Middle East and Europe are hitting Britain and countries worldwide. Last week, the IMF said our UK fiscal discipline stands out with the lowest forecast deficit in the G7 by 2029.

“And today we’ve given the green light to getting North Sea gas from the Jackdaw field, investing the revenues in our clean energy future and supporting British workers.

“In my Budget next week, I will keep up this momentum. Maintaining our fiscal discipline and drive for growth in every postcode, while giving businesses and families some breathing space.”

September’s inflation figure is used for the annual uprating of welfare payments, with the state pension now in line to rise by almost £500 next year.

The figure is also used to calculate increases in business rates in England, with pubs, shops, offices and other hospitality businesses now facing a £1.1bn increase in the collective bill from April, according to tax firm Ryan.

News.title: England dealt harsh lesson in Pakistan collapse
News.content:
Brendon McCullum wants his team to learn how to adapt as they prepare for the World Cup and this was a lesson in how not to master a run chase.

Failing to overhaul 302 is not an embarrassment, but the way England threw away a good start with some brittle batting gives McCullum plenty to ponder.

Spin exposed familiar failings as left-armer Arafat Minhas added six for 40 to his 59 from 58 with the bat, but it was also short balls from the seamers that hurt England. A two-paced pitch made the back-of-a-length delivery tricky, as it had in the match between Sri Lanka and Pakistan on the same ground at the weekend, but England failed to find a way to adjust their tempo.

Ben Duckett, Joe Root and Sam Curran were all dismissed by seamers hitting the pitch hard and forcing them to play square while Arafat exposed limitations against spin. He bowled Harry Brook for five with a beauty that dipped and straightened as he mixed up his arm ball with consistent accuracy to deadly effect.

News.title: Fried chicken and sugary drinks: Tanzania battles a growing obesity problem
News.content:
In early 2025, Said Shukuru, 31, was experiencing life-threatening health concerns. He weighed 150 kg (over 20 stone); his body mass index (BMI) was over 40 and he had a blood pressure of 190/100.

“It was very serious,” says Shukuru. In April last year, he underwent a successful mini gastric bypass operation at the Aga Khan Specialised Polyclinic in Masaki, Dar Es Salaam. His weight has since halved.

Shukuru’s case may be extreme, but his story serves as a warning. Overweight and obesity levels are increasing fast across East Africa, and particularly in Tanzania. Unless the government responds properly, the country faces a looming public health crisis.

Overweight and obesity in Tanzania have grown over the past 40 years because of economic development and liberalisation, urbanisation and increasingly sedentary lifestyles. Traditional diets, based on whole foods, are being replaced by refined and processed products. To make matters worse, chicken and chips, known as kuku chips, and sugary drinks are everywhere.

“When you live in an urban area like Dar (Es Salaam),” says Shukuru, “junk food is cheaper than groceries.”

The origins of these developments lie in Tanzania’s economic history. During the colonial period, fruits and legumes were exported while high-energy, starchy foods like maize were produced for domestic consumption, says Joyce Kinabo, professor of nutrition at Sokoine University.

“Food security was considered as having a lot of maize,” says Kinabo.

News.title: US warns over travel in Kenya as Ebola cases mount
News.content:
The United States has urged citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya, raising its travel alert level after the country reported an eighth case of Ebola.

The East African nation has recorded a rash of cases linked to a Kenyan businessman who died after travelling from Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

DRC is currently enduring the second worst Ebola outbreak on record with more than 4,000 deaths since May, though the true toll is thought to be far higher.

“The level was changed from Level 2 to Level 3 due to health risks,” the US embassy in Kenya said, a day after the State Department issued renewed travel advice for its citizens.

“Reconsider travel in Kenya due to risk of health, crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest and traffic safety. Some areas have increased risk,” it said.

The alert came as Kenyan doctors leaders demanded better protective equipment against the highly infectious virus.

Three of the confirmed Ebola cases are reported to be health staff who cared for the businessman and the others are thought to be relatives who visited him.

News.title: US records first human case of H5N1 this year
News.content:
A man in Washington has tested positive for H5N1, marking the first human case of bird flu in the US this year.

The patient, who works on a dairy farm, was reportedly infected after being exposed to two infected cows.

H5N1 has become endemic on US dairy farms after ‘spilling over’ from birds in 2024, and has since infected more than 1,000 herds across dozens of states.

The person is not seriously ill and is isolating at home, according to the Washington State Department of Health.

Scientists have long warned that if H5N1 mutates and gains the ability to spread person-to-person, it could trigger the next global pandemic – and each new infection gives the virus more opportunities to replicate and change.

Last week, a 50-year-old man in Taiwan was infected with a different strain of bird flu, H7N7, genetic analysis of which showed the virus had undergone adaptations to spread more effectively between mammals.

Of the more than 1,000 people who have contracted H5N1 since it was first detected in the late 1990s, almost half have died.

Its “extraordinarily high” mortality rate means that, were it to gain the ability to spread between people, it would be of “enormous concern”, the World Health Organization (WHO) previously warned.

However, the strain circulating among US dairy cattle, clade 2.3.4.4b, has proven less lethal to humans.

News.title: Job market warning lights ‘flashing red’
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. Wages have grown at the slowest pace in six years in a sign of the cost of living challenges facing the Chancellor ahead of the Budget.

Total pay excluding bonuses grew by 3.7pc in the three months to August, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

It was the weakest growth since November 2020, when Britain was grappling with the second Covid lockdown.

It raises pressure on John Healey as he seeks to give household finances “breathing room” in his first Budget speech next week. Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

5) Barclays private credit loans trigger Bank of England complaint | Watchdog fears that downturn in shadow banking sector might spread across financial system

What happened overnight

Asian shares fell in cautious trading as oil prices stayed high.

Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 declined 1.4pc to 64,008.53, even after AI-related stocks jumped on Wall Street.

South Korea’s tech heavy Kospi dropped 4.3pc to 5,518.53 as Brent crude oil continued to trade around $110 a barrel.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 lost 0.3pc to 8,816.90. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell nearly 1.2pc to 23,889.38, while the Shanghai Composite was down 0.5pc to 3,712.42.

Analysts say investors are also waiting for the upcoming slew of earnings reports from various major companies.

On Wall Street, the S&P 500 rose 0.4pc, coming off its worst week since June, and the Nasdaq composite rallied 1.1pc.

The majority of US stocks outside of AI and tech fell, though, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average finished with a 0.1pc drop.

Sports.title: I used to cry in the back of the car after Chelsea training sessions – I was always playing catch-up, admits Chalobah
Sports.content:
Next

FORMER Chelsea defender Trevoh Chalobah has admitted he used to cry on his way home from training as a youth star.

The centre-back, 27, joined Chelsea at the age of eight and went on to make 151 appearances for the club before leaving for Como this summer.



But Chalobah has admitted he “never really liked football” as a kid and struggled in the early age groups at Chelsea.

He revealed how he was “playing catch-up” with Chelsea youth stars like Mason Mount and Declan Rice, who had joined the club a few years earlier than him.



Speaking to the Athletic, he said: “At Chelsea, I was in the same group as Declan Rice and Mason Mount.

“They’d been playing since they were five. I was always playing catch-up. It was so difficult.



“I used to come in from those sessions and cry in the back of the car of the scout, Ray [Rembridge], who’d brought me to Chelsea.

“I’d say I couldn’t do it anymore. Ray would give me the confidence, a boost — he helped me every day and gave me a work ethic.

“He said that nothing was easy in life and those words never left me.”

The England international said he got into the sport after watching his brother play but didn’t have “natural ability”.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

He added: “My brother (Nathaniel, now at Charlton Athletic) was naturally gifted, so he would always play football in the park.

“I never really liked football. I’d watch him and just do normal kid stuff.

“Fulham saw my brother and took him there. I said, ‘You know what, I might as well just try playing this football and see where this goes’.

“I never really had the natural ability, I just watched my brother and learned from him.”

Chalobah had some great memories with his boyhood club after a handful of loans to Ipswich, Huddersfield, Lorient and Crystal Palace.



He was a regular squad player for the Blues last season and played a total of 47 times across the campaign, scoring three times.

Chalobah won five trophies as a Chelsea player, including the Club World Cup and Uefa Conference League title last season.

Como signed him for a fee of around £31million after manager Cesc Fabregas reached out and explained his vision.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But he insisted it was a “difficult” decision to leave Chelsea and said the club still “means everything” to him.

Chalobah has played a total of eight games for Como so far, starting six games in Serie A.

Sports.title: Joshua Kimmich out of Bayern Munich clash against Arsenal after withdrawing from squad due to death in family
Sports.content:
Next

JOSHUA KIMMICH is OUT of Bayern Munich’s Champions League clash against Arsenal.

The Germany international has withdrawn from the squad following a death in his family.



Bayern host the Gunners in the tournament’s league phase fixture at the Allianz Arena TONIGHT.

Kimmich, 31, was missing from the Bundesliga giant’s final training session ahead of the game.



It has now been revealed that the midfielder will not be available due to a death in his family

The club has confirmed his withdrawal on social media.

It read: “Due to a death in his immediate family, Joshua Kimmich is not in the squad today for the match against Arsenal.

“On behalf of the family, we ask that his privacy and grief be respected, and that further inquiries and reporting be refrained from.

Sports.title: Ex-Fulham goalkeeper Sergio Rico tied up by armed robbers and wife threatened in front of kids during terrifying raid
Sports.content:
Next

FORMER Fulham goalie Sergio Rico and his family have suffered a terrifying armed robbery while they were having dinner at home.

The 33-year-old was tied up after five masked raiders smashed down the front door of the footballer’s property near Seville and threatened his influencer wife Alba Silva in front of their two children, including their baby son.



Alba’s mum reportedly had a gun put to her head at the dinner table by one of the intruders while his accomplices ransacked the house in Bollullos de la Mitacion and took valuables including cash, jewellery and designer handbags.

Police were today investigating the violent break-in after Sergio, who played for Fulham in the 2018/19 season on loan from Sevilla before joining Paris Saint-Germain, although no arrests are yet thought to have been made.



Alba admitted overnight she was still deeply traumatised following Monday night’s violent break-in, saying in a post to her 255,000 Instagram followers: “I’m still in shock after what happened, I am without words.

“But the only really important thing is that thanks to God our family is safe. Thank you to everyone for your concern.”

Sergio, who spent nearly three weeks in a coma and 36 days in intensive care after being hit by a mule cart and runaway horse in May 2023 while he enjoyed downtime at an annual pilgrimage in south-west Spain, has yet to comment on his social media.

But the goalkeeper, currently a free agent after playing for Al-Gharafa in Qatar, has contacted Spanish journalists to admit the gang who targeted them were extremely violent but refute reports he was badly beaten.

As well as Sergio’s mother-in-law and the couple’s children Carla, two last month, and three-month-old baby son Sergio Jr, a female maid was with them when the horror crime unfolded around 10pm on Monday.

The value of the items stolen has not been made public.



The criminals who targeted them have been described locally as non-Spaniards who are probably of “Arabic origin or Albanians.”

Last week former Liverpool goalkeeper Peter Gulasci and his pilates instructor wife Diana Vigh were targeted as they slept in their beds hours ahead of his current club Villarreal’s Champions League clash against Napoli.

He was ruled out of the October 13 match following the couple’s terrifying ordeal.



Four masked men are said to have forced entry to the footballer’s property on a luxury residential estate in Puzol near the east coast Spanish city of Valencia.

The victims’ ordeal lasted for around 45 minutes before the robbers fled in two high-end vehicles.

Respected local paper Las Provincias has revealed the intruders had got away with valuables worth around €200,000 (£170,000) which included jewellery, designer bags and cash.

And it said the robbers had taken advantage of the fact Gulasci and his wife had not activated their alarm to enter the house through a garage window.

The terrified couple are said to have obeyed every order the robbers gave them because their two children were sleeping in the next room and they wanted to make sure they didn’t wake up.



Breaking his silence about the “deeply traumatic” armed robbery he and his family suffered, Gulasci said in a social media post hours after it happened: “Thank you so much for all your messages, kindness and support. We truly appreciate it.

“The events of Monday night were deeply traumatic. Having our home and sense of safety violated is something that will take time to process, but above all, we are grateful that our family is safe.

“We would now like to put this experience behind us, as much as possible, and return to our everyday lives and kindly ask everyone to respect our privacy and allow us to move forward.”



Leeds forward Largie Ramazani, currently on loan at Burnley, fell prey in May to burglars who targeted his luxury home 15 miles from the Villarreal goalkeeper’s pad while he was playing for Valencia.

The intruders are said to have struck in a “meticulously pre-planned raid” after waiting for the Belgian 25-year-old to head to his home stadium for the last game of the season against LaLiga champions Barcelona.

No-one was in the house on the exclusive residential estate of Torre en Conill in Betera just north-west of Valencia when a gang got into the property and took an estimated €100,000 (£86,000) in jewellery and designer clothes.

Brussels-born Ramazani, who began his youth career at Charlton Athletic before signing a four-year deal with Manchester United aged just 16 in July 2017, had posted a video of his home near Valencia on his YouTube channel before the May 23 raid.

The video he published showed exterior and interior footage of the property and led to speculation at the time it could have facilitated the burglars’ raid.



The intruders are understood to have jumped over a wall before getting inside via a window and taking advantage of the fact the alarm was also not switched on.

As well as a suitcase belonging to Ramazani, who signed for Leeds in August 2024 from Spanish side UD Almeria and joined Valencia on loan in August last year, the criminals are understood to have taken property belonging to a brother and two friends living with him.

News of the violent break-in at Gulacsi’s home came hours after police arrested three people suspected of break-ins at homes across Spain’s Catalonia region, including those of Barcelona stars Joan Garcia and Pau Cubarsi.

The two men held have been remanded in prison and a 46-year-old woman released on conditional bail pending an ongoing investigation.

In May former Southampton player Jan Bednarek and his family suffered a terrifying robbery ordeal in their home in Porto in Portugal.



An intruder armed with a knife reportedly threatened the Polish international before escaping with €150,000 (£130,000) in jewellery.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The 30-year-old and his loved ones were not harmed.

Late last week, Brazil winger and former Manchester United player Antony revealed his home in Seville was burgled while he was playing for his current club Real Betis in the Champions League against Porto.

Sports.title: EFL managers involved in furious touchline spat at full-time as reason behind what sparked chaos revealed
Sports.content:
Next

THERE were feisty scenes at the end of Wolves’ Championship clash with Portsmouth as the two managers were involved in a touchline fracas at full-time.

Emotions at Molineux Stadium boiled over on Tuesday night as Terry Devlin hit an 86th-minute equaliser for the visitors to snatch a point on the road after Jordan James’ 62nd-minute opener.

Conceding late on seemed to leave Wolves boss Cesar Peixoto frustrated as he vented those emotions by confronting John Mousinho as the full-time whistle sounded.



He was seen making a talking gesture towards his opposite manager before pointing his finger towards the Pompey gaffer.



Mousinho, 40, responded to the Portuguese by putting his hands on him to try and move him away.

But this only further incensed the 46-year-old who continued to berate the perplexed looking Englishman before coaches and players of both sides rushed over to pile into the fray.

Mousinho eventually walked away from his altercation as the situation calmed down.

He sarcastically told media of the incident: “I shook his hand and then as he walked off he kindly explained to me that I talk too much.

“That was it, I very politely told him I disagreed, that’s my job as head coach. I don’t know what it was all about.

“It was the end of the game, it’s done, shake hands and walk off. That’s what we did [and] we’ll stick to that but the second someone has a pop back then I think it’s fair game.”

He continued: “What are we gonna do, we didn’t do anything right? Just a bit of handbags so I don’t know what the point is.



“If you’re going to do something, do it, don’t tell me I talk too much.”

Peixoto did not address the incident in his own post-match comments, but insisted his Wolves side need to play with more courage.

He said: “I spoke to the players and told them we have to play with courage, as we normally do and as we work during the week.

“If things go wrong, it’s my responsibility, not theirs. I want them to feel free of that pressure. The second half was better, but we scored and then conceded from their only shot inside the box.

“We have to be disappointed with the result, even if it’s one point.”



On throwing away their lead, he was seemingly angry at the amount of time Portsmouth took to restart the game.

He added: “We scored and were managing the game, but we dropped a little deeper than I wanted. I wanted us to keep pushing forward, playing in the same way and trying to find the second goal.

“I think the players were also tired in the final minutes. They wanted to win so much that they pushed us further back than I would have liked.



“Portsmouth scored from a second ball, something we’ve seen happen in games before. It was disappointing because we were in control, but that’s football.

“Portsmouth also took a lot of time to restart the game, and they delayed things throughout the second half.

“I haven’t seen the images, so I can’t be sure, but I don’t know if it was a penalty on Mane either. However, I don’t want to talk about the referee.

“We are capable of doing better, particularly in the first half. We tried in the second, but it’s difficult when the opposition have all 11 players defending deep around the edge of the box.

“You need more mobility and intensity on the ball, and you need to move it quicker to create opportunities to score more goals. Today, we scored only once and conceded a late equaliser.
