World.title: Russia frees US citizen Stephen Hubbard, state media reports
World.content:
President Vladimir Putin says Russia has agreed to release a 74-year-old American citizen who was jailed for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine, state media is reporting.

Stephen Hubbard has been taken to Pulkovo Airport, Putin said, during talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg.

Hubbard, a former teacher originally from Michigan, was sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony in 2024.

Prosecutors had accused him of serving in a defence unit in the eastern city of Izyum when he was captured by Russian forces, shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine two years earlier.

The US State Department had previously classified Hubbard as "wrongfully detained", and on Tuesday, President Donald Trump said that he had raised his case with Putin.

"Watch what happens," Trump told reporters, "we have been focused â on âHubbard".

CBS News, the BBC's US media partner, reported that Hubbard had been in poor health and was expected to be flown to Texas for treatment.

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

Russian state media reported that Witkoff had thanked Putin for Hubbard's release and, on Trump's behalf, for the deal struck with Washington earlier this month to import Russian diesel.

The first shipment under the agreement will leave Russia "in two to three days", Putin said during the meeting, as quoted by state news agency TASS.

The diesel deal has infuriated Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, and seen diplomatic relations between Kyiv and Washington further deteriorate.

During Wednesday's meeting in St Petersburg, Witkoff was filmed by Russian TV saying the deal was an example to Ukraine of what could be achieved by working together.

"Your decision to remove export controls on diesel oil from Russia, not just to the US but also to the world at large in the midst of an economic shock, I think that was really important that that happened," he said.

"I know [President Trump] is deeply grateful for it."

World.title: Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite new optimism
World.content:
The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky before talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country.

Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!"

But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner?

The two men have never been close â that much is obvious â but have they now fallen out once and for all?

Both in rhetoric and actions, the past 10 days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship.

Just listen to the way they talk about each other.

"Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week.

The verbal assault has continued this week.

"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history.

Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously.

In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, saying Benjamin Netanyahu "has no f**king judgement". Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister".

"Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad."

World.title: Katya Adler: France divided over who to blame for riots and what to learn from them
World.content:
"This is not the face of France! You media all focus on the violence and destruction of Saturday's protests. But that's not the majority. It's not 'us'. That's not France!"

Elisabeth was speaking to me in front of a row of smashed shop windows, shattered glass still littering the tree-lined Parisian street. Its walls were daubed with red-lettered graffiti insulting French police and signed with the date of the riots, 17 October.

I'd stopped Elisabeth and her friend to ask their thoughts on what happened on Saturday. Elisabeth was so upset that, when she spoke, she seemed close to tears.

"My friend thinks this is civil war in France but I don't. Saturday is about something else entirely."

But what did happen exactly? Who was behind the riots? While much of the looting seemed opportunistic, the violence looked pre-planned. Why orchestrate it now, after weeks of student protests? And who most stands to gain from the destruction this weekend? Elisabeth wasn't entirely sure.

Different theories are doing the rounds - in and outside France. Black and white answers may be appealing, but the truth is there are many factors at play.

The president of the National Assembly, YaÃ«l Braun-Pivet, has proposed a parliamentary inquiry into the riots and how they were organised.

French intelligence had briefed government circles earlier this month that left-wing anarchist groups were involved in the student protests. Their signature: a capital A, circled in black, was spray-painted on many buildings across France this weekend.

French media have played and replayed a video shot on Saturday showing groups of young men dressed in black, with a black, folded kerchief around their face to hide their identity, apparently attacking a number of police vans with what look like large hammers or machetes.

A French intelligence report dated 29 September, published by Le Figaro newspaper, details the "manipulation" of student demonstrations by student unions and political movements aligned with the radical left.

It suggests the far-left political movement La France Insoumise (LFI) was relying on violence as an electoral strategy ahead of the 2027 presidential elections. LFI denies this.

World.title: Australian MP loses both legs after alleged car attack, husband says
World.content:
Helen Haines, the Australian MP who was hit by a car in what authorities say was a deliberate attack, has lost both her legs, her husband has confirmed.

Phil Haines said the"horrendous incident" caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind are in good shape". He added that the "good news in all this is that she's alive".

The alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, faces multiple charges and appeared in court for the first time on Wednesday.

Nugent was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the independent MP outside her electorate office in the regional town of Wangaratta, about 240km (150miles) northeast of Melbourne.

Haines' "road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter," her husband said at a press conference in Melbourne where she is being treated.

"She is a determined person who will do her best, with our support and love, to recover. And that is what we hope for."

He thanked hospital staff and people, both in Australia and internationally, who have shown their concern for Haines, and urged those who want to show their support to donate to the Save the Children fund.

"Please keep sending Helen your love," he added.

Earlier on Wednesday, Nugent appeared at the local court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Police said more charges may be laid, including attempted murder.

Nugent - a local from the nearby town of Tarrawingee and known as an environmental campaigner - remained silent and emotionless during his brief court appearance.

He did not apply for bail and is due back in court in February. Court documents show he was also charged with cultivating and possessing cannabis.

World.title: Elon Musk confirms he is considering merging Tesla and SpaceX
World.content:
Elon Musk has said he is actively considering merging Tesla and SpaceX, his two biggest companies.

"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts to discuss SpaceX's latest results on Tuesday.

While Musk noted it could not be assumed a merger will go ahead, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies had been formed to examine the move.

"The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," he said. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."

With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (Â£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.

SpaceX builds space rockets as well as Starlink internet satellites and provides a secured satellite network for governments, including the US, through its Starshield business.

That part of the business is currently facing scrutiny over claims Ukraine's access to the network has been limited, leaving it vulnerable to deadly strikes by Russia.

US President Donald Trump has denied either he or Musk ordered the slowdown. Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions.

Starlink's total revenue rose to $5.2bn in the three months to 30 September from $3bn in the same period last year. It is dwarfed by SpaceX's expansion into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, such as Anthropic and Google.

The business generated revenues of $7.5bn over the three months, up from $813m last year.

World.title: Pakistan arrests man wanted by US over $126m postage fraud case
World.content:
Pakistan's cybercrime agency has arrested a man accused of running a counterfeit operation that caused $126 million (Â£94m) in losses to the US Postal service.

Faheem Akram is accused of having sold fake stamps via a fraudulent website in the US since 2023.

He was indicted by a federal grand jury in Florida last month for selling more than five million counterfeit shipping labels to thousands of US customers over the years. Authorities have now shut down the website.

Earlier this month, the US Postal Inspection Service offered a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to his arrest.

According to the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida, the 33-year-old from Khanewal, Pakistan, operated LabelsBank.com.

US prosecutors alleged that he sold counterfeit US postage at a fixed rate regardless of a package's weight, size or destination.

The counterfeit labels, usually sold at $2 each, allegedly allowed customers to ship packages at rates far below legitimate prices, resulting in substantial lost revenue and shipping costs to the Postal Service.

An investigation found that more than 5,200 individuals purchased more than 5.1 million counterfeit shipping labels, the office said in a press release.

Akram is charged with one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States and to make and sell counterfeit postage stamps, five counts of making and selling counterfeit postage stamp labels, and four counts of wire fraud.

If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on the conspiracy and counterfeit postage counts, and 20 years in prison on each wire fraud count, the office said.

World.title: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say
World.content:
Sudan's army has been accused of launching several drone strikes that have reportedly killed more than 300 people, including dozens travelling to a funeral.

The death toll from strikes in two areas of West Kordofan state on Sunday evening was 150, sources told the Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict that erupted in 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

In Abyei, a disputed border area between Sudan and South Sudan, 153 people were killed when drones hit a market on Monday, the region's information minister said.

A military source told the BBC the army had carried out the Abyei attack, saying the market was a fuel supply site for the RSF.

The attack has raised tensions between South Sudan and Sudan, which jointly administer Abyei, as they both claim ownership to the oil-rich region in a dispute that has remained unresolved since South Sudan ceded in 2011.

South Sudan has summoned Sudan's ambassador to lodge a formal protest. There are fears the conflict could spill across the border.

World.title: Gambia to pay victims of Yahya Jammeh's rule from proceeds of his seized US mansion
World.content:
On Tuesday, the Gambia Reparations Commission said it was "pleased to inform victims, survivors and the public that it has received a total of $2,573,414.10" from the sale of Jammeh's property.

It said it was committed to ensuring the funds were managed responsibly and transparently, "with due regard to the rights and needs of victims and survivors".

Jammeh lost to Adama Barrow in the election of 2016, first accepting defeat and then rejecting the results.

He eventually stepped down in 2017 amid intense regional and international pressure.

Troops from several West African nations, including Senegal, had been deployed to The Gambia, threatening to drive Jammeh out of office.

In the end he agreed to step down and went into exile Equatorial Guinea.

A national commission then discovered that the former president had 281 properties in The Gambia, as well as the one in the US and one in Morocco, and controlled more than 100 bank accounts.

There was no way that he could have afforded this on his salary and it concluded that he had misappropriated more than $300m.

Jammeh is accused of presiding over the murder of political opponents, disappearances, rape and torture.

A commission of inquiry found that widespread abuses had resulted in the death of "240-250 Gambians and non-Gambians at the hands of the state or its agents".

World.title: How appeal court’s verdict on nullification of CAMA provision strengthens human rights suits
World.content:
The Court of Appeal in Abuja, on 17 September, upheld a Federal High Court judgement nullifying several provisions of the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA), 2020, Nigeria’s principal corporate regulatory law.

The judgement struck down a string of CAMA provisions which conferred some powers on the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC), to control and intervene in the running of incorporated trustees, including religious bodies and other associations, in certain situations.

Both the Federal High Court and the Court of Appeal ruled concurrently that the provisions infringed upon constitutionally protected rights to freedom of thought, conscience, religion, association, and peaceful assembly.

But the Court of Appeal differed with the lower Federal High Court’s decision striking out the National Assembly’s name as a defendant in the suit filed as a fundamental human rights enforcement action.

In a landmark pronouncement in the judgement, the Court of Appeal held that the lower court’s decision striking out the National Assembly’s name from the suit on the grounds that it was not served with a pre-action notice before the suit was filed “cannot stand.”

The pronouncement on the judgement brings renewed attention to the special status of fundamental human rights suits and the limits of pre-action notice statutorily mandated to be served on some public institutions before suing them in court.

The Court of Appeal’s decision trashed the long-held notion that failure to serve a pre-action notice on some public institutions or serve them within the time stipulated by statute automatically rendered subsequent legal actions against the institutions incompetent.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The court’s three-member panel comprising Abba Mohammed, Donatus Okorowo, and Eberechi Nyesom-Wike ruled that fundamental rights enforcement suits are exempted from such statutory limitations or pre-action notice requirements.

“Since the right of action in fundamental rights enforcement cases is specifically provided by the Constitution, such a right of action cannot be limited or affected by any statutory limitation or requirement of pre-action notice,” Mr Okorowo wrote in the certified true copy of the lead judgement newly obtained by PREMIUM TIMES.

The decision was one of the two interrelated judgements the Court of Appeal delivered on 17 September.

The first, which arose from the appeal filed by the CAC, dealt with the crux of the matter – the legality or otherwise of the disputed CAMA provisions, while the other, which stemmed from the appeal filed by the plaintiff Emmanuel Ekpeyong who commenced the suit at the trial court, centred primarily on the effect of pre-action notice on the matter.

PREMIUM TIMES found after reviewing the verdicts that the Court of Appeal ordered the restoration of the National Assembly as a defendant in the matter.

The appeal court faulted the aspect of the 18 April judgement of James Omotosho of the Federal High Court that failure to serve the National Assembly with pre-action notice made the lawyer’s fundamental rights action against the legislative body incompetent.

Section 21 of the Legislative Houses (Powers and Privileges) Act, 2017, requires anyone intending to sue the National Assembly to give it three months’ notice before instituting the action.

However, Section 46(1) of the Nigerian constitution guarantees the right of any person to approach a court for redress over an alleged violation of their fundamental rights.

The Court of Appeal panel held that the constitutional provision superseded the provision of the Legislative Houses (Powers and Privileges) Act.

Mr Okorowo ruled that “Section 21 is a subsidiary requirement that cannot lawfully clog the right of immediate constitutional access conferred by Section 46(1).” He added that the requirement was void to the extent that it applied to fundamental rights proceedings.

The court also rejected the National Assembly’s claim to immunity, noting that the constitutional provision cited applied only to the removal of a governor or deputy governor.

It therefore held that the “part of the judgement” of the Federal High Court “which held the suit incompetent” against the National Assembly for failure to serve a pre-action notice under Section 21 of the Legislative Houses (Powers and Privileges) Act, 2017, and which accordingly struck out the name of the 1st Respondent, is hereby set aside.”

The court went on to declare that the failure to serve a pre-action notice on the National Assembly “does not render a fundamental rights action incompetent” against the National Assembly. It said the law relied on by the Federal High Court to make such a declaration was “inapplicable to proceedings for the enforcement of rights guaranteed under Chapter IV of the Constitution.”

“The name of the 1st Respondent, the National Assembly, is restored as a party to Suit No. FHC/ABJ/CS/1076/2020,” Mr Okorowo also ruled, while affirming “the substantive determinations” of the Federal High Court on the overall merits of the case. The substantive issue was not a subject of appeal in the particular case.

The suit

Mr Ekpenyong filed the suit less than a month after late President Muhammadu Buhari signed CAMA 2020 into law in August 2020.

The law expanded the CAC’s powers over incorporated trustees, including religious organisations, raising concerns about possible interference with their affairs.

Although the Act introduced several reforms to Nigeria’s corporate environment, its provisions on incorporated trustees, which cover churches, mosques, charities, NGOs and other associations, drew strong objections from religious organisations and civil society groups.

At the centre of the controversy was Section 839, which gave the CAC powers to suspend trustees and appoint interim managers where certain conditions existed, including alleged misconduct or mismanagement, fraud or where intervention was considered necessary in the public interest.

Religious organisations feared the provision could give the government excessive control over their internal affairs.

The Christian Association of Nigeria (CAN) called for the law to be amended, while the CAC maintained that it would not arbitrarily suspend trustees and that its actions remained subject to judicial review.

Amid the ensuing controversies, Mr Ekpenyong instituted the suit on 31 August 2020 at the Federal High Court in Abuja.

He sued the National Assembly, the CAC and the Attorney General of the Federation (AGF), over provisions of CAMA which he argued violated his constitutional rights.

In his suit, Mr Ekpenyong challenged the sections 839, 842 to 848 and 851 of the law, urging the court to rule that the disputed provisions infringed upon his freedom of thought, conscience and religion, freedom of association and peaceful assembly, as well as his right of access to court.

He relied on Sections 38 and 40, among other provisions, of the Nigerian constitution.

Federal High Court judgement

Delivering the judgment in April 2023, Judge James Omotosho agreed that the powers conferred on the CAC to regulate incorporated trustees under Sections 839 and 842 to 848 of CAMA were excessive and infringed Mr Ekpenyong’s rights to freedom of religion and association.

He declared the disputed provisions unconstitutional. He also held that Section 851, which provides for an Administrative Proceedings Committee to hear certain matters under CAMA, was inconsistent with the constitutional provision conferring jurisdiction on the Federal High Court.

But, while ruling in Mr Ekpenyong’s favour on the substantive issues, Mr Omotosho struck out the National Assembly as a defendant on the grounds of the plaintiff’s failure to serve a pre-action notice on the legislative body before instituting the suit.

Appeals

The ruling prompted two separate appeals.

The CAC challenged the decision nullifying the disputed CAMA provisions, while Mr Ekpenyong appealed against the decision to strike out the National Assembly as a respondent to the suit.

Mr Ekpenyong’s appeal challenged the Federal High Court’s decision that failure to serve a pre-action notice could prevent him from pursuing his fundamental rights claims against the National Assembly.

He argued that the lower court erred in law by holding that his action was incompetent against the National Assembly because he had not served the required notice.

He maintained that Section 46(1) of the Constitution did not make pre-action notice a condition for commencing proceedings to enforce fundamental rights guaranteed under Chapter IV.

He also argued that the Fundamental Rights (Enforcement Procedure) Rules were designed to advance applicants’ rights and freedoms, not restrict them.

The lawyer therefore asked the Court of Appeal to set aside the decision removing the National Assembly from the suit.

However, the National Assembly opposed the appeal, arguing that pre-action notice was a condition precedent to instituting proceedings against it.

Its lawyer, Bukola Adeagbo, of the legislature’s Directorate of Legal Services, contended that the failure to serve the notice affected the trial court’s jurisdiction to hear the case.

She also argued that the fundamental rights claims could wait until the required notice had been served and urged the appellate court to dismiss the appeal.

The Attorney-General of the Federation, represented by Samuel Gabriel, a principal state counsel in the Civil Appeals Department, similarly argued that the absence of pre-action notice rendered the suit premature and incompetent.

Mr Gabriel relied on the doctrine of sovereign immunity, contending that the National Assembly enjoyed such immunity and that Section 21 of the Legislative Houses (Powers and Privileges) Act, 2017, was intended to protect the legislature.

He further argued that Mr Ekpenyong’s action was essentially a request for the interpretation of CAMA and did not qualify as a fundamental rights suit.

The CAC did not file a brief in response to the appeal.

Federal High Court’s misapplication of law and internal inconsistency

Rejecting the respondents’ arguments, Mr Okorowo who gave the lead judgement consented to by the two other members of the panel, held that the nature of a suit was determined by the substance of the claim rather than its title or the procedure used to commence it.

The court rejected the reliance on Section 188(10) of the constitution to justify the National Assembly’s claim to immunity.

He ruled that the lower court had misdirected itself in law by striking out the legislature.

He said the lower court’s judge not only misapplied the law to come to that conclusion, but he was also “internally inconsistent with his own reasoning.”

“First, the internal inconsistency is patent,” Mr Okorowo wrote, noting that the judge earlier in the same judgement “correctly held that “fundamental human rights suits are sui generis and are largely not governed by the ordinary rules of civil procedure.”

He added on the basis of the special nature of fundamental rights enforcement suits, the trial judge “refused to strike out the suit for want of locus standi, relying on Paragraph 3(e) of the Preamble to the 2009 Rules, which provides that no human rights case may be dismissed for want of standing (see page 21 of the Judgement at page 169 of the Record).

READ ALSO: Court fines former banker N1m over bank fraud in Lagos

“Yet, after treating the suit as outside ordinary civil procedure for purposes of standing, he subjected the same suit to the ordinary civil-procedure requirement of a statutory pre-action notice, a creature of ordinary procedure and statutory privilege, without reconciling the two positions. The two holdings cannot stand together.

“If the suit is sui generis and distinct from ordinary civil procedure when the objection concerns standing, it does not lose that character when the objection concerns notice.”

The appellate court consequently set aside the part of the lower court’s judgement that removed the National Assembly from the suit.

It declared that the pre-action notice requirement did not apply to proceedings seeking to enforce fundamental rights guaranteed under Chapter IV of the Constitution and ordered that the National Assembly be restored as a party to the case.

The decision is subject to appeal at the Supreme Court.

World.title: 2027: Makinde promises tax breaks, end to militancy under APM’s RESET agenda
World.content:
The presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), Seyi Makinde, has promised to introduce tax incentives for businesses, improve education and security, and address militancy in the Niger Delta if elected President in 2027.

Mr Makinde made the promises on Tuesday at the party’s South-south town hall meeting in Uyo, Akwa Ibom State, where he presented his RESET agenda as a proposed alternative to the policies of the President Bola Tinubu administration.

He said the agenda was designed to restructure Nigeria’s economic, educational, security and political systems to address persistent poverty and improve citizens’ living conditions.

“The RESET agenda is simply to ensure that if Nigeria has not worked well for you as an individual, the way it should, then let us reset Nigeria,” he said.

Mr Makinde, who is also the governor of Oyo State, said his proposed education reforms would focus on developing the skills and knowledge required to build a thriving middle class and expand economic opportunities, particularly for young people.

He said his experience as an entrepreneur had shown that the government alone could not generate the employment and economic expansion Nigeria needed.

“I started my own company at the age of 29. I employed engineers. I took the risk on behalf of the state because government alone cannot provide the employment and expansion that we need,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The APM candidate promised to encourage entrepreneurship and provide tax breaks to businesses, citing his administration’s record of increasing Oyo State’s internally generated revenue without raising taxes.

“The records are there,” he said.

Mr Makinde criticised the federal government’s tax policy, arguing that taxation should target wealth rather than worsen the burden on poor Nigerians.

He said the tax law passed by the government was inconsistent with productivity and accused the authorities of prioritising revenue collection from poor citizens.

“You are supposed to tax wealth. You are not supposed to tax poverty. But they are only interested in taxing poverty,” he said.

The governor also questioned the effectiveness of some of the Tinubu administration’s economic interventions, including the Presidential Initiative on Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) and the naira-for-crude arrangement.

He asked whether the policies had translated into lower transportation costs for millions of Nigerians.

Mr Makinde further challenged the government to publish its petroleum pricing template, arguing that this would enable experts to examine the figures and suggest ways to make fuel pricing more affordable.

“Provide Nigerians with your pricing template. We have Nigerians who can tell us how to make it work for millions of Nigerians,” he said.

Mr Makinde also repeated his allegation that the federal government had spent dividends paid by Nigeria LNG Limited (NLNG) into the Federation Account without distributing the states’ and local governments’ shares.

He said the money should be shared among the three tiers of government in accordance with the Constitution.

“Anything that goes into the Federation Account, according to our Constitution, should be shared between the federal government, state governments and local governments. Let them provide the amounts meant for the states and local governments in Nigeria,” he said.

The governor insisted that he stood by his earlier claim that the federal government had withheld nearly N250 billion due to each state from the NLNG dividend payments.

The Presidency has since rejected his allegation. Presidential spokesperson Bayo Onanuga described the claim as false, according to a statement reported by news organisations on Sunday.

Mr Makinde also pledged to address insecurity, including militancy in the Niger Delta, saying that although militancy had declined in the region, the underlying problem remained unresolved.

He said his administration would work towards ending militancy and improving Nigeria’s security architecture.

Daura, Bala seek support for APM ticket

The party’s vice-presidential candidate, Lawal Daura, said the ticket’s RESET agenda was intended to break what he described as Nigeria’s recurring cycle of poor governance and economic hardship.

He said the programme would focus on education, the economy, security and citizens’ general welfare.

Mr Daura, a former director-general of the State Security Services (DSS), said Nigerians deserved to live with dignity and should not be condemned to poverty in a country with abundant resources.

He also described the APM as a patriotic party committed to putting Nigeria first, urging voters to consider the party’s proposals ahead of the 2027 elections.

The party’s National Chairman, Yusuf Dantalle, said the country needed to reconsider its political and economic arrangements to address insecurity, poverty, inequality and hopelessness.

Mr Dantalle said kidnapping and other security challenges reflected deeper socio-economic and political problems that required more than isolated interventions.

He argued that the proposed reset should lead to a country in which citizens could travel, visit farms and go about their daily activities without fear.

Governor of Bauchi State, Bala Mohammed, also addressed the gathering, urging Nigerians to assess the candidates based on their records, ideas and capacity to address the country’s challenges rather than their age or financial resources.

Mr Mohammed said the South-south region had significant economic potential but needed leadership capable of translating its resources into improved living conditions.

Mr Makinde also expressed confidence that the APM could secure support in the region, arguing that the opposition needed to unite ahead of the 2027 elections.

He alleged that efforts were being made to prevent opposition parties from working together but maintained that the South-south would support his party in the next election.

World.title: 89 CSOs demand release of Nigeria’s investment treaty review, warn of risks to public funds
World.content:
Eighty-nine civil society organisations in Nigeria have called on the federal government to publish its review of the country’s investment treaties, warning that international arbitration mechanisms could expose public funds to costly claims and restrict the government’s ability to enforce environmental and climate regulations.

The groups, including Amnesty International Nigeria, BudgIT, ActionAid Nigeria, Health of Mother Earth Foundation, Policy Alert and Yiaga Africa, also demanded a review of Nigeria’s reliance on the investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) system, which allows foreign investors to challenge certain government measures before international arbitration tribunals.

In a statement issued on 17 October to mark the Global Days of Action to End ISDS, the CSOs called on the federal government and the National Assembly to ensure that investment agreements do not erode environmental protection, public health, fiscal stability and communities’ access to justice.

They also called for improved transparency in investment agreements and relevant dispute-settlement provisions, as well as safeguards to ensure that new offshore petroleum investments do not unnecessarily restrict Nigeria’s regulatory powers.

The statement comes as Nigeria pursues major offshore oil projects and seeks to attract investment in transition minerals, including lithium, despite growing pressure for stronger environmental accountability and climate action.

Investment disputes, public finances

The CSOs warned that ISDS provisions could cost Nigeria substantial compensation claims when foreign investors consider government policies inconsistent with protections under applicable investment treaties.

They said the financial consequences could be huge for a country with limited fiscal space and extensive environmental liabilities, particularly in oil-producing communities.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Public resources spent defending claims or paying awards are resources unavailable for healthcare, education, climate adaptation, clean energy and environmental restoration,” they said.

They explained that the prospect of expensive arbitration could also discourage governments from introducing or strengthening regulations in the public interest, a phenomenon commonly described as regulatory chill.

The CSOs stressed that foreign investors were entitled to fair treatment and due process but should not enjoy exceptional rights that undermine democratic decisions, environmental accountability or access to justice for affected communities.

Nigeria’s record of arbitration disputes

The statement cited three publicly documented investor-state arbitration cases involving Nigeria’s petroleum sector.

Shell Nigeria Ultra Deep Limited initiated proceedings against Nigeria at the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) in 2007. The case was discontinued in 2011.

Shell Petroleum N.V. and Shell Petroleum Development Company of Nigeria Limited initiated another ICSID case in 2021 under the Nigeria-Netherlands bilateral investment treaty. That case was discontinued in October 2022.

In June 2023, Korea National Oil Corporation and its Nigerian subsidiaries initiated another case under the Nigeria-Korea bilateral investment treaty. The case remained pending in the latest records cited by the organisations in 2026.

The CSOs noted that the three cases had not proven Nigeria’s liability in the records they reviewed, but argued that they show the legal and fiscal exposure associated with defending investment disputes.

They also raised concerns about the implications of investment protections for Nigeria’s planned offshore petroleum developments, including Bonga North and Bonga South West/Aparo.

They called on the government to ensure that petroleum agreements, production-sharing arrangements and fiscal incentives preserve its ability to strengthen environmental, climate, public health and fiscal regulations.

Lithium dispute raises fresh concerns

The CSOs also cited the Jupiter Lithium dispute in Kaduna, registered at ICSID in June 2026 under the Nigeria-United Kingdom bilateral investment treaty.

The case, which remained pending, concerns a lithium mining project and shows the potential implications of investment protections for Nigeria’s emerging transition-minerals sector.

The CSOs said the country must ensure that investment arrangements support responsible mining, environmental safeguards and domestic economic benefits rather than reproduce the environmental and social problems associated with oil extraction.

Demand publication of treaty review

A central demand of the CSOs is the immediate publication of the report of a nine-member committee inaugurated by the Attorney-General of the Federation on 8 November 2024 to review Nigeria’s bilateral investment treaties and the Nigerian Investment Promotion Commission Act.

The committee was mandated to examine how investment promotion could be balanced with national interests, environmental protection and sustainable development.

The CSOs said the committee’s findings and recommendations had not been made public and demanded their release without further delay.

If the review remains incomplete, they called on the government to disclose its status and announce a firm completion date.

They also called for open consultations involving the National Assembly, civil society organisations, host communities, labour groups and independent experts.

They further urged the federal government to take lawful steps towards terminating or replacing investment agreements that expose legitimate public-interest regulation to legal and financial risks, while supporting international efforts to move beyond the ISDS system.

They said Nigeria needs investment that supports development without compromising democratic accountability, environmental protection or the rights of its citizens.

World.title: Tinubu failed Nigerians on economy, security – Baba-Ahmed
World.content:
The National Chairman of the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP), Hakeem Baba-Ahmed, has accused President Bola Tinubu’s administration of worsening economic hardship and insecurity, saying Nigerians have yet to feel the benefits of its policies.

Mr Baba-Ahmed said millions of children were unable to attend school because of insecurity, while dangerous roads and the rising cost of living continued to affect Nigerians.

He spoke on Tuesday during an interview on Channels Television’s Politics Today, where he criticised the government’s performance after three and a half years in office.

“Children who live in territories taken by bandits and kidnappers can’t go to school at all,” he said.

The PRP chairman also questioned the government’s economic performance, arguing that official statistics did not reflect the difficulties Nigerians faced in their daily lives.

“Children aren’t going to school; life is more insecure; life is harder. He flashed all the statistics. How can we build an economy?” he asked.

Mr Baba-Ahmed also faulted the pace of road construction, citing the Abuja-Kaduna highway as an example of a road where motorists still face security risks.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He argued that the government should have delivered more infrastructure projects with the revenue generated from oil.

Tinubu has nothing to tell Nigerians

Mr Baba-Ahmed, who was special adviser on political matters in the Office of Vice President Kashim Shettima, also criticised Mr Tinubu’s reported decision to limit his participation in campaign rallies ahead of the 2027 general election, arguing that the president should personally explain his administration’s record to voters.

He said the president appeared to be relying on other political figures to campaign for his re-election rather than directly addressing Nigerians about his policies and their effects.

“He had nothing to say to them; he had nothing to say to Nigerians, which is why he says, ‘Okay, gentlemen, go and campaign for me. I will stay in Abuja and run the country,’” he said.

“You run the country now? Three and a half years, you didn’t run this country. Now you remember that you have to run a country?”

The PRP chairman further questioned the administration’s record on governance, arguing that the government had not adequately addressed the problems confronting the country.

He also stressed the importance of a national census, describing it as a key tool for planning and understanding the country’s demographic strengths and weaknesses.

2027 election

Mr Baba-Ahmed expressed confidence that Mr Tinubu would struggle to win the 2027 presidential election, arguing that the outcome would depend on the credibility of the electoral process.

He warned that a compromised election could threaten Nigeria’s unity, particularly if voters believed their choices had been disregarded.

He said the government and electoral authorities must ensure that citizens in areas affected by banditry and kidnapping could participate in the election.

According to him, insecurity could prevent millions of Nigerians from voting, especially in parts of northern Nigeria where armed groups have restricted movement and disrupted daily life.

He also warned that wealthy political interests could use their financial resources to mobilise large numbers of voters, raising concerns about the influence of money on the electoral process.

Mr Baba-Ahmed acknowledged that allegations of electoral malpractice were not peculiar to Nigeria, but argued that the authorities must take steps to prevent manipulation and limit its impact on election outcomes.

He described the announcement of results as a critical stage of the electoral process, insisting that only officials authorised by law could declare a winner.

INEC communication

The PRP chairman also criticised the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) over what he described as inadequate communication with Nigerians.

Responding to the commission chairman’s position on the declaration of election results, Mr Baba-Ahmed said the law clearly identifies the officials authorised to announce winners.

He agreed that no individual could independently declare a candidate the winner of an election without the legal authority to do so.

However, he said INEC needed to communicate more effectively with the public and explain its role in announcing election results to prevent confusion.

Mr Baba-Ahmed, who once served as INEC secretary, also expressed concern about the possibility of political actors attempting to manipulate the outcome of the 2027 election.

“I’m worried because if they lose, I hope they don’t try to make or turn falsehood into truth. That’s what I’m worried about,” he said.

World.title: Mexico approves Reno Omokri as Nigeria’s ambassador
World.content:
The Mexican government has approved Reno Omokri’s appointment as Nigeria’s ambassador to the country.

Mr Omokri disclosed this in a post shared on X on Tuesday.

He said the Chargé d’Affaires of the Embassy of Mexico, José Flores, delivered the agrément confirming the Mexican government’s acceptance of his appointment.

An agrément is official approval for a diplomat to serve in another country. This marks his formal assumption of duty.

Mr Omokri will also serve as Nigeria’s ambassador to Guatemala, Honduras, and Nicaragua.

He has concurrent accreditation to the three countries.

“To God Be The Glory, The Chargé d’affaires of the Embassy of the United Mexican States in Abuja, Mr José Manuel Briseño Flores, Today In Abuja Delivered The Agrément From The Government of the United Mexican States Accepting Me, Bemigho Reno Omokri, to Serve as Ambassador Extraordinaire and Plenipotentiary of the Federal Republic of Nigeria to the United Mexican States, With Concurrent Accreditation To The Republic of Guatemala, The Republic of Honduras, and The Republic of Nicaragua, to the Director of Protocol of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, His Excellency, Ambassador Babagana Wakil,” he wrote.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

PREMIUM TIMES previously reported that President Bola Tinubu had announced the new ambassadors last year and approved their posting in March.

The president approved the posting of 31 career diplomats and 34 non-career diplomats two years after he recalled the previous ambassadors, which included 41 non-career and 42 career diplomats, in September 2023, without giving a specific reason.

Many of the appointees have since assumed duties.

World.title: My father had covenant with God to die at 100 – Ondo SSG Taiwo Fasoranti
World.content:
Taiwo Fasoranti, the eldest child of the late Afenifere leader Reuben Fasoranti, has said his father had a covenant with God to die at the age of 100.

Mr Fasoranti, who is the Secretary to the Ondo State Government (SSG), disclosed this when Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa paid a condolence visit to the family of the late Afenifere leader at his residence in Akure on Tuesday night.

The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that Mr Fasoranti died on Tuesday evening in his house in Ijapo, Akure.

The SSG said that his father had repeatedly told family members that he had a covenant with God to depart from the world upon attaining the age of 100.

“Baba often told us that he had a covenant with God that whenever he got to 100, he would go. He repeatedly told us that when he died, we should not cry.

“We are not mourning Baba, we are rejoicing.

“Baba has left us a big pair of shoes to step into, but we can only thank God for the legacy of firmness, resilience, hard work and love that he left us with,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The SSG described his father as a devoted parent who was actively involved in the upbringing and education of his children.

He said the family would greatly miss the wise counsel of the late nationalist, whom he described as a man of few words who communicated his thoughts “quietly but effectively.”

He appreciated Governor Aiyedatiwa for identifying with the family during this period, while appealing for prayers to enable the children to sustain their father’s legacies.

Speaking, Mr Aiyedatiwa described the late Afenifere leader as an epitome of humility, kindness and wisdom whose contributions to governance and national development would remain indelible.

“Even at that age, Baba was still influencing decisions of the government. That is to tell you that he was still mentally sound,” he said.

The governor described the deceased as a great educator whose positive influence extended across generations, producing prominent personalities within and outside Nigeria.

“We cannot but celebrate his life and times. We are not mourning. We are just celebrating and thanking God for a life that was well lived,” he said.

The governor said the late nationalist lived a fulfilled life characterised by humility, kindness, wisdom and dedication to the service of humanity.

Mr Aiyedatiwa urged the family and other Nigerians to emulate the virtues of the deceased and continue to make meaningful contributions to society.

Fasoranti: From school teacher to natoinal prominence

The late Afenifere served as a teacher, principal, and educationist. Upon his retirement, he established the Omolere Nursery School and Akure High School, both of which still stand as a monument to his legacy as a school administrator.

He was a highly respected Nigerian elder statesman and progressive politician who began his political journey at the grassroots level, serving diligently as an elected councillor and later as the Chairman of the Akure Local Government.

He served as the Ondo State Commissioner for Finance from 1979 to 1983 during the administration of then-Governor Adekunle Ajasin.

Mr Fasoranti was an ideological disciple of elder statesman and nationalist Obafemi Awolowo.

He was an active member of the Awolowo-led Action Group (AG) from the pre-independence to the First Republic eras, and the Unity Party of Nigeria (UPN) during the Second Republic. During the oppressive military regime of General Sani Abacha in the 1990s,

Mr Fasoranti was part of the National Democratic Coalition (NADECO) formed in 1994 by leading politicians, civil rights activists, retired military officers, and professionals to confront military tyranny and fight for the restoration of democratic rule.

Some NADECO members, including Mr Fasoranti, escaped state-sponsored assassination during the military era.

(NAN)

World.title: Uganda says no active Ebola cases after Nigeria confirms infection
World.content:
Uganda’s Ministry of Health has urged the public to remain calm and vigilant following Nigeria’s confirmation of an Ebola case, clarifying that the infected woman’s transit through Uganda does not establish that she contracted the virus there.

In a public statement issued on Tuesday, the ministry said preliminary information indicated that the Nigerian woman travelled to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) for business and passed through Uganda in early October without showing symptoms.

She reportedly developed symptoms after arriving in Nigeria, where authorities have confirmed an Ebola infection.

“The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said, adding that travel through Uganda alone was insufficient to establish where the infection occurred.

The clarification comes as Nigeria intensifies its response to the confirmed case in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), with health authorities beginning contact tracing to identify people who may have been exposed to the virus.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that Nigeria’s Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, confirmed the case on Tuesday. The patient is receiving treatment in isolation at a private hospital in the FCT, while 44 close contacts, including healthcare workers, patients, caregivers and travel contacts, have been identified.

Active cases

The Ugandan health ministry said it had no confirmed active Ebola cases as of the time of its statement.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

It also said the Nigerian government had yet to provide detailed information about the woman’s travel itinerary and clinical history, which it said would help guide further investigations and any necessary contact tracing.

The Ugandan health ministry said it was working with relevant agencies to strengthen screening and public health controls at points of entry, following the development.

It added that limited provisions had been maintained for humanitarian and diplomatic movements.

The ministry urged residents to practise regular handwashing and use sanitiser as part of efforts to reduce the risk of infection. It also pledged to provide verified updates through its official communication channels.

Regional outbreak

Nigeria’s confirmed case comes amid an ongoing Ebola outbreak linked to the Bundibugyo virus in the DRC, with infections also reported in other countries.

Kenya, which confirmed its first imported case in early October, reported a ninth case on Tuesday. Its health ministry said all nine cases belonged to one known cluster, with the eight surviving patients responding well to supportive care.

The first Kenyan patient had travelled from the DRC through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi. The development has heightened regional concerns about the movement of the virus across borders.

Uganda also recorded Ebola infections earlier in 2026 but subsequently declared its outbreak over after completing the required period without a new confirmed case.

Nigeria’s current case has renewed attention on the risks posed by international travel during an outbreak, as public health authorities work to establish the source of infection and prevent further transmission.

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated materials. Symptoms can include fever, headache, severe weakness, vomiting and diarrhoea.

Health authorities have advised the public to maintain good hand hygiene, avoid contact with the bodily fluids of suspected cases and promptly report possible exposure to public health officials.

Investigations into the Nigerian case and the circumstances surrounding the patient’s travel remain ongoing.

World.title: FAAN begins earning MMA2 revenue as 20-year dispute with Bi-Courtney ends
World.content:
The Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN) has begun earning revenue from the Murtala Muhammed Airport Terminal Two (MMA2) in Lagos following a settlement between the Federal Government and Bi-Courtney Aviation Services Limited over a dispute that lasted nearly two decades.

The Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo, disclosed this on Tuesday during the formalisation of the settlement involving the Federal Government, FAAN, Bi-Courtney and Stabilini Visinoni Limited.

“FAAN had not earned a kobo from MMA2 for the last 20 years because of disputes. Today, FAAN begins to earn its money from MMA2,” Mr Keyamo said.

The agreement provides for the resumption of concession fee payments to FAAN and the reciprocal waiver of specified historical financial and other claims by the parties.

Mr Keyamo said the Federal Executive Council (FEC) approved the framework for the negotiated settlement on 30 April 2026, following discussions aimed at resolving the long-running dispute.

What the settlement changes

Under the revised agreement, Bi-Courtney has agreed to waive its outstanding claims against the Federal Government, while the government and FAAN will relinquish specified historical claims against the concessionaire, including accumulated concession fees and related payments arising before the agreement.

The minister said the arrangement was intended to resolve past disagreements and establish clearer contractual obligations for the parties going forward.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The settlement also addresses a dispute over the General Aviation Terminal (GAT), commonly known as the Old Domestic Airport.

According to Mr Keyamo, the revised agreement recognises the terminal as the property of the Federal Government, to be operated by FAAN.

The minister said the government had agreed to allow Bi-Courtney to expand its apron and accommodate regional flights within Africa at MMA2, subject to the terminal’s capacity.

The agreement also restores rights and provides for separate lease arrangements covering a four-star hotel and conference centre near the airport. The facilities have remained unfinished for years.

Mr Keyamo said the government would retain regulatory oversight over security, access, emergencies and maintenance standards, while the parties would work together to implement the revised arrangements.

Background to the dispute

In April, PREMIUM TIMES had reported that the Federal Government had reached a settlement with Bi-Courtney to resolve the long-running dispute over MMA2 after years of litigation and disagreements over the airport concession.

Mr Keyamo at the time said the Federal Executive Council (FEC) had approved the negotiated settlement, which included concessions by both parties, revised operational arrangements and plans to restore government revenue from the terminal.

The dispute originated from a concession agreement signed on 24 April 2003 involving the Federal Government, Bi-Courtney and Stabilini Visinoni Limited for the design, construction, operation and eventual transfer of the domestic terminal.

The agreement initially covered 12 years from 7 May 2007 but was subsequently extended to 36 years.

Disagreements over contractual obligations, financial claims and the scope of the concession led to multiple court cases across successive administrations.

Bi-Courtney maintained that it had been denied benefits under the concession, while FAAN asserted its own financial entitlements and responsibility to protect public airport assets.

READ ALSO: FAAN steps up airport surveillance as Nigeria confirms Ebola case in Abuja

The dispute also involved the ownership of the General Aviation Terminal and financial claims connected to the Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria.

Mr Keyamo said the latest settlement followed negotiations between the government and the chairman of the Bi-Courtney Group, Wale Babalakin, with legal, commercial and technical teams involved in the process.

He added that the agreement would give Bi-Courtney greater certainty to invest in the terminal while allowing the government to resume revenue collection and plan airport development under the revised framework.

He urged FAAN and Bi-Courtney to ensure that the settlement resulted in completed facilities, reliable services and improved airport operations.

“The travelling public should see the result in functioning facilities and dependable service. That is how the value of this settlement will be measured,” he said.

World.title: Elon Musk ordered reduction in Starshield services for Ukraine – Report
World.content:
File: Elon Musk

Elon Musk ordered a reduction in Starshield services for Ukraine, the Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday, after the tech billionaire said any limits on the SpaceX-operated communications system would ultimately have come from the president.

Musk capped the speed at which Ukrainian equipment could connect to the system, making some of Kyiv’s drones useless, the Journal reported, citing anonymous US officials and people familiar with the matter.

Kyiv has accused Washington of deliberately slowing speeds at which Starshield can be used effectively — a charge denied last week by US President Donald Trump.

Musk had previously said that “any limits on speed or usage” of Starshield systems were “decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” referring to Trump.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that Washington had no prior knowledge of the slowdown.

“The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk,” Rubio said during his trip to India.

“That’s a private company; the president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything… I’m telling you, there was no foreknowledge.”

On Tuesday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that the Pentagon had not directed any changes to Starshield, saying: “We haven’t pulled anything back.”

“Nothing’s changed from our view. We haven’t made any directives or anything like that,” he said.

Trump said last week he did not request any curbs to Starshield, adding: “It wasn’t me. And I don’t think it was Elon.”

Kyiv last week reported restrictions to the service, which it sees as crucial to fending off Moscow’s invasion, shortly after Trump criticized Ukraine and urged it to stop targeting Russian oil refineries.

Ukraine uses Starshield, Starlink’s military-grade satellite service, for its battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russia-occupied territory, and its interceptor drones. It also uses SpaceX’s parallel Starlink civilian satellite system.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv have been increasingly tense in recent days, with Trump calling for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to be replaced after he criticized a US deal allowing more Russian diesel into global markets.

AFP

World.title: Fasoranti was true custodian of Awoism, not slogan chaser — Yoruba Group
World.content:
Pa Fasoranti

…Death ends extraordinary chapter in Yorubaland’s political history

By Dayo Johnson, Akure

The Conscience of Yoruba Nation Group has mourned the death of Afenifere leader, Pa Reuben Fasoranti, describing his passing as the end of an extraordinary chapter in the political history of Yorubaland and Nigeria.

The convener of the group, Abagun Kole Omololu, in a statement, said the organisation received with profound sorrow the news of the death of Fasoranti, whom he described as a steadfast adherent of Awoism and a committed custodian of its ideals.

Omololu said: “His death marks the end of an extraordinary chapter in the political history of Yorubaland and Nigeria.

“With his departure, we have lost a man whose life was defined by an uncommon devotion to principle, an abiding commitment to public service and an unwavering belief in the progressive ideals of Chief Obafemi Awolowo.

“Pa Fasoranti was not merely a follower of Awolowo; he was a steadfast adherent of Awoism and one of its most committed custodians.

“To him, Awoism was neither a convenient political slogan nor a political legacy to be exploited for personal gain.

“It represented a philosophy of governance founded on education, social justice, accountable leadership, genuine federalism and the welfare of ordinary citizens.”

He said Fasoranti’s service as an educationist, his tenure as Commissioner for Finance in the old Ondo State under the progressive administration of Chief Michael Adekunle Ajasin, and his decades of involvement in Afenifere reflected his consistent commitment to those ideals.

Omololu added that Fasoranti remained committed to the belief that political leadership should be judged by its contributions to society rather than the privileges attached to public office.

He said the late elder statesman’s integrity stood in contrast to a political culture in which principles were often sacrificed for expediency.

“Pa Fasoranti’s integrity and steadfastness offer a powerful contrast to a political culture in which principles are too often sacrificed at the altar of expediency.

“He belonged to a generation that understood that public office was a trust, political conviction a responsibility, and honesty an indispensable attribute of leadership.

“His example reminds us that integrity is demonstrated not by what people proclaim, but by the principles they uphold when compromise would be more convenient.

“His advocacy of democratic governance and genuine federalism also reflected his understanding that Nigeria’s stability and prosperity depend on justice, equity and respect for the legitimate aspirations of its constituent peoples,” he said.

According to Omololu, Fasoranti’s death should serve as both a moment of mourning and an opportunity for reflection on the ideals he upheld.

“For the Conscience of Yoruba Nation Group, his passing is both a moment of grief and a solemn call to reflection.

“Awoism must not be reduced to the celebration of Awolowo’s name or the recitation of his achievements. Its authenticity must be measured by the quality of governance, access to education, protection of the vulnerable and the willingness of leaders to place the common good above personal interests.”

The group extended its condolences to the Fasoranti family, Afenifere, the people of Akure and Ondo State, and the Yoruba nation.

Omololu said the late Afenifere leader’s ideals would endure beyond his death, urging political leaders and others to preserve the principles of justice, integrity and public welfare associated with Awoism.

“Pa Fasoranti has departed, but the ideals to which he devoted his life endure.

“The most fitting tribute to his memory is to uphold the principles he cherished and ensure that Awoism remains a living commitment to justice, integrity and the welfare of our people.

“May his soul rest in perfect peace,” he added.

World.title: Mimiko mourns Uduaghan, hails him as detribalised statesman
World.content:
Uduaghan

Ex-Delta governor was bridge-builder across party lines

By Dayo Johnson, Akure

Former Ondo State Governor, Dr. Olusegun Mimiko, has mourned the death of former Delta State Governor, Dr. Emmanuel Eweta Uduaghan, describing him as a detribalised statesman who left indelible footprints in Delta State and Nigeria.

Mimiko, in a statement he personally signed, said he and his wife, Olukemi, received the news of Uduaghan’s death with sadness.

Uduaghan reportedly died in the early hours of Monday, October 19, 2026, after an illness.

“We mourn the departure of Dr. Uduaghan, a complete gentleman, a medical doctor who brought compassion into governance, and a detribalised statesman who left indelible footprints across Delta State and Nigeria,” Mimiko said.

He noted that Uduaghan served Delta State in various capacities, including Commissioner for Health, Secretary to the State Government and governor, discharging his responsibilities with grace, humility and calmness, even in times of crisis.

Describing the late former governor as a bridge-builder, Mimiko said he maintained cordial relationships across political divides.

“He was a bridge-builder and a brother across party lines,” he said.

Mimiko extended his condolences to Uduaghan’s wife, Roli, his children, the Uduaghan family of Abigborodo, the Delta State Government and the people of the state, as well as others mourning his death.

He noted that the loss was particularly painful as it came just days before Uduaghan’s 72nd birthday.

“We pray Almighty God grants his soul eternal rest and grants his family the fortitude to bear this irreplaceable loss.

“May his gentle soul rest in perfect peace,” Mimiko added.

World.title: Fasoranti was steadfast democrat, pillar of Ajasin administration — Ijabiyi
World.content:
Pa Fasoranti

By Dayo Johnson, Akure

The PBAT Mandate Elders Forum, Ondo State, has mourned the death of Pa Reuben Fasoranti, describing him as an educationist, a steadfast advocate of democracy and a key pillar of the administration of the late Governor Michael Adekunle Ajasin.

The forum’s Chairman, Chief Demola Ijabiyi, in a condolence message issued on behalf of the group, described Fasoranti’s death as a profound personal loss and the departure of a towering figure whose life enriched Ondo State, the Yoruba nation and Nigeria.

Recalling their shared political journey under Ajasin, Ijabiyi said his association with the late elder statesman spanned several decades, including their service in the administration of the former governor.

He said: “My association with Pa Fasoranti stretches back several decades, including our memorable service under Governor Michael Adekunle Ajasin.

“During the 1982/83 election campaign, he was Commissioner for Finance and in charge of the re-election campaign, while I served as the campaign manager.

“Pa Fasoranti was the right-hand man of the late sage and one of his most trusted pillars. Together, they administered the old Ondo State with integrity, transparency and an unwavering commitment to the welfare of the people.

“The administration’s monumental achievements became a reference point against which successive administrations in the state have been measured.

“Working alongside him gave me the privilege of witnessing his discipline, sound judgement and devotion to public service.

“He understood that public resources were a sacred trust and that government existed to improve the lives of the people. These convictions guided his conduct throughout his public life.”

The forum noted that Fasoranti brought the same sense of duty to his work as an educationist, public administrator and political leader.

It said he belonged to a generation whose politics were rooted in clear principles, personal sacrifice and service to the common good.

His participation in the National Democratic Coalition (NADECO) and the struggle against military rule, the forum added, further demonstrated his courage and commitment to constitutional government.

“At a difficult period in Nigeria’s history, he stood with others who demanded the restoration of democracy.

“As a leader of Afenifere, he remained a respected voice for Yoruba unity, justice, equity, true federalism and national progress. His quiet dignity and consistency of purpose earned him respect across generations,” the statement read.

Ijabiyi said Fasoranti’s greatest legacy lay in the values he upheld and the example he set for future generations.

“At 100, Baba has completed a remarkable earthly journey. We mourn because we shall miss his presence, wisdom and fatherly counsel. We also give thanks to Almighty God for a long and purposeful life devoted to worthy causes.

“The most fitting tribute we can pay him is to uphold the integrity, discipline and commitment to public welfare that defined his life. Political leaders and younger generations must learn from his example and recognise that lasting honour comes through service.”

The PBAT Mandate Elders Forum extended its condolences to Fasoranti’s children, grandchildren, extended family, political associates, the leadership and members of Afenifere, and the government and people of Ondo State.

“We pray that Almighty God will comfort all who mourn him and grant his soul eternal rest. Pa Reuben Famuyide Fasoranti leaves behind an honoured name and a legacy that will continue to inspire generations,” Ijabiyi added.

World.title: PSG’s Kvaratskhelia set for months out with torn ACL
World.content:
PSG’s Georgian forward #07 Khvicha Kvaratskhelia (C) celebrates Paris Saint-Germain’s victory with teammates at the end of the French L1 football match between Paris Saint-Germain (PSG) and Le Mans FC at the Parc des Princes stadium in Paris on October 10, 2026. (Photo by FRANCK FIFE / AFP)

Paris Saint-Germain winger Khvicha Kvaratskhelia requires surgery after tearing his ACL in the Champions League win against Barcelona, the European champions said on Wednesday.

“Having suffered a torn anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee during yesterday’s match against FC Barcelona, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia is set to undergo surgery in the coming days,” PSG said in a statement.

In more bad news for PSG, the club said forward Ousmane Dembele and central defender Marquinhos will both be sidelined for “several weeks” with injuries.

Kvaratskhelia slumped to the turf without any apparent contact and left the pitch just before the hour mark in the 4-2 league phase victory against Barcelona at the Parc des Princes on Tuesday.

The 25-year-old Georgia international played a leading role in helping PSG to win back-to-back Champions League titles and is one of the contenders for the Ballon d’Or, which will be awarded on Monday.

Dembele, the current Ballon d’Or holder, and Marquinhos both suffered thigh injuries, PSG said.

World.title: Nigerian newspapers review: Experts, opposition take on Oyedele over N4,000/$ crash for naira
World.content:
Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister for the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele
