World.title: Nigeria’s 11m-tonne cold storage gap exposes food supply weakness
World.content:
…as stakeholders list challenges, proffer solutions

By Cynthia Alo

Nigeria has an estimated 11 million tonnes of perishable produce requiring cold storage, but less than 20,000 tonnes of long-term capacity, stakeholders have said.

They blamed short-term financing for blocking investment needed to cut post-harvest losses.

Speaking at the 10th Sustainability Table Series in Lagos, themed, ‘‘Feeding the Future: Resilient Food Systems, Smarter Value Chains & Cold-Chain Infrastructure’’, Managing Director of Mystrose Agro Commodities Ltd and NovaChill, Babatunde Niran-Aluko, said building cold storage at scale requires at least £600 per tonne. Sokoto alone, according to him, produces about 400,000 tonnes of onions, showing the scale of the gap.

Niran-Aluko is building a 20,000-tonne facility in Sokoto that can keep produce for eight to 10 months and cut losses to five per cent, but said it is small against national need.

“My goal is 500,000 tonnes, and we have 11 million tonnes to address. We need 22 of me and we still won’t finish it,” he said.

He said the model will work with cooperatives and aggregators, not individual farmers, and may need government subsidy to stay affordable. He added that many Nigerian investors seek quick returns, not long-term infrastructure.

Country Director, Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition, Dr. Michael Ojo, said cold-chain needs patient capital.

“The banks are short-term, business people seeking investment are short-term, so we cannot solve long-term problems,” he said.

He called for development finance to structure viable models.

Ojo also said Nigeria must move from just growing more food to fixing the whole system — aggregation, logistics, processing, markets and nutrition — including biofortified crops and fortified staples, plus demand creation for nutritious food.

On her part, Founder, Century 21 Foundation, Princess Kemdi Chika-Okafor, called for decentralised, solar-powered hubs near aggregation centres and markets, not one large warehouse.

“When we talk about solar-powered cold storage hubs, we should not focus on a lone warehouse like at the airport. We need to create hubs where we have a lot of food,” she said.

She said pay-as-you-go fees would help smallholders and traders afford storage, while partnerships with NGOs and public institutions could provide cheaper finance.

National President, National Onion Producers, Processors and Marketers Association, Aliyu Isah, said storage must go with inputs and handling facilities.

He listed right seed varieties, fertiliser, chemicals, mechanisation, irrigation, and common centres for cleaning, sorting, grading and packaging. He said lack of sorting machines is blocking market access.

World.title: Nigeria confirms first Ebola case is Bundibugyo strain
World.content:
The first Ebola case detected in Nigeria is the Bundibugyo strain, which is behind a major DR Congo outbreak, and the patient is a diplomat, an emergency meeting heard on Wednesday.

The case in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda to the capital Abuja on October 3, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said.

Since the Ebola outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo in mid-May, the deadly viral haemorrhagic fever has spread to several countries across the continent, including to neighbouring Uganda.

“We did three levels of tests, but all molecular. The strain was Bundibugyo,” Olajumoke Babatunde, director of the public health laboratory service at the NCDC said.

The World Health Organization (WHO) also confirmed that it was the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is still neither a vaccine nor a specific treatment.

“This person is actually a diplomat,” another official said, adding the patient has deteriorated into “multi-organ failure”.

The director general of Africa CDC, Jean Kaseya, warned on Tuesday of “an extremely serious threat” as Kenya also declared its ninth Ebola case.

In several months, the DRC’s Ebola epidemic has become the deadliest in the country’s history, killing 4,381 people out of more than 9,000 confirmed cases, according to the health authorities.

Nigeria has identified 44 contacts that are being monitored, while intensifying efforts to find other people who may have been exposed.

The WHO said in a statement that infection prevention and control was being “ramped up” at the private hospital where the patient sought care.

World.title: Adeleke Initiates Comprehensive Security, Surveillance Project in Osun
World.content:
Yinka Kolawole in Osogbo

Osun State Governor, Ademola Adeleke, has initiated plans for a comprehensive statewide security and surveillance project aimed at strengthening intelligence gathering and protecting lives, businesses and public institutions across the state.

The initiative, being developed in partnership with Hefei Shengwen Information Technology Company Limited, was discussed at a meeting between the governor and executives of the Chinese technology firm last Monday.

The delegation was led by the company’s Director of International Operations, Mr. Cai Jianfei, and its Manager of Overseas Operations, Mr. Nemo Guo.

According to a statement issued yesterday by the governor’s spokesperson, Mallam Olawale Rasheed, the proposed project will involve the deployment of modern security technologies, including drones, radar systems, artificial intelligence-powered cameras, robotics and Internet of Things (IoT) devices across the state.

The technologies are expected to facilitate real-time information gathering and round-the-clock monitoring of security developments through a central Command and Control Centre.

The proposed initiative will also incorporate a Safe School Project and a decentralised mobile application that will enable residents to connect with the Command and Control Centre.

Under the plan, security infrastructure will be extended to schools, banks, industries, farms, mining sites, commercial centres, bus parks, and motor garages, as well as major towns and transportation routes across Osun State.

Speaking at the meeting, Adeleke said the initiative was designed to harness emerging technologies to improve the state’s security architecture and strengthen the protection of residents and businesses.

The governor also referenced his administration’s establishment of the Osun State Security Trust Fund, noting that the proposed technology-driven initiative would complement efforts to address security challenges across the state.

“We plan to create an inclusive security platform that will fully secure and protect our people. From schools, hospitals, businesses and border communities, this initiative is a strategic option,” the governor said.

Cai, who reportedly invited Adeleke for a working visit to China, described the proposed project as an inclusive security initiative designed to integrate the capacity of the state leadership with advanced technology to protect citizens and businesses.

The project is expected to provide a centralised system for monitoring security developments across different locations in the state, although the statement did not specify its implementation timeline, cost, or commencement date.

The initiative came as the Adeleke administration prepares for its second-term inauguration.

World.title: UNODC: Terrorist Groups Use Sexual Violence to Terrorise, Control their Victims
World.content:
Linus Aleke in Abuja

The Country Representative of the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), Cheikh Toure, has said terrorist groups deliberately use sexual and gender-based violence to terrorise, punish, and control their victims.

Speaking at the Second Expert Group Meeting on the ‘Development of a Toolkit for First Emergency Responders in Cases of Sexual and Gender-Based Violence Linked to Terrorism’ held in Abuja, Toure said terrorist groups perpetrate these crimes against women and girls, as well as men and boys, targeting entire communities based on their faith, ethnicity or political identity.

“The harm does not end when an attack is over. Its consequences can endure for years, compounded by stigma, displacement and barriers that prevent survivors from accessing the care and justice they deserve,” he said.

Toure cautioned that the toolkit would only be as effective as the practitioners who helped shape it.

He reiterated that the abduction of 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in April 2014 had shown the world the devastating consequences of Boko Haram’s violence.

According to him, “The abductions led to forced marriages and sexual enslavement associated with the insurgency in the North-East. It demonstrated that such crimes were not isolated incidents but part of a deliberate method of terror.

“This is a global challenge. It is not confined to one religion, ideology or terrorist organisation. That is precisely why this toolkit must draw on experiences from different contexts while remaining firmly anchored in the rights, safety and dignity of those affected.”

Toure said the United Nations General Assembly and Security Council have established clear positions on the abduction of women and girls and the use of sexual violence by terrorist groups.

He explained that Security Council Resolution 2331 of 2016 recognised sexual violence and trafficking as tactics used by terrorist groups, while Resolution 2467 of 2019 called for a survivor-centred approach to addressing conflict-related sexual violence.

He added that the General Assembly had also reaffirmed these commitments through successive reviews of the United Nations Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy.

Toure said that although international commitments were in place, their consistent implementation on the ground remained a challenge in countries such as Nigeria.

“A resolution alone does not reach a survivor. What matters is whether its principles translate into practical action and whether countries can adapt and implement them within their own national systems.

“I therefore trust that Nigeria will demonstrate the commitment required to domesticate this guidance and ensure that survivors across 36 states are not left behind,” he said.

Toure stressed that first emergency responders operated under some of the most challenging conditions imaginable.

“They may arrive during or immediately after an attack, amid continuing insecurity, mass casualties, limited resources and the overriding responsibility to save lives.

“Under such circumstances, signs of sexual violence can easily be missed. Evidence may be destroyed, survivors may become dispersed, and stigma may deepen,” he said.

On his own, the National Security Adviser, Mallam Nuhu Ribadu, said sexual and gender-based violence could leave survivors facing lasting physical injuries, psychological distress, stigma and barriers to rebuilding their lives.

Represented by the National Coordinator of the National Counter Terrorism Centre, Major General Adamu Laka, Ribadu added that families and communities also bore the consequences.

According to him, behind every discussion of response procedures, documentation and accountability lay an important principle: the safety and dignity of survivors must remain the foremost concern.

“For anyone who has experienced sexual violence, the manner in which assistance is first offered can influence their willingness to seek further care, their confidence in public institutions, and their path towards recovery.

“First, emergency responders therefore occupy a critical position. They may be the first to recognise that sexual violence has occurred, the first to receive a disclosure and the first to connect a survivor with medical care or protection services.

“They often work under severe pressure, with limited resources and competing demands,” he said.

Ribadu explained that the toolkit under consideration sought to equip responders with practical guidance for dealing with such circumstances.

He said: “Its development offers an opportunity to strengthen the connection between emergency assistance and survivor protection, and the preservation of information that can support investigations.

“We must keep one clear principle in view: every response should protect survivors from further harm. Urgent care, privacy, dignity and appropriate referrals must guide the initial encounter.

“Responders must also understand the limits of their responsibilities and know when specialist assistance is required.”

World.title: Between Akpabio’s Performance and Battle for 11th Senate Leadership
World.content:
As Senator Godswill Akpabio seeks a second term as President of the Senate, early endorsements expose the emerging succession battle, raising critical questions about legislative performance, institutional independence and the 11th National Assembly. Sunday Aborisade reports.

The declaration by the Senate Chief Whip, Senator Tahir Monguno, that there is “no vacancy” in the office of the Senate President has introduced a fresh dimension to the emerging struggle for the leadership of the 11th National Assembly.

Beyond its immediate political implications, however, the declaration raises fundamental questions about legislative performance, institutional independence, political succession and the extent to which the present Senate can influence the leadership of a chamber whose membership Nigerians are yet to elect.

Monguno’s declaration during last Thursday’s plenary was unequivocal. Expressing confidence that a majority of serving senators would return to the chamber after the 2027 general election, he endorsed the continuation of Senator Godswill Akpabio as Senate President.

His position extended to the Deputy Senate President and other principal officers, signalling a broader preference for continuity in the leadership of the 10th Senate.

Senator Cyril Fasuyi subsequently reinforced the position, maintaining that the Senate presidency was already occupied and should not be treated as an office awaiting a new contest. Akpabio then put the position to a voice vote, with senators responding in support.

Politically, the development was significant. It demonstrated the willingness of Akpabio’s allies to begin consolidating support for his possible return well before the inauguration of the next National Assembly. Institutionally, however, it did not settle the question of who would preside over the Senate after the 2027 elections.

The distinction is crucial. The current Senate can express confidence in its leadership, but it cannot determine the composition or leadership of the 11th Senate. Nigerians will decide who represents them in the next National Assembly, while the senators elected in 2027 will choose their presiding officers in accordance with the Constitution and applicable parliamentary rules.

Akpabio, therefore, faces two separate political tests: securing his return to the Senate and persuading his colleagues in the next Assembly to elect him president. Success in the first will not automatically guarantee success in the second.

The emerging contest is consequently about much more than the survival of an incumbent. It is also a test of the relationship between political loyalty and legislative performance, the independence of parliament under a dominant executive, and the extent to which the leadership of the National Assembly should be determined by institutional considerations rather than the calculations of political power brokers.

Succession battle before the battlefield is formed

The timing of Monguno’s declaration provides an important insight into the political calculations surrounding the Senate presidency.

Akpabio had complained that controversies arising from his comments during deliberations on a bill dealing with attempted suicide were being exploited by political opponents to undermine his reputation ahead of the contest for the next Senate presidency. He had also suggested that the contests for the presidency and vice-presidency were effectively settled, leaving the Senate presidency as a major political prize still attracting attention.

Against this background, Monguno’s intervention can hardly be divorced from the calculations already gathering momentum around the 11th National Assembly.

The declaration appears designed, at least in part, to establish an early narrative of continuity, reassure Akpabio’s supporters and discourage potential challengers from assuming that the position will automatically become available after the next elections.

Yet the strategy presents an interesting paradox. While it may strengthen the incumbent’s standing among his allies, it also draws attention to the political uncertainty surrounding his ambition. If his return were already assured, why would the leadership need to establish so early that there was “no vacancy”?

Of course, an early endorsement is not necessarily evidence of weakness. In parliamentary politics, succession battles frequently begin long before the formal process, as aspirants build alliances, negotiate interests and seek assurances from colleagues.

Nevertheless, the declaration cannot eliminate the uncertainties that will shape the next leadership contest. Senators who endorse Akpabio today may not return in 2027. Those who return may reassess their positions in response to new political alignments, while newly elected senators will enter the chamber with interests and ambitions of their own.

The present Senate may therefore have expressed a preference, but the final political arithmetic remains unsettled.

What exactly is at stake?

The intensity of the emerging contest is understandable. The Senate President occupies one of the most influential positions in Nigeria’s political system, presiding over legislative business, participating in the determination of parliamentary priorities and exercising considerable influence over the allocation of committee responsibilities and the management of the chamber.

The office also places its occupant at the centre of relations between the legislature and the executive, particularly in budgetary proceedings, ministerial confirmations, oversight investigations and deliberations on major government policies.

These responsibilities make the Senate presidency both an institutional office and a significant instrument of political influence.

For Akpabio, retaining the position would mean continuing to shape the legislative agenda during a period when President Bola Tinubu’s administration will be approaching the next general election. For potential challengers, the contest represents an opportunity to influence the direction of the Senate and redefine its relationship with the executive.

However, the national interest demands that the contest should not be reduced to a struggle for political survival or the distribution of parliamentary privileges.

The more important question is whether the next Senate will be led by a presiding officer capable of strengthening legislative independence, improving accountability and restoring public confidence in the National Assembly.

That is the standard against which Akpabio’s third-year performance should be assessed.

Performance versus political loyalty

The central weakness in the emerging succession debate is the tendency to discuss Akpabio’s possible return principally in terms of endorsements, alliances and the number of senators willing to support him.

Those considerations are important in parliamentary politics, but they are insufficient to establish whether another term would serve the interests of the Senate or the Nigerian public.

An incumbent seeking another term should be judged on what he has accomplished, the institutional precedents established under his leadership and the extent to which the Senate has discharged its constitutional responsibilities.

Supporters of Akpabio can point to legislative activity, cooperation with the executive and the passage of government-backed measures as evidence of a productive working relationship between the two arms of government. They may also argue that a stable relationship between the Senate and the presidency can facilitate governance and prevent unnecessary institutional confrontations.

There is merit in that argument. Cooperation between the legislature and executive is not inherently undesirable. Governments require functional legislative institutions to consider proposed laws, approve expenditure and provide the legal framework for implementing public policies.

The problem arises when cooperation becomes indistinguishable from acquiescence.

A legislature that routinely endorses executive proposals without sufficiently interrogating their implications risks weakening the constitutional checks and balances that distinguish democratic government from executive dominance.

Consequently, the pertinent question is not whether Akpabio has maintained a working relationship with the Tinubu administration. It is whether that relationship has enabled the Senate to perform its oversight responsibilities effectively or diminished its willingness to challenge questionable policies and expenditure where necessary.

Has the Senate adequately scrutinised the federal budget and monitored the implementation of appropriations? Has the committees consistently investigated the performance of ministries, departments and agencies? Has oversight findings translated into corrective action, improved public expenditure or greater accountability?

How effectively has the chamber responded to the economic pressures confronting households, the challenges of insecurity, unemployment and the public demand for better governance?

These questions require evidence-based answers rather than political declarations.

The Senate presidency should not be treated as a reward for loyalty to the ruling party, the executive or the incumbent leadership. It is an office whose continued occupation should depend, in part, on the confidence of elected colleagues in the candidate’s ability to lead the institution effectively.

The independence question

Perhaps the most consequential issue confronting Akpabio is the perception of the Senate’s independence under his leadership.

Nigeria’s presidential system deliberately distributes power among the executive, legislature and judiciary. The National Assembly is not expected to operate as an extension of the presidency, just as the executive cannot reasonably expect the legislature to obstruct every government initiative.

The constitutional relationship is one of cooperation within clearly defined boundaries, with each arm retaining the authority and responsibility to perform its assigned functions.

In this arrangement, legislative independence is measured not by the frequency of disagreements with the executive but by the willingness and capacity of lawmakers to make decisions on their merits.

A Senate that supports a sound government proposal is performing its responsibilities. A Senate that rejects or amends a defective proposal after careful examination is doing so as well.

The critical issue is whether senators are free to exercise independent judgment without undue political pressure.

This question becomes particularly important when the ruling party controls the executive and commands substantial influence within the legislature. Under such circumstances, the Senate leadership carries a special responsibility to demonstrate that party affiliation does not override constitutional duty.

For Akpabio, a credible case for continuity would require demonstrating that the Senate has remained capable of holding government accountable, including where such scrutiny might be politically inconvenient.

It would also require showing that oversight is substantive rather than ceremonial, and that legislative decisions are guided by national priorities rather than the preservation of political relationships.

Without such evidence, an endorsement by serving senators may establish the incumbent’s political strength without necessarily resolving questions about his institutional performance.

Can ‘no vacancy’ prevent a contest?

In practical terms, the declaration cannot prevent a contest for the Senate presidency of the 11th National Assembly.

The Constitution provides the framework for the election of the Senate President by senators from among themselves. The relevant constitutional provisions, including Section 50, establish the offices of the presiding officers of the National Assembly and provide for their election.

The process is distinct from the general election through which Nigerians elect members of the Senate.

Akpabio must first secure a Senate seat before he can seek the presidency of the chamber again. Even if he returns, he will have to obtain the support of enough senators in the new Assembly to secure election.

The distinction between returning to the Senate and becoming its president is fundamental. A senator’s electoral victory confers membership of the chamber; it does not automatically confer the authority to preside over it.

Furthermore, the composition of the 11th Senate will depend on the outcome of elections across the country. Some serving senators will retain their seats, others will lose, and new lawmakers will introduce different constituencies, political interests and calculations into the chamber.

The possibility of a changed political configuration makes any attempt to treat the next Senate presidency as a settled matter premature.

Political discussions have also linked other prominent figures to calculations surrounding the contest, including Senator Adams Oshiomhole and Imo State Governor, Hope Uzodimma, who is seeking a return to the Senate. Such calculations underscore the likelihood that the contest will be shaped by a combination of party dynamics, regional considerations, personal ambition and negotiations among lawmakers.

However, potential candidacies and political alignments should not be confused with a settled field of contestants. The actual contest will become clearer as the elections approach and the composition of the next Senate emerges.

Danger of closing the door too early

Monguno’s declaration carries a further political risk: it could be interpreted as an attempt by the present Senate leadership to determine the choices available to its successor.

Although the endorsement has no power to bind the 11th Senate, the language of “no vacancy” may create the impression that the outcome has been predetermined before voters have elected the lawmakers who will make the decision.

Such an impression could provoke resistance among senators who believe the next Assembly should exercise its independence in choosing its leadership.

Indeed, an early declaration of continuity may unintentionally provide potential challengers with a rallying point. They could frame their campaign around the principle that the next Senate should be free to choose its president without being constrained by endorsements issued by the outgoing chamber.

The counterargument from Akpabio’s supporters is equally straightforward: serving senators are entitled to express confidence in their leader, and their endorsement does not prevent future senators from making their own choices.

That position is defensible. Political endorsements are a normal feature of democratic competition, and nothing about the declaration itself establishes that the constitutional process for electing the next Senate President has been displaced.

The controversy should therefore be assessed in proportion to its actual significance. The declaration is politically consequential, but it is not a constitutional guarantee of Akpabio’s return.

Its importance lies in the message it sends: the incumbent’s supporters intend to organise early, project confidence and make continuity a central theme of the succession debate.

Whether that strategy succeeds will depend on the circumstances that emerge after the 2027 elections.

Implications for 11th N’Assembly

The contest has implications extending beyond Akpabio’s personal ambition.

First, it could influence the conduct of the 10th Senate during its remaining months.

If the leadership becomes excessively preoccupied with succession, there is a risk that legislative priorities could be overshadowed by political manoeuvring.

Budget scrutiny, oversight investigations, law reform and other responsibilities requiring sustained attention must not become secondary to the struggle for parliamentary offices.

Second, the contest could affect the relationship between the Senate and the executive. A leadership seeking to retain office may face competing incentives: demonstrate cooperation with the presidency to preserve political support while also showing sufficient independence to satisfy lawmakers and the wider public.

How that balance is managed will influence the Senate’s institutional credibility.

Third, an early succession campaign could deepen divisions within the ruling party or the Senate if competing interests interpret the declaration as an attempt to monopolise the leadership position. Conversely, a transparent process based on consultation and respect for the prerogatives of the next Assembly could produce an orderly transition.

Fourth, the struggle provides an opportunity to reconsider what Nigerians should expect from legislative leadership. The National Assembly has frequently faced public criticism over its relationship with the executive, the cost of governance and the perceived distance between lawmakers and ordinary citizens.

A contest for the Senate presidency should therefore provide an opportunity for candidates to articulate clear commitments to legislative accountability, transparency, effective representation and institutional reform.

The next Senate will inherit substantial responsibilities, including scrutiny of national expenditure, consideration of laws affecting economic recovery and security, and oversight of government agencies responsible for delivering public services.

Its effectiveness will depend not merely on the identity of its president but also on the quality of its membership, the independence of its committees and the willingness of senators to place national interests above narrow political calculations.

The verdict will depend on more than numbers

Ultimately, Akpabio’s greatest challenge may not be defeating a particular rival. It may be persuading enough senators that continuity under his leadership would serve the institutional interests of the next Assembly.

To make that case convincingly, he must demonstrate what the Senate has achieved under his leadership, where it has fallen short and what he intends to do differently if given another opportunity.

He must also confront legitimate questions about legislative independence rather than allowing the succession debate to become a contest of endorsements and political loyalty.

For his supporters, the argument for continuity must rest on demonstrable accomplishments, effective management of the chamber and a credible commitment to stronger legislative oversight.

For potential challengers, the burden is equally demanding. It is not enough to oppose Akpabio or declare that the Senate presidency should change hands. They must explain how their leadership would improve the performance of the institution.

The decision ultimately belongs to the senators who will constitute the 11th National Assembly. Their choice should reflect not only political alliances but also their assessment of the qualities required to lead the chamber through the next phase of Nigeria’s democratic development.

Monguno’s declaration has undoubtedly given Akpabio an early political boost. It has also brought the succession question into sharper focus well before the 2027 elections.

But an endorsement by the present Senate cannot substitute for electoral victory, and electoral victory cannot substitute for the support required to become Senate President.

The real test will be whether Akpabio can return to the chamber, defend his record and persuade a new generation of senators that his continued leadership is preferable to an alternative.

If he succeeds, the declaration may be remembered as an early indication of a successful campaign for continuity. If he fails, it may instead become an example of the limits of political endorsements in a system where the final decision rests with elected lawmakers.

For now, the Senate presidency remains an open political question. The voters will determine the composition of the 11th Senate, and the senators elected will determine who leads it.

Beyond the battle for the office, however, lies a more important question for Nigerian democracy: will the next Senate be remembered for the political interests it serves or for the independence, accountability and quality of legislation it brings to public life?

World.title: Again, Another Non-Nigerian Brings Ebola into Abuja; FG Says Don’t Panic, Stay Vigilant
World.content:
• Govt confirms first case in Abuja, activates emergency response

•44 close contacts identified as tracing begins

• Medical sciences academy seeks implementation of high-alert protocols

•Urges Nigerians to avoid handshakes, unnecessary physical contacts

Emmanuel Addeh and Onyebuchi Ezigbo in Abuja





The federal government yesterday confirmed one case of Ebola disease in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), with the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare revealing that it has activated emergency public health response, including the commencement of contact tracing.

Also, the Academy of Medical Sciences of Nigeria (AMSN) yesterday noted with concern the reported case, but commended the prompt commencement of contact tracing as well as the isolation of the patient and the in-tensified surveillance already underway.

The Academy further recommended the immediate and nationwide implementation of high-alert protocols, draw-ing on the proven measures that enabled Nigeria to contain Ebola in 2014 and to respond to COVID-19 in 2020.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), the epicentre of the disease, has recorded thousands of cases and deaths as health authorities intensify containment efforts. The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, had heightened regional concerns over cross-border transmission, prompting increased surveillance, contact tracing and isolation measures.

Specifically, as of October 20, 2026, at least 4,605 people have died from the ongoing Ebola outbreak in Central and East Africa, according to the US Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), with one death reported in Kenya and two in Uganda.

Besides, the CDC has recorded 9,582 confirmed cases across the affected countries, with investigations and reporting still ongoing. For comparison, the DRC’s 2025 Ebola outbreak, which was declared over on December 1, 2025, recorded 45 deaths from 64 confirmed and probable cases, representing a case fatality rate of 70.3 per cent.

Ebola is a severe and often fatal disease transmitted through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people or contaminated materials. The Bundibugyo strain responsible for the 2026 outbreak is particularly con-cerning because there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment for this strain, making early diagnosis, iso-lation, supportive care and contact tracing essential to containing its spread.

But in the statement conveying the news on the Ebola case, the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Wel-fare, Prof. Ali Pate, said the patient was a woman who recently arrived in Nigeria on an international flight from Uganda.

She was said to be asymmetric and Ebola usually takes about three weeks for symptoms to develop.

And thankfully, Abuja has very well equipped medical laboratories capable of meeting the challenge.

According to the minister, the woman was admitted to a private hospital in the FCT where she received care for several days before diagnosis was confirmed. The statement added that she is currently in isolation and receiv-ing medical care.

Pate said the Federal Ministry of Health and the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and (NCDC) are working closely with FCT Health Services Secretariat and other relevant authorities to contain the infection and prevent further spread.

“Contact tracing has commenced with 44 close contacts identified presently, with public health teams identifying and monitoring people who may have been exposed, including healthcare workers, patients, caregivers and travel contacts,” he said.

He added that surveillance has been intensified and hospitals are receiving immediate support to strengthen infection prevention and control measures.

The federal government called on all public and private healthcare facilities nationwide to be on high alert. It urged healthcare workers to maintain a high index of suspicion, promptly identify and isolate suspected cases, observe strict infection prevention and control measures, and immediately report suspected cases.

The government also issued advisory on what Nigerians should know and do. It said Ebola spreads through direct contact with blood or body fluids of sick people or contaminated materials, and cannot spread before symptoms begin.

It advised Nigerians to remain calm but vigilant, practice regular hand hygiene, avoid contact with body fluids of suspected cases, watch for symptoms including fever, severe weakness, headache, vomiting and diarrhoea, and report possible exposure immediately.

It further urged those contacted during tracing, including airline passengers, to cooperate and avoid rumours and stigma.

“Our assurance to Nigerians (is that) Nigeria successfully contained Ebola in 2014, and we have the experi-ence and public health systems to respond to this case,” Pate said, noting that investigations are ongoing and updates will be provided.

The first known case of Ebola in Nigeria was in a traveller called Patrick Sawyer, exposed in Liberia. On July 17, 2014, while under observation in a Monrovia, Liberia, hospital for possible Ebola, the patient developed a fever and, while symptomatic, left the hospital against medical advice.

Despite advice against travel, on July 20 he flew by commercial airline from Monrovia via Accra, Ghana, to Lomé, Togo, then flew to Lagos. On arrival in the afternoon of July 20, he was acutely ill and immediately transported to a private hospital where he was noted to have fever, vomiting, and diarrhea. During hospital admission, the patient was queried about Ebola and said he had no known exposure; he was initially treated for presumed malaria.

Based on the patient’s failure to respond to malaria treatment and his travel from an Ebola-affected country in the region (2), treating physicians suspected Ebola. The patient was isolated and tested for Ebola virus infection while local public health authorities were alerted about a suspected case of Ebola. A blood specimen sent to Lagos University Teaching Hospital was confirmed positive for acute Ebola virus infection. The index patient died on July 25.

Meanwhile, the AMSN has recommended the immediate and nationwide implementation of high-alert protocols, drawing on the proven measures that enabled Nigeria to contain Ebola in 2014 and to respond to COVID-19.

“These should include: Enhanced screening at airports, seaports and land borders, particularly for travellers from affected countries. (Also) strict infection prevention and control in all public and private health facilities, with adequate personal protective equipment for health workers, rigorous contact tracing, monitoring and follow-up with sustained, accurate public communication through official channels,” it stated.

The academy, in a statement by the President, Prof. Osato Giwa-Osagie; Foundation President, Prof. Oladapo Ashiru and Head of Rapid Response Committee, Prof. Boaz Adegboro, pointed out that health workers must maintain a high index of suspicion, promptly isolate suspected cases and report them immediately to public health authorities.

“The public should understand clearly that Ebola is not an airborne disease. It spreads through direct contact with the blood or other body fluids of a person who is sick with Ebola or has died from it, or through contact with materials contaminated by those fluids. A person with Ebola cannot spread the disease before symptoms begin.

“As a simple and effective precaution, the Academy advises all Nigerians to avoid handshakes and other un-necessary physical contact, including hugging, during this period. We encourage the use of non-contact greet-ings,” the group said.

For information or to report a suspected case, it urged members of the public to call the NCDC toll-free number 6232, which it said is available 24 hours a day as well as seven days a week.

“The Academy stands ready to support the federal government and all stakeholders with expert advice as the response continues,” the group emphasised.

World.title: Gbajabiamila: Draft of National Policing Bill Now Ready, Undergoing Legislative Review
World.content:
• Expected back from justice ministry by October 30 for onward transmission to president

•Submitted along with 29 consequential amendment bills

• Delta approves amendment for state police, to write National Assembly

Deji Elumoye in Abuja and Omon-Julius Onabu in Asaba





The presidency, yesterday, disclosed that the draft of the 2026 National Policing Bill was ready.

Chief of Staff to the President and Chairman of the Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill, Hon. Femi Gbajabiamila, made the disclosure, in a release.

Gbajabiamila said the group had completed the drafting stage of its assignment and had formally submitted the bill, together with 29 consequential amendment bills, to the Federal Ministry of Justice for legislative drafting review and validation.

He said the submission to Attorney General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Lateef Fagbemi, took place on Monday, October, 19, in line with the working group’s work plan.

The chief of staff explained that the ministry’s review would ensure that the bills conformed to legislative drafting standards and conventions, and did not conflict with existing laws.

He said the Ministry of Justice was expected to return the validated draft bills to the working group on or before Friday, October 30 for final consideration before their presentation to President Bola Tinubu, which would mark the conclusion of the group’s mandate.

Gbajabiamila said, “The proposed National Policing Bill seeks to establish the constitutional and legislative framework for a dual policing structure, comprising a Federal Police Service and State Police Services.

“The Working Group remains committed to a rigorous and transparent process that will deliver a comprehensive legislative proposal for consideration by the president and subsequent transmission to the National Assembly.

“The work on preparing the National Policing Bill is proceeding alongside the ongoing consideration of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (Sixth Alteration) Bill, 2026 by the States Houses of Assembly, which must be completed before the bill is transmitted to the National Assembly.”

The presidency had last Thursday hinted that the National Policing Bill would be transmitted to the National Assembly within two weeks.

Gbajabiamila told newsmen after the steering committee’s meeting at State House, Abuja, “The National Policing Bill is more or less ready for transmission to the National Assembly.

“We will probably have one more meeting after this to cross the t’s and dot the i’s and make sure every area is covered. So, we are 90 per cent ready. The governors have one or two observations, and we should be ready in about a week or so.”

He described the bill as “the most consequential bill of the administration so far”, adding that it has undergone strenuous exercises in the last few weeks since the working group’s steering committee began deliberations on August 3.

Commenting on the possibility of the states dragging their feet on the passage of the Sixth Constitution Alteration Bill (State Police), especially against the backdrop of the information that only about six states had passed the amendment, out of the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Gbajabiamila affirmed that there was a “national consensus” among Nigerians on the need for the amendments.

“I see no reason why anyone will want to have a rethink on it,” he said.

Members of the committee present at Thursday’s meeting held at the conference hall of the Chief of Staff Office at State House, Abuja, included Chairman of Nigeria Governors’ Forum and Governor of Kwara State, AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq; Governor Dapo Abiodun of Ogun State; Governor Uba Sani of Kaduna State; Inspector General of Police, Tunji Disu; and Attorney General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, represented by Solicitor General and Permanent Secretary, Federal Ministry of Justice, Mrs Beatrice Jedy-Agba.

Others were Chairman, Policy Advisory Committee, Justice Abdullahi Liman (rtd); Head, Nigeria Police Reform Secretariat, Professor Olu Ogunsakin; Special Adviser to the President on National Assembly Matters (House of Representatives), Dr. Lanre Smart; Senior Special Assistant to the President on Planning and Research, who also doubles as Secretary of the Committee, Nnadubem Moghalu; the representative of President of Nigerian Bar Association; and Assistant Inspector-General of Police (AIG) Abraham Nabhon Thomas, representing the National Security Adviser, among others.

Tinubu had on July 7 inaugurated the Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill to prepare the legal framework for the implementation of state police across the country.

The working group’s inauguration followed National Assembly’s passage of the Constitution Alteration (State Police) Bill, 2026, in which the president proposed a dual policing structure comprising the Federal Police Service and 36 State Police Services.

Tinubu had stated that while the constitutional amendment created the framework for state police, the National Policing Bill would provide the legal structure for its implementation.

He said, “The Constitution Amendment Bill establishes the framework for dual policing, but it does not operationalise it. That work is left to the National Policing Bill.”

According to him, the proposed legislation would address issues necessary for a smooth operationalisation of the state police system.

Tinubu stated, “The proposed National Policing Bill will include provisions on minimum policing standards, state readiness certification, federal-state coordination, accountability, human rights safeguards and fiscal conditions.”

The president said the committee would produce an implementation-ready draft bill immediately after the constitutional amendment process.

“The Working Group has been constituted to produce a technically robust, implementation-ready draft National Policing Bill for transmission to the National Assembly,” Tinubu said.

He said the committee was necessary to avoid delay after the State Police bill was passed.

“We must not wait until the constitutional process is concluded before beginning this important assignment,” he said.

Delta Approves State Police Amendment

Delta State House of Assembly, yesterday, approved the Sixth Alteration Bill of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999 (as amended) to give legislative muscle to the proposed State Police Services in the country.

The approval followed deliberation on a letter from the National Assembly seeking the consideration and concurrence of the 36 States Houses of Assembly in the ongoing constitutional amendment process.

Speaker, Hon. Emomotimi Guwor, read the letter on the floor of the Assembly, outlining the objective of the bill, which sought to provide a constitutional framework for the establishment of State Police Services while preserving the Nigeria Police Force as the Federal Police Service.

Majority Leader, Hon. Emeka Nwaobi, said the proposed amendment aimed to guarantee security of life and property through a dual policing system, allowing states to establish and fund their own police services to address rising cases of insecurity, particularly at the local level.

The lawmakers generally agreed that the bill would strengthen local intelligence gathering, improve response to security challenges, create employment opportunities, and help tackle insecurity at the grassroots more effectively.

Support for the bill was unanimous, with all 23 members present at plenary affirming their support.

While commending the members for their patriotism and overwhelming support for the bill, Guwor stated that the establishment of State Police would ensure a safer environment and engender the desired development of Delta State.

He stated, “Distinguished colleagues, I commend you for approving the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria (Sixth Alteration) Bill, 2026, in line with Section 9 sub-section (2) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (as altered).

“This is a significant step towards the establishment of State Police in Nigeria. It brings us closer to a policing system that is more responsive to our communities, improves intelligence gathering, and strengthens our capacity to tackle security challenges.

“For Delta State, this reform holds great promise for protecting lives and property, sustaining peace and creating a safer environment for investment and development in line with the M.O.R.E Agenda of our amiable Governor, His Excellency, Rt. Hon. (Elder) Sheriff Francis Orohwedor Oborevwori.”

The speaker thereafter directed Clerk of the House, Mr. Otto Aghoghophia, to communicate the resolution of the Delta State House of Assembly to the National Assembly appropriately.

Earlier, the legislators observed one-minute silence in honour of former governor of Delta State, Dr. Emmanuel Eweta Uduaghan, who died on Monday, October 19, three days to his 72nd birthday.

World.title: Tinubu, Awolowo’s Family Mourn as Afenifere Leader, Pa Fasoranti, Dies at 100
World.content:
• President describes elder statesman as an icon and beacon of principle

•Says Nigeria will sorely miss his voice of wisdom, moral authority, and fatherly counsel

•Aiyedatiwa, Falae, Sanwo-Olu, Bamidele grieve

Deji Elumoye, Sunday Aborisade in Abuja, Sunday Ehigiator in Lagos and Fidelis David in Akure





President Bola Tinubu and the Chief Obafemi Awolowo family, yesterday, paid glowing tributes to Afenifere leader, Pa Reuben Fasoranti, who died at the age of 100.

Tinubu, in a tribute, praised the late patriarch and elder statesman as a principled icon and one of the Awolowo progressive family’s last great titans.

According to him, Nigeria will sorely miss Pa Fasoranti’s voice of wisdom, moral authority, and fatherly counsel.

Tinubu, in the 13-paragraph release, stated, “I received with profound sadness the news of the passing of Pa Reuben Famuyide Fasoranti, our father, patriarch, elder statesman, and foremost Afenifere leader, who died at the glorious age of 100.

“On behalf of the federal government and the people of Nigeria, I commiserate with the Fasoranti family, the good people of Akure Kingdom, the government and people of Ondo State and South-west Nigeria, and the entire Afenifere family.

“Pa Fasoranti was an icon, a beacon of principle, and one of the last great titans of Chief Obafemi Awolowo’s progressive family.

“His life, spanning a century, was a lesson in integrity, discipline, selflessness, and unwavering commitment to the Yoruba people and the unity and progress of Nigeria.”

The president added, “From his days as an educationist and principal, to his stewardship as Commissioner for Finance in the old Western Region, and later as the leader of Afenifere, Baba never wavered in his belief in true federalism, social justice, and a Nigeria that works for all.

“Baba made immense contributions to this country and, at the risk of his life, fought for the democracy we enjoy today.

“Pa Fasoranti distinguished himself in every respect: in his disciplined, Spartan way of life, his belief in principles, and his commitment to noble causes.”

Tinubu said, “Our nation will sorely miss his voice of wisdom, moral authority, and fatherly counsel, especially now, when we need his guidance most.

“I recall Baba’s centenary on May 11 this year, when we celebrated not just longevity, but a legacy of honour. He lived a fulfilled life and left indelible footprints in the sands of time.

“I also recall his prayers and counsel when I came to his residence in Akure in 2022 to inform him of my decision to contest the presidency. Pa Fasoranti told me I would be President in his lifetime, and God answered his prayer.”

Tinubu stated, “I had hoped Papa would also be around with us for my second term to witness the full dawn of economic growth and prosperity in the land.

“But we must thank God for Pa Fasoranti’s long life of service, grace and fulfilment.

“May his gentle soul rest in perfect peace. May God comfort all who mourn him and grant his family the fortitude to bear this great loss.”

Aiyedatiwa, Falae Hail Afenifere Leader as ‘One-in-a-Thousand-Years Man’

Fasoranti, who turned 100 years in May, died peacefully in his sleep at his residence, yesterday, October 20, according to his eldest son and Secretary to the Ondo State Government, Dr Taiwo Fasoranti.

Taiwo said the family had been looking forward to celebrating his father’s 101st birthday but had accepted his death as the will of God, describing his century-long life as one worthy of celebration rather than mourning.

He stated, “Baba passed on this evening around 4pm peacefully in his room, in his bed. Baba was 100 years old. He turned 100 in May, and we were all looking forward to his 101st birthday, but God knows best.

“I don’t count it as mourning, but I count it as a time to celebrate his longevity and his influence and impact in the lives of Nigerians, especially Yoruba people.”

He described his late father as a man of few words whose wisdom, firmness, and calm disposition left an enduring impression on those around him.

“My day starts with seeing him in the morning and seeing him when I get back from the office. No matter how late it is, he will still be up waiting for me to come in,” he said, recalling the close relationship they shared until his father’s death.

Fasoranti’s Passing is End of Awolowo’s Political Era, Late Sage’s Family Declares

The Awolowo family mourned the death of Fasoranti, describing his passing as the end of a remarkable era in the political history of Awolowo’s Titans, the Yoruba nation, and Nigeria.

The head of the Awolowo family and Chairman of African Newspapers of Nigeria (ANN) Plc, publishers of the Tribune titles, Ambassador Olatokunbo Awolowo Dosumu, made the assertion in a condolence statement issued yesterday.

Dosumu described Fasoranti as one of the last surviving titans of the political tradition established by the late Chief Obafemi Awolowo, stating that his commitment to the ideals of the late sage remained steadfast throughout his life.

Dosumu stated, “The passing of Chief Reuben Fasaranti at the venerable age of 100 marks the end of a remarkable era in the political history of the Yoruba nation and Nigeria.

“With his departure, we have lost, in a very real sense, the last of the titans of the Awolowo political tradition.”

Dosumu added, “Chief Fasaranti belonged to that extraordinary generation of leaders whose political convictions were rooted in principle, whose commitment to public service was steadfast, and whose loyalty to the ideals and philosophy of Chief Obafemi Awolowo endured through changing times and circumstances.”

He stated, “Throughout his long and eventful life, he remained steadfast in his commitment to the values of justice, equity, progressive governance and the advancement of the common good.

“Neither the passage of time nor the changing fortunes of politics diminished his dedication to the cause he embraced.”

Falae: He’s Exceptional Generational Man

Former Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Chief Olu Fale, described the late elder statesman as his in-law, whom he had known intimately for more than 60 years and considered an extraordinarily rare figure in Nigeria’s political, religious, and social life.

“I’m going to describe Baba Fasoranti as an exceptional generational man, one in a thousand years,” Falae said.

He recalled that throughout their decades-long relationship, he had never witnessed Fasoranti quarrel with anyone or raise his voice at political meetings.

Falae said the late leader was always willing to mediate disputes and help parties reach peaceful resolutions.

He said, “In all that time, I’ve never heard him quarrel with anybody, shout at anyone, even in political meetings. He was always ready to mediate in any dispute brought to his attention.”

Falae said Fasoranti’s influence extended beyond politics to education, community development, and religious life, stating that his commitment to helping disadvantaged children was among the enduring examples of his selflessness.

He recalled that when Fasoranti was the founding principal of Iju/Itaogbolu Grammar School, he admitted pupils from poor backgrounds and allowed them to complete their secondary education on credit, with the opportunity to repay after leaving school.

“No one is perfect, but Baba is as near perfect a human being as I believe you can get in this fallen world,” Falae said, describing his death as a significant loss to Akure, Ondo State, and the Yoruba nation.

Aiyedatiwa: He Was a Beacon of Wisdom

Ondo State Governor, Lucky Aiyedatiwa, described Fasoranti as a patriarch and a beacon of wisdom, integrity and selfless service, whose contributions to the development of Ondo State, Yorubaland, and Nigeria would remain indelible.

In a telephone conversation, he said, “His counsel, fatherly guidance, and principled stand on issues of justice and good governance will be sorely missed.”

The governor commiserated with the Fasoranti family, the people of Akure Kingdom, and the state over the loss.

Sanwo-Olu: It’s End of an Era

Lagos State Governor, Mr. Babajide Sanwo-Olu, described the demise of Pa Reuben Fasoranti, leader of the pan-Yoruba socio-political organisation, Afenifere, as the end of an era.

Sanwo-Olu, who is Chairman of South-West Governors’ Forum, said the glorious exit of Pa Fasoranti, a respected elder statesman, educationist, and progressive, was a big loss to the Yoruba people and Nigeria at large.

In a condolence message personally signed, Sanwo-Olu described the late Pa Fasoranti as a committed leader and a symbol of wisdom, integrity, and selfless service who served the Yoruba people and Nigeria passionately.

He also commiserated with his Ondo State counterpart, Aiyedatiwa; the government and people of Ondo State, particularly the people of Akure Kingdom; the Fasoranti family; and members of Afenifere.

Sanwo-Olu stated, “Baba Fasoranti was a respected and passionate statesman whose contributions to education, leadership and public service remain indelible. He impacted many lives positively through courageous and uncompromising leadership. His commitment to public service and community development was commendable.

“Pa Fasoranti, during his lifetime, made a lot of positive impact in Yorubaland and Nigeria. He did great exploits as the leader of Afenifere by steering the ship of the pan-Yoruba socio-cultural organisation in the right direction.

“We cherish Pa Fasoranti’s commitment to fighting for truth, equity, justice, true federalism and good governance, which he championed for many decades during his lifetime.”

Sanwo-Olu added, “I pray for the repose of the soul of the late Pa Reuben Fasoranti. May God grant the deceased’s family, loved ones, and the Yoruba people the fortitude to bear the irreparable loss of the centenarian.

“On behalf of my family, the government and people of Lagos State, as well as my brother governors in the South-West, I commiserate with the Fasoranti family, Afenifere members and the entire people of Yorubaland over the departure of our respected leader and elder statesman, Pa Reuben Fasoranti.”

Bamidele: Fasoranti’s Death Robs Nigeria of a Patriot, Awoist

Leader of the Senate, Senator Opeyemi Bamidele, described the death of Pa Fasoranti as a monumental loss to Nigeria, saying the late elder statesman devoted his life to national development, progressive politics, and the pursuit of true federalism.

Bamidele, who expressed shock and sadness over the passing of the centenarian, said Fasoranti distinguished himself as a patriot and statesman who consistently placed the national interest above personal and sectional considerations.

In a condolence message, the senate leader said the late Afenifere chieftain left behind an enduring legacy of integrity, selflessness, and commitment to the unity and progress of Nigeria.

Describing him as a patriot par excellence, Bamidele said, “The late centenarian was a patriot par excellence, a statesman of uncommon integrity who consistently placed national interest far above personal or sectional considerations.

“As an educationist, school administrator and community leader, Baba Fasoranti impacted generations of Nigerians and left an indelible mark on our national development trajectory.”

World.title: CAS: Volatility, Contemporary Warfare Makes  Military to Build Relevant Doctrines
World.content:
Linus Aleke in Abuja

The Chief of the Air Staff (CAS), Air Marshal Sunday Kelvin Aneke, has said the volatility, uncertainty, complexity and ambiguity of contemporary warfare placed increasing demands on the military to develop relevant doctrines and innovative operational thinking to prepare personnel for complex security challenges.

He stressed that meeting these demands required not only capable aircraft and modern equipment but also sound doctrines, effective professional military education, informed operational planning and institutions capable of translating lessons from operations into improved combat effectiveness.

Speaking at the commissioning of new vehicles procured for the Air Warfare and Doctrine Centre (AWDC), the CAS commended the Commandant and the entire staff of the Centre for their continued efforts to advance the professional and intellectual capabilities of the Service.

Represented by the Chief of Logistics, Air Vice Marshal Henry Yurkusi, the CAS noted that the Air Warfare and Doctrine Centre occupied an important position in this process, adding: “The Centre’s responsibilities in doctrinal development, research and professional military education are central to our institutional growth.”

The CAS said the Centre’s output helped to shape how the Service understood air power, prepared its personnel and responded to emerging operational requirements.

“It is, therefore, important that the Centre has the necessary resources to support its activities and sustain the tempo required to fulfil its mandate. The vehicles being commissioned today represent a practical investment in that institutional capacity.

“Beyond their immediate transportation function, they will improve the Centre’s ability to coordinate official engagements, supervise activities, support training programmes and facilitate other institutional assignments.

“Their availability is expected to reduce mobility constraints and contribute to more efficient administration. While these vehicles may appear to be a modest addition to the Centre’s overall inventory, their value lies in how effectively they support the work the Centre was established to carry out.”

Air Marshal Aneke stressed that lessons emerging from operations must inform the development and review of doctrine, while training must remain responsive to the realities confronting aircrew and ground personnel.

“We must continually assess whether our concepts, procedures and institutional approaches adequately prepare the Service for present and future challenges.

“In this regard, I expect the Centre to sustain its efforts towards producing sound doctrinal products and competent personnel who can translate professional knowledge into operational advantage,” he concluded.

World.title: Oborevwori Visits Late Uduaghan’s Family, Otuaro, Omo-Agege, Mulade, Other Mourn
World.content:
Sylvester Idowu in Warri

Delta State Governor, Hon. Sheriff Oborevwori, yesterday, visited the family of former governor Emmanuel Eweta Uduaghan, to offer his condolences, following his death on Monday at the age of 71.

Oborevwori, who was accompanied by his wife, Deaconess Tobore Oborevwori, and top government functionaries, described the late Uduaghan as a great leader whose contributions to the development of Delta State would remain indelible.

The governor had earlier joined family members and other dignitaries, including Uduaghan’s daughter, Orode, and former President of the Nigeria Football Federation, Amaju Pinnick, to receive the former governor’s remains at Osubi Airport.

Speaking during the condolence visit to Uduaghan’s widow, Mrs Roli Uduaghan and family members, Oborevwori said the outpouring of grief and the large number of people, who gathered to mourn the former governor reflected the impact he had made on many lives.

He recalled his relationship with the deceased, describing him as his former boss and a man who played a significant role in his political journey.

“He was my boss. He gave me the highest political appointment, Special Adviser, in 2007. That is something that really touches my heart. You are all aware that he supported me throughout this journey,” the governor said.

Oborevwori described Uduaghan as a calm, articulate and thoughtful leader who made significant contributions to the development of the state.

According to him, the number of people who turned out to receive the late governor’s remains and those who visited his family was evidence of the lives he had touched through public service and political appointments.

The governor had earlier signed the condolence register, wrote: “I am saddened by the demise of the former Governor, Dr Emmanuel Eweta Uduaghan. He was a great boss. I commiserate with his beloved wife, children, family members and Deltans over this great loss.

“May God grant the family the fortitude to bear the loss. Your impact in Delta can never be forgotten. Asamaigor, RIP.”

Also, the immediate past deputy governor of Delta State, Dcn. Kingsley Burutu Otuaro, described the death of Uduaghan as a major loss to Delta State and the Niger Delta acknowledging his contributions to governance, peace and regional development.

Otuaro, in a condolence message, said the death of the former governor had robbed the state of an experienced statesman whose leadership and commitment to the wellbeing of the people would remain part of Delta State’s political history.

“Dr. Uduaghan was more than a former governor; he was a father, an elder, a gentleman and a leader whose humility, wisdom and commitment to peace and development touched many lives,” Otuaro said.

Also, a former Deputy President of the Senate, Senator Ovie Omo-Agege, has expressed profound shock over the death of Uduaghan.

In a condolence message personally signed, Senator Omo-Agege described Uduaghan’s death as a profound personal loss, recalling their days together in the James Ibori administration.

“This is a profound loss. We served together under our leader, Chief James Ibori. He was Secretary to the State Government and I was Executive Assistant to the Governor. I knew him as calm in a crisis, loyal, humane and decent. He brought a doctor’s compassion into government.

“Our political paths later diverged, but our respect for each other never did. He remained a brother across party lines: a gentleman, a bridge-builder and a man of peace”, he said.

Similarly, the National Democratic Party (NDP) Candidate for the house of representatives in Warri federal constituency, Chief Mulade Sheriff, in a tribute described the passing of Uduaghan as a monumental loss to the state, Niger Delta and Nigeria as whole.

Mulade described his passing as the fall of an Iroko, the exit of a political colossus, and a monumental loss to Delta State, the Itsekiri Nation, the Niger Delta and Nigeria at large.

The Delta Unity Group (DUG) has also expressed deep shock and profound sorrow on the passing of Uduaghan.

In a statement issued by its National Publicity Secretary, Sir Sunny Areh, the group stated that Dr. Uduaghan’s transition was not just the loss of a former governor but the exit of a unifier.

“For us in DUG, this is not just the loss of a former Governor; it is the exit of a unifier. Dr. Uduaghan was Delta in its truest essence: An Itsekiri by birth, Urhobo by adoption, Isoko by bond, Anioma by love and Ijaw by service. In a state often divided by ethnic fault lines, he lived and led as a bridge. He belonged to all of us, and all of us belonged to him.”

World.title: Transfer update: Ex-Orlando Pirates youth products could command €25 million fee
World.content:
Former Orlando Pirates youngsters Relebohile Mofokeng and Mbekezeli Mbokazi could be worth a combined €25 million in the coming transfer windows as interest in their services continues to grow.

Both players rose through the Buccaneers’ development structures before earning promotion to the senior team, where their performances attracted attention beyond South Africa.

Mofokeng joined the Pirates first team in 2023 and went on to make more than 100 appearances, scoring 29 goals.



His impressive performances earned him three major individual honours at the PSL Awards last season: Players’ Player of the Season, Footballer of the Season and Young Player of the Season.

His progress subsequently earned him a move to Belgian club Union Saint-Gilloise, where he has continued to attract attention.

The 21-year-old is reportedly valued at around €6 million and has been linked with clubs in France and Germany, as reported by Siseko Gwegwe.



His performance has raised the possibility of another move as early as next year. He has enjoyed life at Union and scored on his debut match in the UEFA Europa League.

Orlando Pirates ex-players shining overseas

Mbokazi, meanwhile, joined Pirates’ youth structures in 2024 before being promoted to the senior team in 2025. After making a strong impression during his time with the Buccaneers, the defender secured a move to Major League Soccer side Chicago Fire.

The Bafana Bafana international has continued to attract attention in the United States, with his performances reportedly putting him on the radar of several European clubs.



Mbokazi is currently valued at around €8 million, but that figure could rise to at least €15 million in the next transfer window if interest in the defender translates into concrete offers.

Should the reported valuations materialise, the two former Pirates players could command a combined transfer fee of approximately €25 million.

For Orlando Pirates, the rise of Mofokeng and Mbokazi underlines the potential value of developing young talent, with both players now building careers abroad after progressing through the club’s youth system.

World.title: The Eastern Cape’s Afrikaans communities are battling crime
World.content:
Many Eastern Cape Afrikaans communities have been sheltered from crime.

However, as reported by The South African, Jeffrey’s Bay, a town with a large Afrikaans population, saw crime increase by 64.1% in three months.

The increase in crime isn’t limited to Jeffrey’s Bay in the Sarah Baartman District Municipality.



Across multiple police precincts, crime in Afrikaans communities has slowly risen in the first quarter.

Crime is hurting these underreported communities

Small-town crime is rarely reported in South Africa until something tragic happens.

But these tragic events aren’t isolated.

Instead, they form part of a larger pattern of rising crime.

In Humansdorp, where 90% of the population speaks Afrikaans, drug-related crime has been rapidly increasing.

Overall, crime in Humansdorp is down from its 2024 peak. In the first quarter, crime in Humansdorp dropped 2.1%.



Yet, drug-related crime hasn’t decreased.

Instead, it rose 18.7% in the first quarter compared to the same time last year.

Drug-Related Crime in Sarah Baartman District Municipality

The Sarah Baartman District Municipality is also the second-highest contributor to drug-related crime in the Eastern Cape, only beaten by Nelson Mandela Bay.

Drug-related crime is a precursor to violent crimes, thefts, burglaries, and murders.

Jeffrey’s Bay, where crime is up 64.1% in the first quarter, had an increase of 39.3% in drug-related crime; the most of any Eastern Cape police precinct.

Humansdorp also reported 3 murders, though this is a decrease from the 4 murders reported over the same period last year.

Likewise in Patensie, where 70% of the population speaks Afrikaans, crime is up 12.1% in the first quarter.

Patensie has one quarter of Humansdorp’s population, but reports about one third of the crime.

The most commonly reported crime in Patensie is theft, followed by serious assault. Drug-related crime doesn’t feature as prominently in the South African Police Service (SAPS) data.

Yet, it is slowly rising, according to the most recent quarter’s data.

The community of 8 547 people also reported one murder.

In Pearston, a town of 5 165 people, drug-related crime is up, and so is murder.

In Willowmore, drug-related crime is also slowly rising, as is the case in Stormsrivier.

Then in Kareedouw, where 73% of residents speak Afrikaans as their first language, crime remains unchanged.

But annual reporting shows crime in the police precinct is up 11.8%.

Theft and common assault saw the highest increase.

In 2025, crime in Kareedouw reached its highest level since SAPS started sharing crime statistics.

Hankey, Kliplaat, Paterson, and Steytlerville have all been impacted by a rise in crime in the first quarter.

But this crime data is only a snapshot of this year’s statistics. The second quarter will reveal if these are one-off spikes or part of a worrying trend.

It’s not all bad news for the Eastern Cape’s Afrikaans communities

In Wolwefontein, a town with a population of 1 358, only 2 crimes were reported in the first quarter.

The same is true for Baviaanskloof, another police precinct reporting single-digit crime in the first quarter.

In Jansenville, crime dropped 5.6% in the first quarter.

These communities spotlight how crime doesn’t have to overtake smaller communities.

World.title: Bomb scare at Eastern Cape airport prompts emergency response
World.content:
Police have activated a multidisciplinary response team following a bomb threat at King Phalo International Airport in KuGompo City in the Eastern Cape.

Police spokesperson Brigadier Nobuntu Gantana said officers received an anonymous call alleging that a bomb was on board FlySafair flight FA388 that had landed at the airport from Johannesburg.

All 182 passengers and six crew members safely disembarked from the aircraft, with authorities now managing the scene and investigating the origin of the threat.



Bomb disposal unit and K9 dogs deployed

Gantana confirmed that a multidisciplinary response team had been activated and was at the airport.

The response includes the Bomb Disposal Unit, K9 explosive detection dogs, hostage negotiators, Disaster Management, Airport Security and Emergency Medical Services.

“The scene is being managed by the relevant authorities, and investigations into the origin of the threat are ongoing. No further information is available at this stage,” Gantana said.

Investigation underway

Police have not provided further details about the aircraft, the nature of the alleged threat or whether any suspicious items have been found.

The investigation into the anonymous call is continuing.

Authorities have yet to release additional information about the incident or indicate when normal operations at the airport will resume.



Full FlySafair statement

FlySafair confirms that it was informed of a potential security threat relating to flight FA388, operating from Johannesburg to East London this morning, with 182 passengers and 6 crew on board.

The aircraft continued its journey and landed safely at King Phalo Airport at 08:49. All passengers have since safely disembarked.

All relevant authorities were informed immediately, and we are cooperating fully with them. As confirmed in the media statement issued by the Office of the SAPS Provincial Commissioner, Eastern Cape, a multi-disciplinary response team is on site, and the aircraft is being held as part of standard security protocols. The scene is being managed by the authorities, with the support of King Phalo Airport.

There have been no flight cancellations as a result of this incident, and all other FlySafair operations are running as normal.

We thank our crew and ground staff for managing the situation calmly and in line with established safety and security procedures. We also apologise for any inconvenience caused and thank our passengers for their patience and understanding.

We extend our sincere thanks to the South African Police Service, King Phalo Airport and all the emergency and security teams on site for their swift and professional response.

As this is an active investigation, we are unable to comment further at this stage. Enquiries relating to the investigation should be directed to SAPS: Brigadier Nobuntu Gantana, 082 337 9402.

The safety of our passengers and crew remains our highest priority.
