World.title: NSFAS 2027 applications near 870 000. The clock is ticking
World.content:
NSFAS has received more than 868,000 applications for 2027 funding, with the deadline on 31 October. Image: Pexels

National Student Financial Aid Scheme (NSFAS) 2027 applications are closing in on 870,000.

And there are just days left to apply.

NSFAS says it won’t extend the deadline.

So if you’re planning to study in 2027 and need funding, now’s the time to act.



NSFAS has received 868,626 applications for the 2027 funding cycle, according to its latest application dashboard, dated 19 October.

In a media release on Tuesday, 20 October, the scheme urged students who haven’t yet applied to do so before the deadline.

WHEN DO NSFAS 2027 APPLICATIONS CLOSE?

Applications close at 23:59 on Saturday, 31 October 2026.



There will be no extension. The NSFAS board has already confirmed this.

HOW TO APPLY

NSFAS spokesperson Ishmael Mnisi said applications can be submitted through the official NSFAS website, or the scheme’s official mobile app.

He urged applicants to make sure all their supporting documents are submitted correctly, and that consent forms are completed where required, to help NSFAS verify their applications.



HOW MANY PEOPLE HAVE APPLIED?

Demand has been strong since applications opened on 18 September.

NSFAS received 51,474 applications in the first four days alone.

By 19 October, that figure had grown to more than 868,000.



WHO QUALIFIES?

NSFAS funds qualifying students at public universities and technical and vocational education and training (TVET) colleges.

Applicants generally need a combined gross household income of R350,000 or less a year, or R600,000 or less for applicants with disabilities.

BEWARE OF NSFAS SCAMS

Applying for NSFAS is free.



Never pay anyone to apply on your behalf, and never share your myNSFAS password or one-time PIN (OTP).

You can report NSFAS scams to the Vuvuzela fraud hotline on 0860 247 653.

World.title: Orlando Pirates v African Stars: Date, kickoff time, permutation, predicted starting XI
World.content:
Orlando Pirates will host Namibian champions African Stars on Friday evening as they look to secure their place in the CAF Champions League group stage.

The Buccaneers head into the second leg of the preliminary round with a 1-0 advantage after winning the first leg in Botswana last weekend.

Abdeslam Ouaddou’s side will be determined to finish the job on home soil after suffering an early elimination in the same stage of the competition last season.



Pirates need just a win or a draw to progress to the next round. However, a defeat by a single goal could force the tie into a penalty shootout, depending on the final aggregate score, while losing by two or more goals would see the Buccaneers eliminated.

A potential penalty shootout could present another challenge for the Soweto giants, given their history in penalty shootouts in continental competition.

Having not played a midweek fixture, Pirates have had additional time to prepare for the encounter. The break has also provided an opportunity for injured players to recover ahead of a crucial assignment.



When Are Orlando Pirates Playing African Stars?

The Buccaneers will welcome African Stars to the Orlando Amstel Arena on Friday, 23 October, with kick-off scheduled for 20:00.

Ouaddou is expected to select a strong starting XI as Pirates look to avoid another disappointing early exit from Africa’s premier club competition.

Progressing to the group stage would be an important step for the Buccaneers and could also ease the pressure on the team following last season’s elimination.



Orlando Pirates Predicted Starting XI

Sipho Chaine; Ghampani Lungu, Lebone Seema, Nkosinathi Sibisi, Deon Hotto; Thapelo Mokobodi, Mthetheli Mthiyane; Simphiwe Masilela, Oswin Appollis, Mohau Nkota; Boitumelo Radiopane.

Ouaddou could opt for an attacking approach, with Pirates looking to build on their first-leg advantage and secure qualification in front of their home supporters.

World.title: Buffel the elephant seal spotted at Duiker Island – PHOTO
World.content:
Cape Town’s famous southern elephant seal Buffel has been spotted at Duiker Island looking healthy after concerns about his condition. Image: Image: Jean Tresfon / Facebook

Look up over the Western Cape coastline and you’ll likely spot marine conservation photographer Jean Tresfon flying overhead in his trusty gyrocopter.

For several years, Tresfon has been taking to the skies to capture spectacular aerial photographs of South Africa’s coastline and marine environment, sharing his work with a growing audience on social media.

If you’re not already one of his nearly 76 000 Facebook followers, we strongly suggest you click the ‘follow’ button now.



PICTURES | Is this the BIGGEST great white shark ever spotted in SA waters?

Much-loved

On his most recent excursion, Tresfon photographed Buffel, the much-loved southern elephant seal.

Well-known to Cape Town’s marine community, he was spotted at Duiker Island looking healthy, plump and seemingly in good spirits.



His latest appearance is welcome news after concerns were raised when he recently turned up at Cape Point for his annual moult in poor condition.

At the time, his appearance sparked fears for his wellbeing.

Now, Buffel appears to be doing much better, with his latest sighting offering encouraging news for those who have followed his journey over the years.



Described affectionately as a “blubber submarine”, Buffel was spotted looking fat and healthy.

Buffel’s remarkable journey

Buffel was first tagged in 2016, when he was estimated to be around three years old. That makes him approximately 13 years old today.

Southern elephant seals are among the largest seals in the world, with males capable of growing to enormous sizes. Their lives at sea are punctuated by periods on land, including the annual moult, when they shed their old fur and grow a new coat.



During this process, their appearance can sometimes cause concern among observers, particularly when they look thin or unwell.

A Cape Town marine celebrity

Over the years, Buffel has become something of a celebrity in Cape Town’s marine scene, attracting attention whenever he appears along the coastline.

His latest visit to Duiker Island is likely to be welcomed by the many people who have come to recognise him and follow his movements.



Southern elephant seals typically live for around 14 to 15 years in the wild, although lifespans can vary. At approximately 13, Buffel is an older animal, making his apparent good condition particularly encouraging.

While a sighting alone cannot confirm an animal’s overall health, seeing Buffel looking so well is certainly positive news after the concerns surrounding his previous appearance.

For now, the giant seal appears to be enjoying life – and Cape Town’s marine watchers will be hoping to see plenty more of their favourite blubber submarine.



Picture published with the permission of Jean Tresfon

World.title: KwaThema woman arrested for allegedly staging her own kidnapping
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - A 37-year-old Kwa-Thema woman who was allegedly kidnapped and rescued has been arrested for staging her own kidnapping.

The woman was arrested on Tuesday along with an accomplice.

Investigations revealed that the woman conspired with her accomplice to stage the kidnapping. This was in order to extort money from her cousin.

The duo are expected to appear before court on charges of defeating the ends of justice, extortion and staging a crime scene.

Police spokesperson Colonel Dimakatso Nevhuhulwi says the public are warmed against making false reports or staging criminal incidents.

"These divert critical police resource from genuine cases and undermines efforts to combat crime and protect communities," she says.

World.title: 'Leave us alone!' DC golfers fear worst over Trump's course remodel
World.content:
WASHINGTON - For years, Max Salas has enjoyed teeing off at Washington's East Potomac Golf Links, a public course nestled in the heart of the US capital where ordinary Americans can enjoy a round without breaking the bank.

But President Donald Trump's controversial plans to remodel the course into a facility capable of hosting major championship- caliber events have left the 74-year-old retiree exasperated.

"Leave us alone! Leave us alone!" Salas told AFP when asked what message he would send to Trump.

"What the hell do we need a championship course in a public course?" he said. "We're here, we've been here for years, and it's ridiculous."

Salas is among golfers worried that Trump's proposed overhaul of East Potomac could transform an affordable public amenity into an expensive destination beyond the reach of its regular players.

At the moment, 18 holes at East Potomac costs a maximum of $48.

That's a far cry from the kind of rates often found at privately owned golf courses -- such as those owned by Trump -- where green fees can often run into hundreds of dollars.

Trump, a famously avid golfer, has claimed that East Potomac is not fit for purpose.

World.title: 'To the shelter, quickly!' Air raids reshape Kyiv school life
World.content:
KYIV - When the air raid alert sounded over the Kyiv region, children knew exactly what to do: they grabbed their tiny backpacks and ran towards the shelter, abandoning bikes, toys and even a doll on the school playground.

Teachers scooped up the stragglers and ushered them into the shelter's entrance, while the cleaner scanned the playground, muttering as she checked that no one had been left behind.

"Everyone to the shelter, quickly, quickly, quickly!" said Valentyna Kurinna, director of the UMKA primary school in Kyiv's suburbs.

The risks weighed heavily on everyone's minds.

Just a few days earlier, a drone slammed into the same playground, narrowly missing a grandfather who stayed outside while the children had taken cover underground.

Security camera footage obtained by AFP showed him looking at the sky and running away just a few seconds before the explosion unleashed a huge ball of fire that burned the multicoloured playground.

World.title: Musk backs SpaceX-Tesla merger as rocket firm turns profit
World.content:
NEW YORK - Elon Musk said he would back a merger of SpaceX and Tesla, as his rocket and AI company reported its first quarterly profit since going public, driven by deals to rent out computing power to AI firms.

Asked about a possible tie-up on a call with analysts, Musk said he felt he was "tap dancing through a minefield," but that a combination would be "a good idea."

Shares in SpaceX shot up nearly five percent in after-hours trading following the comments.

Musk said special committees of independent directors at both SpaceX and Tesla have been set up to study the idea at the request of shareholders.

He added that he could not take part in their talks because he has a conflict of interest.

Musk is chief executive of both companies, and also serves as chairman and chief technology officer of SpaceX.

He owned 48.4 percent of SpaceX as of June 30, according to a regulatory filing, and controls more than 82 percent of its voting power through super-voting shares.

He holds about 20 percent of Tesla.

The committees have not agreed on the terms of any deal and there is no guarantee they will, Musk said, cautioning that it would be overstating it to treat a merger as a certainty.

Any deal would need the backing of a majority of all Tesla shares, not just those cast in a vote, which Musk called "quite a high hurdle."

He said the two companies could gain from working together on AI software, chip design, robotics and space-based computing.

His remarks came after SpaceX posted net income of $4.4 billion for the July-September period, compared with a loss of $1.1 billion a year earlier.

Revenue jumped 161 percent to $14.6 billion. The quarterly results follow a bumpy start on Wall Street.

SpaceX began trading on the Nasdaq on June 12 after an IPO priced at $135 a share that raised about $85.7 billion.

Its first earnings report as a listed company showed second-quarter revenue of $7.8 billion and a net loss of $541 million.

The AI division, which SpaceX now calls "Super Intelligence," drove the turnaround. Super Intelligence is US President Donald Trump's preferred term for AI.

The unit's revenue rose more than nine times from a year earlier to $7.6 billion, overtaking the Starlink satellite internet business as the company's largest source of sales.

- Cloud computing -

SpaceX credited new cloud services agreements, wider adoption of its Grok chatbot and its acquisition of Cursor, an artificial intelligence coding startup.

SpaceX’s cloud customers include Anthropic, which agreed in May to pay nearly $45 billion over three years for computing power at SpaceX's Colossus data centres.

Google signed on in June, agreeing to pay $920 million a month from October through June 2029.

The AI unit turned an operating profit of $431 million, compared with a loss of $1.7 billion a year earlier.

As with other AI companies, spending remains heavy.

SpaceX invested $19.6 billion in the quarter, $16.4 billion of it in AI, bringing capital spending for the first nine months of the year to $48 billion.

Its computing capacity reached 1.7 gigawatts, up from 0.6 gigawatts a year earlier.

Musk said he was "fairly confident" SpaceX could bring an additional 10 gigawatts of computing capacity online in 2027.

That would come on top of the roughly 2.5 to 3.0 gigawatts it expects to have running by the end of this year.

He added that power, cooling and electrical equipment were "somewhat of a limiting factor."

Revenue at the Starlink satellite internet unit grew 69 percent to $5.2 billion, and consumer subscribers reached 13.6 million.

Average monthly revenue per consumer, however, fell to $69 from $83 a year earlier.

SpaceX also completed the first revenue-generating flight of Starship, the giant rocket central to Musk's Mars ambitions and to deploying satellites at scale.

The flight carried 26 next-generation Starlink satellites into orbit.

World.title: Bomb threat at King Phalo International Airport
World.content:
KUGOMPO CITY - Police have responded to a bomb threat at the King Phalo International Airport in KuGompo City in the Eastern Cape.

Provincial police have said a caller, using an unknown number, alleged that there was a bomb inside an aircraft that landed at the airport.

The aircraft is being held at the airport as part of standard security protocols. All 184 passengers on board have safely gotten off the flight.

A multidisciplinary response team, including the bomb disposal unit, K9 explosive detection dogs, hostage negotiators, disaster management, airport security and emergency medical services, is at the scene.

Police spokesperson Brigadier Nobantu Gantana says they are investigating the origin of the threat.

They are also urging the public not to speculate on the matter.

World.title: Joburg Zoo to keep its elephants after activists demanded their removal
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The High Court in Johannesburg has ruled that Lammie, Ramadiba and Mopane can remain at the Johannesburg Zoo under an extended permit.

Animal Law Reform and the EMS Foundation had sought to have the elephants removed and relocated to a sanctuary. However, their application was dismissed.

They argued that the elephants were housed in conditions that neglected their physical, emotional and social needs.

Joburg City Parks and Zoo says that they have caregivers and a veterinary team that closely monitor the elephants, and they are doing well.

World.title: AKA murder trial hears surveillance analyst was threatened
World.content:
DURBAN - A surveillance analyst has told the Durban High Court that he received threats after testifying in the trial into the murders of Kiernan “AKA” Forbes and Tebello “Tibz” Motsoane.

On Monday, CCTV footage from King Shaka International Airport was played in court. It showed a man believed to be one of the accused following Forbes and his entourage after they arrived in Durban.

The man appeared to maintain a safe distance from the group while seemingly speaking on his phone.

Forbes and Motsoane were killed on the same day.

Seven men are on trial for their murders. They have pleaded not guilty to charges that include murder, attempted murder and unlawful possession of firearms.

A ballistics expert has also linked bullet casings recovered from two separate shootings to the same firearm.

The State is seeking to establish whether firearms allegedly used in the killings are linked to other cases.

World.title: PSG late show downs Barca in Champions League, Liverpool fight back
World.content:
PARIS - Holders Paris Saint-Germain made it three wins from three in this season's Champions League, beating Barcelona 4-2 thanks to late goals from Vitinha and Fabian Ruiz on Tuesday, while Liverpool clinched a dramatic comeback victory over Villarreal.

Phil Foden scored a hat-trick as Manchester City thrashed AEK Athens 5-1, while there were also much-needed wins for Roma and Napoli.

PSG kept their place at the top of the league-phase table, but could yet count the cost of injuries suffered by Ousmane Dembele, Marquinhos and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia at the Parc des Princes.

"We don't feel superior to any team but we trust in ourselves, in everyone who starts and who comes off the bench," Paris midfielder Ruiz told Movistar. "There's still a long way to go."

Barcelona twice levelled against the two-time defending champions, but were ultimately well beaten as they slipped to their first defeat of the season.

"We tried to play how we want to play, we pressed them very high. There were a lot of fantastic things on show today," said Flick, whose team had won their previous 11 games in all competitions this term.

Kvaratskhelia hit the post, Dembele hobbled off and Ferran Torres was denied by Barca goalkeeper Joan Garcia in a fast-paced opening.

PSG took a deserved lead in the 38th minute as Desire Doue collected the ball outside the area and thumped a shot into the bottom corner.

Garcia made another excellent save shortly after the break from Achraf Hakimi, before Xavi Espart burst through to level for Barca against the run of play.

Kvaratskhelia and Marquinhos both pulled up injured within seconds of each other and had to leave the field.

The home team continued to press, though, and Lucas Hernandez restored their advantage 18 minutes from time with a brilliant header.

Lamine Yamal powered past Warren Zaire-Emery to equalise again seven minutes later.

But Vitinha hammered home from outside the box in the 81st minute and Ruiz's tap-in gave Luis Enrique's team a second straight 4-2 Champions League win after seeing off Man City by the same scoreline last week.

- Liverpool fight back -

World.title: From Babu to Sakaja, Aladwa and Winnie Odinga: Nairobi race crowded ahead of 2027
World.content:
Babu Owino, Johnson Sakaja and George Aladwa are among the leaders eyeing Nairobi’s gubernatorial seat ahead of the 2027 General Election. [Courtesy, Standard]

The contests for Nairobi’s Gubernatorial and Senatorial seats are gaining momentum, with three political outfits now gearing up for what promises to be a bare-knuckle fight for the control of the capital.

With less than a year to the high-stakes 2027 elections, the two seats have attracted a crowded field from across the political divide, even as political camps continue to mobilise their machinery to capture the city’s vast voter blocs.

World.title: Judge certifies fresh bid to jail Sakaja, Charles Kerich over Sh76.7m debt as urgent
World.content:
Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja. [File, Standard]

The High Court has certified as urgent a fresh application seeking to have Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja, former Finance Executive Charles Kerich and two other county officials jailed over an alleged breach of a court-approved payment plan in a Sh106.7 million legal fees dispute.

Justice Francis Gikonyo certified the application by Kwengu & Company Advocates seeking to reinstate a three-month jail sentence previously imposed on Kerich and hold Sakaja, current Finance County Executive Committee Member Ibrahim Auma Nyangoya and Chief Officer for Finance Asha Abdi accountable for the alleged failure to pay Sh76.7 million.

World.title: Kenya confirms third Ebola case
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kenya has confirmed a third case of Ebola involving a 65-year-old woman who is a close relative of the first two patients.

The Ministry of Health, in a statement, said the woman developed a fever, sore throat and malaise while in quarantine, prompting her isolation and testing.

Her samples tested positive for Ebola at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI).

According to the Health Director-General Patrick Amoth, the patient has been transferred to an infectious disease unit, where she is receiving supportive care and being monitored.

“Having been in quarantine, she was diagnosed early and is currently receiving supportive care, improving her chances of recovery while limiting the risk of further spread of the disease,” the statement read.

The second patient, on the other hand, is in stable condition and responding well to supportive care.

The latest case brings the number of confirmed Ebola infections in Kenya to three.

According to the Ministry, of the 130 contacts identified so far, 127 had been traced and placed in quarantine, with efforts ongoing to trace the remaining three.

World.title: Motorists, households face fresh fuel price hikes
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

EPRA attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East. [FIle, Standard]

The Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) has increased fuel prices, raising the cost of super petrol by Sh12.93 per litre, diesel by Sh9.90, and kerosene by Sh28.49.

The new prices, effective from October 15 to November 14, 2026, will see motorists in Nairobi pay up to Sh226.96 per litre for super petrol, Sh227.76 for diesel, and Sh219.85 for kerosene.

EPRA Director-General Edward Mwirigi Kinyua attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East, which has disrupted petroleum supply chains and driven up the cost of importing fuel.

The rise in kerosene prices is likely to hit low-income households that rely on the fuel for cooking and lighting.

Meanwhile, higher diesel prices could raise the cost of transporting goods and operating public service vehicles, potentially driving up fares and commodity prices.

Diesel is a key fuel for the country's freight transport sector and a significant portion of public service vehicle operations, meaning the increase could have a ripple effect across the economy.

The latest review comes after EPRA maintained pump prices during the September 15 to October 14 pricing period, despite a decline in the cost of importing petrol.

World.title: Oburu Oginga to leave hospital soon - ODM
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

ODM SG Catherine Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician.

ODM Secretary General Catherine Omanyo has dismissed social media reports about the health of party leader Oburu Oginga, saying he is recovering well and is expected to be discharged from hospital either today or tomorrow.

Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician, accusing them of exploiting his health condition to attract online attention and increase engagement.

“It's unfortunate what I've been reading on social media. Those people who are seeking to have more likes or viewers, they will be disappointed because he's up, he's well, he's fine. In fact, he's headed home either today or tomorrow,” she said.

Omanyo insisted that the reports had exaggerated his situation, dismissing claims of his death and assuring the public that he was doing well.

She noted that health conditions could fluctuate, saying Oburu's position as ODM party leader had made his well-being a subject of heightened public interest.

“Everybody, everybody, including you and me, our health is not static. You can be under the weather any time. It's just that he's a party leader, and it makes breaking news,” Omanyo said.

She urged social media users to exercise restraint when discussing the health of public figures, warning against spreading unverified reports, particularly claims of death, before confirmation from credible sources.

Her remarks come amid growing speculation on social media about Oburu's health, with some users circulating unverified claims about his condition.

World.title: Kenya declares Ebola a formidable epidemic disease, sets new rules
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, who declared Ebola caused by the Bundibugyo virus a formidable epidemic disease under the Public Health Act. [File,Standard]

Kenya has declared Ebola virus a formidable epidemic disease, introducing new rules governing screening, isolation, quarantine, contact tracing and the handling of bodies.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale issued the declaration through a legal notice published in the Kenya Gazette on Monday, October 12, under Section 35 of the Public Health Act.

The declaration follows Kenya’s confirmation of its first imported case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease on October 6, after a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo travelled through Uganda to Nairobi. The patient died despite receiving supportive treatment.

The case prompted health authorities to trace people who may have come into contact with the patient and strengthen screening at points of entry.

In an update on October 12, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Kenya had listed 127 contacts, with 94 in quarantine, and screened more than 665,000 travellers at points of entry.

WHO also supplied protective equipment and testing materials worth about US$70,000 to support the response.

The government published two legal notices on October 12. Legal Notice No. 203 declares the disease a formidable epidemic, while Legal Notice No. 204 establishes the Public Health (Ebola Disease) Rules, 2026.

The regulations provide for screening at points of entry, medical assessment, isolation, referral, quarantine and monitoring.

They also assign responsibilities to transport operators, health facilities, medical practitioners and laboratories.

Health authorities will conduct investigations and contact tracing, while designated health facilities will manage suspected and confirmed cases. The rules also provide for the inspection and decontamination of premises.

The regulations cover the safe and dignified disposal of bodies, burial procedures, record-keeping, transportation and repatriation. They also address public communication, media houses’ responsibilities in public sensitisation and assistance from enforcement agencies.

The rules provide for offences and penalties, although the Gazette extract does not specify the penalties for individual violations.

What the declaration means

Bundibugyo virus disease is a form of Ebola that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person or contaminated materials.

Contact with the body of someone who has died from the disease can also expose people to infection during unsafe burial practices.

Symptoms can include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache and sore throat, followed by vomiting and diarrhoea. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days.

WHO says no approved vaccine or specific treatment currently exists for the Bundibugyo strain, making early detection, isolation, supportive care and contact tracing central to controlling its spread.

The health agency has advised against travel or trade restrictions on Kenya, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo based on the information available.

The new rules establish a legal framework for managing the disease, from identifying suspected infections and monitoring contacts to caring for patients and preventing exposure during burials.

World.title: Agriculture Minister: “Egypt Forum” showcases state’s vision for next 3 years with participation of all segments of society
World.content:
Minister of Agriculture and Land Reclamation Alaa Farouk emphasized the importance of the “Egypt 2026 Forum” in showcasing the Egyptian state’s vision for the next three years, noting that the forum witnesses wide participation from various segments of society, political parties and decision-makers.

In a statement on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, Farouk stated that the forum reflects the Egyptian state’s keenness on societal participation and opening spaces between the government, the people, experts and specialists regarding public policies, national projects and development programs implemented over past years and their impact on improving citizens’ lives.

He added that the file of food security and rural development comes at the forefront of the Egyptian state’s priorities, contributing to turning challenges into promising opportunities.

He pointed out that the Egyptian state has adopted an integrated reform and executive path that balances giant horizontal expansion for land reclamation with vertical expansion based on scientific research and digital transformation, aiming to maximize added value, achieve self-sufficiency, narrow the import gap and provide safe food for citizens at affordable prices.

Farouk explained that the agricultural sector witnessed a radical transformation driven by the state’s vision towards horizontal land reclamation and the rational management of water resources.

The state implemented a package of the largest land reclamation projects in its history, which increased the agricultural area and doubled production. These include the New Delta project with an area of 2.2 million feddans, the Toshka project with an area of 1.1 million feddans, the North and Central Sinai Development project covering about 456,000 feddans, the New Egyptian Rural Development project spanning 1.5 million feddans, and projects in South Upper Egypt and the New Valley covering 650,000 feddans, he said.

Farouk noted that the state has taken numerous proactive measures to support urban development, particularly the agricultural sector, to secure the food and agricultural product needs of the great people of Egypt during periods when many countries—including developed ones—failed to achieve this goal and some even imposed restrictive policies on their agricultural exports.

He stressed that at a time when the world was losing millions of hectares annually due to desertification, soil degradation, drought and unfavorable climate change, the Egyptian state managed to add more agricultural land through reclaiming over 3.5 million feddans of desert.

World.title: Egypt seeks to accelerate oil, gas investments
World.content:
Minister of Petroleum and Mineral Resources Karim Badawi met with Cypriot Energy Minister Michael Damianos, East Mediterranean Gas Forum Secretary-General Osama Mobarez and executives of international oil and gas companies operating in Egypt to discuss ways to accelerate investment and increase production.

The meeting took place during a roundtable titled “The Future of Energy in Egypt,” held on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, as part of the Mediterranean Offshore Conference and Exhibition (MOC).

Discussions focused on accelerating the development of discoveries and connecting them to existing infrastructure, maximizing the economic returns from oil and gas resources, strengthening regional cooperation and consolidating Egypt’s position as a regional hub for energy trading and trade.

Badawi said partnerships with investors were based on mutual interests, stressing that the success of companies operating in Egypt translates into success for the country’s oil and gas sector and the Egyptian state.

He affirmed the ministry’s commitment to addressing challenges facing its partners and providing the necessary conditions for expanding investments to generate sustainable economic returns for all parties.

The minister said declining production had been one of the sector’s most significant challenges, requiring efforts to stimulate investment, accelerate exploration and development activities and improve operational efficiency. He stressed that the ministry was focused on strengthening cooperation with partners, addressing factors affecting production and establishing more sustainable foundations for growth in the coming years.

Badawi added that the current phase required more effective partnerships through direct dialogue with companies to identify their needs and proposals, determine measures to accelerate investment decisions and project implementation and enhance the competitiveness of investment in Egypt’s oil and gas sector.

He also highlighted the importance of regional cooperation among Eastern Mediterranean countries and leveraging available resources and existing infrastructure to generate greater economic value from discovered gas reserves and support the development of new resources.

Egypt has significant advantages that position it to play an increasingly central role in the regional energy system, Badawi said, citing its advanced natural gas infrastructure, transportation networks, gas reception and trading facilities and liquefaction capabilities, as well as its strategic location linking production areas with consumer markets.

The ministry is looking to work with its partners to maximize the economic benefits of these assets and facilities, reducing project costs, improving efficiency and enhancing investment viability, he added.

For his part, Mobarez said Egypt’s energy future was closely linked to the future of regional cooperation, given the Eastern Mediterranean’s discovered natural gas resources and promising potential, which require increased investment and the development of infrastructure to unlock their value.

The main challenge, he said, lies in accessing these resources and converting them into sustainable economic value by developing viable projects, accelerating the development of discoveries and connecting them to target markets.

Achieving this requires clear regulatory frameworks and investment-friendly policies that enable the private sector to play an effective role in financing and implementing projects, as well as developing the infrastructure needed to transport gas to markets, Mobarez said.

He added that the East Mediterranean Gas Forum works to strengthen cooperation among governments, oil and gas companies, technology and services providers, financial institutions and regulatory authorities. Its efforts aim to identify priority projects, attract further investment and accelerate the implementation of infrastructure needed to maximize the use of the region’s resources.

Company executives and international partners said Egypt had significant competitive advantages that strengthened its ability to attract investment and reinforced its role in the regional energy sector. These included advanced infrastructure, transportation networks and gas facilities, its strategic geographical location, accumulated technical and technological expertise and the availability of data to support exploration activities and investment decisions.

Participants said these advantages offered promising opportunities to accelerate project implementation and maximize the use of resources in Egypt and the Eastern Mediterranean. They emphasized the importance of continuing to develop government-investor partnerships based on transparency, mutual trust and shared interests.

They also said the settlement of outstanding dues owed to companies had helped strengthen confidence in Egypt’s oil and gas investment climate and encouraged new investments to accelerate the development of discoveries and connect them to the national grid as quickly as possible, boosting production and maximizing economic returns.

Sustaining investment flows, participants stressed, requires a stable and predictable investment environment, clear and flexible regulatory frameworks, and long-term partnerships between the government and private sector. Such conditions would help companies make investment decisions more quickly and ensure projects are implemented according to target schedules.

They further noted that the true value of resources lies not merely in discovering them, but in the sector’s ability to develop, produce and market them efficiently. This requires flexible and innovative business models and the adoption of advanced technologies and artificial intelligence tools to improve operational efficiency, reduce costs and accelerate exploration, development and production.

The discussions underscored the importance of greater integration and cooperation among Eastern Mediterranean countries and companies operating in the region, alongside the development of regulatory and commercial frameworks and coordinated efforts to develop resources, provide infrastructure, transport gas and connect supplies to markets. These measures would support energy security, optimize the economic use of resources and strengthen prospects for sustainable development across the region.

The Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources said the roundtable reflected its commitment to deepening direct dialogue with investment partners and identifying practical solutions to the challenges facing the sector. The efforts aim to increase investment, accelerate resource development, raise production levels, maximize the use of Egypt’s infrastructure and consolidate the country’s position as a regional hub for energy trading and trade.

World.title: Egyptian Navy celebrates 59th anniversary commemorating sinking “Eilat” destroyer
World.content:
The Egyptian Navy celebrated its 59th anniversary, commemorating October 21, 1967, the day Egyptian naval forces changed the concepts of naval warfare worldwide by successfully sinking the Israeli destroyer Eilat off the coast of the city of Port Said.

Speaking at a press conference on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, held to mark the occasion, Commander of the Egyptian Navy Lieutenant General Mahmoud Adel Fawzy affirmed that this historic anniversary serves as an inspiration and a driving force for building the future.

He noted that the Navy continues to implement its development and modernization plans in accordance with the strategic vision of the political leadership and the General Command of the Armed Forces. These efforts aim to strengthen combat capabilities, localize armament and naval shipbuilding and enhance the training and qualification of combat personnel, enabling the Navy to carry out all missions assigned to it across the country’s various strategic directions.

World.title: Greek Ambassador: Egypt-Greece ties offer strong foundation for partnership
World.content:
Greek Ambassador to Egypt Nikolaos Papageorgiou said Egyptian-Greek relations represent an advanced model of strategic partnership rooted in a deep historical and civilizational legacy and longstanding human and cultural ties.

He added that relations between the two countries continue to develop, reflecting their commitment to expanding bilateral cooperation in ways that serve the interests of both peoples and support regional stability.

In exclusive remarks on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, to the Middle East News Agency (MENA) on the sidelines of the Mediterranean Offshore Conference and Exhibition at the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, Papageorgiou said ties between Cairo and Athens were built on solid historical and human foundations that had acquired renewed strategic significance over the centuries, establishing a strong basis for understanding and coordination across various fields.

He stressed that the challenges and transformations facing the region underscore the importance of partnerships built on mutual trust, shared interests and a long-term vision.

The ambassador said sustained communication, exchanges of visits and delegations, and growing political, economic and cultural cooperation reflected the vitality of bilateral relations and their ability to adapt to regional and international developments.

Cairo and Athens have promising opportunities to deepen cooperation and broaden their partnership, drawing on their shared strategic interests and pivotal positions in the Eastern Mediterranean, he added.

Papageorgiou noted that Egyptian-Greek relations extend beyond political and economic cooperation, deriving much of their strength from civilizational and human ties forged over centuries. These connections have built enduring bridges of understanding between the two peoples, giving the partnership a depth that transcends immediate interests and supports a more sustainable vision for the future.

Cooperation between the two countries also extends to vital sectors, including energy and electricity interconnection, he said, noting that their complementary capabilities offer opportunities to strengthen economic cooperation and expand connectivity between Egypt and Europe through Greece.

The ambassador added that Egypt and Greece possess complementary capabilities in the natural gas sector, creating further opportunities for cooperation and enhancing energy security in the region and Europe.

Papageorgiou described Alexandria as one of the most prominent living symbols of Egyptian-Greek ties, uniquely demonstrating how cities can embrace cultural diversity and create common ground between civilizations.

He noted that throughout its history, Alexandria has maintained a distinguished position as a center of science, knowledge, trade and human interaction.

Alexandria is not merely a testament to a shared history but also a living civilizational asset that can be built upon to promote cultural dialogue and understanding among peoples, he said. The city’s historical and human significance gives it an important role in supporting bilateral relations and strengthening their popular and cultural dimensions.

The ambassador said interaction between Egyptians and Greeks had continued across successive generations, with the Greek community in Egypt helping strengthen social and cultural ties. This has made relations between the two countries a model of coexistence and cultural exchange, as well as an important pillar of their contemporary partnership.

He expressed appreciation for initiatives and events highlighting Alexandria’s heritage, describing the preservation of its civilizational legacy and the promotion of its value among younger generations as a shared responsibility.

Such efforts also help strengthen Alexandria’s position on the international cultural map and open broader opportunities for cultural and tourism exchanges, he added.

Papageorgiou concluded that Egyptian-Greek relations have solid foundations for further development, supported by their shared history, strategic interests and close human ties. Building on these foundations would strengthen the bilateral partnership, broaden cooperation and reinforce both countries’ roles in promoting regional and international stability, understanding and integration.

World.title: To save the midterms, Trump is recharging the grievance politics that made him president
World.content:
Donald Trump is playing one of his final cards in the midterm election race: fear of an American civilizational collapse.

To hear the president, the greatest current threat to Americans is not the prohibitive cost of groceries, gasoline, diesel and housing; his Iran war quagmire; or concerns that AI could wipe out jobs and even humanity.

It’s that White, Christian culture could be destroyed unless his Republican monopoly on Washington power is preserved in the midterm elections.

In one of the most foreboding closing arguments of any of his political campaigns, Trump is flinging racially charged rhetoric; conjuring Islamophobic paranoia; and stirring up false visions of kids being mutilated in mass transgender surgeries without parental consent. He’s also acting as an arbiter of others’ faith and American identify.

“Americans are going to stand up and declare that we will protect our civilization, we will preserve our religion, our values and our heritage, and we will never let our nation be conquered or destroyed by people that hate us,” Trump said at a rally in Kansas on Monday, at which he also used an antisemitic slur.

At his most vulnerable political moment in nearly six years as president, Trump isn’t responding with compelling, innovative defenses of his record on affordability or foreign policy. He’s intensifying the scorched-earth imagery that made his name and seeking to replenish power by weaponizing painful national divides.

In an example of his willingness to wade into some of the most sensitive cultural issues, Trump warned at his Kansas event that Democratic Senate nominee Adam Hamilton told people to “repent because you were born White.” This was a misrepresentation of the candidate’s far more expansive remarks on race, self-reflection and personal faith.

But getting the details right is hardly the point.

President Donald Trump and Sen. Roger Marshall greet each other during a rally in Park City, Kansas, on Monday. Jonathan Ernst/Reuters

Trump’s anti-Muslim imagery

Trump has also been claiming that US-born Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is a “jihadist,” a smear he repeated Tuesday night in North Carolina. And he has been referring to El-Sayed as “Mohammed” on the basis that if “you have any problem with names, just call the guy Mohammed. You’ll probably be right.”

Such stereotyping is not merely aimed at disqualifying a political foe. It implies that everyone who shares that person’s faith or ethnic characteristics lacks the distinguishing humanity of an individual and is not authentically American.

The president offered another glimpse into his mindset in Kansas when he used “Shylock” — an antisemitic slur — to defend GOP Sen. Roger Marshall against criticism over medical billing practices. This time, he can’t say he was unaware of the term’s insinuations: He caused a storm by using it publicly in 2025.

The president is going beyond generalizing over religion and race.

He warned in Arizona this month that a Democratic Congress would lead to widespread gender transitions of children in schools. “They want to mutilate, cut your children. It’s unbelievable, what they do. … Your son leaves as Jimmy and comes back home in three days as Janet, and they don’t even ask you,” he said. He told similar baseless tales in Georgia last week and in North Carolina on Tuesday evening.

In recent days, he’s stoked fears that the rioting rocking France will cross the Atlantic if the Democrats win, after a campaign in which he’s warned socialists and communists want to obliterate the republic. He again demonized Somali-born Minnesota Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar on Tuesday, dismissing the idea that the naturalized American citizen is entitled to constitutional rights because she is originally from a “shithouse” country.

The president has also sought to foster religious intolerance by implying that the faithful who do not share his sympathizers’ specific political creed are a national threat. On Monday, he mocked Hamilton’s religious credentials as a leader in the United Methodist Church of the Resurrection. “He doesn’t act like a pastor because his views aren’t of a pastor,” Trump said.

While admitting he’s hardly a Bible aficionado, Trump nevertheless portrayed himself as a pseudo-prophet, claiming that an unnamed Texas religious leader had been correct to predict that “he’s going to lead us to a period of time … in Christianity that nobody else can do.”

Trump has long sought to identify enemies and outsiders against whom to define himself. He’s most politically effective when he has a foil. And many politicians are guilty of exaggeration. Some, like Trump, sometimes dole out vindictive comments framed as jokes to create a layer of political cover. Vice President JD Vance, for instance, tapped into the theme of un-American outsiders, quipping Monday that a protester at one of his events must have crossed the border illegally to behave in such a manner.

Many liberals have meanwhile tended to assume that all Trump’s supporters share the apparent racial and religious prejudices of their movement’s leader. That’s not a fair criticism of voters who find the totality of his message appealing.

It is not necessarily racist to worry that Democrats didn’t properly secure the southern border. Some Americans genuinely worry whether expanding Muslim or other faith communities will fully integrate or change the character of their cities and customs. And it’s perfectly appropriate for issues like a candidate’s views on the Middle East or groups like the Muslim Brotherhood to be litigated in campaign debates. El-Sayed has hardly been unwilling to address them.

Yet Trump is going much further than simply throwing out “red meat” to supporters, in the phraseology of political consultants. It’s not credible that such a sophisticated political operator is mindlessly blurting out random thoughts during his onstage weave. The repetition of searing themes and the frequent resort to racial or religious tropes is creating a pattern of fear.

Trump’s return to some of his most inflammatory imagery coincides with a swing through red states in a last-ditch bid to jolt turnout among the most conservative voters as he tries to save vulnerable Republican candidates. His decade in top-flight politics has shown his dark rhetoric can be a rallying cry.

But even for Trump, in a political career that has always flouted decorum, the latest demagoguery is stark. It comes across as a deliberate attempt at distraction; an effort to reframe the stakes of an election dominated by concerns about affordability — and voter economic plights worsened by his war in Iran.

It’s unclear whether it will work. If he can animate low-intensity voters who have shown up only when he’s on the ballot, maybe he’ll save some red-state Republicans who never expected they’d face a fight for their careers in 2026.

But White House strategists show they understand how his outlandish comments can alienate more moderate voters by not sending him this week to swing states with the tightest races.

And Mark Sanford, the Republican former governor of South Carolina, told CNN’s Erin Burnett on Tuesday that concentrating on false stories about transgender kids was unlikely to mitigate GOP vulnerabilities.

“I think it’s off-topic because the preponderance of folks that I talked to in and around South Carolina are worried about the economy, they’re worried about affordability. They’re worried about inflation,” Sanford said. “I guess it’s a way of changing the subject if what’s going on isn’t working for you … but I don’t see this as the issue that’s going to move swing voters.”

President Donald Trump looks at supporters during a campaign rally to support Republican House candidate Ed Gallrein and Senate candidate Andy Barr in Highland Heights, Kentucky, on October 17. Kevin Lamarque/Reuters

Trump’s rhetorical barrage is shocking, even for him

The cacophony of Trump’s two terms has sometimes dimmed shock over his antics or simply exhausted his critics as he floods the zone with acrimony. American politics, of course, has long been scarred by racism. Bigotry has periodically rushed to the surface of political life, often when cultivated by a politician who sees it as a vehicle to amass more power.

Yet it’s still remarkable to witness a president, a head of state, so consciously using his megaphone to tear at national racial, religious and cultural divides. When past presidents like Richard Nixon, Ronald Reagan or George H.W. Bush — or even Lyndon Johnson, who passed the Civil Rights Act — wanted to play a race card for political reasons, they did it implicitly or metaphorically.

Trump doesn’t do such subtlety. By lashing out at undocumented migrants, minority lawmakers and transgender citizens, he seems to be deliberately trying to delineate who belongs in America and benefits from its rights — a path that is both threatening to individual citizens and national unity.

But for all its ferocity, the message this time around hints at vulnerability.

In Trump’s presidential campaigns, his search for outside foes on whom to blame America’s woes was often a galvanizing force for his movement. Now, with his popularity near record lows, the strongman’s conceit of a nation besieged by outsiders suggests a diminished leader making a last stand — rather than one with the capacity to expand his appeal through persuasion.

And with polls showing majorities of Americans sour on Trump’s performance, economic management and signature foreign war, his attempt at inflammatory distraction seems unlikely to prevail. No wonder the GOP views November 3 with growing trepidation.

World.title: The big questions about who’s to blame for Starshield disruptions in Ukraine
World.content:
So, who slowed down a crucial satellite communications system used by Ukraine, making the country more vulnerable to Russian attacks in recent days?

Even some key Republicans are demanding answers and promising consequences for those responsible.

But the Trump administration and its top ally, Elon Musk, have so far offered a confusing, incomplete and sometimes contradictory set of answers.

The administration has disowned responsibility, but the disruption came right as Trump sharply turned away from Ukraine and toward Russia in its yearslong war. And Musk seemed to repeatedly point the finger toward Trump last week.

The controversy began a week ago when Ukraine accused Musk’s SpaceX of severely hindering its defense by suddenly limiting its Starlink internet service, which uses satellites in low orbit. Ukraine has used Starlink and a related military-grade service, Starshield, to communicate quickly and to both launch and prevent drone attacks.

(Ukraine has also accused the Trump administration of limiting intelligence-sharing about impending Russian attacks — a charge the US government denies.)

What everyone has claimed

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has pointed at the Trump administration.

Reuters also reported Thursday, citing anonymous sources, that the White House sent a message to the Defense Department to slow down the Starshield system. CNN has not confirmed that reporting. Multiple sources told CNN that the direction didn’t come from Trump, who also denied being involved.

Zelensky pointed at the White House during an interview on NBC’s “Meet the Press” on Sunday. He said: “Of course the message came from government,” while adding that SpaceX carried out the order.

The next day, Zelensky sought to emphasize the price of such limitations by posting a blurred image of a child he said was killed by a Russian Shahed drone.

And Musk also seemed to gesture in the US government’s direction on Wednesday. Responding to Ukraine’s former defense minister on X, Musk emphasized that Starshield was “owned and controlled by the US government.”

“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said.

When another X user claimed, alongside a series of claims, that “Starshield is under U.S. government control. That is who made last night’s call,” Musk responded: “True.”

(SpaceX has not responded to a question from CNN about whether Musk was explicitly confirming Trump and his administration were responsible for the Starshield slowdown. And his comments could seemingly have some wiggle room, which we’ll get to.)

But the Trump administration has denied involvement and even at times questioned whether there was a disruption.

Trump said flatly on Friday, “I didn’t do that.” He added: “I don’t know if it was anybody, because it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon.”

On Saturday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio suggested Zelensky didn’t know “what he’s talking about” and called reports of a White House role in the Starlink disruptions “categorically false.”

“Nothing to do with the White House,” Rubio said, adding: “No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it.”

Trump signaled Monday that he still didn’t know who was responsible.

“I don’t know who it was, but I’d like to find out,” he said.

The apparent contradictions

But some of these comments are difficult to reconcile.

Trump on Friday also seemed to question whether there even was a slowdown. He said he didn’t “even think it was slowed down,” and that “I think it’s probably functioning.”

“They say it’s the same as it always has been,” Trump added.

Rubio in his comments Friday also claimed that Starshield — which is, again, the military-grade version of Starlink — was “not at this moment available to Ukraine” and “has nothing to do with Ukraine.” But Bloomberg reported two years ago that Ukraine had been given access to Starshield. And in comments Monday in Uzbekistan, Rubio confirmed that “Ukraine has benefited from it.”

Musk’s comments are also somewhat confusing. While he seemed to point at the administration and Trump for any Starshield decisions, he added that Starlink — the civilian version — “cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.” That could be read to suggest there was a dispute about Ukraine’s use of Starlink, as well.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth pointed in the same direction Tuesday, after this article initially published. He said that “we haven’t pulled anything back,” but that “there are terms of service that obviously need to be complied to” when using Starlink, which he said it has the power to address.

Also, two senior US officials have told CNN that the Starshield order did not come from Trump.

Breaking down the claims

It’s worth emphasizing that this episode didn’t happen in a vacuum. It comes amid multiple signs of Trump moving away from Ukraine and increasingly cozying up to Russia.

Trump has taken to blaming Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries for high diesel prices (despite compelling evidence that the Iran war is the main culprit for the prices). He has also recently delayed major new sanctions on Russia. And he sought to import Russian diesel, while upping the pressure on Ukraine to concede more to Moscow to end the war, which began with Russia’s unprovoked invasion in 2022.

The Starlink controversy also comes as Ukraine has accused the administration of withholding vital intelligence-sharing. That’s another charge the Trump administration denies, despite CNN having previously reported that it threatened to do just that.

Musk’s decision to at least gesture toward Trump is also extremely notable, given the SpaceX CEO is a major Trump ally and the biggest benefactor of Trump’s political party in the midterm elections. He’s spent hundreds of millions of dollars for the Republican Party.

Musk could have said Starshield speed decisions are decided by the federal government and stopped there. But he continued by saying, “and ultimately POTUS.” And then he also did the “True” post.

Amid the confusion, some congressional Republicans are demanding answers.

They include retiring Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska and vulnerable Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania. Fitzpatrick vowed Monday on X that those limiting Starshield “will be fully investigated and will be held fully accountable.” He also promised congressional hearings and “immediate harsh and punitive budget cuts to any responsible agency or agency head.”

Outgoing Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Cornyn of Texas have also joined with Democrats to demand accountability, with Tillis calling it either “an unacceptable error or lapse” or a conscious “decision to clear the field for a Russian attack.”

Answers may not be imminent, but this controversy could return to the fore should Democrats control one or both chambers of Congress come January.

CORRECTION: This story has been updated to correct Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick’s first name.

World.title: Pentagon grants DHS permission to test heat ray weapon for potential use at border
World.content:
The Pentagon has given the Department of Homeland Security permission to test a military-grade heat ray and develop tactics to potentially use it in operations at the southern US border, according to a memo signed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last month and obtained by CNN.

The heat ray, officially known as the Active Denial System, is a nonlethal weapon that shoots an invisible beam of electromagnetic waves that can reach a little more than half a mile away, according to the US military.

The energy beam causes a burning sensation when it comes into contact with the human skin — which Pentagon officials have previously compared to feeling a blast of heat when opening a hot oven. Military officials have said the resulting “tingling effect” lasts between 10 and 15 minutes but also generates “an instinctive and irresistible urge to run from the effect.”

Deploying the heat ray at the US border would be an unprecedented step, even for the Trump administration, which has made border security and clamping down on immigration a top priority. The DHS request did not specify where or how the weapon would be tested and how it might eventually be used, but over the years, there have been internal discussions about potentially using it for crowd dispersal along the US-Mexico border, according to current and former Customs and Border Protection officials.

US officials had also considered deploying the system during moments of domestic unrest, including at the end of President Donald Trump’s first term when protests erupted over the murder of George Floyd, according to a former US official familiar with those discussions.

The memo authorizes the “temporary loan” of one ADS system for seven months, starting in September, and states that it “shall not be operated by DoW (Department of War) personnel,” appearing to absolve the Pentagon of any responsibility for how the directed-energy system may ultimately be deployed.

It also states that DHS is solely responsible for “system employment, use and development of tactics, techniques and procedures.” At the end of the seven-month loan period, DHS can submit an additional request for further use of the Pentagon system in border operations based on need, a defense official told CNN.

“CBP is continually evaluating new technologies, especially those that enhance operational effectiveness and strengthen mission capabilities,” a Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said in a statement to CNN.

The Pentagon referred CNN to DHS when asked for comment.

The US military briefly deployed the system to Afghanistan nearly two decades ago but ultimately declined to use it during active combat operations. The US military also considered using the system for crowd control purposes at US facilities abroad where terrorist detainees were being held at the time but ultimately declined to employ it for that purpose as well, according to a source familiar with those previous internal considerations.

Customs and Border Protection officials have previously entertained the idea of using the system in areas where there’s a high concentration of illegal crossings. Border officials have occasionally discussed potentially using the system as a crowd dispersal tool, but it has never been deployed.

Concerns over effectiveness and legality

Officials ran into hurdles over legalities, use of force, effectiveness, and potential issues over sovereignty, particularly if the system was deployed on people in Mexico who had not yet crossed into the US. Chief among those concerns, however, was whether people could be harmed, either directly or indirectly, by the weapon.

“Even if they’re chasing people back to the river, you don’t want them to go in and drown,” a former CBP official told CNN. “For the cost, for the training and for the policies you’re going to create, is the juice worth the squeeze?”

El Centro sector, which covers around 70 miles along the US-Mexico border, evaluated the system several years ago, when Rodney Scott, who now serves as CBP commissioner, helmed that sector, according to a CBP official.

At the time, officials were discussing whether the system might help agents with an influx of illegal crossings along the nearby river by discouraging people from trying to cross in that area or pushing them to get out of the water.

One of the considerations at the time was whether the system might result in more rescues if people were incapacitated by the technology, the official said, though it’s unclear why it wasn’t deployed.

In 2018, prior to midterms, CBP officials also weighed using it against migrants, but then-Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen shot it down.

“The issue was treating immigrants and citizens like enemy combatants,” a former DHS official familiar with previous discussions about using the weapon against migrants told CNN. “Thematically, inhumane treatments typically get rejected.”

Some Border Patrol agents have more recently cast doubt over whether they need the tool at all amid low border crossings and an increase in personnel, according to another former CBP official.

World.title: Rioting in France gives Trump a new talking point as he tries to stave off GOP midterm losses
World.content:
As Kansans were waiting for President Donald Trump to arrive at his rally in Wichita this week, they were treated to a new addition to the pre-show program: footage of this weekend’s violent protests in France, most of it clipped from Fox News, aired on large screens.

That the unrest was unfolding 4,700 miles away from the Heartland Credit Union Arena seemed immaterial to the point Trump and his team were trying to make. This could happen here, Trump would later warn his crowd, if Democrats win in November’s midterms.

“When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical ‘Dumocrats’ want to do to America,” he said Monday.

France, he claimed, was being “conquered, looted and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists who hate Christianity” and “the Western civilization itself.”

President Donald Trump points to a member of the crowd during a campaign rally in Park City, Kansas, on Monday. Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images

It’s a theme the president briefly returned to Tuesday night in North Carolina. “Do you believe what’s going on in France? That’s never going to go on over here,” Trump told rally attendees. “I promise you, that’s never going on in here.”

With a narrowing window for harsh political winds to shift, Trump and Republicans have seized on the violence as they make their final arguments to American voters. To some of Trump’s advisers, the unrest has looked a little like an “October surprise” that some believe could help improve what had been dire prospects for victory in just two weeks.

The torched cars, graffiti and looted shops are all a cautionary tale, they have warned, and the inevitable result of liberal policies — particularly on immigration — that they have been warning against for years.

There is little evidence the violence in France over the weekend was carried out by illegal immigrants, or immigrants of any kind. The demonstrations began as a student movement demanding better funding and improvements at schools. Labor unions and other groups joined to protest high living costs and record fuel prices.

What led to the scenes of violence is a matter of dispute among France’s political leaders, and has led to a round of finger-pointing.

Trump, along with right-wing leaders in France, used the scenes to accuse French President Emmanuel Macron and other European centrists of failing to get a handle on uncontrolled migration from the Middle East and Africa.

“Our country is caught in a vice…between violence and powerlessness,” Marine Le Pen, the far-right leader, said, suggesting only her firm hand could restore order amid Macron’s “chaos.”

Le Pen, who is standing in the presidential election for the far-right National Rally party, has sought to inject the issue of migration into the debate, blaming the violence on delinquents from France’s banlieues, poor urban areas where much of the country’s migrant population lives.

France protests turn violent 20 photos An elderly man uses a gas mask to protect from the smoke from tear gas during demonstration against the “high cost of living”, at the Place des Terreaux in Lyon, on Saturday. Jeff Pachoud/AFP/Getty Images

Trump stopped short Tuesday of saying whether he would endorse Le Pen in next year’s election, where she is a front-runner. But he nonetheless appeared to be echoing her arguments, and insisted Macron had ignored his advice to crack down on migration.

“Some people think it’s a little controversial. I don’t care,” Trump said in the Oval Office on Tuesday. “It’s an immigration problem. We have people that poured into France, and they were also unchecked, unvetted, like with (President Joe) Biden when he was doing. We don’t do that.”

Earlier in the day, he specifically invoked “what is taking place in France” in pledging that the spending in outside money he oversees will top $400 million by Election Day.

It may be too early to tell whether Trump’s decision to seize on the images from France will have a determinative effect among American midterm voters. Most say their primary concerns are the high cost of living, and Trump’s immigration agenda has become unpopular, with majorities of Americans saying in polls his administration has gone too far in deporting undocumented immigrants from the United States.

Trump, however, has chafed at recommendations from political advisers that he not mention immigration as much as he stumps for Republican candidates. As he shines a spotlight on the situation in Europe, he has once again made a hardline approach to immigration a centerpiece of his pitch.

“If you want to see what is at stake in this election,” Trump said ominously in Kansas on Monday, “just look at what’s happening in France.”

Other Republicans have followed suit. Vice President JD Vance wrote on X that immigration was to blame for the violence.

“Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion,” he wrote in a post that featured video of the fire that destroyed the historic town hall in Limoges, the town in central France famous for its porcelain. “They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility.”

Trump referred approvingly to Vance’s post in the Oval Office on Tuesday, and insisted that concerns about education or costs were not driving the scenes of unrest.

“It’s not about education. It’s about immigration,” he said. “It’s about illegal people coming in who basically hate France. They hate the people. They hate everything.”

This story has been updated with additional details.

World.title: Liberia: Mo Ali Challenges Grand Gedeh University Graduates
World.content:
Mr. Mo Ali, Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation

Zwedru City, Grand Gedeh County — In a stirring commencement address during Grand Gedeh University’s historic convocation over the weekend, Mo Ali, Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation (LWSC), challenged both public officials and the graduates to measure leadership by outcomes rather than titles or ceremony.

By Franklin Doloquee From Zwedru City, Grand Gedeh

Speaking before a crowd of graduates, faculty, local officials, educators, government officials and community residents, Ali said appointments and honorifics are only the beginning.



He said real achievement is demonstrated by the tangible improvements leaders produce for ordinary citizens.

Colorful banners bearing the university seal fluttered in a warm breeze while applause rose and fell as his remarks underscored the convocation’s theme: “Accountability Is the Test of Leadership.”

‘Power must produce results’

Ali told the assembly, urging officials at every level to hold themselves to higher standards.

He described the too-common celebration of appointments — public congratulations, photographs and social media fanfare — as premature if they are not followed by measurable gains in service delivery.

“When someone is appointed to lead an institution, the appointment is not the achievement. The achievement is what that person accomplishes with the responsibility entrusted to them,” the LWSC boss stated.

He illustrated his point with concrete examples. For families who wait each day for clean water, an impressive title means little if taps remain dry.

For communities suffering from poor sanitation, a decorated office or an official vehicle offers no relief.

“A minister should be assessed not simply by meetings attended, but by policies implemented and improvements achieved,” he said, adding that legislators should be evaluated on the quality of representation, lawmaking and oversight, and public managers by how well their institutions perform.

He acknowledged that public institutions often operate under severe resource constraints, from tight budgets to aging infrastructure.

Yet he insisted those obstacles should spur creativity and discipline rather than provide perpetual excuses for inaction.

“Leadership is not the absence of difficulties. It is the responsibility to confront them and demonstrate progress,” Ali intimated, his voice steady as he paced a short stage set against the silhouette of the university’s main building.

Addressing the graduates directly, Ali urged them to be problem-solvers, innovators, entrepreneurs and professionals committed to serving their communities.

He reminded them that change does not require national fame. Small, local improvements a successful shop that provides jobs, a better-stocked clinic, a repaired school roof, or a community-led sanitation drive transform lives even if they do not make headlines.

“You do not have to wait until you become nationally prominent before contributing to Grand Gedeh,” he asserted.

Ali also counseled the new graduates on the nature of public life and the temporary privileges of office.

In a section he titled: “The Day Nobody Calls You ‘Honorable,’” he reminded them that official recognition and attention ebb over time.

“The official vehicle may be returned. The telephone may stop ringing.

The invitations may become fewer,” he said.

Rather than mourn this normal change, Ali suggested officials and citizens alike should focus on the substance of their work and the legacy of service they leave behind.

The convocation included several other speakers who echoed calls for accountability and community engagement, and the ceremony featured traditional music, student presentations, and the presentation of diplomas to hundreds of graduates who celebrated with relatives and friends.

In conversations after the ceremony, many attendees expressed optimism that the university’s new alumni, equipped with fresh skills and energy, will play active roles in improving local health care, education, water access, and small business growth across Grand Gedeh County.

Ali closed his remarks by challenging both officials and citizens to keep asking pragmatic questions about leadership: Will services become more reliable? Will public resources be managed responsibly? Will projects be completed on time and to standard? He said those questions should guide public assessment of leaders and serve as the yardstick for progress.

As graduates dispersed into the late afternoon heat, the convocation left a clear message: authority is not valuable for its own sake; it’s worth is proven by the concrete benefits it brings to people’s daily lives.

Thousands Turn Out to Celebrate Graduates at Historic Commencement Ceremony

Thousands of graduates, family members and well-wishers including many Liberians packed the grounds to celebrate the University of Grand Gedeh’s historic commencement ceremony.

The atmosphere was jubilant and colorful as crowds gathered to honor the students who received the university’s final batch of associate degrees before the institution transitions to full university status.

The eighth and final associate-degree commencement drew huge numbers from across the region.

Graduates marched in rows, their gowns and caps fluttering in the breeze, while proud parents, siblings and friends cheered from shaded stands and along the walkways.

Vendors moved through the crowds selling cold drinks, snacks and flowers and the air filled with congratulatory shouts, camera clicks and the low hum of excited conversation.

For many of the graduates, the ceremony was more than a formal rite of passage it represented hope and a tangible step toward improved opportunities.

Several graduates described the degree as a “big boost” for their futures, saying it will strengthen their chances for employment, further study, and community leadership.

One graduate embraced relatives and wiped away tears of joy, while others posed for photographs, their faces beaming with relief and pride.

Speakers at the event emphasized the milestone significance of this graduating class.

University officials lauded the students’ perseverance and dedication, noting the institution’s achievement in becoming a full degree-granting university. Government and community leaders who attended the program highlighted the positive impact the university’s upgrade will have on local education, job creation, and regional development.

The ceremony blended formal protocol with vibrant local culture. Traditional music and dances punctuated the program, and speakers often paused for rounds of applause and cheers. Guests waved national and university flags as the graduates processed; colorful fabrics and patterned attire added to the festive scene.

Organizers took care to ensure the event ran smoothly. Ushers guided guests, security personnel maintained order, and medical staff were on hand for any emergencies. Despite the large turnout, volunteers and staff coordinated seating, the diploma distribution, and the procession with practiced efficiency.

As the ceremony closed, many graduates lingered on the grounds, exchanging congratulations and making plans for the future. For the university and its community, the day marked both an ending and a beginning: a celebration of achievement and a hopeful look ahead now that the institution has attained full university status.
