World.title: Uganda: Uganda Has No Active Ebola Cases, Health Ministry Assures Public
World.content:
A tent used to isolate Ebola patients is disinfected in Bunia, DR Congo (file photo).

Uganda has reiterated there are no confirmed active Ebola cases, following reports of a confirmed infection in Nigeria involving a woman who travelled to the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) for business.

In a statement, the Director General of Health Services in the Ministry of Health, Prof. Charles Olaro

said preliminary information indicated that the woman transited through Uganda in early October without showing symptoms but developed them after arriving in Nigeria.

He cautioned against concluding that the infection originated in Uganda, noting that investigations were still underway to establish where the woman was exposed to the virus.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation," Prof Olaro said.

He added that Uganda had no confirmed active Ebola cases at the time of the statement and urged the public to remain calm as authorities continued to monitor the situation.

"We wish to clarify that, as at the time of this statement, Uganda has NO confirmed active Ebola cases," Prof. Olaro said.

The Ministry added that the government of Nigeria had not yet provided detailed information about the woman's travel itinerary and clinical history, which would help guide further investigations and determine whether contact tracing was necessary.

Meanwhile, the Ministry said it would work with relevant government agencies to strengthen screening and public health controls at Uganda's points of entry.

It noted that limited provisions had been maintained for humanitarian and diplomatic movement and that additional measures would be taken to reinforce public health safeguards.

The Ministry urged Ugandans to remain vigilant and observe preventive hygiene measures, including regular handwashing and the use of sanitiser.

"We urge the public to remain calm, vigilant and to practice regular handwashing and sanitising," the statement said.

The Ministry said it would continue to provide verified information through its official communication channels as investigations progressed.

World.title: Kenya: Kenya Confirms Ninth Ebola Case, Says All Patients Improving
World.content:
Health workers in protective gear inside the Ebola treatment centre at Buniaâs referral hospital in Ituri province, eastern DRC, October 2026.

In a statement published on its X account on Tuesday and signed by Patrick Amoth, the Director-General for Health, the ministry said all nine cases belonged to one known cluster.

Kenya has confirmed a ninth case of Ebola, with health authorities saying all eight surviving patients are improving.

The latest Kenyan case involves a 24-year-old man who is a close relative of the first patient. He developed symptoms while in quarantine and tested positive on 19 October, according to the Kenyan Ministry of Health.

In a statement published on its X account on Tuesday and signed by Patrick Amoth, the Director-General for Health, the ministry said all nine cases belonged to one known cluster, with no evidence of transmission beyond the group.



Kenya's first patient was a 40-year-old man who travelled from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on 3 October. He died at a Nairobi hospital on 5 October.

Treatment and contact tracing

The ministry said the eight surviving patients were stable and responding well to supportive care. It added that it had received 500 doses of medicine to support treatment for confirmed patients.

Contact tracing has also progressed, with 134 of the 135 identified contacts (99.3 per cent) traced and placed in quarantine.

The ministry said contacts who entered quarantine on 6 October and remain symptom-free would complete their 21-day monitoring period and begin returning home from 25 October.

It added that authorities had distributed protective equipment, diagnostic kits, and sample-collection materials to high-risk counties, and established a dedicated laboratory at Kenyatta National Hospital to support testing and prevent disruption to other hospital laboratory services.

Kenya, it noted, has not imposed restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings. The cases in Kenya are linked to the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the DRC, where the Bundibugyo virus has caused thousands of infections and deaths.

WHO reported more than 8,700 confirmed cases and more than 4,200 deaths in the DRC as of 6 October, with transmission continuing across dozens of health zones.

Nigeria confirms first case

The Kenyan update comes as Nigeria confronts its own Ebola infection, with the federal government confirming the first case in Abuja on Tuesday.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that the patient was a woman who arrived in Nigeria on an international flight from Uganda. She is receiving treatment in isolation at a private hospital in the Federal Capital Territory.

Close 

In a statement signed by the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, the federal government said it had begun contact tracing and identified 44 close contacts, including healthcare workers, patients, caregivers, and travel contacts.

The government urged healthcare facilities nationwide to remain vigilant, promptly isolate suspected cases, maintain strict infection prevention measures and report suspected infections to public health authorities.

The development has heightened concerns about cross-border transmission, particularly as the outbreak in East and Central Africa coincides with frequent international travel and movement between countries.

Nigeria's response includes surveillance, laboratory testing, isolation and contact tracing to identify possible infections and limit further transmission.

World.title: Nigeria: 12 Years After First Outbreak, Nigeria Records Fresh Ebola Case
World.content:
A tent used to isolate Ebola patients is disinfected in Bunia, DR Congo (file photo).

Twelve years after Nigeria was declared free of Ebola following an outbreak that killed eight people, the country has confirmed a new case of the disease in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).

The federal government disclosed the case on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, following laboratory confirmation of the infection in a woman who recently arrived in Nigeria on an international flight from Uganda.

The patient had been admitted to a private hospital in Abuja, where she received treatment for several days before the diagnosis was confirmed.

The coordinating minister of health and social welfare, Prof. Muhammad Ali Pate, announced the development in a statement, adding that the woman was in isolation and receiving medical care.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

He said 44 close contacts had been identified as authorities intensified efforts to contain the infection and prevent further transmission.

According to the minister, contact tracing had commenced, with public health teams working to identify and monitor people who might have been exposed to the virus, including healthcare workers, patients, caregivers and travel contacts.

He added that surveillance had been intensified and the hospital where the patient received treatment was receiving immediate support to strengthen infection prevention and control measures.

Pate directed public and private healthcare facilities nationwide to remain on high alert and maintain a high index of suspicion for possible Ebola cases.

He also urged healthcare workers to identify and isolate suspected cases promptly, observe strict infection prevention and control measures, and immediately report suspected infections to public health authorities.

The minister advised Nigerians to remain calm but vigilant, stressing that early detection and compliance with public health measures were critical to preventing further transmission.

He said containing the infection would require public cooperation and coordinated action by the federal government, FCT authorities and other partners.

Pate assured Nigerians that investigations were ongoing and pledged that the government would continue to provide accurate and timely updates.

Remembering Nigeria's 2014 Ebola Battle

Nigeria's first major encounter with Ebola occurred in July 2014, when an infected Liberian-American, Patrick Sawyer, arrived in Lagos by air.

Sawyer was admitted to a private hospital, where he died five days later. His arrival triggered an outbreak investigation in Lagos, a densely populated commercial city with extensive domestic and international travel connections.

The incident posed a significant risk of wider transmission because Sawyer had interacted with people at the airport and in healthcare facilities before his infection was confirmed.

However, Nigeria's response, including the sacrifice of the late Dr Ameyo Stella Adadevoh, demonstrated how rapid case identification, contact tracing, isolation, coordinated emergency management and public awareness could help contain a dangerous infectious disease.

According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), the outbreak resulted in 20 cases and eight deaths, including the index case. Nigeria was officially declared free of Ebola transmission on October 20, 2014, after completing the required 42-day period without a new case.

The response involved the Federal Ministry of Health, Lagos State authorities, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), international health partners and other stakeholders.

An emergency operations structure was established to coordinate the response, investigate suspected infections, identify contacts and monitor people who might have been exposed.

Public awareness campaigns and engagement with community, traditional and religious leaders also helped communicate the risks associated with the disease.

The successful containment of the 2014 outbreak established Nigeria as an example of how a country could interrupt transmission even when confronted with a potentially devastating epidemic.

However, the confirmation of another case 12 years later underscores the fact that previous success does not eliminate the risk of new infections entering the country.

Nigeria's Ebola Preparedness

Before the latest confirmation, Nigeria had intensified its preparedness following the spread of Ebola in parts of Central and East Africa.

On October 6, 2026, the NCDC announced heightened vigilance after Kenya confirmed an imported case linked to an outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

At the time, the agency said Nigeria had no confirmed Ebola case.

It also disclosed that preparedness activities were being strengthened in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, Port Health Services, state governments and other partners.

The measures included surveillance, early detection, laboratory diagnosis, isolation and referral, contact tracing, infection prevention and control, risk communication, and the protection of healthcare workers.

The NCDC also reported that a national Ebola preparedness tabletop simulation exercise had been conducted to test response arrangements and identify gaps requiring attention.

LEADERSHIP reports that President Bola Tinubu established a Presidential Task Force on Ebola Virus Disease Preparedness and Emerging Public Health Threats in June 2026. The task force was created to strengthen national preparedness and prevent the importation and spread of the disease following outbreaks in the DRC and elsewhere in the region.

It is chaired by the Chief of Staff to the President, Femi Gbajabiamila, and comprises representatives of relevant ministries, departments and agencies, state governments and public health partners.

Its responsibilities include coordinating the national response, overseeing the implementation of Nigeria's Ebola preparedness plan, reviewing surveillance reports and coordinating decisions on emergency measures.

As part of the preparations, Tinubu approved the release of N10 billion in emergency intervention funding to strengthen the NCDC's operational capacity and support critical public health response activities.

The confirmation in Abuja now puts these preparedness arrangements to a practical test.

Expert Calls for Calm, Effective Risk Communication

Meanwhile, an infectious disease expert, Dr Oladipo Elijah Kolawole, has urged Nigerians to remain calm but vigilant following the federal government's confirmation of an Ebola case in the FCT.

Kolawole, an associate professor of infectious diseases, pathogen genomics and molecular epidemiology at Adeleke University and founder of Helix Biogen Institute, told LEADERSHIP that early detection and strict adherence to public health measures were critical to containing the disease and preventing wider transmission.

He advised Nigerians to practise regular hand hygiene, avoid direct contact with the bodily fluids of sick individuals and promptly report suspected cases to health authorities.

The expert stressed that public vigilance and evidence-based interventions, rather than panic, were essential to managing the situation.

He urged the government to prioritise rapid case investigation, contact tracing, laboratory confirmation and effective risk communication to contain the infection.

Kolawole also called for stronger infection prevention and control measures in healthcare facilities, noting that transparency, preparedness and a coordinated public health response would be crucial to preventing further transmission.

Close 

How Ebola Spreads and What Nigerians Should Know

Ebola is a severe viral disease that can cause serious illness and death.

The virus spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person who is sick or has died, or through contact with contaminated objects and materials.

It is not spread simply because an infected person is in the same room, nor through ordinary casual contact without the necessary exposure.

Symptoms

Symptoms can include fever, severe weakness, headache, muscle pain, vomiting and diarrhoea. Some patients may develop bleeding, although this does not occur in every case.

The incubation period generally ranges from two to 21 days.

Precautions

The federal government has advised Nigerians to practise regular hand hygiene, avoid contact with the bodily fluids of anyone suspected of having the disease and report possible exposure to public health authorities.

Anyone who develops compatible symptoms after possible exposure should contact public health authorities for guidance rather than visiting a healthcare facility without prior notification.

People identified by contact-tracing teams should cooperate with health officials and follow instructions on monitoring and other recommended public health measures.

Assurance to Nigerians

The Federal Ministry of Health has said Nigeria successfully contained Ebola in 2014 and has the experience and public health systems to respond to the current case.

However, the ministry stressed that containing the disease requires everyone to play their part.

World.title: Africa: Every Country Has a Balance Sheet - Development Cooperation Should Start There
World.content:
Ovidiu Bujorean, chief executive officer of OviBees Ventures, spoke with Alexia Latortue, Head of Secretariat of the Future of Development Cooperation Coalition, for the fourth conversation of Wave 2 of the RootsToFoods Capital Series

In a RootsToFoods Capital Series interview, Alexia Latortue, Head of Secretariat of the Future of Development Cooperation Coalition and former U.S. Treasury Assistant Secretary, explains why a system designed after the Second World War must be redesigned around countries’ own visions, and why she is not in the camp that says aid is dead.

Ovidiu Bujorean, chief executive officer of OviBees Ventures, spoke with Alexia Latortue, Head of Secretariat of the Future of Development Cooperation Coalition, for the fourth conversation of Wave 2 of the RootsToFoods Capital Series. Latortue has worked inside CGAP at the World Bank, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the Millennium Challenge Corporation and the U.S. Treasury, where she was Senate-confirmed Assistant Secretary for International Trade and Development. The Coalition, co-hosted by the African Center for Economic Transformation (ACET) and the Center for Global Development (CGD) and co-chaired by former Nigerian Vice President Yemi Osinbajo and former Spanish Foreign Minister Arancha González Laya, is reimagining how development cooperation delivers.

The pattern she saw across all four was the same. “Institutions generally are full of inertia, and individual people within institutions have a lot of power to move that inertia,” she said. She points to the push under Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen to evolve the multilateral development banks, treating climate and development as intertwined and stretching their balance sheets. It took a leader willing to back her team, deep technical evidence, trust built with borrowing and donor countries alike, and a political window opened by rising debt and fiscal pressure. Hence her impatience with one familiar objection: “I don’t really buy it when people say we’ve tried it before.”



In the Coalition’s consultations, emerging-market participants rarely started with aid, or even with finance as the binding constraint, she said. They started with whether a country has a clear, shared vision for its own development and the ability to execute it, and with the freedom to learn from the Gulf on one issue and Kenya on another. “It’s not a north-south thing at all.”

“Every country, even the poorest country, has assets and liabilities.”

Alexia Latortue, Head of Secretariat, Future of Development Cooperation Coalition

That is the premise of the Coalition’s first report, The Development Balance Sheet, published in May 2026. Assets include a capacity to innovate, tax revenue, access to borrowing and natural resources; liabilities include unsustainable debt, a changing climate, weak institutions and illicit outflows. A country that knows what it prioritizes can then articulate which external partnerships it needs, financial but also technological and knowledge-based. The lens is wide: Nigeria, the report notes, receives more than 7.5 times as much in remittances as in official development assistance.

The Coalition’s next paper proposes four purposes for development cooperation: ending deprivation and protecting people in crisis; economic transformation, the strongest call from emerging markets; advancing the common good on challenges “that have no passports,” such as climate change and pandemics; and creating knowledge and innovation. Without that clarity, she said, actors work at cross purposes and trust erodes.

Five years out, she hopes to see more confident governments that set their own trajectory and pick fewer, longer-term partnerships at greater scale, and partners that state their comparative advantage against a country’s plan instead of producing “50 different country plans for Malawi from different people around the world, but not Malawi.” Accountability would follow outcomes rather than money disbursed, with countries engaging one another as peers: “really treating countries as equals.”

On reforming the system from inside, she was direct. “I think every institution needs fresh air,” she said, not least because the post-1945 architecture no longer reflects the world. But she is “a big believer in being bold, but also in building, not destroying,” since insiders often hold the information that accelerates change. She also wants institutions to plan for their own end: “Every time we create something new, an institution or a fund, we never have sunset clauses.”

On aid, she drew a careful line. Official development assistance fell 23.1 percent in real terms in 2025, according to OECD preliminary data, the largest annual drop on record. Latortue noted that ODA has long been a small part of what drives development success, while remaining vital in humanitarian crises and in fragile settings where extreme poverty is concentrated. “I am not in the camp of people who say ODA is dead,” she said. “Because it’s small and because it’s so precious, and because used well it can be so catalytic, we had better use it exceptionally well.”

The need to look at a much wider range of financial flows, she argued, is “not linked to ODA falling. It’s linked to the fact that this is what drives development”: domestic public and private investment, foreign investment and local savings. Nor should anyone conclude that the private sector can do it all. Chief executives she met in Kigali told her the same thing, she said: “We can come in, we have financing, we have ideas, but I need rule of law. I need a capable workforce that is healthy, that is educated.”

The most promising signs of change are already visible, she said. Rwanda insists that partners align with its national vision, and finances near-universal health insurance creatively, including through solidarity between better-off and poorer Rwandans. And the multilateral development banks, while “not there yet,” are starting to act as enablers rather than only financiers, especially in middle-income countries, using guarantees “to unlock even institutional investors in your own country.”

Close 

Asked for the most underrated skill for anyone reforming a large institution from within, Latortue kept it short: “Leaving their egos at the door.”

Alexia Latortue spoke with Ovidiu Bujorean, chief executive officer of OviBees Ventures and host and designer of the RootsToFoods Capital Series, for Episode 9 of the series, the fourth episode of Wave 2. Latortue is Head of Secretariat of the Future of Development Cooperation Coalition, a Distinguished Non-Resident Fellow at the Center for Global Development and a member of the board of ODI Global, and previously served as Assistant Secretary for International Trade and Development at the U.S. Treasury. The views expressed are her own. RootsToFoods Capital Series is produced by OviBees Ventures, with AV Ventures, an ACDI/VOCA affiliate, as founding partner, and is distributed in partnership with AllAfrica Global Media. Wave 2 continues November 3 with Kanini Mutooni of the Draper Richards Kaplan Foundation and Dr. Frank Aswani of the African Venture Philanthropy Alliance.

World.title: Libya: How People in Libya and Beyond Are Living With Khadafi's Legacy, 15 Years On
World.content:
Fifteen years ago today, Moamer Kadhafi was captured and killed by rebel fighters, ending 42 years of one-man rule over Libya. RFI spoke to Libya specialist Virginie Collombier about what "Khadafism" stood for, who still believes in it and whether the removal of its architect has made life better for the country's people.

Kadhafi seized power in Libya in a military coup in 1969 and went on to build one of the most idiosyncratic states of the 20th century.

Funded by vast oil wealth and enforced by ruthless repression, it was guided by his Green Book - a manifesto proposing a "third way" between capitalism and communism, and officially called the Jamahiriya - or "state of the masses".

Kadhafi cast himself as a champion of Arab - and subsequently African - liberation, and backed armed groups abroad, which brought years of Western and United Nations sanctions.



His fall in 2011, following an uprising and a Western-backed military intervention, left Libya split between rival governments in the country's east and west. Many Africans blame his removal for the instability that has since spread across the Sahel.

In February this year, Kadhafi's son Saif al-Islam, long seen as his political heir, was assassinated, leaving his supporters without a leader.

We asked Virginie Collombier, a professor at Luiss Guido Carli University in Rome and a specialist on Libya, what survives of Kadhafi's ideas and influence, in Libya and beyond.

RFI: Is Kadhafism simply the Green Book - the text which set out a third way, anti-capitalist and anti-Marxist, to shape the political, economic and social life of the Jamahiriya?

The Green Book is often seen as the symbol of Kadhafism, and it's the central doctrinal text: a third way meant to offer an alternative to the two great ideologies of the 20th century, capitalism and communism. But Kadhafi's way of governing was based on a much broader set of ideas and institutions.

The fundamental idea was that sovereignty should belong directly to the masses. People organise themselves at grassroots level through popular committees, which are then connected to the government and the executive branch. There was also a distinctive economic outlook, often likened to socialism, though it took different forms and shifted over time. And there were doctrinal elements drawn from Islam, which likewise evolved.

In foreign policy, the main principles revolved around Arab nationalism, then African nationalism, and a revolutionary anti-imperialist theory. Remember that Kadhafi took power in 1969, when the Cold War was at its height. Pan-Arab nationalist movements, notably [Gamal Abdel] Nasser's in Egypt but also in Syria and Iraq, had already transformed the region. Kadhafi arrived somewhat late, and his approach to power was heavily influenced by what was happening elsewhere at the time.

RFI: In the West, Kadhafism is associated with political repression, regional conflict and alleged support for international terrorism. Why have his revolutionary ideology, Arab nationalism and pan-Africanism taken a back seat?

First, because these are not things that are particularly appreciated in the West. Kadhafi very quickly found himself in direct confrontation with the United States and France. There were repeated attempts by a number of Western powers to eliminate him, directly or indirectly.

His "third way" was also fundamentally at odds with parliamentary democracy. Behind the rhetoric of mass democracy, the system was highly centralised. Repression was severe and fell on every kind of opposition: political, of course, but also views that challenged the idea of Libya as above all an Arab nation, denying the country's ethnic and linguistic diversity.

His economic policies also generated strong opposition, with many people badly hit by the nationalisation of property, including homes.

Alongside the repression, the system used local levels of power to install loyal interlocutors on the ground - in effect a policy of repression, and reward for the regime's local representatives.

The redistribution of wealth through the central state [notably oil resources from 1960s onwards] also reinforced the concentration of power.

Finally, by positioning himself as a leader of anti-imperialism and opposition to European colonialism, Kadhafi backed a number of movements that the West regarded as terrorist: national liberation movements in Africa, but also in Northern Ireland and Palestine.

The regime went as far as supporting terrorist attacks, which led to major US and then UN sanctions lasting more than 20 years.

Ukrainian forces operating in western Libya as covert war grows

RFI: The Arab League dropped Kadhafi, yet many African heads of state continued to back him after the first UN embargo in 1992. Why was Kadhafism less successful in the Arab world than in Africa?

Tensions between Kadhafi and other Arab leaders emerged very quickly. He was a flamboyant figure who soon fell out with several Middle Eastern governments, particularly Egypt's, because he wanted to be the leader of the Arab world. He was also seen as a troublemaker - relations with France, and especially the US, were very strained.

So he changed tack, shifting from Arab nationalism to Africa: its future, decolonisation and development. He pursued a series of African policies, including support for development and investment, which quickly made him an admired figure overall, although his popularity varied from country to country.

RFI: What remains of Kadhafi's legacy in Africa? Libya specialist Vincent Hugeux says Africa is "short on heroes", which made Kadhafi "an icon by default".

It's now 2026. For the younger generation, who makes up the majority of the continent's population, Kadhafi is a distant memory. They often have other reference points, but it's true that iconic figures are thin on the ground. Among some African elites, Kadhafi did a lot of good, so there's a certain nostalgia.

There may also be, and it's surely grown in recent years, deep resentment, even anger, towards the countries that took part in overthrowing him. They say, with some justification: "You removed the regime without any clear plan for what would come next."

Removing Kadhafi profoundly destabilised the whole region. Through a domino effect, it had severe and damaging repercussions, particularly in the Sahel, in terms of insecurity, instability and the spread of jihadism. It isn't the only explanation, but there is maybe a feeling that the military operation that toppled him in 2011 had many harmful consequences for Africa.

Libya's Al-Khadim airbase becomes a hub for Russian arms in the Sahel

RFI: Libya was the only country to see foreign intervention during the Arab Spring pro-democracy protests - a "humanitarian" intervention by the West carried out without the African Union's backing.

Unlike what happened in most countries in the region in 2011 and 2012, Libya was the only state where Western powers chose to intervene.

There were attempts at mediation, notably under South African leadership, to find a compromise between the protesters, or opponents of Kadhafi, and the regime. But Western powers set these mediation efforts aside and gave them no serious consideration. That remains a major source of tension and criticism among African elites.

The intervention was also seen as a betrayal by Russia, which has since used its veto to block any form of intervention proposed at the Security Council. In 2011, Moscow abstained on Resolution 1973. The West had presented it as a text embodying the "responsibility to protect" demonstrators and civilians. In practice, that responsibility was very quickly turned into a military intervention with the clear aim of toppling the regime.

RFI: Why has the Kadhafist movement in Libya never recovered since the 2011 revolution?

The year 2011 was particularly complex. Unlike in Egypt or Tunisia, where a popular movement brought down a regime and replaced it with another, three things overlapped in Libya.

There was a popular movement that quickly became militarised and was met with repression. At the same time, the confrontation between the regime and its opponents was compounded by a deep division in the country between pro and anti-Kadhafi forces, both armed. This turned the conflict into a genuine civil war.

Finally, and above all, foreign military intervention added another layer of complexity and strengthened the various anti-Kadhafi factions on the ground.

When the regime collapsed, the country was deeply divided between the victorious revolutionaries and the defeated, who were marginalised and sidelined for several years.

In this divided Libya, the two rival camps realised that, for security and political reasons, they needed to bring in a number of figures from the Kadhafi era. From 2017-18 onwards, a process of absorption and co-option began, with a number of former prominent figures aligning themselves with either Khalifa Haftar [leader of the Libyan National Army] or the Tripoli government.

Close 

Those who refused to join that system were, to varying degrees, allied with Saif al-Islam Khadafi. But although he was politically charismatic, he had no army or real militia capable of mobilising people. Nor did he have the financial means to do so, which put him at a disadvantage.

Following his assassination in February 2026, his movement is in real crisis. There's no figure for supporters to rally around and no real political project either. Among Kadhafi's surviving children, it seems that no one has the desire or the ability to play that mobilising role.

Libya's road to democracy remains blocked as political stalemate endures

RFI: The writer Jean-Louis Gouraud, who knew Kadhafi well, wrote in his 2023 book that "Kadhafism was nothing other than Kadhafi". Do you agree?

Kadhafism was indeed very much centred on Kadhafi as a person, on a highly personalised system of power closely tied to him. At the same time, Kadhafi was the product of a society and a rather particular history.

In some respects there was something very Libyan about him. In a way he organised around himself a system closely tied to his country's social structures and history. This is what is sometimes called the "Libyan personality".

It reflects quite well what Libyan society went through in terms of profound upheaval: from the colonial period to independence and the discovery of oil - and the brutal way that transformed society and the role of the state.

We tend to forget that Libya and its people spent several decades largely cut off from the rest of the world because of sanctions and embargoes. That still shapes the Libyan personality today, even though new generations have of course come along.

So yes, in some respects you could say Kadhafism was Kadhafi. But it's also the reflection of a country's history, and upheavals in a society that we haven't yet properly analysed or understood and which are quite unusual.

This article has been adapted from an interview in French by Anne Bernas.

World.title: Sudan: As Sudan War Spills Into Central African Republic, UN Warns Against Early Peacekeeper Exit
World.content:
The UN warned on Tuesday against a premature withdrawal of its peacekeepers as the war in Sudan spills over into the Central African Republic (CAR).

CAR continues to face a resurgence of deadly violence in the east despite the disarmament of nearly 2,000 fighters and the gradual completion of the latest electoral cycle, the Security Council heard.

Illustrating the current fragility, the top UN official in the country, Valentine Rugwabiza, highlighted an attack on 30 June by different armed groups on Am-Dafock, bordering Sudan, which killed civilians, members of national security forces, displaced 17,000 civilians and injured six UN peacekeepers.



However, without peacekeeping mission MINUSCA's rapid response, she said, attacks in the border area with Chad and Sudan would have resulted in significantly more fatalities and State authority could not have been restored after only five days of control by the armed group, whose fighters retreated across the border into Sudan.

"In this regard, I plead with the council, as it prepares to renew MINUSCA's mandate, to maintain MINUSCA with adequate force levels and capabilities during the critical consolidation phase," she stressed.

Regional instability

While Bangui consolidates its authority and continues disarming rebel groups, violence is multiplying in the east, driven in part by the war in Sudan that is complicating plans for a gradual MINUSCA troop drawdown, Ms. Rugwabiza said.

The situation in the northeast and southeast remained particularly worrying, notably around mining sites and along the corridors traditionally used by pastoral farmers - often the source of community tensions.

Abducted children, attacked villages

In the southeast, 26 serious incidents were recorded, attributed to suspected members of the Lord's Resistance Army (LRA - a long-established armed group of Ugandan origin - between June and September.

They included reports of rapes and sexual slavery and the abduction of 68 civilians, around 40 of them children.

At the same time, the Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé (AAKG) militia continues to threaten local populations.

However, Ms. Rugwabiza announced Monday's release of three hostages held since December 2025, including the sub-prefect of Bambouti, following several months of mediation with local leaders.

Peace progress

This violence contrasts with advances in the peace process. Since July 2025, 1,907 fighters have been disarmed and demobilised, but their economic re-integration remains difficult and some cannot be located.

Politically, elections are ending. As of 1 October, 127 of the 177 municipalities had installed their municipal councils. The remaining polls, postponed for lack of financial and logistical resources, are due to be held on 25 October.

Yet, this institutional progress is not enough to improve living conditions. Nearly two million Central Africans, or 31 per cent of the population, faced acute food insecurity between April and August.

At the beginning of October, the UN humanitarian plan was only 46.6 per cent funded.

Peacekeeping dilemma

It is in this context that the Security Council must decide, before mid-November, whether to renew MINUSCA's mandate. The mission has already closed several bases in regions deemed sufficiently stable and transferred certain responsibilities to national authorities.

MINUSCA was deployed in 2014, a year after Séléka, a predominantly Muslim coalition, seized power by force and overthrew then-President François Bozizé, triggering a spiral of violence, looting, massacres of civilians and sexual violence.

More than 10 years later, Séléka has been dissolved, two presidential elections have been held and a 2019 peace agreement has brought 14 armed groups into a political process.

Vast areas remain unstable

Meanwhile, vast areas remain unstable. Right now, the UN peacekeeping mission maintains more than 12,000 peacekeepers.

Close 

According to Ms. Rugwabiza, initial assessments show no major deterioration in security in the localities affected by base closures. But, this reorganisation relies in particular on long-range patrols and on strengthening Central African forces.

Divided Security Council

The issue has divided Security Council members. The United States has already argued for larger troop reductions while other countries warn against a hasty withdrawal.

The UN Secretary-General recommended extending the mandate by one year while preserving the military capabilities needed for rapid intervention.

After more than a decade of MINUSCA's presence, CAR has recovered some of its institutions and territory. However, the violence that persists at its borders is a reminder of how dependent these gains remain on international support.

World.title: Former McDonald's exec spills the beans on why healthier menu favorite got the axe
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

McDonald's is looking to expand its chicken offerings, including potentially bringing back grilled chicken sandwiches — a menu item the fast-food giant discontinued in 2020.

At a September investor meeting, McDonald's executives discussed plans to expand the chain's chicken lineup, including grilled chicken sandwiches and wraps, as demand for protein options grows, according to Restaurant Dive.

The renewed interest comes years after McDonald's pulled its grilled chicken sandwich from U.S. menus, raising questions about why the healthier offering disappeared in the first place.

MCDONALD'S EXECUTIVE REVEALS SIMPLE MENU HACKS TO HELP CUSTOMERS PACK MORE PROTEIN INTO MEALS

Chef Mike Haracz, who served as McDonald's manager of culinary innovation from 2015 to 2019, told Fox News Digital why the grilled chicken sandwich ultimately failed to make the cut — and whether it could find its way back to the menu.

The reason was simple: Not enough customers were ordering it, Haracz said.

"For many of the menu items at McDonald's, and this is true for any corporate chain restaurant, there is a certain sales threshold that means it will be profitable, and it makes sense to have in the restaurant," Haracz said.

"Once [those] sales dips below a certain level, it does not make financial sense to keep it on the menu, as you will end up throwing away product."

In 1993, McDonald's introduced a grilled chicken sandwich as a healthier menu offering, but it did not stand the test of time.

MCDONALD'S BRINGS BACK POPULAR ITEM FOR SHORT TIME AS ONE STATE GETS A TREAT

The sandwich consisted of a marinated skinless chicken breast filet, lettuce, tomato, sweet red onion, Monterey Jack cheese and an herb sauce, all piled on a bun, according to a 1993 press release about the menu item.

McDonald's unveiled a more natural preparation of its grilled chicken in 2015, announcing on its website that it would be cooked using only canola oil, olive oil, and real spices and herbs.

The chain revamped the sandwich that year, introducing the Artisan Grilled Chicken Sandwich.

Ultimately, though, the grilled chicken sandwich lost its spot at McDonald's in 2020, when the chain also removed salads from its U.S. menus, according to Business Insider.

In his role at McDonald's, Haracz formulated new menu items for U.S. locations.

CLICK HERE TO 

People looking for healthier options at McDonald's appreciated the grilled chicken offering — especially parents, Haracz noted, because while their kids might have been excited about eating a Happy Meal, the parents were not as interested.

Like many other menu items, the grilled chicken sandwich was cooked on the flattop and held in the universal holding cabinets, or UHCs.

Ultimately, it came down to simple dollars and cents.

Space is valuable at McDonald's, Haracz noted, with each location organized to make every square inch profitable.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

If an item is taking up space but not making money, it's probably not going to last too long, he said.

Consumer satisfaction played a big role, Haracz said, adding that he thinks the grilled chicken sandwich's flavor profile didn't always wow guests.

"McDonald's also realized once it gets to a point, there may be menu cannibalization, [which] means instead of ordering Chicken McNuggets, I might order the chicken sandwich," Haracz said. "Well, if we take the chicken sandwich away, are they still going to order Chicken McNuggets or other items? Most likely they are."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Could the grilled chicken sandwich make a comeback? Haracz thinks it's possible.

"I do think there's a chance it could come back because many chains are dealing with the fact that beef prices are rising, and a way to offset that is to offer a more affordable protein option, which would be chicken," he said.

Haracz said he's not sure if there will be a renaissance of grilled chicken specifically.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Certainly chicken items, in general, will be more popular, not only because of the beef prices, but also, that is a bigger profit margin if McDonald's develops it appropriately."

Fox News Digital reached out to McDonald's for comment.

World.title: DAVID MARCUS: The 5 factors that could decide Michigan's tight and ugly senate race
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Michigan senate race between Republican candidate Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has turned into the marquee matchup of the 2026 midterm, both as a test of the far left’s ability to compete in middle America and as a referendum on President Donald Trump’s leadership. So what will tip the balance?

While many of the basic factors of this contest have already been built in, such as El-Sayed’s disdain for Israel, and Rogers, somewhat qualified, support for the president’s policies, there are a few points emerging that could prove decisive in the final two weeks.

MORNING GLORY: THE POLLS GOT MICHIGAN BADLY WRONG. NOW DEMOCRATS MAY FACE A BIGGER RECKONING

Here are five factors that still could sway who some late deciders vote for, or whether they turn out to vote at all.

1. Temperament

Policy differences aside, Mike Rogers and Abdul El-Sayed are very different people with very different temperaments, and voters Fox News Digital spoke with in Michigan could see, in the same temperamental attributes, either a positive or negative light.

For example, Leon in Detroit, a city employee in his 40s who supported El -Sayed’s opponent Haley Stevens in the primary, said of Abdul, "He just comes off arrogant, like he’s talking down to everybody," but young voters I spoke with in Grand Rapids called this attitude, "confidence," and "assertiveness."

DAVID MARCUS: WHY ABDUL EL-SAYED’S ANTI-BILLIONAIRE SCREEDS MAY NOT PLAY IN GRAND RAPIDS

On the ground, one could almost describe the race as a Thanksgiving dinner in which Rogers is your calm, conservative, wealthy uncle and El-Sayed is the new college boyfriend who keeps talking about how terrible American capitalism is and why the football game on tv is toxic, Michigan voters must choose who they hope will be there next year..

LEE CARTER: 2026 ELECTION COULD ALL COME DOWN TO JUST ONE TYPE OF VOTER

2. Get Out The Vote Campaigns

Back in August, when El-Sayed won a one point victory over Stevens, despite polls showing him up by double digits, it was the aggressive far left ground game, especially in semi urban areas like Dearborn, from groups like the Democratic Socialists of America that saved his bacon.

FOX NEWS POLL: MICHIGAN VOTERS SPLIT BETWEEN EL-SAYED AND ROGERS

As Tiffany Justice, Senior Advisor for Citizen’s Alliance told Fox News Digital, " Michigan elections are won at the margins, and the voters who decide them are working-class conservatives who agree with us but don't have a habit of voting. A TV ad won't get them there. A neighbor knocking on their door, looking them in the eye, and personally inviting them to the polls will."

Rogers claims that the GOP ground game has been improving in the Wolverine State, and he better hope so, in fact the money men on the right might need to shift a bit from ads on screens to faces at screen doors.

TRUMP CAMPAIGN INSIDER REVEALS STRATEGY BEHIND MIDTERM BLITZ THAT WHITE HOUSE HOPES PAYS OFF BIG

3. Donald Trump

You didn’t really think we could leave the president out of this, did you? El-Sayed has dared Trump to campaign with Rogers in Michigan, and Trump has decided to oblige him with a rally set for Sunday, October 25th, just a day after former President Barack Obama will rally with Abdul.

MIKE ROGERS PRESSES CNN'S DANA BASH ON WHY THE PRESS IS 'EAGER' TO DEFEND ABDUL EL-SAYED

Rogers, for his part, has distanced himself from Trump both on the conflict in Iran and on the Canadian tariff war, and notably has done so with no blowback from the commander in chief, a Trump rally will bring out much needed MAGA voters, but could it also alienate independent voters just days before the election.

4. French Riots

El-Sayed’s family ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, as well as his past statements in support of it, have become central to this race, even after Abdul’s hand-waving "sort of" disavowal of the group in a testy town hall exchange, and the backdrop to this issue is the pro Islamist riots in France.

COULD FRANCE'S RIOTS HAPPEN HERE? EXPERTS SEE PARALLELS IN SOCIALISM, IMMIGRATION — AND KEY DIFFERENCES

Americans, including voters in Michigan, are increasingly looking towards Europe, with its burning buildings in Limoges and trampling of free speech in London, as a warning of what happens when a nation has untrammeled immigration without assimilation.

LIZ PEEK: TWO TROUBLED SENATE RACES COULD SPOIL DEMOCRATS' BLUE-WAVE FANTASY

If these riots persist and get worse, both Rogers and El-Sayed will have to address them and the undertones will be clear as day to Michigan voters.

5. The Final Debate

On Wednesday, Rogers and El-Sayed will take the stage for their second and final debate, the first having been contentious, but arguably without a knockout blow for either man. The electorate is much more keyed in than it was on October 8th, when they first sparred, making this the biggest chance either side has to attract new votes.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

How aggressive will El-Sayed be, and can he do it without voters like Leon thinking he is condescending? Can Mike Rogers keep his cool, and should he? In a race this close, one viral moment could make all the difference.

With 2 weeks left to go, the Michigan senate race sits on a knife’s edge, and any of these 5 factors could tip it to one side or to the other.

World.title: ELI STEELE: California forces companies to mine the past for slavery's sins
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Editor's note: This op-ed is part of a series by Eli Steele exploring White guilt in America and the West. Steele is the director of the newly released documentary essay, "White Guilt." See the film at WhiteGuiltFilm.com.

I am a native Californian, and I will never get over the absurdity of seeing California and slavery in the same sentence. I believe I saw it for the first time during the height of the Black Lives Matter unrest. I remembered how I learned in my San Jose elementary school that California entered the Union in 1850 as a free state. Yet here we are again, this time with AB 2599, the Truth in Disclosure Act.

On September 30, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed the act into law. "This is a bill that requires large companies that operated before 1965 to search their records for ties to slavery going back to 1849 and then we make it public," Newsom said. "These are insurance policies on enslaved people. Human beings used as collateral, quite literally as collateral for loans."

REPARATIONS ACTIVISTS CELEBRATE 'IMPORTANT VICTORY' AFTER NEWSOM SIGNS FIRST-EVER CORPORATE SLAVERY BILL

I first learned about these atrocities as a child, and they made me understand how total the dehumanization of slavery was. This history should be learned, but there is something profoundly different about turning history into a legal obligation, sworn under penalty of perjury. This comes at a time when most California students, including Black students, are underperforming in reading and math. So why does Sacramento want to excavate corporate records from 1849 rather than fix the classrooms today?

I believe the point of this investigation is not to discover more history, since we have historians for that, but to unearth confessions that can be commodified as grievances. To see why, you have to understand that White guilt is transactional.

SMITHSONIAN SCREENING DISPUTE PUTS MUSEUM'S COMMITMENT TO DIVERSE VIEWS ON TRIAL: 'RIGHT KIND OF BLACK?'

When I mention White guilt, many people tell me they feel none. Of course they don't. You cannot feel guilt for what you have not done. But, that is not White guilt. "White guilt doesn't have anything to do with actual feelings of guilt," my father, Shelby Steele, author, columnist and Hoover Institution Senior Fellow, says in our new documentary, "White Guilt." White guilt is the collective guilt that says all Whites must carry the sins of the slave masters and segregationists forever.

Activists on the Left have leveraged this accusation for power since the 1960s, and it has produced a terror in many whites, the terror of being tied to this racist past. Those Whites, especially liberal Whites, want innocence most of all, the ability to say, "I am not like those racist whites."

ELI STEELE: NYC ICE SHOOTING EXPOSES HOW WHITE GUILT ERASES PERSONAL RESPONSIBILITY

Black leaders understood early on, as my father did in the 1960s, that Whites would do anything out of their deep, existential desire for innocence. That is what gives White guilt its transactional nature.

My father has said that White guilt is "quite literally the same thing as Black power." From Jesse Jackson, Al Sharpton to Black Lives Matter, these leaders knew their power was in selling Black victimization. Whites bought innocence with everything from endless programs of dependency to lowered education standards. Both sides of this White guilt — Black power symbiosis get what they want, and that is the trap.

ELI STEELE: THE TERROR OF BEING CALLED RACIST IS CRUSHING FREE SPEECH IN AMERICA

In order to keep the lucrative White guilt grift alive, Black leaders have to keep Blacks locked into permanent victimhood, and Whites have to remain condemned as eternally guilty. As America continues to make racial progress, this symbiosis has moved further left, and further into the past, in search of more grievances.

Our state is busy chasing the ghost of past crimes while ignoring the very crimes of miseducation taking place today.

It was California’s reparations task force that demanded AB 2599. This new law applies to any company doing business in California that takes in more than $100 million a year worldwide and existed in some form by the end of 1964.

Once the legislature funds it, any such company will be legally bound to go through its records, and the records of its parent companies, subsidiaries and predecessors, back to 1849. It must report any findings that the company sold or leased slaves, used them as collateral for loans, or insured them. The first filings are due as early as January 15, 2029, and the records will be kept online indefinitely. Every filing will be a confession made under oath, and every confession becomes one more grievance on the public record, available to the activists for as long as the database exists.

Newsom bought his own racial innocence by signing into law the demand that more Black victimization be found. Imagine if Newsom had refused to sign. He would have been blasted as the governor who protected the companies that exploited slaves.

Right there is the very terror that White guilt deploys to kill any reasonable objections. And the corporations on the target list will confess to the sins of their predecessors and buy their innocence with statements of regret and funding for programs and initiatives. None of them will risk the stigmatization that comes with fighting a slavery disclosure law.

REPARATIONS ADVOCATES SLAM CASH COMPENSATION ‘HANDOUT’ LABEL, POINT TO PAST GOVERNMENT REMEDIES

On the same day, Newsom vetoed a bill to exempt reparations payments from state income tax. Where there was no innocence to be gained, he refused to cost his state actual revenue.

On the other side of the bargain are the sellers, and their product is Black victimization. The author of the bill, Democratic Assemblymember Isaac Bryan, told CalMatters which companies he expects to file. "I'm thinking agriculture. I'm thinking banking, insurance. I'm thinking anything in the financial sector." Then he said about what comes next. "Once the public has this disclosure and we have a full accounting of the impact, then it's up to us to decide what that means and what we're going to do about it."

If that last line comes off as a threat, it is because it is. Bryan is telling these companies that once the grievance is documented, lawmakers will set the price of penance. And what this statement also reveals is that this is nothing more than a fishing expedition to find the crime to fuel the White guilt-Black power symbiosis.

CALIFORNIA COUNTY APPROVES REPARATIONS PLAN AS NEIGHBORING SCHOOL DISTRICT 'BLACK THRIVING' EFFORT STALLS

That is why the left will never let the White guilt — Black power symbiosis die out. Kristin Nimmers, policy and campaign manager for the California Black Power Network, told Fox News Digital that "a single check is not going to holistically repair our communities." She wants "a harm-based approach, so whoever was harmed should be entitled to that repair."

The rest of us are chum in this transaction, Black children most of all. California released its new test scores on October 15. Only 33.7% of Black students met the state standard in English. In math, it was 21.5%. Our state is busy chasing the ghost of past crimes while ignoring the very crimes of miseducation taking place today.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

But the White guilt-Black power symbiosis never had any interest in doing the hard work of developing young minds into individual talents. Instead, this symbiosis will wait for the companies to report back on the sins of their predecessors, and then its elites will hold up the evidence as yet more proof that California and America are systemically racist.

The past will be dragged into the present as if no progress had ever been made, the accusation refreshed and sharpened for another generation. And worst of all, the Black children who needed a state that believed in their future will instead be told that the sins in that database, from 1849, are what has been holding them back all along.
