World.title: Gavin Newsom’s legislative minions just got a lesson in constitutional supremacy
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

It is no surprise that a unanimous three-judge panel of the Ninth Circuit just enjoined the blatantly unconstitutional attempt by the "No-Longer-So-Golden State" to impose restrictions on the ability of ICE and other federal agents to enforce federal immigration law. That panel was doing exactly what federal courts are supposed to do — uphold the U.S. Constitution.

On October 14 in U.S. v. California, the court tossed the so-called "No Vigilantes Act" (NVA) onto the ash heap. This law was part of the state’s continuing effort to obstruct federal immigration enforcement, which has included relentless public attacks by the governor and state officials on federal agents just trying to do their job of enforcing the law. That includes noxious claims like Newsom likening them to the thuggish "secret police" of an "authoritarian" state.

The NVA required any non-uniformed "federal law enforcement officer" operating in California to "visibly display identification" when carrying out federal law enforcement duties. A federal agent violating this requirement could be criminally prosecuted by the state.

FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS NEW YORK LAW BANNING ICE AGENTS FROM WEARING MASKS

As the Ninth Circuit pointed out, the Supremacy Clause in Article VI makes the "Constitution, and the Laws of the United States … the Supreme Law of the Land." In other words, federal law not only overrides any state law to the contrary, but it requires what is called "intergovernmental immunity." Under "the intergovernmental immunity component of the Supremacy Clause … states may not directly regulate the Federal Government’s operations or property." The panel cites to a 1996 Ninth Circuit decision, Blackburn v. U.S., on this issue, but then points out that this basic legal principle — that states cannot interfere in federal functions — goes all the way back to one of the most seminal Supreme Court cases in our history, McCulloch v. Maryland (1819). "It is the very essence of Supremacy," said the Court in McCulloch, "to remove all obstacles to its action within its own sphere, and so to modify every power vested in subordinate governments, as to exempt its own operations from their own influence." That is why "States have no power … to retard, impede, burden, or in any manner control the operations of the constitutional laws enacted by Congress to carry into execution the powers vested in the General Government."

California tried to argue that the NVA was constitutional because it did not "substantially burden" federal law enforcement. But the Ninth Circuit shot that down, too, saying any attempt by a state law to directly regulate "the conduct of the United States … is void irrespective of whether the regulated activities are essential to federal functions or operations, and irrespective of the degree to which the state law interferes with such functions or operations."

What made this law even worse was its threat to criminally prosecute federal agents. This is especially ironic because California attempted to do with the NVA what the Supreme Court specifically told the state it couldn’t do 136 years ago in another seminal case, In re Neagle (1890), also cited by the Ninth Circuit panel. That decision reads like a Hollywood movie but also demonstrates just how bizarre state officials have acted in California for a long time, not just in today’s heated political arena.

In re Neagle involved the state of California trying to prosecute a U.S. Marshal for murder. Marshal David Neagle was acting as a bodyguard for Supreme Court Justice Stephen Field, a job the U.S. Marshal’s Service still carries out today. He shot and killed the former chief justice of California’s state supreme court, David Terry, at a railway station in the San Joaquin Valley, after Terry tried to assassinate Field. Terry was known for his violent temper and apparently had a grudge against Field for a court decision involving the prior divorce of Terry’s current wife.

DOJ DEMANDS SANCTUARY STATES END 'BLATANTLY UNLAWFUL' ANTI-ICE POLICY AS A MATTER OF LIFE AND DEATH

The Ninth Circuit quoted the Supreme Court’s opinion in Neagle that even the "most unquestionable and most universally applicable of state laws, such as those concerning murder, will not be allowed to control the conduct a marshal of the United States acting under and in pursuance of the laws of the United States." California couldn’t prosecute a U.S. Marshal then for doing his job, and it cannot criminally prosecute federal agents now who are "acting under and in pursuance of the [immigration] laws of the United States." End of story, end of case, end of unconstitutional state law.

By the way, a second law enacted by California’s constitutionally ignorant legislators, the "No Secret Police Act," was already enjoined by a lower court for the same reason. That law made it a criminal offense for federal agents to wear "a facial covering that conceals or obscures their facial identity." You know, the same agents who have been villainized, doxxed, followed home, harassed, run down by cars, and shot at by thugs who masquerade as protesters.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

As the Ninth Circuit correctly recognized, the lawlessness occurring in California is not limited to thugs. Perhaps some remedial courses on the Constitution for Governor Newsom and the California legislature may be in order.

World.title: Trump's MOAB threat could put Iran's deepest bunkers in America's crosshairs
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Take President Donald Trump’s threat on the MOAB seriously. The U.S. Air Force’s GBU-43 Massive Ordnance Air Blast weapon, nicknamed the "mother of all bombs," could figure prominently in any new airstrike plans targeting Iran.

"The mother of all bombs is not nuclear," Trump said. "This is just an extremely large bomb. It’s like a tiny nuclear bomb, but the mother of all bombs is one big bomb, but it’s not nuclear."

"I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to," Trump said.

FRESH ACTIVITY EMERGES AT IRAN’S DEEPLY BURIED NUCLEAR SITE AS TRUMP WARNS IRAN NOT TO ‘GET CUTE’

He’s right. The U.S. has a range of precision weapons that can knock out any suspicious target in Iran, including the construction activity at Pickaxe mountain. Admiral Bradley Cooper, Commander, United States Central Command, has detailed knowledge of high-value Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps sites that could be MOAB targets.

President Trump has said he won’t strike Iran prior to the mid-terms, but clearly he is looking at Central Command’s strike briefing charts in great detail. And he wants Iran to know it.

Here are four reasons the MOAB is a formidable threat.

Trump ordered the first use of a MOAB in Afghanistan in April 2017

The MOAB was dropped on April 13, 2017, on a cave complex in Nangarhar Province, Afghanistan. "There was no surprise," then-Secretary of Defense James Mattis said of the MOAB. "The battle was going on, and we were going to use what was necessary to break ISIS," he added. Mattis said he wasn’t going to waste time "digging into tunnels to count bodies"; CNN reported 94 ISIS fighters killed.

Too big for U.S. bombers

While America’s B-2, B-52 and B-1 bombers can easily carry the weight of the 21,000-lb. MOAB, the problem is the shape. The MOAB used in 2017 was too big to fit on the standard racks and rotary launchers in the bomber weapons bays. For the Afghanistan mission, the MOAB was loaded on a special cradle and slid out of the back ramp of an MC-130 while in flight. Don’t worry about the MC-130s. Yes, the basic C-130 is a cargo plane, but the Special Operations versions like the MC-130 are adapted for clandestine missions. This is also where air dominance over Iran comes in handy. The initial weeks of Operation Epic Fury knocked out Iran’s Russian-built integrated air defenses. Subsequent strikes by CENTCOM have prevented Iran from reconstituting their air defenses. MC-130s on a MOAB mission might also get help with electronic warfare and other attack suppression from the Space Force, U.S. Air Force, and U.S. Navy carrier-based aircraft like the EA-18G, F-35C and E-2D.

MOAB is a precision weapon

The clue is the official designation of GBU-43 which stands for Guided Bomb Unit. Small drogue parachutes stabilize the MOAB upon release and then the satellite-guidance kit guides the bomb to the designated point of impact. MOAB is actually an air burst; earlier, smaller heavy air blast weapons were used in World War II and in Vietnam under the name "daisy-cutter." The theory behind an air burst is to maximize blast effect without muffling by the ground.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Built for the Iraq war

The MOAB was built in great haste by the Air Force Research Lab just prior to Operation Iraqi Freedom in 2003. At the time, reports suggested Iraq might have built large underground bunkers for dictator Saddam Hussein’s loyal troops. Saddam Hussein back in 1991 had famously taunted the U.S.-led Coalition about engaging in "the mother of all battles," which, of course, turned out to be the airpower-led victory of Operation Desert Storm.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Trump’s decision to bring up the MOAB is all about keeping military pressure on the IRGC as the U.S. naval blockade squeezes their oil revenue. The MOAB would be an intimidation weapon for knocking out military targets. IRGC commanders would face major losses. And it’s also a reminder that the U.S. can carry out any military strike deemed necessary, to prevent Iran’s path to a nuclear weapon and stop their terrorism.

World.title: Alabama governor commutes death sentence as doubts emerge about evidence in murder conviction
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey, a Republican, commuted the sentence of a death row inmate on Tuesday after the current Jefferson County district attorney and several former judges and prosecutors raised concerns about his conviction.

The governor said she was commuting Toforest Johnson’s death sentence to life in prison without parole. Johnson, who has long maintained his innocence, was convicted in the 1995 murder of Jefferson County Deputy Sheriff William Hardy. He remains incarcerated at the Holman Correctional Facility.

"When presented with Mr. Johnson’s case, I had concerns there was not enough direct evidence to carry out the most serious punishment, death," Ivey said in a statement. "My decision is not a determination of innocence, but a recognition that the circumstances of this case justify commuting his death sentence to life imprisonment, without possibility of parole."

Ivey has commuted the death sentences of three death row inmates since she became governor in 2017. She has also overseen 27 executions during her tenure, which will end in January because she is term-limited and cannot run for re-election.

GOP GOV DEWINE URGES OHIO TO ABOLISH THE DEATH PENALTY, SAYS IT IS NO LONGER A DETERRENT

The governor spared his life despite Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall urging her last week to reject the clemency request and "respect the jury's decision" and the rulings of the courts reviewing Johnson's case.

On July 19, 1995, Hardy was shot twice in the head as he was working off-duty security outside a hotel in Birmingham. Johnson said he was on the other side of the city when the shooting happened.

One of Johnson’s attorneys, Ty Alper, said he and his client are grateful to Ivey for "diligently reviewing Toforest’s case and taking action to spare an innocent man from execution," but added that they will continue to fight to overturn the conviction.

"Toforest Johnson is innocent. Now it is up to the courts to overturn his conviction and grant him a new trial. We will keep fighting until he is home with his family," Alper said in a statement.

LAWYERS, EXPERTS URGE TENNESSEE GOVERNOR TO COMMUTE CHRISTA PIKE’S SENTENCE AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION

Johnson's attorneys have waged a yearslong legal battle to secure a new trial. His push for a new trial has received national attention and attracted widespread support, including from prominent lawyers, such as the original prosecutor in his case, as well as celebrities such as Kim Kardashian.

Several former judges and prosecutors have joined supporters seeking a new trial for Johnson over questions about his conviction. Former Alabama Attorney General Bill Baxley, former Chief Justices of the Alabama Supreme Court Sonny Hornsby and Drayton Nabers and other former judges and prosecutors have submitted briefs or written editorials backing a new trial.

Jefferson County District Attorney Danny Carr, who was elected in 2018, is among those who have backed Johnson’s call for a new trial. In 2024, Carr wrote in a court filing that the "evidence in this case has unraveled over 20 years."

Carr said that credible alibi witnesses placed Johnson in another area at the time of the shooting. He also said there are multiple reasons to doubt the key prosecution witness, who "claimed she overheard Johnson confess to the murder on a three-way phone call on which she was eavesdropping."

LONGEST-SERVING US PRISONER DIES AT 101 AFTER ESCAPING DEATH PENALTY 8 TIMES

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The woman testified during Johnson's 1998 trial that she was eavesdropping on a phone call when she heard a man she believed was Johnson admitting to the shooting.

She received a $5,000 reward in 2001 for her assistance in the case.

Johnson’s lawyers said that the state withheld evidence of monetary incentive for her testimony.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: Russia frees American Stephen Hubbard, 74, as Trump envoy meets with Putin
World.content:
American Stephen Hubbard was released by Russia on Wednesday, the latest sign of warmer ties with the Kremlin as Washington pressures Kyiv to agree to a deal that ends Moscow’s war.

The news of Hubbard’s release followed talks between U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff and President Vladimir Putin early Wednesday. Putin said that Hubbard, 74, was at the airport and Witkoff thanked the Russian leader for his release.

Washington has courted the Kremlin for weeks, and the release of Hubbard — a retired Michigan schoolteacher detained in Ukraine in 2022 — will give President Donald Trump a victory to tout after backlash at home and abroad for his tilt away from Ukraine.

Trump said Tuesday that he had raised with Putin the idea of releasing Hubbard, who was being held in Russia on charges he denies of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine.

The meeting in St. Petersburg, which Jared Kushner was expected to join virtually, comes after the American negotiators met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European leaders in the Norwegian capital, Oslo.

Ukraine brought forward new ideas and proposals at those talks, a U.S. official told NBC News, adding that “meaningful progress” was made as the Trump administration intensifies its peace push.

Diplomacy has made little headway for months, and this renewed American effort has fueled backlash at home and abroad given a series of apparent moves to withhold support from Ukraine and align more closely with Russia.

Witkoff was greeted by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the international airport outside St. Petersburg, Russia, on Wednesday. TASS via AP

Trump renewed his pressure campaign, which has fueled concern that the U.S. is no longer committed to Kyiv’s defense against its Moscow invaders.

“We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.”

Kremlin adviser Yuri Ushakov said that Ukraine would dominate the talks between Putin and Witkoff at the Constantine Palace in St. Petersburg. Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev was also due to join, Ushakov said.

Witkoff leaves the Grand Hotel in Oslo, Noway, on Tuesday, before Ukraine talks. Jonas Been Henriksen / AFP via Getty Images

The goal for the meeting with Putin was to build on the progress made in Oslo, discuss the proposals with Russia and create a pathway toward direct negotiations, the U.S. official said.

Zelenskyy said that a potential trilateral leaders’ meeting was “one of the important ideas” raised in Oslo after Tuesday’s talks, which also included the leaders of Norway and Finland.

Putin has so far insisted any meeting with Zelenskyy could only happen once a deal is finalized and take place in Moscow, a nonstarter for the Ukrainians. The Kremlin has also shown little sign of shifting from its hardline demands, which include seizing Ukraine’s entire eastern Donbas region.

Trump signed a diesel fuel deal with Russia earlier this month and waived new sanctions on Moscow, while Kyiv says it received no advanced warning about at least three major Russian attacks and that restrictions on Elon Musk’s Starshield satellite service continue to hamper its aerial defenses and battlefield operations.

Zelenskyy and Witkoff embrace, accompanied by Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, right, and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, left, during their meeting in Oslo on Tuesday. Heiko Junge / AFP via Getty

After the talks with Witkoff on Tuesday, Zelenskyy told reporters the recent issues on security cooperation with the U.S. have been resolved.

“We are thankful that intelligence works now — I am speaking about early warning systems, which are very important for our people, for our children and civilians,” he said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the talks in Oslo “positive,” but said “nothing unexpected” came out of them. “Armed with those ideas,” Witkoff will go to St. Petersburg, Rubio said, and share them with the Russian side “and let’s see if we can make some progress.”

Destroyed cars among debris in the courtyard of a residential building following a Russian drone attack on Kyiv on Wednesday. Serhii Okunev / AFP via Getty

Rubio once again denied that the White House was behind any slowdown to Ukraine’s use of the internet service, saying this was an issue for Musk and SpaceX. Musk himself said last week any decision was down to Trump.

Deadly Russian attacks continued to hit Ukraine, meanwhile, with at least nine civilians killed across the country on Wednesday as Moscow ramps up its strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of winter.

Authorities in Russia’s border Bryansk region said Wednesday one person was killed in a Ukrainian strike.

World.title: Woman sexually assaulted at fraternity near University of Chicago, lawsuit alleges
World.content:
A 19-year-old woman filed a lawsuit Monday alleging she was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago in February amid heightened scrutiny of sexual misconduct on college campuses.

The college student, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, sued in Cook County Circuit Court, alleging that the sexual assault took place during a party at the Alpha Delta Phi fraternity house on Feb. 7. It names Alpha Delta Phi Inc. and Chicago Society of Alpha Delta Phi as defendants.

“The grief that this has imposed upon me is indescribable,” Doe told NBC News in an interview. “It is the first thing I think about whenever I wake up every day and the last thing I think about whenever I fall asleep.”

Doe’s case comes weeks after a former Cornell University student claimed in a lawsuit that she was gang-raped at a fraternity party, causing national outrage, and just days after a woman reported that she was sexually assaulted at a party hosted by a different fraternity near the University of Chicago.

The University of Chicago, which does not recognize fraternities as official student organizations, said in a statement that it was “prepared to help the Chicago Police Department” in its investigation.

“These allegations are very disturbing to the University community,” said a university spokesperson, Gerald McSwiggan. “The University of Chicago is committed to addressing and preventing incidents of sexual assault.”

Alpha Delta Phi’s national team said in a statement that it is aware of the allegations and that it “suspended the member involved.”

“The conduct described is deeply troubling and inconsistent with our values,” it said. “We are committed to the safety and well-being of our members and communities and will cooperate with law enforcement as appropriate.”

Alpha Delta Phi’s Chicago chapter referred all requests to its national organization.

Doe — who is not a student at the University of Chicago — said she learned about the party on Instagram and had gone to parties at the fraternity house previously. That night, she said, she went to the party with several friends, none of whom are students at the university.

Doe said she was dancing with friends when a fraternity brother approached her. The fraternity brother offered her a shot, which she said immediately made her feel unsteady and lightheaded, according to the lawsuit.

She said she had had only two drinks before she took the shot, spaced out over roughly two hours. She described having the “spins” and feeling as though her “vision was underwater.”

“I know myself, and that was not the amount with how intoxicated I felt after the shot that I took with him,” she said. “I’ve never felt like that before.”

She added that she watched the fraternity brother pour the shot and did not notice anything “odd.”

The fraternity member then directed Doe to follow him to a secluded bedroom on a different floor of the fraternity house, according to the lawsuit. Doe expressed her unsteadiness and lightheadedness, which the fraternity member ignored, the lawsuit says.

The fraternity brother began to make “unwanted and nonconsensual sexual advances” on the woman, the lawsuit says. It says she “lost all physical and verbal ability to refuse” the fraternity member’s alleged sexual advances.

“I remember backing onto the bed because I knew what was about to happen, but I just — I didn’t feel like I was strong enough to get out,” she told NBC News.

The lawsuit says that although her verbal ability was limited, she managed to plead with the fraternity brother to wear a condom, which he refused to do. The fraternity brother then penetrated her “without her consent,” the lawsuit says.

After the alleged encounter, the man left Doe alone and unconscious, according to the suit. It alleges that other fraternity brothers initially blocked her friend from going upstairs to find her.

Her friend found her unconscious and helped her out of the house, according to the complaint. She said that she faintly remembers her shirt being on backward when she woke up but that she was not sure how she got her clothes on.

She struggled to speak and walk as they escorted her out of the home, according to the lawsuit. Doe said she slept over at her friend’s dorm room that night.

The next morning, Doe found bloodstains in her underwear and went to the hospital, where she reported the incident to the Chicago Police Department, according to a police report. Doe told police she believed the alcohol was laced with something, according to the report.

Police confirmed that a 19-year-old who reported a sexual assault at the fraternity house took herself to Illinois Masonic Hospital for treatment on Feb. 8. Doe received a sexual assault evidence collection kit at the hospital, according to the police report.

Days later, the woman was contacted by the University of Chicago Police Department, which she said was investigating her case. Doe said that university police spoke with her for roughly 30 minutes over the phone but that she has not heard from them since. The university police department declined to give Doe records related to her case without a subpoena, she alleges in her lawsuit.

A spokesperson for the city’s police department said it was investigating the incident; the spokesperson did not answer questions about the university police department’s involvement in the case.

Doe is seeking a trial by jury and an amount in excess of $200,000, plus costs.

Doe’s lawyer, Mike Grieco of Gould Grieco & Hensley, said the aim is to also “ensure that this doesn’t happen again, and to help reform” policies within the university.

The University of Chicago has been roiled in recent days by a separate allegation of a sexual assault at a fraternity party near campus. A 21-year-old woman told police she was sexually assaulted this month at a party held at the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity house, just off campus. Chicago police said no arrests have been made in either case.

“At the end of the day, what happened to me is not unique, and it’s not rare. It happens way more than people realize,” Doe said. “There are so many other survivors out there who suffer in silence.”

World.title: Russians locked out of bank accounts and apartments as Ukraine hits data centers
World.content:
While most Yandex services have been coming back online, three people told NBC News they had been left locked out of their disposable cash and savings for days after disruptions to Yandex Pay, a digital payment service that many Russians use.

Irina, 21, said that in the future she will diversify her deposits across different banks and have a “substantial cash reserve” just in case.

Yandex said Oct. 9 that no employees were hurt and that it is working to restore service.

“Data centers are the iron heart of Yandex,” the statement said. “Their operation is critical for services that have become part of people’s everyday lives.”

Anastasiya Mityaeva, 25, who splits her time between Moscow and the southern city of Krasnodar, said she was “shocked” by the outages, which initially left her family worried about being able to pay down their mortgage after her account, her mother’s account and her grandmother’s account were all inaccessible.

“The uncertainty was scary,” said Mityaeva, who has 2 million followers on TikTok and is originally from Russian-annexed Crimea. “We realized just how much hangs on Yandex. We did not quite appreciate it before.”

Mityaeva, who regained access to her money after several days, also had issues calling a taxi on the first day of the outages and encountered problems with the system to enter her apartment building. Her Yandex home voice assistant, equivalent to an Amazon Echo, stopped responding to requests to play music and turn off the lights.

She did not blame the company, saying Yandex was a “hostage of the situation,” adding: “I understand that this was not up to them. This came from the outside.”

Others were more critical of the company. Viktoria, 30, a barista from Moscow, said she plans to stop using Yandex completely after she was unable to access her money during the outages, describing it as the last straw after other recent issues.

She said Saturday that she once again had access to her money through Yandex Pay but that the service was displaying the wrong balance on her account.

Three taxi drivers in Moscow, who use Yandex’s taxi application to take orders and get paid, all told NBC News they could not see how much money they were making and could not withdraw their earnings during the outage. One of the drivers said he has stopped working altogether until the problem gets fixed. He is originally from Kyrgyzstan and did not know why the outages were happening.
