World.title: Secret Service study explores how to prevent workplace violence
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Secret Service, best known for protecting presidents and dignitaries, is leveraging its vast intelligence gathering, research capabilities and other tools to help prevent workplace violence.

A new report seen by NBC News from the Secret Service’s National Threat Assessment Center analyzed 50 cases of workplace violence over the past decade to seek common motivations, tactics and warning signs, including the shooting at the Capital Gazette in 2018 in Annapolis, Maryland, in which a gunman killed five employees. In the incidents under review, 119 were killed and 128 were injured. The report was born of the center’s examination of mass attacks, which found most of the targeted locations were businesses.

“Which is why we launched this initiative,” said Lina Alathari, who leads the threat assessment center. “To look at how can we prevent targeted workplace violence. What is the thinking, behavior and circumstances of workplace attackers?”

The threat assessment center was developed to study how other kinds of attacks could be prevented. Officials use that knowledge and apply it in other situations, such as school shootings, mass attacks and now workplace violence.

The report, expected to be released Wednesday, is intended to provide guidance to businesses, human resources officials, local law enforcement agencies and mental health professionals who mitigate workplace risks.

Alathari said there are almost always warning signs before someone attacks. While the reviewed cases do not suggest that attackers belong to any specific demographic group, they do share similar patterns.

“Grievances are always the No. 1 motive that might sort of trigger someone to carry out an attack,” Alathari said.

Retail and service businesses are the most frequently attacked, because the public often has easy access, followed by manufacturing and healthcare facilities.

The connection between a targeted business and a perpetrator is typically direct and personal; 16 of the attackers were actively employed at the sites they targeted. Others are tied through current or estranged romantic partners, she said.

According to the Secret Service’s research, more than 40% of the suspects in cases of such violence had histories of domestic violence, but they were not always charged with crimes related to that violence, the report found.

Given the prevalence of violence against intimate partners, the study urges workplaces to recognize signs and support employees.

“That includes empowering those who may be experiencing stalking, harassing, threats from romantic partners or other relatives to feel connected enough to come forward and ask for help,” Alathari said.

Most of the attackers used firearms, but others used knives, explosives or vehicles. Nearly 25% of the attacks involved more than one weapon. The resolutions of the incidents varied; in more than 75% of them, attackers stopped causing harm on their own and were arrested at the scene. Nearly half died by suicide. In 14% of the studied cases, law enforcement ended the violence by killing the suspect.

The National Threat Assessment Center Team described one case in which the suspect had been fired but the employee’s badge access remained active and allowed the attacker to return and gain access. It advised people to look for common warning signs: changes in behavior, depression, increased absenteeism, discussion of weapons, expression of violent thoughts or any kind of threats against co-workers.

Last year, the Secret Service led 400 training sessions on preventing mass violence for roughly 50,000 participants nationwide.

“There are always opportunities for intervention, and what I can tell you is that the cost of inaction can be deadly,” Alathari said.

World.title: Texas couple charged in shooting death of Missouri high schooler on her way to the zoo
World.content:
A couple from Texas were charged this week in the deadly freeway shooting of a 17-year-old high school girl who was driving to the zoo for a Halloween celebration.

The St. Louis County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office in Missouri charged Willie Herndon, 42, with first-degree murder and armed criminal action in connection with last week’s attack, which killed Alyssa Wilson, authorities said Monday.

Taiya Herndon, who investigators said is his wife, is charged with hindering prosecution, accused of driving her husband to an Illinois hotel 12 miles from St. Louis, prosecuting attorney Melissa Price Smith said at a news conference Monday.

It’s not clear whether either of the two, from Arlington, Texas, has a lawyer. The state public defender’s office for the area did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Alyssa Wilson. Photo courtesy Robert Hickman via KSDK

The attack killed Alyssa, who was on the precipice of adulthood and optimistic about the journey ahead, her father, Robert Hickman, said at the news conference.

“Alyssa was 17, excited about her life, excited about her future,” he said as he teared up.

The shooting occurred around 7 p.m. Wednesday, when Alyssa was driving south on Interstate 170 in Overland, Missouri, just northwest of St. Louis, said Jack Abell, chief deputy commander of the region’s Major Case Squad. She was on her way to Halloween festivities at the St. Louis Zoo, known as “Boo at the Zoo,” Abell said.

According to security video, Alyssa was traveling south and had just passed a white Buick Enclave that was stopped on the shoulder when the sound of a single round was heard, Abell said at the news conference.

“A person exited the vehicle and stood outside for a short period of time,” he said. “There was a gunshot, got back in the vehicle. The vehicle turned its hazards off and continued on.”

Robert Hickman at a news conference in St. Louis on Monday. KSDK

The round went through the rear of the red Buick Encore that Alyssa was driving, Abell said. First responders found Alyssa with a gunshot wound, he said. She was rushed to Barnes-Jewish Hospital in St. Louis, where she was pronounced dead.

The Herndons had no connection to the girl, Abell said.

Wilson was 60 days from turning 18, said Hickman, her father.

“We were getting ready to take our first family vacation together to go to Disney for her to see her favorite person in the world, Princess Tiana,” he said, referring to the character from the animated movie “The Princess and the Frog.”

“Unfortunately, she’s not going to get to do that anymore,” Hickman said. “This was a senseless act.”

The couple were found after investigators used security video of the shooting, as well as automated license plate readers, to track that Buick, which had an out-of-state registration, Abell said.

The vehicle was under surveillance for “long hours” before investigators saw the couple come out of the hotel in Caseyville, where they were taken into custody Friday, he said.

A judge-approved search in Illinois turned up a gun, as well as “supporting evidence,” Abell said, and investigators were analyzing a shell casing found alongside the freeway in Overland.

Major Crimes Unit investigators interviewed Willie Herndon, he said, and came away with a better understanding of the crime.

“During the interview, Willie Herndon provided details regarding his involvement in the incident and additional information pertaining to possible ongoing investigations in other areas,” Abell said. “Those investigations are continuing as we speak.”

The region’s top prosecutor, Price Smith, said charges were filed in Missouri on Friday. Bail in those cases was set at $1 million for Willie Herndon and $500,000 for Taiya Herndon, to be posted in full, the Major Case Squad said in a statement.

The two were being held as prosecutors await extradition to Missouri, authorities said.

Inmate records for the St. Clair County Jail in Illinois show Taiya Herndon is being held on an out-of-state warrant with no bail. The records say she was booked Saturday.

No jail records for Willie Herndon were available.

Alongside 20 or so Major Crimes Unit investigators, the case received help from law enforcement far and wide, authorities said.

“The case was solved within 36 hours due to the collaborative efforts of the FBI, ATF and the many law enforcement agencies that are in this room,” FBI St. Louis Assistant Special Agent in Charge Dave Herr said at Monday’s news conference.

Abell said he could not discuss a possible motive because cases that may be connected to the attack were still under investigation.

World.title: Heath Ledger and James Avery honored by former co-stars on ‘Dancing with the Stars’
World.content:
There was not a dry eye in the ballroom Tuesday night after celebrities competing on “Dancing with the Stars” paid tribute to those who left an impact on them, who included actors Heath Ledger and James Avery.

The dedication week is a tradition for the reality series, often leading to emotional moments on the normally lighthearted dance series. Among those competing this season are actors Julia Stiles and Tatyana Ali, who chose to honor their former co-stars.

Stiles reflected on her time with Ledger while they were filming their ’90s rom-com “10 Things I Hate About You,” in which Ledger’s role as the mischievous Patrick Verona solidified him as a teen heartthrob. Ledger died in 2008 of an accidental overdose caused by mixing painkillers and sedatives that were prescribed to him.

In her rehearsal package, Stiles recalled how authentic Ledger was during the filming. She teared up talking about how easy it was working with him.

She and her partner, Ezra Sosa, did a contemporary dance to a cover of Frankie Valli’s “Can’t Take My Eyes Off of You.” It was an homage to a famous scene from the movie in which Ledger’s character serenades Stiles.

“I have so many great memories, but I’m also sad, because I really wish that I could pick up the phone and be like: ‘Hey, dude, people really care about that movie. We did something special,’” Stiles said. “And I can’t do that.”

Before the episode aired, the partners posted a joint Instagram statement saying the dance was about honoring “a film that changed so many lives, and someone whose impact continues to be felt by generations.”

Stiles ended her dance by placing a rose down in front of a photo of Ledger. When she turned back, the entire main cast of “10 Things I Hate About You” was on the dance floor to join her.

Actors Andrew Keegan, Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Larisa Oleynik, Susan May Pratt and Gabrielle Union joined hands with Stiles as the music faded.

Judge Derek Hough thanked the cast for joining Stiles for the moment after the performance ended.

“I mean, how cool is it to have created something that will last forever, you know?” Hough said. “And tonight, this performance will last forever, as well. It was a perfect combination of joy, fun and emotion.”

Stiles earned a combined total of 36 from the four judges, her best score of the competition series so far.

Another poignant dedication came from the former cast members of the “Fresh Prince of Bel-Air,” as Ali and Alfonso Ribeiro danced in honor of Avery, their on-screen father. Avery, who portrayed Uncle Phil on the series, died on New Year’s Eve in 2013 following complications from open-heart surgery.

Before the episode, Ali posted a TikTok video explaining how much Avery meant to her. She spoke about how he offered her mentorship and “poured” into her at a young age.

“I met him when I was 11 years old,” Ali said. “Every holiday, James would give me a baby doll. I have a collection of beautiful baby dolls. And he told me, ‘I’m giving you these dolls because they look like you, and I always want you to know how beautiful you are.’”

In the segment showing her rehearsals, Ali said she “loved him a lot.”

Ribeiro called it a blessing of his life to be able to do the dance with Ali.

Ribeiro, Ali and her partner, Jan Ravnik, danced a Viennese waltz to Nancy Wilson’s “(You Don’t Know) How Glad I Am.” The song was a cover recorded by Ali, who said Wilson was one of Avery’s favorite artists.

During the dance, Ravnik left Ali on the dance floor and allowed Ribeiro to end the performance with her. The two shared a tearful hug when the music stopped, with a portrait of Avery on display behind them.

The four judges gave Ali a combined score of 32, her best of the season.

Judge Carrie Ann Inaba said she felt honored to be able to watch the former on-screen siblings dance together.

“Dance plays a role in our lives, like, a real role,” Inaba said. “And tonight, I saw it play this role right here live. And you dance like — it was like watching an old Hollywood film come to life, and all of your grace.”

World.title: Armed federal agents knock on doors looking for noncitizen voters
World.content:
Armed and in uniform, federal agents from the Department of Homeland Security have been knocking on doors in several states to ask residents about their immigration status — and to inquire if they have registered to vote or cast votes in past elections, a CBS News Investigation has found.

The operation is part of an effort to root out potential noncitizen voters ahead of the midterms. DHS has alleged that there could be as many as 250,000 citizens illegally registered to vote, although election experts have disputed the accuracy of this figure. Just 156 people have been charged with voting-fraud related offenses since the beginning of the Trump administration, according to the Department of Justice. There are 227 million registered voters in the U.S.

Critics say that sending armed federal agents to the doors of U.S. residents could be intimidating for legal voters.

"What we're seeing now is the federal government is inserting itself into the state process for verifying their voter roles in an unprecedented way," said Jessica Marsden, a lawyer for Protect Democracy, a left-leaning advocacy group that is suing the federal agency over the door-knocking campaign. "And they are doing it in a way that seems maximally designed to scare lawful voters from participating."

Photos posted by HSI NorCal of Homeland Security agents knocking on doors in the San Francisco area. X/@HSINorCal

The home visits ramped up in September, in the thick of the midterm campaign season, and continued over the past weekend. The Justice Department announced Monday that Homeland Security agents in California arrested more than 20 people, all of them green card holders, on allegations they had illegally registered or cast a vote.

As part of that roundup, dozens of federal agents descended on the residence of a 72-year-old man from Belize, who was taken from his home in his pajamas and arrested on charges he allegedly voted illegally in the past four elections.

"HSI is actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found," said a DHS spokesperson. "Under President Trump, HSI is committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens and only American citizens are electing American leaders."

Eric Balliet, a former Homeland Security Investigations agent, said the door-knocking operation is a significant departure from traditional law enforcement activities.

"In my 23 years with HSI, I never engaged in or was aware of any incident of initiative that sent Special Agents to private residences to verify the eligibility of voters," Balliet said, who served in the federal government under multiple administrations.

In June, the DHS directed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, to assist in deportations of alleged noncitizen voters. Homeland Security Investigations, the agency conducting the at-home visits, is one of the enforcement arms of ICE and typically focuses on criminal cross border investigations like child exploitation, drug smuggling and money laundering.

Months later after the announcement, hundreds of agents were pulled off their cases and assigned to track down alleged noncitizen voters as part of a "surge" initiative, according to internal documents reviewed by CBS News. The directive, first reported by CNN, describes a "Criminal Voter Fraud " initiative that includes "field reviews" in at least six states including California, Georgia, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.

Photos and videos posted on X show agents from Homeland Security Investigations, some of whom are carrying firearms, approaching houses and knocking on doors, under captions like, "AMERICAN ELECTIONS ARE FOR AMERICANS."

One photo from Kansas City HSI's account shows four agents at the door of a woman standing on her porch holding a child's hand.

Homeland Security agents making an arrest in the Kansas City area. X/@HSIKansasCity

The woman is identified in a Department of Justice press release as Mariana Alexandra Dewey, a Peruvian national who was charged with four counts of voter-fraud related crimes including illegally casting a ballot in the 2024 election. Her case has not yet been heard. Her lawyer declined to respond to CBS News' request for comment.

For civil rights advocates, the show of force has sparked concerns about the chilling effect it could have on legal voters.

"It is sending the signal to a much broader community, do not show up at the polls. Do not vote," said Dr. Carol Anderson, a professor of African American Studies at Emory University.

"And so if you are somebody who has registered to vote and you're a naturalized citizen, what you see in that community is that — because this is not a regime that makes those discernments — that you're gonna stay away from the voting booth."

A DHS spokesperson said, "DHS and DOJ are laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens… Those who are here legally and are not breaking other laws have nothing to fear."

"Target List"

In one video, agents are filmed holding a document that says, "Target List."

That list can be far reaching, said a HSI agent familiar with the initiative who asked to speak anonymously. DHS pulls from internal databases, voter rolls, and other datasets. Then employees attempt to match names against citizenship data provided by the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, or USCIS.

In September, a USCIS whistleblower said that employees were asked to review the voter information of tens of thousands of individuals across the country, including citizens. Employees were given quotas to investigate 40 subjects a day, which is a rate of roughly 12 minutes per subject.

DHS has defended the data matching program and the work USCIS has done to identify potential noncitizen voters.

"Far from being rushed or untrained, these investigative efforts are conducted diligently and professionally," said a DHS spokesperson. "There is no quota on criminality. DHS will pursue each and every illegal voter to the fullest extent of the law ."

"There's every reason to expect that there are many, many more false positives in these lists," said Marsden.

She noted that Homeland Security officials initially said they had identified nearly 16,000 noncitizens on Nevada's voter rolls, but ultimately they were unable to provide evidence of a single illegally registered voter.

World.title: American Stephen Hubbard released by Russia, Steve Witkoff says
World.content:
Stephen Hubbard, a U.S. citizen who was jailed in Russia for more than four years after being accused of fighting for Ukraine, has been released from custody, U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff confirmed Wednesday during a meeting with President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.

Trump administration officials, including Witkoff, were in St. Petersburg Wednesday for talks with Putin and other senior Russian officials that focused on the Ukraine war, but included other matters. Russian state news agencies, citing Putin, said Hubbard was at St. Petersburg's Pulkovo Airport.

Video from the meeting showed Witkoff thanking Putin for freeing the American.

"I wanted to thank you very much. The president sends his thanks. Our whole nation sends it's thanks," Witkoff said. "Because of you, he's going home to his family."

Hubbard, a 74-year-old Michigan native, was the last American in Russia whom the State Department had formally declared wrongfully detained. As many as 10 other Americans, including dual nationals, remain in Russian custody.

Hubbard, who is in poor health, was expected to be flown to Texas for treatment at a military hospital.

Stephen Hubbard, a U.S. citizen accused of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine against Russia, is seen inside an enclosure for defendants as he attends a court hearing in Moscow, Oct. 7, 2024. Moscow City Court Press Service/Handout/REUTERS

President Trump hinted at a possible breakthrough in the case on Tuesday, telling reporters in the Oval Office he had personally pressed Russian President Vladimir Putin to secure Hubbard's release.

"Everybody's been after Hubbard for a long time, long before I got here," Mr. Trump said. "I've been talking to President Putin about Mr. Hubbard. I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him."

"I'd love to get him back," Mr. Trump added. "It's time to have Mr. Hubbard back."

A retired school teacher who served in the U.S. National Guard and Air Force, Hubbard was captured in Ukraine shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of the country in February 2022. Russian authorities accused him of manning a checkpoint for mercenaries. He was sentenced in 2024 to almost seven years in a penal colony.

Hubbard's family had little contact with him while he was detained, and they have maintained his innocence.

It was not immediately clear what the U.S. had agreed to, if anything, to secure Hubbard's release, which came after Mr. Trump announced Friday that his administration would waive some sanctions on Russia just two days before they were due to take effect. That decision by Mr. Trump was praised by Putin but criticized harshly by members of Congress, including some Republicans.

Hubbard's release follows the return of American Robert Gilman, who was freed from Russian custody in August after his health deteriorated to a life-threatening condition. A former Marine who spent more than four years imprisoned in Russia, Gilman was granted a humanitarian pardon following a direct appeal by Mr. Trump to Putin.

Early last year, Russia released American school teacher Marc Fogel, and in 2024 journalist Evan Gershkovich and Marine veteran Paul Whelan were among those released from Russian custody in a complicated multi-country prisoner swap.

The State Department maintains a Level 4 "Do Not Travel" advisory for Russia, warning U.S. nationals against all travel to the country due to the risk of wrongful detention, arbitrary enforcement of local laws and limited U.S. consular assistance.

The Trump administration last year established a new designation for countries that are deemed "state sponsors of wrongful detention," CBS News previously reported. The measure gives the State Department expanded authority to impose sanctions, export controls and travel restrictions on countries that use detained Americans as political leverage.

Despite its lengthy history of imprisoning Americans on questionable charges, Russia has not faced the designation, which was applied to Iran in February and Afghanistan in March.

Some Americans jailed in Russia have not been declared wrongfully detained by the U.S. government, including Aleksandr Antonov, who was arrested in Russia last year and sentenced to six years in prison.

His family argues that he was detained because he is a U.S. citizen, and they have urged the State Department to prioritize his case. CBS News reported earlier this year on an internal debate within the department over whether to designate him as wrongfully detained.

World.title: Memphis fails to pass 1-year data center moratorium, opts for shorter-term ban
World.content:
In a heated city council meeting on Tuesday, leaders in Memphis, Tennessee, voted against a moratorium that would have paused data center development for a year in the city, which has become a hotspot for the facilities driven by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI.

Instead, city council members passed a substitute ordinance — which some said they received on short notice and did not have time to review — that would halt construction of data centers for 135 days.

Residents and activists have pushed back against data center development in the region for years, starting with the construction of SpaceXAI's Colossus 1 data center in 2024. The company has also built two other data centers and has two under construction in Memphis and the surrounding region, including across the state border in Southaven, Mississippi.

Also in Southaven, a plant powering the company's data centers is using methane gas turbines, which prompted a lawsuit from the NAACP and other organizations over alleged pollution.

SpaceXAI did not reply to a request for comment. The Trump administration moved to dismiss the case, but earlier Tuesday, a Mississippi federal judge blocked that bid.

Supporters of data centers argue they are needed to support the growth of artificial intelligence technology. Advocates also say they will create much-needed jobs, although experts counter many of those jobs are in the construction industry and therefore temporary.

The moratorium would have paused the construction of new data centers for a year, allowing the city to adopt permanent zoning and development regulations as well as establish disclosure requirements for data center applicants. It also would have provided the opportunity to study impacts on air quality, electrical infrastructure, water protection and noise. The moratorium would not have halted existing data center operations.

The language of the ordinance that was passed Tuesday states that it is intended to complement Memphis Mayor Paul Young's executive order to establish a 90-day period to study the impacts of data center development.

Many attendees in the chambers appeared shocked and confused at the proposal for the new ordinance. A few members of the crowd remained in the chambers following the vote where they sang, chanted and vocalized their frustrations.

FILE -- Construction on a SpaceXAI data center on Riverport Road in Memphis, Tennessee, on April 25, 2025. Photo by Brandon Dill/The Washington Post via Getty Images

The city council's move comes after a postponement of the vote earlier this month spurred protests in the chambers and resulted in an early end to an Oct. 6 meeting.

Community members' opposition to data center development in Memphis is reflective of the broader attitude across America in recent months. According to a recent Pew Research Center survey, over half of Americans say they're not comfortable with a new data center operating in their area — a sentiment that's spilling over into city council meetings and town halls across the country.

Ahead of the vote, KeShaun Pearson, the executive director of the Memphis Community Against Pollution, said that community members were concerned about what they feel has been a lack of transparency from local government officials and data centers' environmental impact.

"It's as if the people who have been elected to protect us and to stand up to corporations and be that representative have just completely abdicated that responsibility, and left us to fend for ourselves," he said.

Pearson and his brother, Tennessee Rep. Justin Pearson, were among a handful of people barred from city council meetings following the protests at city hall earlier this month.

A federal judge lifted the ban and the two were present during the vote. Pearson and the group have sued the city council over the ban.

World.title: Ohio race takes ugly turn with ad featuring Amy Acton's mother
World.content:
A new attack ad features the estranged mother of Democratic candidate for Ohio governor Amy Acton calling her a "liar" and defending her GOP opponent Vivek Ramaswamy. Acton's campaign and her brother denounced the ad as a "despicable low."

Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, whose husband was accused of raping Acton when she was a child, says in the spot, "It's not easy for a mother to say this, but Amy was a serious problem. She is a liar; she lies about her past."

Acton's brother, Philip Stearns, lashed out at Ramaswamy in response: "It's not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother's husband into a political talking point."

He said that after their stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested and charged, he and Acton were removed from the Arthurs' custody and lived with their father.

"Our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," Stearns said. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core – a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants."

Ramaswamy told reporters Tuesday it was "an ad from our campaign," according to The Columbus Dispatch. He defended the content of the ad, saying: "Every person who appears to know her the best … have told voters not to vote for her but to vote for me instead."

The origins of the ad, which circulated on social media on Monday night, were initially unclear. It lacks the mandatory disclosure of who paid for and authorized the commercial. It has not aired on TV or cable but has spread widely on social media.

Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy, but said in a statement on Tuesday, "We don't know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke out about Amy in 2020, but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor."

The state Republican Party did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Acton, who served as the state's public health commissioner under GOP Gov. Mike DeWine during the pandemic, has previously talked about being abused by her now-deceased stepfather. According to court records provided by the campaign, in 1978, Arthur was charged with raping Acton, when she was between 10 and 12 years old. He entered a not guilty plea.

Acton has also detailed struggles throughout her early childhood with poverty and homelessness, and records provided by her campaign show that the family lived in a tent for a year.

Acton told the Youngstown Vindicator in 2019 that once she and her brother were able to go live with their father, their lives became more stable.

"In the courthouse after they were charged, I went to give her a kiss, and she just turned her cheek away," Acton told The Vindicator seven years ago. "That was the last time I ever saw her." Her campaign says that court date remains the last time Acton saw her mother.

Her mother and her stepfather, released on bond, left Ohio without facing charges, the news site said. Warrants were issued for Cledith Arthur's arrest at least twice in the next few years, according to court records. Donna and Cledith Arthur lived in Pennsylvania until Cledith's death in 2004.

Ramaswamy's backers have launched other personal attacks against Acton, who has been leading in polls over the last month.

Other aspects of Acton's personal life have also resurfaced during the election, including an incident when police were called to her home in 2019 during what was characterized as a domestic dispute.

World.title: Florida executes man who killed deputy after fighting for gun
World.content:
Florida carried out its 18th execution of the year on Tuesday under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis' aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term.

William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder for the 1986 shooting of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski.

The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves by the shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response.

A medic was called into the chamber a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.

Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation's aging death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of the country in total executions.

Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year. Another execution is scheduled for November, which would tie that mark if both are carried out as planned.

DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims' families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out.

Reaves fought with deputy after dropping gun

According to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves acknowledged that he had placed the call at a payphone outside the store.

While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves' shorts, officials said. The men struggled over the firearm and Reaves eventually regained control over it. Investigators said the deputy attempted to run away before Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds.

Reaves was initially convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and subsequent appeals have been unsuccessful.

The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves' final appeals last week.

William Reaves, 77, was sentenced to death after being convicted of first-degree murder for the 1986 shooting of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. CBS Miami/AP

One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida's method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.

The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states like Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.

Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter on Monday asking him to stop the execution.

Final appeals for Reaves were still pending before the U.S. Supreme Court.

Florida close to matching last year's record-setting number of executions

A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. in 2025. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half the 31 total executions in the U.S. so far this year. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.

Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. 5. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

World.title: Musk chose to restrict Ukraine's access to SpaceX network, sources say
World.content:
A decision by Elon Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, people familiar with the matter told CBS News.

The satellite service, which is used for drone operations, hitting certain targets and protecting sites in Ukraine, was slowed significantly last week.

Musk held multiple conversations with administration officials leading up to the order, the sources said. He wanted clarity on the president's thinking on the matter. Musk has expressed distaste with his company being seen as profiting from the continued war between Russia and Ukraine.

It's not clear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed.

Musk licenses SpaceX's Starshield technology to the U.S. government. He said last week the U.S. controls who can access the technology and what level of service those users receive.

"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk, the world's richest person, wrote on X.

Musk did not reply to a request for comment. CBS News has reached out to the White House and the Pentagon for comment.

The Wall Street Journal was first to report on Musk's order.

The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some officials inside the administration, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications.

Mr. Trump said Monday he was seeking details on who ordered the slowdown.

"I don't know who it was, but I'd like to find out," he said.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Tuesday the Pentagon has not manipulated the service.

"We haven't pulled anything back. There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to. And that's where Starlink has the option to make those decisions, but nothing's changed from our view. We haven't made any directives or anything like that," Hegseth told reporters, adding that "we wish the Ukrainians, obviously, success."

Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday there were still limits on Ukraine's Starshield service.

What is Starshield?

Starshield is a military-grade satellite network made by SpaceX for the U.S. government and its partners. It runs on similar technology to its civilian sister, Starlink.

The U.S. government pays to use Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia

Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances.

There is no working alternative to Starlink, which has put a massive constellation of low-earth satellites into orbit, and no direct competitor comes close.

What happened in Ukraine?

Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including a throttling effect that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions.

Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr speed cap, that is, the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates faster than the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable.

Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr. Strike drones equipped with Starshield cruise at 160 km/h or higher, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes.

Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr, making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.

Zelensky said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Shahed attack drones.

The Ukrainian leader wrote on X last week that "the Russians are trying to take advantage of the problems with Starlink in Ukraine, as our interceptor drones depend on this connection among other things."

Zelensky has suggested there are still some restrictions. He told NBC News over the weekend the maximum speed was 161 km/hr, and he said Tuesday that he'd spoken with Secretary of State Marco Rubio about "the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored."

The apparent restrictions drew swift pushback from U.S. lawmakers, with a bipartisan group of senators asking the Defense Department's internal watchdog to investigate last week.

"There needs to be an investigation, we need to find out who these people are because lives are at risk and lives are lost over these things," Republican Rep. Mike Turner of Ohio said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" over the weekend.

Why have Trump and Zelensky clashed?

Beyond the Starshield disruptions, Zelensky has said in recent days that Russia struck Ukraine without warning from the U.S., and deliveries of key interceptor missiles to Ukraine have slowed down.

A senior Pentagon official told CBS News on Monday there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."

Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent weeks, accusing him of not doing enough to seek an end to the Russia-Ukraine war.

The U.S. president argues the war is responsible for high energy prices. His administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel earlier this month in an effort to ease pressure on the price of the commodity, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. Mr. Trump also waived sanctions on Russia last week.

Mr. Trump said earlier this month that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire." Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

The Russian government never confirmed that it had agreed to a ceasefire.

In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," and argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," as he urged both sides to make a deal while adding that the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin.

"I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said.

World.title: The AI doom scenario you've never heard of may be hardest to stop
World.content:
It seems that almost daily, a big tech company releases a new AI-driven digital assistant. Muse by Meta, Gemini by Google, dots by OpenAI. By the time this article is published, a new one from [insert tech company here] will probably have a press release touting its ability to manage your work and life — to take things off your plate, automate your processes, speed up your tedious tasks. It sounds helpful and, to lower the bar, harmless.

But some researchers say this is the beginning of a treacherous path for humankind, one where bots take more and more off our plate until all that's left is an empty vessel, and we human users become nothing more than thoughtless "approvers."

It's not just a threat to jobs. They warn that allowing our skills and knowledge to deteriorate, and surrendering our critical thinking to AI, poses an existential danger to humanity.

One term for this path is "gradual disempowerment" — a scenario where AI displaces human labor in the economy, replaces human decision-making in all key societal concerns, erodes human creativity, and degrades human cognition along the way.

And though the word "gradual" is in the name, that does not mean the problem is something to worry about far in the future, according to experts.

"I put gradual disempowerment on the very top of my list," said Jay Chooi, the founder and CEO of Robocurve, a company that tracks and measures AI-driven robotics capabilities.

Chooi believes gradual disempowerment is just as worrisome as the threat of engineered pandemics and more destructive cyberattacks, which could be accelerated by capable AI.

"It's a civilization-scale problem," Chooi said of gradual disempowerment. "A lot of people feel very powerless, because it requires a lot of effort and a whole-of-society approach to solve it."

What is "gradual disempowerment" and how could AI cause it?

The term "gradual disempowerment" stems from a paper published in early 2025.

At the heart of the gradual disempowerment scenario is AI technology continuing to advance in capabilities, as it has rapidly since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022.

AI models may soon be better at nearly all cognitive tasks than humans — solving frontier math problems, doing hard science, coding, writing and creating art and music, to name a few of the areas where AI increasingly excels. At the same time, advances in robotics could lead to AI-powered robots performing better than humans at physical labor like packing boxes, constructing homes, building cars, painting murals, mining for rare minerals, and even building IKEA furniture.

We like to think that in an ideal world, the best applicant generally gets the job, and they are paid based on the level of demand for their skills. But imagine if a human is never the best person for the job. That's a world that some AI prognosticators and whistleblowers expect.

It's a world where an AI agent or AI-enabled robot is better at every task and sub-task that it takes to do my job and your job. They move faster than us, think deeper, have more patience and stamina. They more cordially answer phones, do more thorough research, and more dexterously wield a scalpel or a nail file. Plus, they never need to sleep or take sick days, they never show up hungover or moody, and they never threaten to leave for a better job.

To picture gradual disempowerment more clearly, here's a scenario: Let's say you run Hammer Co., a company that manufactures hammers. You have line workers who shape the steel heads and wooden handles and then fit them together, and managers who keep the factory running smoothly. You have people who maintain your supply chain and teams to handle marketing, sales, accounting, and all the other functions that help your business thrive.

But then a tech company comes out with AI-powered Hammer Bots. The robot workers can make hammers far faster than your human workers, while AI agents can run the business side with little oversight. They'll work all night, never make mistakes, and cost far less than your happy, well-paid staff. You don't want to fire your human workers. You see them around town and have known their families for years, after all.

But your competitor gets the Hammer Bots. Most customers just want the cheapest hammers — they don't care who or what makes them. As CEO of Hammer Co. you either compete or die. So you fire all your humans and get Hammer Bots to replace them.

Now, try to envision this is the case for every company, and every job. With normal free-market incentives, the company that stays loyal to its human employees will be outcompeted by the company that gets AI to do the work instead.

Here's where gradual disempowerment comes into play.

The fewer humans that participate in labor, and the more work that's outsourced to AI agents, the more humanity becomes dependent on AI for decision-making and the more human skills deteriorate. How long until the finer points of hammer-making will be forgotten?

With AI making all our complex decisions for us, humans become less capable of understanding and overseeing those decisions or of pushing back against them.

"If people aren't actually practicing the skills that the agents are doing for them, they lose the ability to have that skill, and so now you become reliant," said Margaret Mitchell, an AI research scientist at Hugging Face and co-author of another recent paper on the importance of keeping humans in the loop in an AI world.

"What happens when something goes wrong? There's no human you can point to who can fix it. So now you've become fully dependent on these systems to fix themselves, and what if that's not possible?"

A risk to democratic governance

It's not just economics and labor at risk. Take the military, for example. All or most decisions in war involve humans today, even if AI contributes to the process, but the balance is likely to shift as the technology becomes more capable.

If the United States uses AI to make decisions in battle, its enemies across the field will be pressured to do the same. The side that leans more heavily on humans will be slower and less efficient. Human soldiers need food and rest. Robot soldiers will not. Human decision-makers are limited in the scenarios they can conceive and plan for; AIs can take into account all of human knowledge.

"The states need citizens. They need us because we pay taxes and we fight for the states in the military," said Jan Kulveit, a co-author of the gradual disempowerment paper and co-founder of ACS Research Group.

States also use people to enforce laws. But what if law enforcement is all automated in the future?

"If, or when, existing states don't need their citizens, they're less likely to be democratic," said Kulveit.

Kulveit compares theoretical future countries that are mostly run by AI to oil states today. He said the oil states tend to be authoritarian because they don't rely on most of their citizens to pay taxes and don't need citizens' votes to rule. States that rely on AI to run the economy and military could have similar outcomes, said Kulveit.

If that is the case, and citizens no longer are the backbone of labor or warfare in a world of gradual disempowerment, then humans lose perhaps their greatest leverage against those in power.

"A lot of people are talking about rogue AI hacking into data centers and taking over the world, but it is not in the mainstream consciousness that like AI could literally take over the world just by continuing to do what it's supposed to do, which is automating everything," said Jay Chooi of Robocurve.

"Organizations are all going to have a very strong economic pressure, and political pressure, to phase out humans and move work more and more into robots or AI."

How does humanity avoid gradual disempowerment?

Humans ceding control to AI, say the gradual disempowerment authors, is almost a natural transition once very advanced AI is here.

Gradual disempowerment "does not need to emerge from a deliberate scheme or powergrab by AI systems," wrote Kulveit and his colleagues. "In the short-term, it is being incentivized by the perceived value that AI systems can bring to economic, cultural and state functions."

"We can't be in the situation where we are competing with the machines," said Kulveit. "Because if we are just competing with the machines, we will probably lose."

The gradual disempowerment authors believe stopping our disempowerment may be a heavy lift for humanity, since it involves complex systems that feed into each other — government, culture, and the economy.

"This may be a bigger challenge than merely preventing AI systems from pursuing overtly harmful goals," they write.

One first step in slowing disempowerment is keeping indicators of how much work is being ceded to AI, and of what kind of specific jobs AI systems are capable of handling. If thousands of workers are being displaced by AI in, say, call center jobs, it helps to know that in granular detail.

But measurement isn't enough without action, Mitchell said. She argues that removing humans from the loop in AI processes both worsens oversight and degrades the skills of the human overseer. Therefore, companies and leadership in all fields must take proactive steps to keep humans engaged.

"This general practice within tech is we want our systems to be frictionless," said Mitchell, referring to the idea that everything should move fast and without obstacles. "There's this sense that the less friction the better, but there's been a push within the more ethical AI community that strategic friction can be good because it can draw people's attention to critical issues that otherwise they might overlook."

Mitchell argues that strategic friction — keeping humans in the work loop at predetermined steps — can be done both by developers of AI, companies like OpenAI and Anthropic and Google, and by companies and organizations that deploy AI. Thoughtful and purposeful design of AI can benefit society as a whole, and the individuals who use it.

Kulveit agrees that AI should be thoughtfully designed to add value to humans, not necessarily replace our every task.

"You want to carve out places where we agree that we will not allow competitive pressures to remove humans from the loop," he said. "It would be nice if the companies train the AIs to be more complementary to humans. Currently, the AIs are implicitly trained to be a replacement for humans. But you can imagine training the AIs so they are better at explaining to us what's happening."

Kulveit is describing AI that doesn't just spew out the answers to whatever question you ask it, at the very least in sectors where it is critical to include human expertise and decision-making, like war. Quick and easy answers can be helpful, but they can also make you dependent and credulous, believing anything the chatbot tells you, whether right or wrong.

But AI can be more than that. It can help you not just by doing the work for you, but by educating you along the way. That way the human worker continues to learn while using AI as a partner, not a substitute.

"There has been such a singular focus on capability or functionality of these systems to the detriment of people, to the detriment of users," said Mitchell. "If your only goal is to get a high score on a benchmark, then you are not going to be taking into account cognitive support design. But if your goal is to make a system that works really well for people — like if the race is for a utility as opposed to benchmark score — then you end up designing fundamentally different systems."

If gradual disempowerment really is a large-scale risk, compared to more talked-about doom scenarios — like AI helping to design bioweapons or chemical weapons — it may suffer from a relative lack of vividness.

"We know what it means for a robot to take over the world. We know what it means for countries to nuke each other," said Chooi. "AI taking over the world is very legible in the human consciousness. But gradual disempowerment? No one has made a movie about gradual disempowerment."

But to Chooi, gradual disempowerment is very easy to picture.

"All the organizations have the incentives to adopt it and phase out humans," he said. "This is a very logical conclusion. It's not very hard to see it."

World.title: The often neglected AI doom scenario that poses a different kind of threat to humanity
World.content: An AI doom scenario that isn't well-known Some researchers warn that as artificial intelligence agents take on more and more tasks, humans could end up giving up their critical thinking skills in a scenario they call "gradual disempowerment." Jay Chooi, co-founder and CEO of Robocurve, a company that tracks AI-driven robots, joins CBS News to discuss. More

World.title: 2025 policing trend: Fewer serious crimes, more minor arrests
World.content:
2025 policing trend: Fewer serious crimes, more minor arrests

toggle caption i Spencer Platt/Getty Images/Getty Images North America

Arrests for low-level crimes, including vagrancy and drug possession, rose in the U.S. from 2024 to 2025 even as rates of violent crime including homicide plummeted to historic national lows, according to a new analysis of federal data from the criminal justice and immigration reforms advocacy group FWD.us.

Zoë Towns, the executive director of FWD.us, spoke to NPR ahead of the report's release on Wednesday.

"This increase signals a really troubling return to some of the extreme law and order policies that defined the American criminal justice system during the 80s and the 90s," Towns said, referring to the era's tough-on-crime policies, including mandatory minimum prison sentences, that led to a massive rise in incarceration in the U.S. for decades.

Sponsor Message

The report analyzes publicly available FBI and immigration arrest data and does not include details of whether charges were dropped or if people served any time in jail or prison.

Still, Towns said, "An arrest has life-changing consequences for the person involved and for their family. It can mean days or months in jail. It can mean a lost job. It can mean missed rent or a missed mortgage payment," and can mean families separated, she said.

A representative for the FBI didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on this analysis.

The findings

Four states, California, Hawaii, Nevada and Arizona, accounted for over half the increase in vagrancy arrests, according to the report. The legal definition of vagrancy is "roaming from place to place without a permanent job, home, or material resources." In practice, it is disproportionately enforced against people experiencing homelessness.

FWD.us found arrests for vagrancy were up 44% (22,769 in 2024 to 32,728 in 2025).

Two demographic groups made up the majority of arrests: Asian Americans, as well as Native Hawaiian and other Pacific Islanders. Although AANHPI people make up only about 7% of the US population, they accounted for 17% of the increase in vagrancy arrests, largely in Hawaii, according to FWD.us

Sponsor Message

Marijuana possession arrests went up 6%, mainly in Southern states that have not yet legalized the drug. The report showed there were 190,182 arrests in 2024 and 201,273 a year later.

There was a stark racial disparity between those arrested for marijuana possession: Black people accounted for 83% of the national increase in marijuana arrests in 2025 and nearly half of all cannabis arrests were of Black people (45%).

Arrests for possession of drugs other than marijuana rose marginally between 2024 to 2025. The report found a national increase of 3% in arrests or 508,087 in 2024 and 523,520 in 2025.

This increase appears to be tied to the unraveling of policies that decriminalized drug possession in some states.

Voters in California (which saw the biggest jump in arrests for drug possession) back in 2024 voted to roll back a measure that had reclassified drug possession from a felony to a misdemeanor. Proposition 36, approved by voters, increased criminal penalties for repeat thieves and drug users. FWD.us says drug possession arrests rose by over 14,000 in a single year following its passage.

That same year Oregon similarly reinstated a policy that made simple drug possession a criminal offense again. That resulted in a 39% increase (2,205) in non-marijuana drug possession arrests.

The report also highlights the vast increase (188%) in arrests for immigration violations in that time — a trend NPR has previously covered. In 2024, there were a reported 109,936 immigration violation arrests. A year later, in 2025, those arrests totaled 316,304.

Why is this happening now?

FWD.us ties the increases, in part, to changes at the federal level.

The data reviewed by FWD.us covers the first full year of President Trump's second term in office. In that time the administration leaned on a tough-on-crime message.

It supercharged its deportation efforts, arresting hundreds of thousands nationwide — many of whom had no criminal convictions. Millions of federal dollars have also been sent to local police through the 287(g) program, which allows local police to make immigration arrests.

Sponsor Message

FWD believes federal deployments of immigration officers and the National Guard may have also led to increased policing and subsequently more arrests.

In summer 2025, Trump claimed American cities including Washington, D.C., were suffering from a "crime emergency" — despite data showing violent crime in the city were at a record low in 2024. He sent hundreds of National Guard troops to the city.

FWD.us found that arrests in D.C. for marijuana possession "more than doubled" following the Trump administration's deployment of National Guard into the city.

Vagrancy arrests may also be tied to actions by the Supreme Court, according to FWD's report. Two years ago, the judges ruled that cities can ban people from sleeping and camping in public places. The ruling allowed Oregon and dozens of other Western localities to limit where individuals living in cars, parks and other encampments stayed.

Insha Rahman, president and director of the criminal justice reform nonprofit Vera Institute, says there are still "incredibly positive trends" showing crime across the board is down.

Adult arrests for drug crimes peaked in 2006 at about 1.7 million, more than 2.5 times the number recorded in 1980.

And has continued a downward trend.

Rahman says this decrease "speaks to the resilience of states and localities that have continued to double down and invest in what works." Vera was not involved in the FWD.us report.

That includes investing in treatment and diversion programs that offer assistance to people struggling with addiction, community violence intervention programs, youth services, counseling and alternative response programs.

World.title: Expecting a baby? 5 tips to help you prepare for pregnancy costs
World.content:
Expecting a baby? 5 tips to help you prepare for pregnancy costs

Oona Zenda/KFF Health News

As Grace Griffin and her husband were welcoming their long-awaited baby — a daughter — Griffin found herself worried about looming medical bills and unsure whether the family could pay for the care needed.

"This whole experience has me wondering (keeping me up at night, actually): Can we ever afford to have another child?"

— Grace Griffin, Calumet, Michigan

Grace and Daniel Griffin, both 26, knew money would be tight once they had their first child. So, even before the Calumet, Mich., couple tried to conceive, they began crunching the numbers to figure out the cost of pregnancy.

"We wanted to save up enough to pay for those medical bills right away, if possible," Grace said.

Sponsor Message

But the cost estimator that she found linked to her UnitedHealthcare student plan asked for medical billing codes for each procedure that Grace was likely to receive. That's information she didn't have.

toggle caption i Patricia Griffin

So, she kept digging until she found the Summary of Benefits and Coverage information on the health plan's website, which estimated out-of-pocket costs for a routine pregnancy and delivery at about $2,700.

"We thought, 'OK, that's doable,'" she said. "We should be able to save up that much and pay for that out of pocket."

But as the expenses piled up, it was clear the estimate wasn't even close.

Early in the pregnancy, Grace met her $500 deductible, the out-of-pocket cost she had to pay before insurance pitched in. Her plan also required her to pay 20% coinsurance for in-network care. This meant that for every $100 billed for things like routine blood work and other needed care, she was on the hook for $20.

"When I started getting lab work is when we started realizing expenses would add up quickly," Grace said. Routine blood tests to check iron levels or for gestational diabetes were a couple of hundred dollars every visit, she said.

In June, after what Grace described as a routine pregnancy and delivery, the couple welcomed their daughter. Then the Griffins received an "explanation of benefits" notice that showed the hospital charged about $18,000 for the delivery, with the family on the hook for a sizable portion.

Sponsor Message

"I thought, 'Oh no, it's going to be a lot,'" she said. "Much more than we budgeted for."

She was right.

In early October, Grace said, her family's out-of-pocket expenses had totaled more than $9,000, over three times the general estimate published by her insurer for pregnancy-related costs.

Meanwhile, Grace and Daniel are scrambling to cover their bills.

For years, federal lawmakers have tried to remedy this issue, said Sabrina Corlette, a research professor and co-director of Georgetown University's Center on Health Insurance Reforms. To make healthcare costs more transparent and accessible to patients, Congress required insurers to provide consumers with an individualized "advanced explanation of benefits" estimating what scheduled care would cost them. The rule, part of the 2020 No Surprises Act, was due to take effect on Jan. 1, 2022, but federal regulators have yet to make that happen, despite ongoing pressure from members of Congress.

"So, it's basically 4 1/2 years since this was supposed to be available, and I think it's a source of a lot of frustration for a lot of folks," Corlette said. "People have a right under the law to know these things."

Meanwhile, she said, another change is pending. Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, long-standing maternity billing codes that bundle much of pregnancy care will be replaced with more detailed coding for prenatal care, labor, delivery and postpartum care.

The change could make it easier to see what individual services cost, but Corlette said it's not yet clear whether the change will make it easier for people trying to stick to a budget.

"I could see where it might be advantageous to the provider," she said. "But I'm not sure I'm seeing benefits to the patient."

Until out-of-pocket maternity expenses get easier to estimate, here are some tips to help you budget for the cost of pregnancy.

1. Enroll your baby before the clock runs out

Oona Zenda/KFF Health News

Ensuring your newborn has health coverage is one of the first paperwork responsibilities that parents face in the whirlwind of bringing a baby home.

Birth creates what's known as a special enrollment opportunity, meaning you don't have to wait until the annual open-enrollment period to sign up a newborn.

Many employer health plans require parents to request enrollment within 30 days of birth. Marketplace plans — for those who buy their own insurance rather than get it from an employer or the government — generally allow 60 days. Wait too long, and your baby may be left uninsured until the following year.

Sponsor Message

Michelle Critzer of Ventura, Calif., learned that lesson the hard way. She works as a sales rep and is the mother of a toddler and a newborn. Her second son, Hudson, was born in February, and Critzer missed the enrollment deadline for him. Ever since, she has been asking her insurer to make an exception — so far, without success.

"The way they set hard must-do's within 30 days of having a baby is actually insanity," she said.

The family was able to enroll Hudson in a health plan through Critzer's husband's workplace, which has a 60-day enrollment window. But that coverage is not nearly as robust as Critzer's insurance, she said. Still, she's grateful to have Hudson insured while she continues pressing her own plan to enroll him.

Oona Zenda/KFF Health News

2. Ask about must-know numbers, like your MOOP

Budgeting for a pregnancy often begins with a tally of the expected expenses. The deductible is the amount you'll pay before much of your insurance coverage kicks in.

After that, you'll likely face copayments — fixed fees paid each time you receive service, regardless of the size of the bill.

Coinsurance is another expected expense, but as Grace discovered, it can be especially tricky to estimate. Coinsurance requires the patient to pay a percentage of the cost for each service received.

MOOP, which stands for "maximum out-of-pocket" expense, is another must-know number. Your plan's MOOP is the ceiling on what you'll pay each year for covered, in-network services (care that your health plan has contracted to pay at negotiated, lower rates).

Think of it as doomsday prepping. Some people get comfort from knowing and planning for the worst-case scenario. Under the Affordable Care Act, in 2026 the amount a person has to pay out of pocket for in-network care is capped at $10,600 for an individual and $21,200 for a family. Your plan might set a lower maximum, but once your spending reaches your plan's limit, insurance pays 100% of all further in-network costs for that year.

Sponsor Message

One complication to be aware of: If your pregnancy overlaps two plan years, the tally of your out-of-pocket expenses resets to zero at the beginning of the second year, and you could find yourself maxing out your out-of-pocket expenses two years in a row.

Some plans have two MOOPs, one for in-network services and another for out-of-network benefits. Insurance plans usually track those expenses separately, and the out-of-network MOOP can be double the in-network limit. That's more incentive to meticulously seek out in-network care.

Oona Zenda/KFF Health News

As a family, the Griffins had an $18,000 MOOP, and Grace's individual maximum was $9,000.

3. Choose in-network care, when you can

You picked an obstetrician in your plan, but don't assume others on the care team are in-network providers.

Ask about the hospital, labs and imaging facilities your doctor's office may use. Corlette, of Georgetown's Center on Health Insurance Reforms, suggests that patients explicitly tell the doctor's office to send tests to an in-network provider.

Federal law protects patients who go to an in-network hospital or other in-network facility from out-of-network "surprise bills" issued by out-of-network providers.

4. Check every bill — and don't be afraid to file an appeal

Oona Zenda/KFF Health News

The Affordable Care Act requires certain recommended prenatal services to be covered without any additional cost to you. Among them: prenatal visits, folic acid, anxiety and depression screening, and breastfeeding and lactation counseling and supplies.

Still, these costs sometimes get mistakenly passed on to the patient.

To protect against billing errors, Corlette suggests patients become familiar with these pregnancy-related services and then check every bill.

If your insurer refuses to pay for a covered charge, consider filing an appeal.

5. Seek help before the bills pile up

Most hospitals offer financial assistance programs. Find out whether yours will work with you, either to reduce your bill or to offer a manageable payment plan. Your doctor or other providers might also offer assistance, if you ask.

Sponsor Message

Oona Zenda/KFF Health News

Corlette said to make sure any arrangement is formally agreed upon in advance so the account isn't unexpectedly turned over to collections.

Also investigate other assistance.

Grace Griffin qualified for Michigan's Rx Kids program, which provides eligible families in certain communities with $1,500 during pregnancy and $500 a month for the baby's first six months or year of life.

That money has helped keep the medical bills from devouring the Griffins' emergency savings.

"It takes a lot of pressure off," she said.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling and journalism.
