World.title: LeBron James talks smack with Knicks fans in victorious 76ers debut
World.content:
LeBron James talks smack with Knicks fans in victorious 76ers debut

toggle caption i Frank Franklin II/AP

NEW YORK — LeBron James got the business from Knicks fans still gloating and riding an emotional high from an NBA championship banner celebration.

As he stepped to the free-throw line for the Philadelphia 76ers early in Tuesday night's season opener, Knicks fans erupted toward James with chants of "We don't want you! We don't want you!"

Such a rude reception from New Yorkers to one of the city's newest residents.

The shouts of rejection came in part because there was a plausible scenario under which James would have opened the season at Madison Square Garden in a Knicks uniform.

James and his agent, Rich Paul, had said the Knicks would have been James' first choice in free agency had New York not won its first NBA championship since 1973 last season.

Sponsor Message

Knicks fans said, we're good.

The 41-year-old James got the final word as the Sixers won 106-100.

James talked smack with fans in the lower level. Yes, that was Spike Lee trying to play peacemaker.

James finished with 14 points and nine rebounds and had plenty of help in getting the W from new Sixers and holdovers. Tyrese Maxey scored 28 points, Jaylen Brown had 19, Joel Embiid had 13 points and 11 rebounds, and the Sixers ruined the Knicks' championship party.

A good night in New York totally spoiled? Not quite, according to James.

"I wouldn't say that," James said. "It was a great night for New York fans. Fifty-plus years. I was a part of that at one point where we hadn't won a major championship in Cleveland in over 50 years. The fans will never forget this moment."

James' first basket for the Sixers was not nearly as memorable. He took a feed from Embiid in the paint and went up strong for an uncontested right-handed layup.

Just two points. Just one bucket of what the Sixers expect to be many, many more over the next two seasons as the NBA's career scoring leader opened his record 24th season.

Embiid appeared to wonder during the national anthem where the Knicks' championship banner was hanging in the rafters as James sat nearby on the bench with his head bowed and hands clasped.

Sponsor Message

The banner was indeed raised in a pregame ceremony.

It's the same kind of celebration the 76ers expect James, Embiid and the rest of a stout starting lineup to deliver on opening night next season.

It's the thrill of the chase, to end a championship drought — much like he did to break that drought in Cleveland — that in part drives James to keep playing after racking up a list of accomplishments unrivaled by his peers.

toggle caption i Frank Franklin II/AP

Sixers hope new starting five can jell and make title run

The Sixers got a first look at the potent lineup they put together this summer in hopes of winning their first title since 1983. James and a fellow All-Star in Brown started alongside holdovers Embiid, Maxey and VJ Edgecombe.

There are some questions about how that All-Star starting four plus Edgecombe will coexist when all have been the primary ballhandlers on their respective teams in the past. Who gets the ball in crunch time? Who has to sacrifice the most? Who has the most to gain?

Watching the answers unfold in real time will be fascinating for the Sixers and their fans.

The chemistry looked strong throughout the night. James hit Brown cutting to the basket to earn the assist on the former Celtics star's first points with the Sixers. The Sixers closed the third quarter with an 11-0 run, capped by Brown's second straight 3-pointer that came at the buzzer and gave Philadelphia an 83-76 lead.

"We did that on the fly," James said.

The offseason all the way through the countdown to the Sixers' home opener Thursday against Cleveland has been a swirl of excitement in Philadelphia. James jerseys are flying off the racks. Murals of him have popped up all over the city. He drew more than 10,000 fans to a public scrimmage and preseason games were sold out. There's a fascination with his helicopter rides from the Sixers' facility in New Jersey to New York.

Sponsor Message

Even his younger teammates admitted to being a bit awestruck when they first met James.

The Sixers entered the Garden almost unrecognizable from when they played there in early May in a second-round playoff series. They lost twice in New York and the Knicks finished the sweep in Philadelphia.

The Sixers loaded up with talent and pushed the payroll so they could challenge the Knicks.

"It's certainly been fun these first few weeks," coach Nick Nurse said. "These guys have been really great."

There's not much left for James to accomplish, except win that fifth ring.

Philadelphia is waiting.

World.title: FAA clears the way for airlines to put Boeing's long-delayed 737 Max 10 into service
World.content:
FAA clears the way for airlines to put Boeing's long-delayed 737 Max 10 into service

toggle caption i Lindsey Wasson/AP

Nearly a decade after Boeing unveiled its largest 737 Max jet, the company has cleared a major hurdle in its effort to bring the plane to airlines. The Federal Aviation Administration approved the Max 10 for passenger service Tuesday, ending years of delays.

The 737 Max 10's certification represents another milestone in Boeing's efforts to restore its reputation and financial footing after years of safety, quality and production challenges. With production approved, the aircraft can now be sold to domestic and foreign carriers.

Sponsor Message

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the certification followed "extensive safety reviews," including thousands of hours of test flights, and called it a major win for American manufacturing.

"To think that it took us almost 10 years to get here. We all probably had a little less gray hair 10 years ago," Duffy said during a visit to Boeing's manufacturing plant Tuesday in Everett, Washington.

The Max 10 is an important piece of the company's effort to regain ground in the narrow-body market. For airlines, the larger plane offers a way to carry more passengers on a single flight, potentially lowering costs per seat. For travelers, it could eventually mean more seats on popular routes, though the impact on fares will depend on how airlines deploy the planes and how much competition they face.

Stephanie Pope, president and CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, said during Duffy's visit that the certification "clears the path to deliver an airplane that will set a new standard in commercial aviation." The Max 10 will typically seat 185-210 passengers, according to Boeing, compared with 175-195 on the Max 9 and 160-180 on the Max 8.

"Today is a very, very special day. It caps years of hard work and dedication by many," Pope said. "It marks another major milestone in our recovery, and it unlocks a key to our future growth."

Sponsor Message

The company expects to begin deliveries in 2027.

toggle caption i Lindsey Wasson/AP

The single-aisle jet was introduced at the Paris air show in 2017 to help Boeing compete with rival Airbus. But technical and regulatory hurdles repeatedly delayed certification.

Boeing's struggles have been particularly acute since two deadly crashes involving the smaller Max 8 killed 346 people in 2018 and 2019 off the coast of Indonesia and in Ethiopia. In 2024, a panel flew off of an Alaska Airlines Max 9 in midair, renewing scrutiny of Boeing's manufacturing and safety practices.

The delays have held up a key part of Boeing's business. More than 30 customers worldwide have ordered 1,555 Max 10s that Boeing has yet to deliver, accounting for more than 30% of its total 737 Max backlog.

Major customers include United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, American Airlines and Ryanair. Alaska Airlines joined that list in January, ordering 105 Max 10s, with options for 35 more.

The Max 10 is intended to compete with Airbus's A321neo model family, which entered service in 2017. The largest A321neo can carry more passengers and fly farther without refueling than the Max 10.

Still, Boeing designed the Max 10 to carry more passengers while burning less fuel than older aircraft — a potentially attractive combination for airlines facing soaring jet fuel costs amid the U.S. war with Iran. Those rising costs have put added pressure on airlines to control expenses.

Certification means the FAA has determined that the Max 10's design meets safety standards, following engineering reviews and flight testing. But Boeing must continue to show it can consistently build the aircraft to the approved design, and each plane must be cleared before it can fly passengers.

The Max 10's certification completes the lineup of four 737 Max models. The FAA cleared the Max 7 for airline operations in August.

Pope on Tuesday described the certification of both the Max 7 and Max 10 in the same year as a sign of the company's resilience.

Sponsor Message

In the wake of the fatal Max 8 crashes, the FAA overhauled how it certifies Boeing aircraft. But over the past 18 months, the agency has gradually eased some of its restrictions on the company, increasing the limit on how many planes Boeing can produce. In July, the FAA also said Boeing could once again issue airworthiness certificates for its 737 Max and 787 planes at the end of production, allowing the company to take back some responsibility for determining whether finished aircraft are ready to fly.

World.title: Zelenskyy says early warning system for Russian missile attacks resumes
World.content:
Zelenskyy says early warning system for Russian missile attacks resumes

toggle caption i Andrii Marienko/AP

KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners about incoming Russian missiles following recent strikes that he said occurred without enough notice, leaving civilians vulnerable.

For at least a week, the Ukrainian leader has said that his country has not received early warnings about ballistic missiles aimed at the capital. Such intelligence, he said, saves lives by allowing the public to be alerted and giving military units time to try to intercept the missiles.

Zelenskyy said the change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including a phone call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"We are thankful that intelligence works now, and I'm speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," Zelenskyy said on a visit to Norway. "So we are thankful to American side now that it works."

Sponsor Message

Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio acknowledged mutual frustration between the U.S. and Ukraine over intelligence sharing and weapons supplies but emphatically denied that the Trump administration has made any changes to previous policy on either issue.

US envoy to go to St. Petersburg

In other developments, Russia unleashed another missile and drone blitz of civilian areas in Ukraine, killing at least nine people, officials said, as Zelenskyy sought more American and European help.

Zelenskyy was joined in Norway by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end the war. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb also met with the Ukrainian president in Norway's capital.

toggle caption i Cornelius Poppe/NTB Scanpix via AP

Gahr Støre said Witkoff planned to fly to St. Petersburg on Wednesday to meet with Russian leaders, exchange ideas from the Oslo meeting and share proposals from European and American colleagues.

"Today was a good day for peace," Stubb said.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow is willing to listen to new U.S. proposals about Ukraine but doesn't expect any "miracle" from Washington.

At the White House, President Donald Trump stepped up the pressure on Zelenskyy to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two men have soured again.

"We want Zelenskyy to make a deal," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. "We've given a lot to Ukraine. We've gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss."

If that doesn't happen, "I think it's going to be a very bad thing."

Zelenskyy speaks with Rubio after US support slows

The conversation with Rubio came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers Monday that he believes "some political decision has been made to slow down ... support for us."

Sponsor Message

Ukraine has nearly run out of American-made Patriot air-defense interceptors that it needs to stop Russian ballistic missiles, according to Zelenskyy, who has pleaded for Washington to send more. But he said the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that other countries have purchased for Ukraine.

The Ukrainian leader also said speed restrictions were still in place on his country's use of Starshield, the military-grade version of U.S. company SpaceX's satellite internet service Starlink, hampering battlefield operations.

Trump also has waived sanctions on Russia, a move that Zelenskyy slammed as helping Putin push on with Moscow's full-scale invasion, which will hit the five-year mark in February.

Zelenskyy said he had "a substantive conversation" with Rubio.

"I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position," Zelenskyy said on social media.

Rubio, who arrived Tuesday in India on an official trip, denied that the U.S. is withholding assistance from Ukraine.

"Nothing has changed," he told reporters.

The Patriot ammunition Ukraine needs is in short supply and is also required elsewhere in the world, Rubio said.

"There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," he said.

Europe tries to make up for waning US supplies

European countries, worried about Russia's plans on the continent and viewing Ukraine as a bulwark against Moscow's ambitions, are trying to take up the slack of any falloff in U.S. supplies, but some key assets are American-made.

European countries and European Union institutions have allocated 237 billion euros ($266 billion) to support Ukraine, compared with 115 billion euros ($129 billion) from the U.S., according to Germany's Kiel Institute, which tracks assistance to Kyiv.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Tuesday questioned whether U.S. negotiators have been honest brokers in peace efforts. Ukrainian officials say the Trump administration has encouraged Kyiv to surrender land to Russia in return for peace.

Sponsor Message

"Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now," Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin's terms "because Europe has been supporting Ukraine," Kallas said.

Russian attacks cause power outages in 12 Ukrainian regions

Four people were killed and 27 others wounded, including children, in Russian missile and drone attacks on the Kyiv region over the past day, regional police said.

Three were killed and six were wounded in the Obukhiv district, where warehouses were damaged, police said. In the Bucha district, one woman was killed and 21 people were wounded, eight of them children, while hundreds of buildings were damaged, according to police.

On Tuesday morning, three people were killed and four injured when two vehicles caught fire in a Russian attack on the Kyiv-Odesa highway, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. The dead included the driver of a shuttle bus that was hit. The bus transports people from Kyiv to the National Military Memorial Cemetery.

Two more people were killed in a Russian attack Tuesday on warehouses on the outskirts of Dnipro in central Ukraine, authorities said.

National grid operator Ukrenergo reported power outages in 12 regions of Ukraine following the Russian attacks.

The Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement that its forces carried out drone strikes on logistics centers, port infrastructure and three cargo ships in the port of Reni in the Odesa region. It said that another bulk carrier was hit at sea on its way to Odesa.

Meanwhile, air defenses intercepted 136 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions overnight, the ministry said.

World.title: France announces nightly curfews 'for as long as necessary' in Paris and other cities
World.content:
France announces nightly curfews 'for as long as necessary' in Paris and other cities

toggle caption i Christophe Ena/AP

PARIS — Fresh curfews were being imposed across the city centers of Paris and Lyon on Tuesday after the first quiet night since France's most destructive rioting in years, as Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said a "massive" security operation was planned for new protests Saturday.

Paris police said the curfew in two designated zones — around Place de la République and the Les Halles shopping district — had restored "public peace" overnight and would remain in place "for as long as necessary." The curfew zones leave out other areas hit on Saturday, including the Champs-Elysées and the area around the Saint-Lazare train station and parts of the Rue de Turbigo in central Paris, where protesters set up barricades and lit fires.

In Lyon, one of France's largest cities, authorities also renewed a curfew in the city center from 9 p.m. to 6 a.m., saying no disturbances had been recorded overnight.

Sponsor Message

Marseille, France's second-largest city, imposed a curfew for unaccompanied minors starting Tuesday night. Lecornu said the targeted curfews "helped keep last night calm."

Student unions and groups from the " yellow vest " movement, whose protests over fuel prices shook France in 2018 and 2019, have called for another day of protests Saturday.

Soldiers from Sentinelle, the anti-terrorism operation that has patrolled French cities since the 2015 Islamic State group attacks, will take over guarding sensitive sites to free up more police officers and gendarmes for crowd control, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told lawmakers Tuesday.

"The deployment (of police forces) for next Saturday will be massive," Lecornu told the National Assembly, France's lower house of parliament, without giving figures.

toggle caption i Emma Da Silva/AP

Suspect held over Limoges city hall fire

Police on Tuesday arrested a suspect in the arson attack that charred the historic city hall in Limoges, in central France, Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said, adding that the person was being held in police custody and may not have acted alone.

French media reported that the suspect was close to radical environmentalist movements and was on a watchlist of people considered potential threats to national security. Darmanin declined to comment on the suspect's profile, but said far-left groups appeared to have organized to attack symbols of the state throughout France.

Sponsor Message

Footage of the 143-year-old building in flames, its bell tower collapsing, spread widely online over the weekend. U.S. Vice President JD Vance shared it on X, blaming the unrest on immigration and writing, "I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn." President Donald Trump, who also relayed the video, said migrants had "taken over France."

French officials have instead blamed the violence on far-left groups and opportunistic looters. At least 2,400 people were arrested after rioters in cities across France on Saturday clashed with police, set cars on fire and stormed public buildings, during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.

On Sunday evening, small groups set fire to trash bins, bicycles and other objects in the streets and looted businesses in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and other cities.

In Paris on Monday night, a police helicopter circled over Place de la République overnight, a central point in the weekend clashes, sweeping the square with a searchlight to check that the curfew was being respected.

Early Tuesday morning, workers used a crane to remove a giant fluorescent yellow vest draped over the statue at the center of the square, then used pressure washers to blast graffiti off the monument.

Louise Belanger, a volunteer who came to help with the cleanup, said she still could not apprehend the level of violence. "Normally when you are 20 you should be optimistic, you should be starting to build something (...) If you are only anger and violence, what are you going to do? This is sad for everybody in society," she said.

toggle caption i Christophe Ena/AP

Courts promise 'extremely firm' response

Speaking in Lille, northern France, Darmanin said 149 people had been jailed nationwide as of Tuesday at noon. According to the Justice Ministry, of the roughly 2,400 people arrested since Saturday, more than 800 have been sent before prosecutors, most of whom were either put on trial immediately or ordered to appear at a later hearing.

Sponsor Message

In Paris alone, about 300 people have been sent before prosecutors following the Oct. 17 protests, the city prosecutor's office said in a statement.

Darmanin said he had asked prosecutors to appeal any sentence they considered too lenient. "People with no criminal record ending up in prison for property crimes is extremely rare, if not unheard of," he said, arguing that the French justice system will be "extremely firm."

In Lille, he said, three men aged 20 to 25 with no criminal record were each sentenced to 10 months in prison and jailed immediately for looting a video game store in the city's old town.

The National Assembly is launching an inquiry into the Oct. 17 violence and the authorities' policing strategy, its speaker, Yaël Braun-Pivet, said, with findings expected "by the end of the year."

Protests continued Tuesday on a smaller scale. Some 400 people, mostly high school and university students, marched in the western city of Rennes, and about 750 in Lyon, under pouring rain.

World.title: United Nations report highlights significant increase in U.S. climate pollution
World.content:
United Nations report highlights significant increase in U.S. climate pollution

toggle caption i Charlie Riedel/AP

Countries are not doing enough to cut emissions that cause climate change, according to a new report from United Nations scientists. And the United States is a big part of the problem.

The U.S. sticks out as the only major economy where planet-warming pollution increased dramatically last year, the report notes.

It finds that last year, the U.S. was tied with Russia as the G20 countries with the most per capita emissions of carbon dioxide and other planet-warning gases. China emits significantly more total greenhouse gases each year than the U.S., but has more than four times the population.

Sponsor Message

Overall, global emissions were basically the same last year as they were the previous year.

U.S. emissions grew because of increased electricity demand, as well as Trump administration policies that support the burning of fossil fuels. The Trump administration has ordered coal-fired power plants in the U.S. to stay open longer than planned, rolled back fuel-efficiency standards for vehicles and ended tax credits for solar and wind projects .

Those policies have made the U.S. an outlier when it comes to escalating greenhouse gas emissions, says Inger Andersen, the executive director of the U.N. Environment Programme.

"Right now, everybody is scrambling a little bit regarding energy security," Andersen says, pointing to global oil and gas disruptions stemming from the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

Despite the geopolitical upheaval, "several G20 members have shown sustained emissions reduction," she notes.

That includes the European Union, which has invested heavily in energy-efficient appliances and renewable electricity sources such as wind and solar, partly in reaction to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The U.S. is pulling out of U.N. climate work

The Trump administration has withdrawn from the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement, and is working to remove the U.S. from all U.N. climate work, arguing the international system imposes unfair burdens on Americans. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency now says greenhouse gases do not pose a threat to human health and welfare, reversing its previous position.

Sponsor Message

The new report includes a statement from the U.S. government, saying the U.S. "does not endorse or agree with its analysis or conclusions, and has not provided comments to this report." The U.S. State Department did not respond to NPR's questions.

The new report, which is compiled annually by an international group of scientists, comes less than a month before global climate talks kick off in Turkey. World leaders will gather to discuss how to speed investments in clean energy and how to pay for the costs of dealing with climate change. The Trump administration will not participate in those talks.

Still, whether or not American leaders formally participate in international climate efforts, the effects of America's reliance on oil, gas and coal are being felt around the world, the U.N. warns. Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, trapping extra heat that warms the entire planet. The effects of all that pollution are felt globally.

The Earth is about 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit (1.5 degrees Celsius) warmer on average than it was in the mid-1800s, according to the World Meteorological Organization . That warming is driving widespread disasters, from deadly heat waves and floods to more intense storms and wildfires.

"All countries, especially the big emitters, must do more," says U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres. "Every fraction of a degree matters."

The Earth is on track for 5 degrees Fahrenheit of warming this century

Right now, the planet is on track for upwards of 5 degrees Fahrenheit (2.8 degrees Celsius) of warming this century, which would cause catastrophic impacts , such as massive sea level rise and the mass extinction of plants and animals, the report warns.

The U.N. Paris Climate agreement sets a goal of limiting warming to well below 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit (2 degrees Celsius), in the hopes of avoiding such cataclysms.

This is the first year the annual report has acknowledged that even lower targets are now out of reach. However, it finds it is still possible to keep warming below 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit, if global greenhouse gas emissions fall by about 25% in the next decade.

Sponsor Message

But countries are currently lagging far behind that goal.

Under the Paris agreement, about two thirds of countries have submitted formal, up-to-date plans for cutting their greenhouse gas emissions. If they all follow through on those plans, it would reduce emissions by about 15% in the next decade — far less than the 25% needed.

World.title: More than 1.5 million Canadian Crime Stoppers tips leaked, CBC exclusive finds
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Andrew Rivard spotted a Crime Stoppers ad offering a $2,000 reward for tips in the winter of 2025, he decided to report what he knew about illegal cigarette sales in his neighbourhood.

Rivard’s original tip shows he disclosed his full name. He says he trusted the organization’s long-standing promise to protect the identities of all tipsters.

"I was told nothing would come of it; no one would come to me with, you know, I guess, resentment," Rivard said. "I just was hoping it would be that exactly — anonymous."

But the Manitoba man's report — along with information from more than 1.5 million other tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years — was exposed in a massive data breach , an exclusive CBC investigation has found.

The personal information captured in some compromised tips was detailed enough for CBC to contact more than a dozen tipsters — including Rivard — who reacted with shock and fear for their safety.

"It’s very scary, to be honest," said Rivard, who now worries his home address and phone number may be used by criminals for retaliation.

Rivard’s original tip as it appeared in the leaked data, including his full name. CBC retroactively redacted other personally identifiable information. (Valérie Ouellet/CBC)

The data was stolen last March by hacktivist collective Internet Yiff Machine. In a manifesto, the group said it wanted to disprove the claim by P3 Global Intel — the company hired by Crime Stoppers to manage its tips — that the platform was "anonymous" and "secure."

A copy of the hacked data was made available to researchers and journalists, including CBC, by Distributed Denial of Secrets , a U.S. non-profit that archives and publishes hacked and leaked documents it deems to be in the public interest.

CBC took extensive precautions to protect this sensitive data throughout its investigation. Our security measures included, but were not limited to, encryption and working in a self-contained, offline environment. The sensitive information was only accessible to a small number of CBC journalists working on the project. Ultimately, CBC intends to destroy its copy of the dataset.

Beyond confirming they were hacked over six months ago, the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association (CCSA) and individual chapters have not spoken about the extent of the breach, only saying they await a detailed report from Navigate360, the company that owns the P3 platform.

This is the first time precise figures on how many Canadian tipsters were compromised in the breach — and the severity of the information exposed — have been made public.

Our interviews and analysis of Canadian content in the leaked data suggest that Crime Stoppers, along with the company it contracted to manage its database, failed to protect tipsters' identities, left personal information unredacted and improperly retained decades of sensitive records.

"For a system that has been designed to promise anonymity to the users, that has failed categorically," said Prof. Ali Dehghantanha, the Canada Research Chair in Cybersecurity and Threat Intelligence at the University of Guelph.

He’s one of two experts who were shown our methodology and limited samples of the data from a secure CBC laptop.

After seeing CBC’s main findings, the RCMP shared concerns that the breach could “jeopardize public safety, including the safety of tipsters, individuals identified in tips and police officers," it said in a statement, adding it was originally told the leak did not include Canadian data or personal information.

CBC also shared the same information with the CCSA, which declined an interview.

In a written statement, the organization’s president, David J. Forster, said they “recognize the concern and uncertainty this incident has created, particularly for people who trust Crime Stoppers with sensitive information.”

There are currently 68 Crime Stoppers chapters registered as non-profits in Canada, according to data from the Canada Revenue Agency .

Professor Ali Dehghantanha is one of two cybersecurity experts who examined samples of the data. (Li Yanjun/CBC)

Tips about high-profile Canadian investigations

Crime Stoppers is a network of civilian-run non-profits that collects anonymous tips on crime and suspicious activity. It operates independently of law enforcement, though it refers a portion of tips back to them to assist in investigations.

The organization often appeals to the public, in partnership with police, for help with unsolved crimes and to advance investigations — all with the promise of anonymity for tipsters who contact them.

CBC’s analysis of Canadian tips found mentions of many high-profile cases that generated significant public attention — from Barry and Honey Sherman’s murders to Amber Tuccaro's disappearance , Montreal’s Luka Magnotta case and, more recently, the international manhunt for Ryan Wedding .

Many of the tips dealt with serious allegations, with some people explicitly saying they feared retribution for speaking out.

Citizens called with information about alleged murderers, terrorists and pedophiles or incriminating details about people they were close to, like family members on the run or breaching court orders.

In 2012, police asked for the public’s help in identifying the voice of a man with a connection to missing Indigenous woman Amber Tuccaro. CBC found hundreds of tips mentioning her disappearance in the leaked Crime Stoppers tips. (Valérie Ouellet/CBC)

A third of all tips talked about drugs and drug trafficking; hundreds reported suspicious activity in their neighbourhoods, often naming individuals and implicating organized crime, biker gangs or drug cartels — including the Hells Angels, Rock Machine and Outlaws, as well as B.C.’s Red Scorpions and Independent Soldiers.

Notes in the data from Crime Stoppers staff suggest some of those tips led to real-life consequences: Nearly 49,000 tips were linked to a case cleared by an arrest or criminal charges, while nearly 1,000 tipsters were approved for cash rewards.

"I am concerned. I am really worried," said Dehghantanha, who has conducted digital forensics investigations for over a decade.

“I am really concerned about these records … being in the hands of the wrong people, while those people who have been impacted are not aware of that and do not have any support.”

WATCH | CBC finds Canadians' personal information in leaked Crime Stoppers tips: Over a million Canadian tips leaked from Crime Stoppers database | Duration closed caption 5:32 A CBC News investigation found more than a million tips submitted to Crime Stoppers in Canada over the past 25 years were exposed in a massive data breach. About half the leaked Canadian tips obtained by CBC contained personal information.

That's exactly the situation one Canadian woman is facing. CBC agreed to withhold her identity given her safety concerns.

She gave a tip about the murder of a loved one, which was unsolved at the time.

"I just feel all the anxiety and scared feeling come back," said the woman. Police have now charged an individual with murder.

"They were capable of hurting my loved one. They could come back and hurt one of us."

Tipsters self-identified in over 4,300 tips, data suggests

More than 850,000 tips — about half of all Canadian records identified by CBC — included personally identifiable information about tipsters, individuals named in allegations and even Crime Stoppers staff and police.

Street addresses and phone numbers appeared most frequently, alongside tens of thousands of personal emails, licence plates and hundreds of banking details related to cash rewards — information that could all be used to uncover an individual's identity.

We could not determine in every instance whether the information belonged to a tipster, a victim or those accused of a crime.

However, CBC found that in over 4,300 reports, tipsters introduced themselves with a full name, although Crime Stoppers explicitly tells the public to avoid including identifying details . Still, this represented a fraction of reports, at less than one per cent of all entries over 25 years. CBC wasn't able to verify whether all names were legitimate.

In 2021, police sought the public's help in identifying a suspect caught on video near the home of billionaire philanthropists Barry and Honey Sherman. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

Despite hundreds of those tips containing clear staff warnings that a tipster had "self-identified" or had been "exposed," the information still appeared in the database unredacted.

Storing all these data points together is a gold mine for fraudsters, said Dehghantanha.

"Imagine I am calling you and talking about the tip that you have provided and asking for more information. Immediately, I build ... trust," he said.

A name or phone number on a list might not seem like much, but it’s enough to do serious damage, said Ben Coon, chief intelligence officer of U.S. cybersecurity firm Unit 221B, who was also shown limited samples of the data.

"From what I saw, there's so much low-hanging fruit here that we could ask questions," said Coon, who said the data could be used for crimes ranging from financial fraud and extortion to money laundering.

Beyond what was collected, experts say the decision to store decades of historical tips in a single place defies basic data retention standards.

"If a tip is closed, does that need to stay online?" said Coon. "The answer to that, to me, is no."

Both experts agree that even though Crime Stoppers uses a third party to manage its data, it is still responsible for auditing how well it is secured.

"You can always outsource the operation … [and] the work," said Dehghantanha. "But you cannot outsource the accountability. You are always accountable when you are collecting the data."

Hacker claims data not publicly available online

Both cybersecurity experts said they were surprised CBC had found the data as they couldn’t locate copies of it online, which they said was reassuring. But they added that once a dataset has been leaked, it’s generally available somewhere.

In an email exchange with CBC News in September, someone purporting to represent Internet Yiff Machine wrote, "I briefly attempted to sell it publicly; however, changed my mind and no copy has made it into the public yet."

They added that the security measures of P3, which was storing Crime Stoppers' tips, were "terrible" and that the platform is still vulnerable.

"I wouldn’t trust [the hackers] at all," said Dehghantanha. "Selling [data] on the underground market is not that difficult, right…. There is a demand."

Internet Yiff Machine’s manifesto includes lines critical of police departments and for-profit prisons. (Valérie Ouellet/CBC)

In a statement, the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association said, "If there is information within the leaked records that could identify people who submitted tips, it is an extremely serious issue." It added that protecting people's safety and anonymity is its "highest priority."

It did not directly comment on the precise figures shared by CBC, but said that it has been communicating with the third-party platform "to assess what records may have been affected, what personal information may have been exposed and what measures were taken to enhance the security of the platform."

"With regard to notifying individuals identified in the records, CCSA has concerns about doing so without jeopardizing the anonymity and safety of tipsters," it said, adding that "the information available to us does not distinguish people who submitted tips from people identified in them."

"We will share further verified information as it becomes available, while ensuring that our communications do not create additional risks for individuals."

Navigate360, the U.S.-based company that owns the P3 platform, did not respond to CBC's requests for comment, which included questions about what security measures it had taken since the hack, whether it had shared reports with Crime Stoppers about the compromised data and whether it was still collecting tips.

The RCMP told CBC that at the time of the leak, it was “advised that Canadian data had not been affected based on the results of the preliminary personally identifiable information (PII) assessment."

"Then, in May 2026, the RCMP was informed by Crime Stoppers that the data breach did include Canadian data but would not contain PII of persons who have reported.”

The national police service added that it is now “engaged with the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association to determine the full scope of the incident."

It stated that it has not received reports of anyone being threatened as a result of the breach and advised anyone with concerns about their submitted information to contact the organization or their local chapter.

The Toronto Police Service, which uses tips from Toronto Crime Stoppers — the chapter with the most tips in the leak — told CBC that the group had notified it of a hack in March, but that it "has not received any information indicating the safety of officers, tipsters or members of the public has been compromised."

As for Rivard, the Manitoba man whose tip was exposed in the leak, he says Crime Stoppers should have been more transparent.

"It might have been embarrassing, but own up to it, just tell the public, let them know, and they might have your trust after, they might not: Let them decide."

World.title: Canadian housing market 'on its knees' as odds of Bank of Canada rate hike rise
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Bank of Canada has not raised interest rates since July 2023.

And while an eighth-consecutive hold is widely-predicted next week, a growing number of economists and traders are now expecting the central bank to hike its trend-setting rate to tamp down stubborn inflation.

Mortgage and debt experts say higher rates would have significant impacts on Canada's sagging real estate market. Payments on variable-rate mortgages would rise immediately, along with rates for new fixed mortgages. The pool of eligible buyers would shrink, shifting power from sellers to those who can qualify for the financing needed to make a purchase. Home prices could dip lower.

"The housing market is kind of on its knees right now, and rising rates is like tossing a drowning guy an anchor," said Scott Terrio, manager of consumer insolvency at Ontario-based Hoyes Michalos & Associates.

He says a hike "would reverberate massively."

Could an interest rate hike see home prices fall?

The volume of home sales nationwide is currently at a 25-year low, says Ben Rabidoux of Ontario-based Edge Realty Analytics.

He describes confidence among buyers today as "unbelievably weak across the country," owing to a slew of economic uncertainties ranging from the Canada-U.S. trade war to the impact of AI on jobs.

"The reality is that when we look at per capita home sales, we're already back to 1990s levels, which [was] a really terrible recessionary environment."

On home prices, Rabidoux believes "a gradual grind lower over the next three or six months is very plausible" if interest rates start rising.

WATCH | How AI is changing the real estate business: That perfect Ontario real estate listing might be staged by AI. Here's what to watch for | Duration closed caption 3:08 If you've been looking to buy a home in Ontario, you may have seen a few listings where the furniture doesn't look quite right. That's because many of them are being staged virtually, using AI. Experts say there are benefits and drawbacks. CBC's Talia Ricci breaks down what you need to know.

Last week, the Canadian Real Estate Association downgraded its forecast for 2026 home sales activity for a third straight quarter.

The industry group referenced a "notably more hawkish tone from the Bank of Canada," as it called for 444,530 homes to be sold by year-end, a 5.2 per cent drop from 2025.

The Bank of Canada's policy rate has stood still at 2.25 per cent since a quarter-point cut in October 2025.

Governor Tiff Macklem has recently warned the bank may need to raise borrowing costs if energy prices remain elevated. On Saturday, he said there is "no resolution in sight for the conflict in the Middle East" that has roiled global energy markets for the past several months.

On Monday, the latest inflation data from Statistics Canada put a spotlight on soaring energy costs. The report showed rising fuel prices have yet to meaningfully spill into other sectors of the economy. However, the Bank of Canada's latest survey, also released on Monday, found businesses are bracing for higher prices.

Odds of rate hike 'not a slam dunk'

The consensus in a recent Bloomberg survey still points to a hold, but so far this week, the Bank of Montreal, RBC Dominion Securities and Desjardins Group have flipped their predictions for Oct. 28 from a hold to a hike.

According to Bloomberg data, traders in the overnight swap market now put the odds of a 25-basis point rate hike from the Bank of Canada next week at 87 per cent, up from 70 per cent earlier this week. Swap market data measures the gap between today's interest rate and the future rate traders are betting on.

WATCH | U.S. tariffs take toll: Canada's economy still resilient, but U.S. trade war taking its toll | Duration closed caption 2:00 Canada's economy has shown resilience in the face of punishing U.S. tariffs, but new import bans on a range of Canadian products are creating further drag. Accounting firm Deloitte has lowered its growth forecast for next year by 20 per cent.

Derek Holt, head of capital markets economics at Scotiabank, is among those calling for a rate hike.

"It's not a slam dunk call, but there is probably enough supporting evidence for a hike," he wrote in a research note on Monday.

Macquarie Group economist David Doyle agrees. He predicts the Bank of Canada will raise its policy rate by 125 basis points by the end of 2027.

"Our baseline case remains for a rate hike at this month's meeting," he wrote in a note to clients on Monday. "We continue to see a steady rate hike cycle ahead."

Leah Zlatkin, a licensed mortgage broker and an expert commentator with LowestRates.ca, agrees.

"If there is a hike, I do think it's gonna be a cycle," Zlatkin said.

She points to a recent price drop in the notoriously expensive Greater Toronto Area as a sign that now is a "good time to buy."

"There's a possibility [that] housing prices are going to continue falling, but the reality is, if you'll qualify for the property today, then you'll qualify again later on if rates rise."

World.title: Ryan Wedding ally 'Tupac,' who allegedly offered cosmetic surgery to locate murder target, requests bail
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A man with alleged ties to the Montreal underworld — who goes by the aliases Tupac and Kim Jong-Un — is asking to be released on bail, a year after he was arrested for allegedly helping accused cocaine kingpin Ryan Wedding set up the assassination of an FBI informant.

Atna Ohna, identified in court documents as a hitman for Wedding's purported drug-smuggling network, is scheduled to appear in Quebec Superior Court in Montreal for a two-day hearing beginning Wednesday.

U.S. federal prosecutors want Ohna extradited to stand trial in Los Angeles on conspiracy charges related to murder, drug trafficking and witness tampering.

Montreal police have described Ohna as one the city's most prominent organized crime figures.

According to Canadian court documents, Ohna made multiple efforts to help locate the target of Wedding's purported murder plot. One such attempt included enlisting the assistance of an acquaintance and telling her Wedding would pay for a "Brazilian butt lift" and breast augmentation surgery.

Montreal-born FBI witness Jonathan Acebedo-Garcia was killed in Medellin, Colombia, in January 2025. (Submitted by name withheld)

Ohna was purportedly given $150,000 cash, plus 30 kilograms cocaine and a bejewelled red necklace, for his role in tracking down the victim, Jonathan Acebedo-Garcia, court documents say. The former Wedding associate turned FBI informant was shot in the head while having lunch in Medellin, Colombia, in January 2025.

A U.S. grand jury later indicted Wedding, Ohna and others — including a self-described " cocaine lawyer ," a crime blogger and an escort service operator — for their purported roles in orchestrating the killing.

The 41-year-old — whose last name is sometimes spelled Onha — has been in custody in Quebec and fighting extradition since his arrest last November as part of an FBI-led takedown targeting Wedding and his allies.

Ohna's lawyer, Danièle Roy, did not respond to requests for comment on the allegations surrounding her client.

In a separate case, Quebec Superior Court w as shown a police surveillance photo of Ohna meeting in a Laval park in May 2020 with four men police identified as high-ranking organized crime figures, including Hells Angels members.

Ohna, second from right, is seen in this police surveillance photo taken in May 2020 in a park in Laval, Que. A court heard Ohna was seen meeting with high-ranking organized crime figures, including Hells Angels members Gilles Lambert and François Vachon. (Quebec Superior Court of Justice)

Minh Tri Truong, a former Montreal police commander, previously told Radio-Canada that Ohna himself has been the target of assassination plots.

"There have been several hits out on him," Truong said. "He's been warned multiple times."

According to court documents, Ohna goes by aliases including Tupac and Kim Jong-Un. (Radio-Canada)

Mysterious assassination in 2023

A summary of U.S. prosecutors' evidence against Wedding, Ohna and other defendants — filed in Quebec Superior Court amid extradition proceedings — suggests the man known as Tupac had worked for Wedding before.

The court documents state that a co-operating witness is expected to testify at trial that in November 2023, Ohna killed an unnamed "rival gang member" on behalf of Wedding. Neither defendant is charged in connection with the purported assassination.

That month, Hells Angels-linked crime boss Gregory Woolley was gunned down in a Lamborghini SUV in a parking lot in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Que.

A separate, burnt-out vehicle believed to be connected to the shooting was later found on a Montreal street, 40 kilometres away.

The shooter has not been identified.

A burnt-out car on a Montreal sidestreet is thought to be connected to the shooting death of Gregory Woolley, a well-known organized crime figure in Quebec who was shot and killed in a parking lot in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Que., on Nov. 17, 2023. (Mathieu Wagner/CBC/Radio-Canada)

U.S. authorities allege Wedding and his second-in-command, Andrew Clark, led an international network of "sicarios" — contract killers — to eliminate perceived rivals of their $1-billion US cocaine empire.

Wedding, a former Team Canada Olympic snowboarder, was captured in Mexico last January and flown to California after a high-profile international search. He has pleaded not guilty to charges including conspiracy to export cocaine and murder in connection with a continuing criminal enterprise. He's set to stand trial next year .

CBC News previously reported Clark, a fellow Canadian known as The Dictator, also turned FBI informant after his arrest.

Although public records don't name Clark as the co-operating witness, lawyers for Ohna and another co-accused recently told a judge it's "obvious" that he must be the informant.

Wedding's second-in-command, fellow Canadian Andrew Clark, was arrested in Mexico in October 2024. (Omar García Harfuch/Facebook)

As for Ohna, court documents say he leveraged his connection to a Montreal woman — who wanted to date him — to obtain information on Acebedo-Garcia, the target of the 2025 murder plot.

At Wedding's request, U.S. prosecutors say Ohna later obtained Acebedo-Garcia's phone number and reached him through Threema, an encrypted messaging app.

Acebedo-Garcia purportedly acknowledged to Ohna he had been working with the FBI and said he had "no choice" but to co-operate.

He was shot in the head five times on Jan. 31, 2025, before the gunman took off on a motorcycle. The shooter has not been identified, but court documents suggest he may have been part of a hit squad hired through a Colombian crime syndicate once linked to the late drug lord Pablo Escobar.

CBC News senior reporter Thomas Daigle has extensively covered the case of Ryan Wedding. He can be reached by email at thomas.daigle@cbc.ca.

World.title: Smith says it’s time to 'move forward' in a united Canada, but vows to fight for Alberta autonomy
World.content:
Danielle Smith says it's time for province to 'move forward'

Alberta Premier Smith pledges to honour 'remain' vote | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 14:45

World.title: Problem gambling jumps, suicides triple in Ontario after expansion of online casinos
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This story is part of a CBC News series examining the public health impacts of online gambling.

Anna, a 51-year-old single mother of two teens, says online slot machine games cost her nearly everything.

And even at that point, the Ontario resident says it was hard to stop.

"The amount of money that I spent and lost — it was astronomical," she told a recent meeting of Gamblers Anonymous in Toronto, which CBC News was invited to witness.

The peer support group has been a lifeline that helped her stop betting and break free from inducements and marketing she would receive from the betting apps, she says.

"If I had gone a little while without gambling, they would literally send me thousands of dollars to say 'free money' to keep you going," she recalled.

WATCH | 'Anna' kicked her betting habit with help from Gamblers Anonymous: Gamblers Anonymous helped 'Anna' kick her addiction | Duration closed caption 1:18 Anna says Gamblers Anonymous helped her find connection to recover from her addiction last year.

She’s not alone.

The number of problem gamblers in Ontario has spiked and gambling-related suicides have tripled since the expansion of private online casino games and sports betting in 2022, CBC News has learned.

Nearly 130,000 Ontarians now show signs of gambling problems, compared with roughly 43,000 in 2018, a tripling of the number of people who meet the criteria of gambling too frequently, losing money and struggling with addiction.

These estimates are based on new research from the Alberta Gambling Research Institute (AGRI), which found a 0.5 per cent jump in Ontario’s rates of problem gambling compared to 2018. Their analysis uses the "Problem Gambling Severity Index" and data from Statistics Canada’s 2025 Canadian Community Health Survey.

AGRI researcher Carrie Shaw says the research is "brand new" and significant, showing that six months after Ontario’s private casinos opened in 2022, the number of problem gamblers in the province climbed while dropping in the rest of Canada.

"In Ontario’s market, gambling is very much normalized through access and s," said Shaw, who presented her findings at an AGRI conference in May.

"It's true across Canada, but more so in Ontario, given the amount of exposure there is," she said.

Carrie Shaw of the Alberta Gambling Research Institute found rising rates of problem gambling in Ontario after the 2022 online expansion of online betting. (CBC)

In July, Alberta joined Ontario in legalizing online gambling run by private companies. Everywhere else in Canada, it is illegal.

"With online gambling ... the barriers to access are completely removed. You can access it anytime from your computer, your mobile phone, any time of day or night," Shaw said. "You can be sitting at your desk at work and still be engaging."

Gambling suicides rising

The Office of the Chief Coroner of Ontario also reports a spike in gambling-related suicides in the years after Ontario began allowing online betting.

Before Ontario’s expansion, the province had an average of five gambling-related suicides each year from 2016 to 2021. That number tripled after 2022.

Matthew Young, chief research officer for non-profit gambling research network Greo Evidence Insights, says he called on government two years ago to do a better job of tracking online gambling activity for fear of increased addiction, bankruptcies and suicides.

"We warned that we might be seeing the harms that we're now seeing in the data," he said.

Those calls were ignored, he says.

A study published in the September 2026 American Journal of Preventive Medicine found a dramatic jump in the number of people with gambling disorders showing up at Ontario hospital emergency departments in distress.

A March 2026 study in the Canadian Medical Association Journal (CMAJ) found a 95.5 per cent increase in men and boys making gambling-related calls to ConnexOntario, the province's 24-hour mental health and addictions help line, over the last decade.

Young calls it "unfathomable" that Canada changed the Criminal Code to allow online gambling and that provinces are opening their markets without proper study of the potential public health impacts.

WATCH | Gambling addiction needs better monitoring, says expert: Gambling researcher says Canada needs better addiction monitoring | Duration closed caption 0:48 Matthew Young, addictions researcher, says there was no harm analysis done before Canada opened the floodgates to online gambling.

Young says that amid lobbying to legalize online gambling in other provinces, he would like to see better monitoring and for a share of the billions in revenues to be dedicated to independent research into ways to curb addiction and gambling-related harms.

Greo Evidence Insights was formerly known as the Ontario Problem Gambling Research Centre.

Ontario defunded it in 2019.

Are you, or someone you know, suffering from gambling? Support is available.

World.title: More than 16 years after BP's Deepwater Horizon disaster, marine life has not recovered
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

More than 16 years after one of the deadliest oil spills in history, a highly comprehensive study has found that life in the waters of the Gulf of Mexico remains severely in decline.

The Deepwater Horizon oil rig, operated by BP off the coast of Louisiana, exploded on April 20, 2010 — killing 11 people and injuring 17 others. During the three months that followed, as much as 4.9 million barrels of oil gushed into the Gulf, according to a U.S. government task force. The environmental catastrophe had a devastating impact on marine life, which continues today.

"A lot of things died right off the bat," said Tracey Sutton, a biological oceanographer at the Guy Harvey Oceanographic Research Center of NOVA Southeastern University whose team has been studying the impacts of the spill for years.

Their research found that some species declined by 60 to 85 per cent in the immediate three and a half years after the spill. Sutton's latest report, combining another eight years of detailed scanning and sampling, was just published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Time hasn't helped the situation, according to the authors.

"That low state has just maintained low," Sutton said, explaining that the dense patches of prey that predators need are missing, resulting in a "decline in things like deep-diving whales and dolphins" as well as fishes, shrimps and squids.

The immediate aftermath of the Deepwater Horizon spill killed lots of marine life, and the authors of a new study say that decline has persisted. (Charlie Riedel/The Associated Press)

Lingering in the deep

The most likely cause of this decline, the study suggests, is the Deepwater Horizon disaster, not least of which because their sampling is still finding remnants of all that spilled oil.

"What we've seen is the persistence of some of the worst components in the oil … polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, or PAHs. That's the really bad stuff," Sutton told CBC News.

The study found these oil-derived compounds inside the muscle tissue and eggs of deep-sea fishes and squid, potentially affecting health and reproduction. The authors also suggest these lingering PAHs can affect some male fishes' sense of smell, which they use to find mates.

Deepsea experts who weren't involved with the research say the study accounted for the natural factors that might affect fish abundance, such as temperature, availability of food and oxygen.

"They eliminate any other factors," said Fabio De Leo, senior scientist at Ocean Networks Canada and a professor at the University of Victoria. "And so the probable cause here is the 87 days of gushing oil through the Gulf for Mexico."

Parsing out environmental factors is a sign of the report's strength, says Kelly Robinson, an associate professor at the School of Biological Sciences at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette.

"Sometimes when you work on data, it can show you a different side," said Robinson. "But if it keeps showing you the same message, that's probably what's happening.”

More than a decade later, researchers say chemical compounds from the oil spill have made their way into fish tissue. (Rich Matthews/The Associated Press)

Diverse and essential

Experts say that the negative effect on species has a larger effect for the whole Gulf ecosystem and its role in helping capture carbon in its depths.

The deep pelagic zone, where Sutton and his team surveyed sampled fishes, crustaceans and cephalopods (such as squid) for years, is an umbrella term for a range of depths — anywhere from around 200 metres to 1,500 metres below the surface.

While sunlight stops relatively high up in that zone, the biodiversity doesn't. Lanternfish, stingrays, sperm whales, krill and many more aquatic species are all normally found throughout these depths and regularly migrate between them.

"You have to remember that these animals feed at the surface," De Leo said. “They migrate downwards and then they respire at that [level]. So the carbon dioxide gets dissolved into the water and there are nutrients that they regenerate back into the water."

"They are a train that's moving energy from the surface to the deep very efficiently," Robinson adds. "And so if we see a decline in that, it's like taking cars away from a train, right? All of a sudden you're not moving as much material."

These species effectively act as a "biological pump" for carbon, and it's one of the ways that oceans help absorb carbon dioxide from the surface, including the excess greenhouse gases humans are pumping into the atmosphere. The waters still dissolve CO2 on their own, but this study shows how pollution can weaken this service that the oceans provide.

Oil booms like this were deployed to try and contain the oil spill, but the volume proved too much and many failed. (Carlos Barria/Reuters)

Risk of future offshore drilling

The Trump administration's promise to "drill, baby, drill" has led to a push for the U.S. to extract more oil and natural gas, including new areas of offshore oil exploration.

In Canada, economic uncertainty has led to the Carney government's support for Pacific Link, a proposed oil pipeline from Alberta to B.C's coast, destined for overseas markets. Despite promised ocean protections , experts fear a long-lasting impact if an oil tanker were to be damaged and leak.

"There's more discussion about increasing oil transport in these areas of the Pacific," De Leo told CBC News from Victoria.

"We're unlikely to have something of [Deepwater Horizon’s] magnitude but there's potentially more risk if there's more traffic," De Leo said.

World.title: Carney government has no launch date planned for proposed sovereign wealth fund
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Nearly six months after announcing plans to create a sovereign wealth fund, the federal government is still not sure when it will be launched, or how exactly it will work.

In April, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada will launch its first-ever national sovereign wealth fund, with seed funding of $25 billion over three years, to be called the Canada Strong Fund.

Carney said the fund will draw on international examples, such as Norway, but will invest only domestically, be arm's-length from the government and focus on funding major Canadian projects in fields such as energy, infrastructure, agriculture and technology.

The fund would work in conjunction with private investors and is expected to include a "retail investment product" for ordinary Canadians to buy into the fund. The details of how that would work have not been announced.

The plan was outlined in the spring economic update in April, but since then, the government hasn't said when it will roll out, nor has it announced who will be running the arm's-length agency responsible for administering the fund.

At the time it was announced, some experts criticized the proposal, noting there are already a number of federal programs available to finance and de-risk private sector projects.

Similar federal programs such as the Canada Infrastructure Bank, the Canada Indigenous Loan Guarantee Corporation and the $15 - billion arm's-length Canada Growth Fund already exist.

"I don't know why specifically there's a need to set up a special fund for this," said Dana Galizia, associate economics professor at Carleton University. "That doesn't mean it's a bad idea. It just means that, without the details, I'm not really clear on what the value is here."

It also faced criticism, notably from members of the Conservative Party, for being funded by debt. Other jurisdictions with similar funds, including Alberta and Norway, invest revenues from oil and gas. They are often used as a way to spend surplus money.

"Generally, sovereign wealth funds are generated from surpluses accumulated by the government," Conservative finance critic Michael Chong said on Tuesday. "The government of Canada is not currently in a surplus."

He added that the fund is "an example of many announcements the government has made that they either have either failed to provide sufficient financial information about or have failed to execute upon."

John Fragos, spokesperson for Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, said the upcoming fall budget will include a "significant" update on the sovereign wealth fund.

"In due course, we'll have outlined who the CEO will be, who the board will be. Reiterating that because this is a novel project, we can draw on best practices around the world and here in Canada and we can see what has not worked," said Fragos.

More work remains

In addition to needing to create a Crown corporation and appoint people to it, Fragos said the federal government has undertaken a mandate review of all of the federal investment programs to ensure they're not overlapping. The review is ongoing.

He said developing the "retail" component for Canadians to buy into the fund is also taking time, because it's a concept without an existing template from other countries.

Another potential element of the fund includes selling federal assets, such as opening up airports to private investment, and using that money to invest. But — again — the details of what exactly that looks like have not been made public.

"I think there's a really interesting opportunity here with this fund, where you could take some of the proceeds from those sales and then you could use it to build the fund," said Colin Busby, director of policy engagement with the C.D. Howe Institute.

He also said, even if it's operated at an arm's length, the fund will need to consider what projects and companies get investments.

"By picking and choosing winners in very distinct parts of the country, it creates a bit of a hurdle and a bit of a political challenge for the government in doing so," Busby said.

World.title: UN retreats from 1.5 C global warming limit and proposes a plan B
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Avoiding 1.5 C of warming above pre-industrial levels is now impossible, and a new pathway to limit peak warming and then bring temperatures back down will be needed, according to an annual UN report on global climate action.

The UN's proposed new best-case pathway is to limit global warming to 1.7-1.8 C, and then eventually bring temperatures back to 1.5 C by the end of the 21st century. It's a sobering change in messaging, but not surprising given that the UN had released a related report this summer already suggesting a possible overshoot of 1.5 C.

The plan B message comes from the UN Environment Programme's Emissions Gap Report, which studies the impacts of countries' climate policies and then projects how much warming they could cause. These projections then guide negotiations at the annual UN climate conference in November, which will be in Turkey this year.

The reports have shown steady, albeit inadequate improvement in temperature projections since the global 2015 Paris Agreement was signed. This year's report, however, includes the impacts of the new U.S. administration under President Donald Trump.

"The U.S.A. no longer has a net-zero emissions goal or target," said Anne Olhoff, director of the UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre, a research institute.

"It's the second largest emitter globally, so it does affect global projections as well."

Passengers walk beneath a sign for the upcoming COP31 UN Climate Summit at the Istanbul Airport in Turkey. The UN's latest pathway report guides negotiations at the summit. (Emrah Gurel/The Associated Press)

Limiting 'overshoot'

Global warming averages have temporarily surpassed the 1.5 C limit several times over the past few years.

The year 2024 was the hottest year on record, reaching 1.55 C above pre-industrial levels. Scientists widely expect 2027 to break that record, another sign that the 1.5 C limit could be permanently crossed.

"It is not time to throw in the towel and give up — to the contrary. This is about how to find our way back, and finding our way back as quickly as possible with as low an overshoot as possible," said Inger Andersen, the executive director of UNEP.

The 1.5 C goal was especially precious for low-lying coastal and island nations, who face an existential threat from rising sea levels. Past 1.5 C of warming, those countries may have to relocate large portions of their populations, or move their entire countries away. These countries have vehemently pushed back on abandoning the 1.5 C goal, and said that the world must fulfill its obligations under the Paris treaty.

"1.5 C must remain the North Star, and overshoot cannot become an excuse for further inaction," the Alliance of Small Island States said in September .

What's the new pathway?

The UNEP's report says that warming could be limited to 1.7-1.8 C under a best-case scenario. To achieve this, global greenhouse gas emissions will have to be reduced 18 per cent by 2030. They will further have to come down 45 per cent by 2035 and 69 per cent by 2040.

The plan B pathway requires countries to pledge stronger emissions targets than they already have — and to deliver on net-zero promises.

There are some positive signs. Renewables like solar and wind power are growing fast and the world's clean electricity goals could be reached if trends continue.

"We see that renewable electricity capacity expansion has been three times higher than expected at the time of the adoption of the Paris Agreement, and we also see that solar [panel] capacity increase has been seven times higher than expected. We need to expand that," Olhoff said.

On the other hand, emissions from the burning of fossil fuels have headed in the wrong direction. The report says that the share of oil in global energy will have to come down 30 per cent and gas by 35 per cent by 2040 to stay on the UN's new pathway.

WATCH | Global action on fossil fuel transition: Canada taking part in summit on phasing out fossil fuels | Duration closed caption 2:44 Dozens of countries are meeting in Colombia for the first summit focused entirely on the transition away from fossil fuels. Canada is sending a delegation to negotiate but is also the largest oil and gas producer who'll be at the table.

Current plans not enough, UN says

Despite those daunting challenges, Andersen stressed that the new pathway "is the only way that we can get back to a semblance of a reality that is still largely manageable without major impacts."

A solar facility in Beijing, China. Solar capacity has increased seven times higher than expected, says Anne Olhoff, director of the UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre. (Achmad Ibrahim/The Associated Press)

The report looked at various levels of climate actions, from the least to most optimistic: the current policies countries have in place, their proposed climate plans that they have submitted to the UN, and all of the pledges they have made (their proposed plans plus other net-zero promises made by governments).

Both current and proposed climate plans are not enough, the report says. If current policies continue without countries making improvements, global warming could reach 2.8 C. In the most optimistic scenario, where countries fulfill all of their pledges, warming would still reach 2.1 C.

And the U.S. under Trump is a major sticking point. The withdrawal of the U.S. from the Paris Agreement and its abandonment of climate action could, on its own, lead to 0.1 C of additional warming.

"Climate impacts will not shield anyone, and that we are seeing and will continue to see impacts on every nation on the planet, including the U.S.," Andersen said.
