SENEGAL · MARKETS

Key Facts — The country Senegal is a West African democracy and new oil and gas producer that uses the CFA franc, a currency tied to the euro.

— What happened Senegal bonds in dollars had their steepest fall since early September after the Assembly speaker threatened on Monday 19 October to block the revised 2026 budget.

— Who is behind it Ousmane Sonko, sacked as prime minister on 22 May, now leads both the National Assembly and the ruling party PASTEF.

— The votes PASTEF holds 130 of the 165 seats in the National Assembly, so the budget cannot pass without its lawmakers.

— The money at stake The budget is tied to a US$2.2 billion IMF programme, agreed by staff on 1 September, that still needs board approval.

— His objections Sonko rejects cuts of FCFA 555 billion (about US$950 million) in investment spending and the planned phase-out of fuel subsidies.

— Still open No agreement was reached on Tuesday 20 October, and the plenary vote planned for Friday 23 October has been pushed to next week.

Senegal bonds denominated in dollars suffered their sharpest fall since early September, Dakaractu reported on Tuesday 20 October 2026. Seneweb, another Dakar news site, tied the drop to a press conference where Ousmane Sonko, the head of parliament, threatened to block the budget.

For US holders of Senegal bonds, the fight matters because the budget is a condition of a US$2.2 billion IMF programme. Sonko said the bill must not be voted as written, and the government has pushed the plenary vote back.

What Sonko Said on Monday 19 October

Sonko, the leader of the ruling PASTEF party, told a press conference in Dakar that the revised 2026 budget should not be voted. He accused the government of drifting from the party’s programme and said President Faye cannot run PASTEF without PASTEF.

He also said his party was not there to block, and that any blockage would be the exclusive responsibility of the executive. At the end of the session he offered a frank and sincere dialogue, Dakaractu reported.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Senegal Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who Holds Power in Dakar

President Bassirou Diomaye Faye sacked Sonko and his government on Friday 22 May, then named Ahmadou Al Aminou Lô prime minister. The Assembly elected Sonko as its speaker on Tuesday 26 May, so the man the president fired controls the chamber that passes budgets.

PASTEF, short for African Patriots of Senegal for Work, Ethics and Fraternity, won 130 of 165 seats in the November 2024 election, Ndarinfo noted. The constitution bars the president from dissolving the Assembly in its first two years, so Wednesday 2 December 2026 is the earliest date.

What He Wants Changed

Sonko rejects the cuts of FCFA 555 billion (about US$950 million) in investment spending in the revised budget, Le Soleil reported from the press conference. He also objects to lower budgets for the education, family and vocational training ministries.

On fuel, he said the subsidy bill would fall to FCFA 552 billion (about US$945 million) in 2026 from FCFA 790 billion (about US$1.35 billion). He expects diesel to rise from FCFA 755 (about US$1.29) a litre to FCFA 867 (about US$1.48), then FCFA 910 (about US$1.56) by 2027.

Why Bond Investors Reacted

On Tuesday 1 September the International Monetary Fund said its staff had agreed a 36-month programme of about US$2.2 billion with Senegal. The programme still needs the approval of the IMF board, and Ndarinfo wrote that the revised budget is among its conditions.

At the same press conference Sonko criticised the G20 Common Framework, the Group of 20 process for restructuring the debts of poor countries. Dakaractu reported that the threat puts the debt restructuring at risk and could disturb the IMF timetable, both key to Senegal bonds.

Talks Failed on Tuesday Night

PASTEF’s parliamentary group said on Tuesday 20 October that a long committee day brought some compromises but no solid consensus with the government. At the government’s request, the committee meets again on Thursday 22 October, and the plenary vote planned for Friday 23 October moves to next week.

Former prime minister Amadou Ba warned that FCFA 540 billion (about US$924 million) of energy subsidies would lack funding without the revised budget. The lawmaker asked the president, the government and the Assembly to start talks at once, Le Soleil reported on Wednesday 21 October.

What It Means for US Readers

Holders of Senegal bonds, including US emerging-market funds, now face a political risk on top of the credit risk. S&P Global Ratings cut Senegal to CC on Friday 4 September and called a distressed exchange or default extremely likely, Senego reported.

A delay in the revised budget could hold up the IMF board vote and the debt talks that bondholders await. Readers can follow the earlier steps in our reports on Senegal’s 2027 budget deficit and the debt restructuring plan.

What Is Not Known

The local reports give no price level for the Senegal bonds, so the size of the fall in cents on the dollar is open. Nor is it known which two points still divide PASTEF and the government, because the group’s statement lists none.

It is open whether PASTEF lawmakers will vote the revised budget next week, and when the IMF board will take up the programme. Whether President Faye will try to dissolve the Assembly once that power opens on 2 December is also unsettled.

More: Senegal news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Senegal bonds fall on 20 October?

Ousmane Sonko said on Monday 19 October that his party would not vote the revised 2026 budget as drafted. Dakaractu and Seneweb reported the sharpest fall in the bonds since early September.

Is Ousmane Sonko still prime minister?

No, President Bassirou Diomaye Faye dismissed him on 22 May 2026. He is now speaker of the National Assembly and leader of the PASTEF party.

Can the Assembly really block the budget?

PASTEF holds 130 of 165 seats, so the budget cannot pass without its votes. The constitution gives the Assembly 60 days to vote a finance bill.

What does the IMF programme have to do with it?

The IMF staff agreed on 1 September to a US$2.2 billion, 36-month programme that still needs board approval. Ndarinfo wrote that the revised budget is among its conditions.

When is the next step?

The finance committee meets again on Thursday 22 October. The plenary vote, first planned for Friday 23 October, has been moved to next week.

World.title: Panama Telethon Aims at Quake Homes Oct 24
World.content:
The Catedral San Juan Bautista in Chitré, Herrera province, the Azuero city that hosts the telethon (file photo: Gualberto107, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

PANAMA · EARTHQUAKE RECOVERY

Key Facts — The country Panama, a Central American nation that uses the US dollar and runs the Panama Canal, is rebuilding after a magnitude 7.7 earthquake on Friday 9 October 2026.

— Why it matters Thousands of families in the central provinces cannot yet return home, and a private fundraiser now adds to the state-led recovery that the United States is helping to fund.

— Why now The civic group Club Activo 20-30 announced its special telethon on Tuesday 20 October 2026, four days before the broadcast.

— What happened The Teletón 20-30 will run on Saturday 24 October at the Azuero Convention Center in Chitré to raise money for new homes, with the state audit office overseeing the funds.

— The numbers Official counts list 9,124 damaged homes, 2,318 of them total losses, and 3,827 people in 55 shelters, while the telethon plans homes of about 43 square meters, reportedly at US$19,000 each.

— What it means for you US donors should wait for the official donation channels, and travelers to Azuero should expect continued disruption in a region where thousands still lack a safe home.

— Still open The fundraising goal, the donation channels, the building schedule and how telethon homes will fit with the 1,300 houses planned by the housing ministry.

— Power Index Panama ranks 11th of 14 in Panama ranks 11th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 34.2 points (October 2026 edition).

A Panama telethon on Saturday 24 October 2026 will raise money to build homes for families who lost theirs in the 9 October earthquake, the civic group Club Activo 20-30 announced on Tuesday 20 October. The event, called the Teletón 20-30, will be held at the Azuero Convention Center in Chitré, the capital of Herrera province, and broadcast on television and online platforms from noon.

For US readers the telethon is the private side of a recovery that Washington has already joined, since US Ambassador Kevin Marino Cabrera announced a further US$1 million on Monday 19 October to hire engineers to assess damaged homes. Panama uses the US dollar in daily life, so every amount in this article is in US$.

The US Geological Survey measured the 9 October quake at magnitude 7.7, while Panama’s civil protection agency Sinaproc and several local outlets cite 7.5. This article uses the US figure and names the difference where it matters.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Panama ranks 11th of 14 with 34.2 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (64); weakest: military means (11). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the Panama Telethon Will Fund

Club Activo 20-30 says the money will go to building and rebuilding houses in Herrera, Los Santos, Coclé and Veraguas, the central provinces named in the announcement. Telethon president Giacomo Tamburelli said families with disabled members, mostly children, will come first, and the homes will be about 43 square meters (463 square feet) with accessibility features.

La Prensa reported that each house built with the Panama telethon money will cost US$19,000. The organizers have not published a fundraising goal in the coverage reviewed.

The special edition changes the telethon’s original aim, which was to raise money for four hospitals in Coclé, Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos, Mi Diario reported. Tamburelli said the effort does not replace government housing programs and is meant to start a national action table of civic clubs, authorities, private companies and other organizations.

Who Will Oversee the Money

Comptroller General Anel Flores, who heads the state audit office known as the Contraloría, backed the event and promised that every dollar raised will be audited. La Estrella de Panamá reported that Flores said his office had reviewed the organizer’s financial statements and found them in order.

The housing ministry, known as Miviot, will assess each case house by house together with the Contraloría and without intermediaries, Flores said, as La Estrella de Panamá reported. He also warned that the emergency will not end in the next weeks, saying in Spanish that it “does not end in December.”

How Big the Housing Damage Is

A joint report by the national emergency operations center and Sinaproc, covering 9 to 19 October, counted 9,124 damaged homes where 29,952 people lived. Of those homes, 2,318 were total losses, 5,546 had moderate or partial damage and 1,260 had light damage, La Estrella reported.

Los Santos and Herrera hold 74% of the home inspections, La Estrella reported, with 4,211 and 2,552 damaged homes, according to La Prensa. La Estrella put total-loss homes at 971 in Los Santos and 743 in Herrera.

A total of 3,827 people remain in 55 shelters across seven territories, and 2,672 of them, or 69.8%, are in Veraguas, according to the same report. The count also lists 27 injured people and damage to 576 schools, 42 health facilities and 69 roads and bridges.

How the Government Plan Compares

Miviot has announced 1,300 houses at four sites, at an average tender cost of US$25,000 each plus about US$2,000 for demolition and site preparation, La Prensa reported. Our earlier report Panama Quake Rebuilding Plan Promises 1,300 Homes covers that plan.

La Prensa calculated that rebuilding the 2,318 total-loss homes at US$27,000 each would cost about US$62.6 million. At the telethon’s US$19,000 unit cost the same count would come to about US$44 million, which is our own arithmetic and not a budget.

Other private efforts are running alongside, including a campaign that places shipping-container homes as temporary shelter at about US$8,000 each, La Prensa reported. That campaign is funded by private donations and citizen contributions.

The US Role in the Recovery

Ambassador Cabrera’s US$1 million will pay a specialist firm to evaluate homes and infrastructure, Telemetro reported. Kit Miyamoto, chief executive of the structural engineering firm Miyamoto International, said the assessments will show how to repair each home and what it will cost.

Earlier the US Embassy delivered 17 heavy cargo trucks worth US$2.1 million to Panama’s border service SENAFRONT on 13 October, Telemetro reported. Our report US Gives 17 Trucks for Panama Quake Relief has the details.

What It Means for You

The organizers say donation channels for the Panama telethon will appear on the official Teletón 20-30 social media accounts, Mi Diario reported, so US donors should use only channels published there. No international payment route was named in the coverage reviewed.

Travelers planning trips to Azuero should expect continued disruption, since damage spans five provinces and thousands of people are still sheltered. Our guides Panama Geopolitics Explained 2026 and Panama and Its Neighbours in Central America set out the wider picture.

Residents and expats based in the capital can find day-to-day context in our Panama City expat city guide. For investors, the housing bill is a public and private spending line still being sized, with no budget figure fixed yet.

What Is Not Known

The organizers’ own announcement and the Comptroller’s statement could not be opened for this article, which rests on five Panamanian outlets that agree on the date, the venue and the aim. No fundraising target, donation channel or building schedule has been published in the coverage reviewed.

Outlets differ on the closing time of the Panama telethon, with La Estrella, Mi Diario and Eco TV reporting midnight and Panamá América reporting 1:00 in the morning. Tamburelli cited more than 2,700 homes in ruins, which is above the 2,318 total-loss count in the official report, and no source explains the gap.

It is not known where the first telethon homes will be built or how they will be coordinated with the 1,300 houses Miviot has planned. The US$19,000 unit cost comes from one outlet and has not been confirmed by the organizers.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Panama telethon for earthquake victims?

It is on Saturday 24 October 2026 at the Azuero Convention Center in Chitré. Outlets give the closing time as midnight or 1:00 a.m.

What will the telethon money pay for?

It will pay to build homes for families who lost theirs on 9 October in Herrera, Los Santos, Coclé and Veraguas. Families with disabled members, mostly children, come first.

Who will audit the donations?

Comptroller General Anel Flores said the state audit office will audit every dollar raised. Miviot will assess each case house by house with the Contraloría.

How many homes did the earthquake damage?

An official report for 9 to 19 October counted 9,124 damaged homes, including 2,318 total losses. A further 3,827 people remain in shelters.

Can people in the United States donate?

The organizers say donation channels will be published on the official Teletón 20-30 social media accounts. No international payment route has been named yet.

Sources: Panamá América, 20 October 2026; La Estrella de Panamá, 20 October 2026; La Estrella de Panamá, 20 October 2026 (damage report); Mi Diario, 20 October 2026; Telemetro, 20 October 2026; Eco TV Panamá, 20 October 2026; La Prensa, 21 October 2026; Telemetro, 19 October 2026 (US$1 million); Telemetro, 13 October 2026 (trucks); US Geological Survey, M 7.7 event page.

World.title: Paraguay Votes to Ban Marriage Under 18
World.content:
The Metropolitan Cathedral in Asunción, Paraguay (Photo: Chipachyryry, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons)

PARAGUAY · CHILDREN’S RIGHTS

Key Facts — The country Paraguay, a landlocked South American country led by President Santiago Peña of the Colorado Party, is a security partner of the United States.

— Why it matters Paraguay’s Civil Code lets 16- and 17-year-olds marry with the consent of parents, a guardian or a judge, and the bill would end legal marriage under 18.

— Why now The Chamber of Deputies passed the bill on Tuesday 20 October 2026 and sent it to the Senate.

— What happened Deputies voted 23 in favour, 15 against and 9 blank to set 18 as the minimum age for marriage, with no exceptions.

— The numbers A coalition of children’s rights groups counted 6,111 adolescents aged 15 to 17 in marriages or early unions in 2025, and 5,625 of them were female.

— What it means for you If the Senate agrees, no one under 18 could marry in Paraguay, and a marriage between a minor and an adult would be expressly prohibited.

— Still open Whether the Senate takes up the bill, passes it unchanged or changes it, and when.

— Power Index Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 in Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 36.0 points (October 2026 edition).

Paraguay’s Chamber of Deputies voted on Tuesday 20 October 2026 to ban marriage under 18 with no exceptions, ending the rule that lets 16- and 17-year-olds wed with parental or judicial consent. The bill passed by 23 votes to 15, with 9 blank votes, and now goes to the Senate.

For US readers, the vote comes from a close Washington partner, one day after Paraguay and the United States signed two security deals in Asunción during a visit by US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau. It also follows Paraguay’s acceptance of United Nations recommendations to end such exceptions, according to a coalition of children’s rights groups.

Our earlier report, Paraguay Signs 2 Security Deals With US, covers the Landau visit. The sources reviewed for this article do not link the marriage vote to those talks.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 with 36.0 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (55); weakest: future resources (13). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the Bill Changes

The bill amends article 17 of the Civil Code and cancels the provisions added by Law 1 of 1992 and Law 5419 of 2015, which allow marriage from age 16. Today the Civil Code sets 18 as the general minimum age, but 16- and 17-year-olds may marry with the consent of their parents, a guardian or a judge.

The text also expressly prohibits marriage between a minor and an adult, and any breach would be reported to the Public Ministry, Paraguay’s prosecution service, for investigation. Marriages that are already being formalised and involve anyone under 18 would be suspended until both partners reach 18.

For marriages already celebrated between people under 18, a transitional rule keeps their property separate until the age requirement is met. The sources reviewed do not say whether those marriages would stay legally valid.

Walter Gutiérrez, the minister of children and adolescence, said on a local radio station that Paraguay had already raised the minimum age once, from 14 to 16 with parental authorisation. Under the new bill, he said, the exception clause is simply deleted, which fixes 18 as the strict minimum.

How Deputies Voted

The tally was 23 in favour, 15 against and 9 blank, as given by the EFE news agency and the Paraguayan outlet RDN. The Chamber approved the bill after its Children and Adolescence Commission issued a favourable opinion.

Deputy Dalia Estigarribia of the opposition Authentic Radical Liberal Party (PLRA), who chairs that commission, defended the bill and argued for ending the exceptions. She filed it in December 2024 with deputies Johanna Ortega, Guillermo Rodríguez and Walter García, EFE said.

“We are going to do justice by the girls, many of them handed over to early marriages authorised by their parents or by a judge,” Estigarribia said in remarks quoted by RDN and translated here. She also noted that international bodies have been calling for the exception to go.

Deputy Yamil Esgaib of the ruling Colorado Party (ANR), who chairs the Justice, Labour and Social Security Commission, asked colleagues to reject the bill. He argued that its legal consequences need study, especially when a teenager becomes pregnant, and that the reach of de facto unions needs to be defined.

RDN said Esgaib also described early marriage as a way out of adolescent pregnancy, and that the Colorado Party did not vote as one bloc. Some Colorados backed the ban, others opposed it and a third group voted blank, and Deputy Rocío Abed, from the camp of President Peña, announced she would vote yes.

How Common Is Marriage Under 18 in Paraguay

The coalition of children’s rights groups known as CDIA said 6,111 adolescents aged 15 to 17 lived in marriages or early unions in Paraguay in 2025. Of those, 5,625 were female and 486 were male, based on the national statistics institute’s 2025 household survey.

The 2025 survey recorded no legal marriages, against an estimate of 745 in 2024, which CDIA said may reflect a change in how marital status is recorded and not a real decline. The group called the practice a serious violation of rights that affects girls and adolescent women disproportionately.

The Ministry of Children and Adolescence, known as Minna, backs the bill. Gutiérrez said the ministry sent a favourable technical opinion to the Chamber and will repeat it if the Senate asks.

What Happens Next

The bill now moves to the Senate, which must study it and decide whether to back the ban. RDN said the Chamber had put off the debate several times before this vote.

The sources reviewed give no date for the Senate debate. Until senators act, the exception for 16- and 17-year-olds stays in force.

What It Means for You

For families and couples in Paraguay, the bill would make 18 the only age at which anyone can marry, with no waiver from parents or a judge. Nothing changes yet, because the Senate has still to act and the bill is not law.

For US readers, the vote shows how Paraguayan lawmakers handle a child-rights question while Washington is building closer security ties with Asunción. Our guides Paraguay Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026 and Paraguay Geopolitics Explained 2026 show who holds power and how the country positions itself abroad.

Residents and visitors can find day-to-day information in our Asunción expat city guide. Our Paraguay flood report covers the other major story in the country this week.

What Is Not Known

The Senate has not announced when it will take up the bill, and the sources reviewed give no timetable. It is also not known whether senators will keep the Chamber’s text, change it or reject it.

It is not clear whether marriages already celebrated between people under 18 stay valid, because the sources describe only a transitional rule on separate property. The Chamber’s own full text was not opened for this article, so these details rest on its communiqué as relayed by EFE and on Paraguayan newspaper reports.

EFE’s write-up of the CDIA bulletin says 83% of the 6,111 adolescents were female, but its own counts of 5,625 females and 486 males work out to about 92%. We therefore use the counts and not the percentage.

The survey recorded no legal marriages in 2025, so it is unclear how many of the 6,111 are legal marriages that the bill would cover. CDIA itself cautioned that the zero may reflect a change in recording, and it cited an estimate of 745 legal marriages for 2024.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Paraguay’s lower house vote on?

The Chamber of Deputies voted on 20 October 2026 for a bill that sets 18 as the minimum marriage age with no exceptions. The vote was 23 in favour, 15 against and 9 blank.

What is the current marriage age in Paraguay?

The Civil Code sets 18 as the general minimum age, with an exception for 16- and 17-year-olds who have the consent of parents, a guardian or a judge. The bill would remove that exception.

Is the ban on marriage under 18 law yet?

No, because the bill still has to pass the Senate. The sources reviewed give no date for that debate.

How many adolescents are in early unions in Paraguay?

A coalition of children’s rights groups counted 6,111 adolescents aged 15 to 17 in marriages or early unions in 2025. Of those, 5,625 were female and 486 were male.

Why does it matter for US readers?

The vote came a day after Paraguay and the United States signed two security deals in Asunción. It shows how lawmakers in a close Washington partner handle a child-rights question.

Sources: EFE via Infobae, 20 October 2026; Diario HOY, 20 October 2026; La Nación, 20 October 2026; RDN, 20 October 2026; Diario HOY on Minna, 20 October 2026; EFE via Infobae on the CDIA bulletin, 11 October 2026; Paraguay Chamber of Deputies.

World.title: Uruguay Teen Found in Argentina After 2 Days
World.content:
The General Artigas International Bridge over the Uruguay River, which links Paysandú in Uruguay with Colón in Argentina, in a 2008 file photo (Photo: Dario Alpern, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

URUGUAY · CRIME

Key Facts — The country Uruguay is a small South American democracy between Argentina and Brazil, and the city of Paysandú sits on the Uruguay River, facing Argentina’s Entre Ríos Province.

— Why it matters The case joins child safety, online grooming and cross-border justice, and shows two neighbouring police forces and prosecutors acting together within about two days.

— Why now Argentine prosecutors updated the case on Tuesday 20 October 2026, two days after the raid in Campana that ended the search.

— What happened A 15-year-old girl missing from Paysandú since Friday 16 October was found on Sunday 18 October in Campana, Argentina, and a 37-year-old man was detained.

— The numbers The search lasted about two days, one 37-year-old man is detained, and detectives seized one vehicle, two laptops and several mobile phones.

— What it means for you Parents and travellers see how a game chat can lead to a border crossing, and Argentina’s free trafficking line 145 is open to anyone.

— Still open Whether the man is tried in Uruguay or Argentina, and how a minor crossed the bridge with no exit recorded.

— Power Index Uruguay ranks 7th of 14 in Uruguay ranks 7th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 45.9 points (October 2026 edition).

A Uruguay teen found in Argentina on Sunday 18 October 2026 is now at the centre of a cross-border human-trafficking case. Argentine prosecutors said on Tuesday 20 October that the 15-year-old is in good health and that the 37-year-old man detained with her refused to testify.

US parents will recognise parts of the pattern the prosecutors describe: an Amber alert, contact through an online game and a messaging app, and an adult who allegedly ran escort advertising sites. This report does not name the girl or her family, because the prosecutor in Paysandú asked the public to respect their privacy.

Everything below about the suspect is an allegation, and he has not been convicted of any offence. The facts come from the Argentine federal police, the two prosecutors and Uruguayan news outlets that quote them.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Uruguay ranks 7th of 14 with 45.9 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (88); weakest: future resources (23). Alignment group: Hedging. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

How the Uruguay Teen Found in Argentina Was Traced

The girl vanished from her family home in Paysandú, a city in western Uruguay, on the morning of Friday 16 October. Uruguayan police say the family filed the report at about 2:45 p.m. that day.

Uruguay issued an Amber alert in the early hours of Saturday 17 October, and Argentina activated its own child-search alert, Alerta Sofía, on Sunday. Interpol’s Montevideo office also circulated a yellow notice, the agency’s alert for missing persons.

Argentina’s federal police say camera footage from the General Artigas International Bridge, which links Paysandú with Colón in Argentina, shows the girl leaving a vehicle before the migration post. She then continued on foot across the bridge, and no exit from Uruguay was recorded.

The driver, a man with Argentine and Uruguayan citizenship, entered Uruguay at 7:00 a.m. on 16 October and returned to Argentina at 8:15 a.m., the federal police say. Footage shows him as the only occupant of the vehicle on the way back.

A Paysandú court issued an arrest warrant on Saturday 17 October, and Interpol then circulated a red notice, its request to locate and detain a suspect. Detectives in Campana, a city in Buenos Aires Province, found a likely address and watched the house.

A raid on Sunday 18 October ended the search. Detectives rescued the girl and detained the man, and seized a vehicle, two laptops, several mobile phones and documents.

Argentina’s national programme for victims of trafficking assisted the girl, and the Campana municipal children’s service took her into temporary care. Uruguay’s police director, José Azambuya, said on Monday 19 October that she was in “perfect condition”.

What Argentine Prosecutors Say

Federal prosecutor Josefina Minatta of Concepción del Uruguay, the Argentine city handling the case, said the file is provisionally classed as human trafficking. She told Uruguayan broadcasters on Tuesday 20 October that the man heard the charge and the evidence but gave no defence statement.

Minatta said the man ran online escort advertising pages and took commissions from them. That is the prosecutor’s statement, not a court finding, and the suspect is presumed innocent.

She said the contact began through the girl’s family, because the man got close to the girl’s sister and even invited the whole family on a trip. The father became suspicious and cut contact, but the man kept writing to the girl through an online game and WhatsApp, Minatta said.

Minatta said the girl described feeling unwell and low, and accepted what she took to be an offer of help. She said the girl soon realised the place was not what she expected, had to throw away her phone, and felt relief when police arrived.

Minatta also appealed to parents, saying that groups that recruit young people look for teenagers who feel isolated or bullied. She said the girl’s father had told investigators that his daughter was unhappy at school.

The phones, laptops and vehicle will be examined by forensic experts, Minatta said. The girl will give testimony in a Gesell chamber, a special interview room for children, and her return to Paysandú will be authorised after specialists in trafficking cases report.

Uruguay Seeks a Trial at Home

Joaquín Suárez, the prosecutor in Paysandú, wants the man tried in Uruguay, according to Telenoche, and Minatta said he plans to ask for the man’s extradition. Suárez told a news conference on Monday 19 October that the finding is a good result but that the case now enters a new stage of gathering evidence and clarifying how the girl was moved.

Suárez has argued, according to broadcaster Telenoche, that the first possible offence was taking a minor out of Uruguay without her parents’ permission. Minatta said the Argentine side may add a migration offence, because the girl crossed the border without the legal authorisation required for a minor.

Minatta said it is still unclear how the crossing happened without that authorisation. Suárez called the situation one of “enormous risk” and thanked police in both countries for the rapid response.

Azambuya said Argentina placed its federal forces and the Entre Ríos provincial police at Uruguay’s disposal. He called relations with the Argentine authorities excellent.

What It Means for You

Parents in the United States will see a familiar pattern in the prosecutors’ account: first contact through a game, then private messages, then a meeting arranged behind the family’s back. The case shows how quickly a missing-child alert, a border camera and two countries’ police can work together.

Anyone in Argentina can report a suspected trafficking case free and anonymously, around the clock, on the national line 145, which the federal police published with the rescue. Families travelling with minors across the Paysandú-Colón bridge should check the current paperwork rules with the consulate or border authorities before they go.

For background on the country, see our guides Uruguay Geopolitics Explained 2026 and Uruguay in Latin America 2026: Role, Weight, Allies. Our Montevideo city guide and Best Places to Live in Uruguay for Expats 2026, Ranked cover daily life, and we also covered Uruguay Teen Gets 6 Years for 5 Killings, a separate case.

What Is Not Known

The court files are not public, so the accounts of both prosecutors reach us through the Argentine government release and Uruguayan news outlets that quote them. We could not confirm how many people other than the suspect, if any, are being investigated.

Early Uruguayan reports on Sunday 18 October said the girl was driven across the bridge and gave the man’s age as 38. The Argentine federal police and prosecutor later said she crossed on foot and that he is 37, and this article follows those accounts.

It is not known when or whether the man will be moved to Uruguay, or which country’s court will try him. Nor is it known how the girl passed the crossing with no exit recorded, or whether the checks at the bridge will change.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where was the Uruguay teen found?

She was found on Sunday 18 October 2026 in a house in Campana, a city in Buenos Aires Province, Argentina. Federal detectives rescued her during a raid and she is in good health.

Who is detained and what is the charge?

A 37-year-old man with Argentine and Uruguayan citizenship was detained at the house. Argentine prosecutors have provisionally classed the case as human trafficking for sexual exploitation, and he has not been convicted.

How did she cross the border?

The Argentine federal police say camera footage shows her leaving a vehicle before the migration post on the General Artigas Bridge and walking across. Prosecutors say it is still unclear how this happened without the authorisation required for a minor.

Will the man be extradited to Uruguay?

The prosecutor in Paysandú wants him tried in Uruguay, and Prosecutor Minatta said he plans to ask for extradition. No transfer date has been announced, and the man also faces proceedings in Argentina.

Can I report suspected trafficking in Argentina?

Yes, the national line 145 takes reports free of charge and anonymously, every day of the year. The federal police published the number with their account of the rescue.

Sources: Argentina Ministry of Security, federal police release, 19 October 2026; Subrayado, 20 October 2026; El País Uruguay, 20 October 2026; Montevideo Portal, 19 October 2026; Telenoche, 18 October 2026; El País Uruguay, 19 October 2026.

MOROCCO · WATER

Key Facts — The country Morocco is a North African kingdom and a free trade partner of the United States, with a long record of drought.

— What happened The European Union’s lending arm lists a proposed Morocco water loan of 130 million euros (about US$146 million) for the state utility ONEE.

— The project It would help pay for drinking water production works with a total cost of about 262 million euros (about US$294 million).

— The status The project is still under appraisal, and the bank published its summary sheet on Tuesday 13 October 2026; no loan has been signed.

— The goal More treated water of better quality, and less electricity burned for each cubic metre produced and delivered.

— What it means for you Water supply shapes Moroccan farm exports, tourism and growth, and European lenders are now lining up behind the state utility.

— Still open The interest rate, the term, the sites and the signing date have not been published.

The European Investment Bank is weighing a Morocco water loan of 130 million euros (about US$146 million) for the state utility ONEE. The bank listed it on Tuesday 13 October 2026, and the business daily LesEco.ma reported it on Tuesday 20 October.

For US readers, the Morocco water loan shows European lenders moving to secure water supply in a US trade partner and farm exporter. The project is still under appraisal, so nothing is signed.

What the European Investment Bank Has Listed

The European Investment Bank, owned by the European Union’s member states, lends money for public projects at home and abroad. Its sheet shows a Morocco water loan of about 130 million euros (about US$146 million) in a project costing 262 million euros (about US$294 million).

The promoter is ONEE, the Office National de l’Électricité et de l’Eau Potable, which produces and sells drinking water and electricity across Morocco. The sheet says the project is under appraisal, the stage before the bank’s board approves any loan.

What the Money Would Buy

The sheet says the Morocco water loan would reinforce drinking water production and raise the efficiency of ONEE’s plants. The aim is more treated water, of better quality, for users across the country.

A second goal is energy efficiency in producing and delivering the water, which LesEco.ma describes as using less electricity per cubic metre. The bank says some of the works may need an environmental and social impact study before they go ahead.

The Next Slice of a Longer Programme

The new proposal is called AEP3 Tranches B and C, after an earlier slice signed on 22 May 2025. That first tranche was a loan of 70 million euros (about US$79 million) in a project costing 140 million euros (about US$157 million).

The first loan backed ONEE’s 2025 to 2030 equipment plan, which its board approved on 21 April 2025. The new Morocco water loan would nearly double the bank’s support for the same programme.

Europe’s Growing Bet on ONEE

On 28 July 2026 the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, a separate multinational lender, announced 250 million euros (about US$281 million) for ONEE. It was its first Morocco loan backed by Tamwilcom, the national credit guarantee institution.

The deal, split into committed and uncommitted parts, is covered in this report on the EBRD water security loan. Together, the two European banks could put hundreds of millions of dollars into the same state utility.

Why Water Is a Pressure Point

Morocco has endured years of drought that cut harvests and slowed growth. The ministry’s water platform Maadialna put national dam reservoirs at 65.7 percent full on 12 October 2026, which is about 11.1 billion cubic metres.

Even so, the state is building 14 large dams, detailed in this report on Morocco’s dam programme. Dams store rain, but treatment plants decide how much of it reaches taps, which is where the new money would work.

What It Means for US Readers

Morocco has had a free trade agreement with the United States since 2006, so its water security matters to American exporters and bondholders. Farm exports such as citrus and tomatoes, which depend on irrigation, feel any shortage first.

Morocco will also co-host the 2030 men’s World Cup with Spain and Portugal, which will bring large crowds to its cities. For now, European banks rather than American ones are the main outside financiers of its water works.

What Is Not Known

The sheet gives no interest rate, repayment term or signing date for the proposed loan. It does not say which towns, plants or pipelines would benefit, or how much extra water the works would deliver.

The sheet names no lender for the other 132 million euros (about US$148 million) of the project cost. The bank’s guarantee cover also depends on the availability of European Union funds set aside for the southern neighbourhood.

More: Morocco news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How big is the proposed Morocco water loan?

The bank lists a Morocco water loan of 130 million euros (about US$146 million) for ONEE. The total project cost is about 262 million euros (about US$294 million).

Who would receive the Morocco water loan?

The borrower would be ONEE, the state office for electricity and drinking water. It produces and transports drinking water across the kingdom.

Has the loan been approved or signed?

No. The bank’s sheet, published on 13 October 2026, shows the project under appraisal, and the bank board has not approved it.

What would the money pay for?

It would pay for stronger and more efficient drinking water production, with better quality and less energy used per cubic metre. The sites have not been named.

Is this the first European loan to ONEE for water?

No. The EIB signed 70 million euros (about US$79 million) in 2025, and the EBRD announced 250 million euros (about US$281 million) in 2026.

Sources: European Investment Bank, project sheet ONEE Production Eau Potable AEP3 Tranches B & C, 13 October 2026; LesEco.ma, Eau potable : la BEI envisage un prêt de 130 millions d’euros à l’ONEE, 20 October 2026; European Investment Bank, project sheet ONEE Production Eau Potable III AEP3 Tranche A, 8 May 2025; EBRD, EBRD and ONEE strengthen water security in Morocco, 28 July 2026; Maadialna, Ministry of Equipment and Water, 12 October 2026.

World.title: Costa Rica Panel OKs US$17.6M University Cut
World.content:
The Plaza de la Democracia in San José, where protesters gathered during the 20 October march against budget cuts (file photo: Rodrigo Fernández, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

COSTA RICA · BUDGET

Key Facts — The country Costa Rica, a Central American democracy, funds its five public universities through a special higher-education fund known as FEES.

— Why it matters The cut and a frozen judicial budget test the first national budget of President Laura Fernández and Finance Minister Rodrigo Chaves, and the frozen funds touch agencies that work with US authorities on drug cases.

— Why now A legislative committee sent the 2027 budget to the full Assembly late on Tuesday 20 October 2026 with the cut inside, hours after thousands marched in San José.

— What happened The committee voted 6 to 5 to take ₡8.048 billion (US$17.6 million) from the university fund, after an earlier vote rejected the cut because a governing-party lawmaker voted against it by mistake.

— The numbers The 2027 budget totals ₡12.4 trillion (US$27.1 billion), ₡29.844 billion (US$65.2 million) of judicial spending stays frozen, and only 25 of 137 motions were voted.

— What it means for you Costa Rican students face uncertainty over places and regional campuses, and visitors to San José may meet protest road closures near the Assembly.

— Still open Whether the universities sue, and whether the full Assembly keeps the cut in two debates before the 29 November deadline.

— Power Index Costa Rica ranks 9th of 14 in Costa Rica ranks 9th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 36.5 points (October 2026 edition).

A Costa Rican congressional committee sent the 2027 national budget to the full Assembly late on Tuesday 20 October 2026 with a Costa Rica university cut of ₡8.048 billion (US$17.6 million) still inside it, hours after thousands of people marched through San José against the measure. The cut comes out of the Special Fund for Higher Education, known as FEES, and the budget committee approved the whole plan by six votes to five.

For US readers, the same budget keeps ₡29.844 billion (US$65.2 million) of judicial spending frozen and blocks the filling of more than 400 vacant judicial posts, including at the Judicial Investigation Agency, known as the OIJ, and the Public Prosecutor’s Office. The OIJ’s Interpol office handed a Russian suspect to US authorities last week, and on 16 October the US Embassy called Costa Rica a key partner against organized crime.

All conversions here use the dollar sell rate of ₡457.54 that the Finance Ministry published for 21 October 2026, so they are approximate. The 2027 budget totals ₡12.4 trillion (US$27.1 billion) and now goes to the full Legislative Assembly for two debates and a final vote.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Costa Rica ranks 9th of 14 with 36.5 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (75); weakest: military means (0). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB). See the full index, the business lens and the data →

How the Costa Rica University Cut Passed

The Legislative Assembly’s budget committee, known as Hacendarios, first rejected the cut on Monday 19 October when Kattia Ulate, a deputy of the governing Pueblo Soberano party (PPSO), voted with the opposition. Ulate later said she had voted incorrectly, and her party asked for a second vote.

That evening the committee approved motion 16 by six votes to five, moving ₡8.048 billion (US$17.6 million) out of FEES to help pay the state’s unpaid employer contributions to Jupema, the teachers’ pension fund. PPSO is the governing party under President Laura Fernández, and Nogui Acosta, who leads the PPSO group in the Assembly, also chairs the committee.

Costa Rica has five public universities: the University of Costa Rica (UCR), the National University (UNA), the Costa Rica Institute of Technology (TEC), the State Distance University (UNED) and the National Technical University (UTN). The cut takes ₡1.899 billion (US$4.2 million) from each of UCR, UNA, TEC and UNED, and ₡448 million (US$1.0 million) from UTN.

UCR rector Carlos Araya called the cut unconstitutional, saying the money was agreed in November 2025 by a liaison commission of government and rectors and that the Constitutional Court has barred lawmakers from reducing such agreed funds. He said the universities would go to court if the decision was not reversed by 11:59 p.m. on Tuesday.

What the Universities Say They Would Lose

The National Council of Rectors, known as Conare, estimates that the proposed cuts to university money across the 2026 and 2027 budgets could reach about ₡26 billion (US$56.8 million). The government’s proposal for the FEES budget itself was a 0% increase, and La Nación reported that talks between rectors and the government ended without agreement.

Araya said the UCR campus at Paraíso depends entirely on the money being cut, and a UCR student leader put that campus at 500 students and an academic centre in Limón at 400. Semanario Universidad also reported that UNA rector Jorge Herrera, who leads Conare, said part of the money is committed to labs, classrooms, libraries and residences at regional campuses, and that losing it would put 417 planned engineering places in Liberia, Nicoya, Sarapiquí, Pérez Zeledón and Coto at risk.

Education Minister Leonardo Sánchez argues that TEC holds substantial reserves, while university officials say much of that money cannot legally pay operating costs. After the march, Acosta said it reflected specific groups and was focused mainly on the universities, and that the way universities use their funds should be reviewed.

Thousands March on the Assembly

The march was called for 9 a.m. at the Fuente de la Hispanidad in San Pedro de Montes de Oca and walked to the Legislative Assembly in central San José, where La Nación said the Plaza de la Democracia was packed. Students, professors and staff from all five public universities joined unions and groups from health, agriculture, culture and labor rights, and opposition deputies took part.

Organizers expected 25,000 to 30,000 people, UTN director William Rojas told La Nación, while the outlets reviewed describe thousands and give no official count. Rain fell during the march, parts of Avenida Segunda stayed closed to traffic at 2:30 p.m., and the rectors watched the committee session from the public gallery.

The Rest of the 2027 Budget

Of 137 motions filed, only 25 were voted before the 11:30 p.m. deadline, and the committee’s rules then discarded the rest and forced the final vote. La Nación reported that only motion 16 won approval among the university cuts, while motion 104, which would have taken a further ₡8.918 billion (US$19.5 million) from university operating costs, and motion 105 on UCR math and science fairs did not pass.

The budget cuts the judiciary by about ₡10 billion (about US$22 million), a figure La Nación puts at ₡10.5 billion and CR Hoy at ₡10 billion, and keeps the freeze of ₡29.844 billion (US$65.2 million) that the opposition tried to remove. La Nación said budget rules 11 and 12 also freeze the filling of more than 400 vacant posts in judicial programs, including the OIJ and the Public Prosecutor’s Office, which pursue drug trafficking and organized crime.

The committee also moved ₡250 billion (US$546 million) from lines of the health insurer CCSS, the child nutrition centers Cen-Cinai, the housing bank Banhvi and the social aid agency IMAS to other social programs, including non-contributory pensions, Avancemos scholarships and school meals. The budget also raises funding for six ministries, including the Presidency and Finance ministries that former president Rodrigo Chaves leads.

Why the Budget Is Tight

The Tico Times reported on 19 October that 2026 revenue is about ₡400 billion (US$874 million) below budget and that the Finance Ministry is asking lawmakers to close the gap with spending cuts and new borrowing. It cited the Comptroller General’s Office, which projects that the financial deficit would rise from 4.3% to 4.8% of gross domestic product, the largest deterioration since 2020.

What It Means for You

For US readers following Costa Rica, the vote shows that the governing party can pass its cuts six to five when its committee members vote together. The details to watch are the 2026 deficit the Comptroller projects at 4.8% of output and the frozen judicial budget, which touches agencies that work with US authorities on drug cases, as we covered in Costa Rica Extradites Five Men to US on Drug Charges.

Costa Rican students and families face uncertainty over scholarships, new places and regional campuses until the full Assembly votes and any court challenge is settled. Our guides Costa Rica Explained: The Country, Its Politics, Its Economy and What to Watch and Costa Rica’s Economy Cools but Stays Solid in 2026 set out the politics and the economy behind the budget.

Visitors and residents in San José should check for street closures near the Assembly on protest days, since parts of Avenida Segunda stayed closed on Tuesday afternoon. Our San José city guide and What to Do in San José in October 2026: Iron Maiden and Tango cover getting around the capital.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the universities filed a court challenge after the 11:59 p.m. deadline Araya set, and the Constitutional Court precedent he cited was not reviewed for this article. No official count of marchers was found, and the organizers’ forecast of 25,000 to 30,000 is not a headcount.

The full Assembly can still change the budget in two debates before the 29 November deadline, so the cut and the judiciary freeze are not final. The size of the judicial cut also differs by source, at ₡10.5 billion in La Nación and ₡10 billion in CR Hoy, so the exact figure is unconfirmed.

The Assembly’s own committee record could not be opened for this article, so the vote counts and amounts rest on four Costa Rican outlets that agree with one another. The dollar figures follow the Finance Ministry’s 21 October sell rate and will move with the exchange rate.

Frequently Asked Questions

How big is the Costa Rica university cut?

The committee approved a cut of ₡8.048 billion (US$17.6 million) to the Special Fund for Higher Education. The money is meant to help pay the state’s unpaid employer contributions to the teachers’ pension fund Jupema.

Why was the vote held twice?

The first vote rejected the cut on Monday 19 October after PPSO deputy Kattia Ulate voted against it. She later said she had voted incorrectly, and the committee approved the cut six to five that evening.

Is the university cut final?

No, the budget still needs two debates and a final vote in the full Legislative Assembly, which has until 29 November. The universities have also said they could go to court.

Who marched on 20 October?

Students, professors and staff from the five public universities marched with unions and social groups from San José to the Legislative Assembly. Organizers expected 25,000 to 30,000 people, but no official count has been published.

Does the budget affect US cooperation on crime?

The budget keeps ₡29.844 billion (US$65.2 million) of judicial spending frozen and blocks more than 400 vacant posts, including at the OIJ and the Public Prosecutor’s Office. The sources reviewed do not say how the freeze would affect cooperation with US authorities.

Sources: La Nación, 20 October 2026 (committee vote); La Nación, 20 October 2026 (rectors); La Nación, 20 October 2026 (march); CR Hoy, 20 October 2026; Semanario Universidad, 20 October 2026; Semanario Universidad, 20 October 2026 (UN rapporteur); The Tico Times, 20 October 2026; The Tico Times, 19 October 2026; The Tico Times, 18 October 2026; Costa Rica Finance Ministry exchange-rate indicator, 21 October 2026.

World.title: Guyana father reportedly confesses to throwing 6-year-old who couldn’t swim to drown after spiritual advisor told him the boy wasn’t his
World.content:
Guyana father reportedly confesses to throwing 6-year-old who couldn’t swim to drown after spiritual advisor told him the boy wasn’t his

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 45-year-old father in Guyana has reportedly confessed to killing his six-year-old son by throwing him into the water, knowing he could not swim, after allegedly being told by a spiritual advisor that the child was not biologically his.

Bharrat Jaikarran is accused of killing his son, Orlando Jaikarran, whose decomposing body was discovered early Tuesday morning, October 20, in a canal at Bath Settlement, West Coast Berbice. The boy had been missing since October 14.

According to the Guyana Chronicle, Jaikarran reportedly told investigators that he had consulted a pujari, a Hindu religious officiant who conducts religious ceremonies and may also provide spiritual guidance. He claimed the spiritual advisor told him Orlando was not his biological son, although that allegation has not been independently verified.

Investigators were reportedly told that Jaikarran rode his motorcycle to an area near the sea dam, left it there and returned home to collect Orlando. He allegedly took the child back to the location and threw him into the water despite knowing that the six-year-old could not swim.

The father reportedly admitted knowing that a neighbour had surveillance cameras but believed his movements would not raise suspicion because Orlando frequently accompanied him on early-morning fishing trips.

According to News Room Guyana, police obtained information from the father that led them to the child’s body. Investigators also reviewed surveillance footage reportedly showing the father travelling with the child before returning alone.

Jaikarran had initially reported Orlando missing and denied harming him. However, as investigators gathered evidence, he reportedly confessed to the killing and provided information that led police to the location of the boy’s remains.

The tragedy has sparked outrage in Guyana, with Minister of Human Services and Social Security Vindhya Persaud condemning the killing and warning against religious figures who make harmful claims under the guise of spiritual guidance.

The case has also raised concerns about the influence of spiritual beliefs and the devastating consequences of acting on unverified claims.

Jaikarran remains in police custody as investigators continue their investigation. A post-mortem examination is expected to establish Orlando’s cause of death.

World.title: Triple murder trial of Christian Espat and Michael Brown delayed until 2027 as prosecution introduces new evidence
World.content:
Triple murder trial of Christian Espat and Michael Brown delayed until 2027 as prosecution introduces new evidence

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The long-awaited triple murder trial of Christian Espat, 31, and Michael Brown, 25, has been postponed until January 2027 after the prosecution sought to introduce additional cellphone evidence just days before the proceedings were scheduled to begin.

The two men appeared before Justice Nigel Pilgrim in the High Court on Tuesday, October 20, in connection with the October 2023 shooting deaths of three-year-old Amarie Esmeralda Rodriguez, her father Delmar Rodriguez, and Carlos Leonardo Chi in San Pedro Town.

The prosecution informed the court that additional digital evidence had emerged following discussions with a witness. The evidence reportedly includes cellphone records, a forensic report and photographs that the Crown considers crucial to its case.

Defense attorneys Dickie Bradley and Leeroy Banner, representing Espat, and Dr. Lynden Jones, representing Brown, objected to the late disclosure, arguing that they needed sufficient time to independently examine the material.

Jones told the court that he received notice of the additional evidence late Friday, October 16, and raised concerns about discrepancies in the number of photographs disclosed. He also questioned why digital files reportedly obtained in 2023 carried modification dates from October 2026.

Although Justice Pilgrim acknowledged that the evidence was being introduced unusually late, he ruled that the prosecution could submit it, emphasizing the importance of allowing relevant forensic and digital evidence to be considered in determining the accused men’s guilt or innocence.

The judge subsequently scheduled another case management conference for December 3, 2026, and set the trial for January 19 to 29, 2027, declaring that it would proceed on those dates “come hell or high water.”

The October 22, 2023 shooting in San Pedro’s San Pedrito area also left several other people injured. Espat and Brown were subsequently charged with three counts each of murder, attempted murder and use of deadly means of harm.

The trial has faced previous procedural disputes, including a June 2026 ruling allowing two prosecution witnesses to testify virtually after they expressed fears for their safety.

Justice Pilgrim also invited defense attorneys to submit bail applications on behalf of their clients, who have remained on remand since 2023.

Both men were further remanded to the Belize Central Prison pending the next hearing.

World.title: 19-year-old Adam Reynolds charged in violent $89,900 Burrell Boom home invasion after stolen SUV recovered
World.content:
19-year-old Adam Reynolds charged in violent $89,900 Burrell Boom home invasion after stolen SUV recovered

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 19-year-old Ladyville resident has been charged with aggravated burglary following a violent home invasion in Burrell Boom Village during which four armed intruders allegedly tied up a businessman and escaped with nearly $90,000 in cash and valuables, including his SUV.

Adam Abraham Reynolds, a labourer of Vista Del Mar, Ladyville, appeared before a Belize City magistrate on Tuesday, October 20, where he was arraigned on a single count of aggravated burglary in connection with the October 14 attack on a 53-year-old businessman at El Chiclero Resort.

According to police reports, the man was asleep inside his condominium around 4:50 a.m. when he was awakened by loud noises. An intruder allegedly jumped onto his bed and pressed a pillow against his face. As he struggled, a second man entered and struck him with an object resembling a firearm, causing an injury to his face.

The businessman was then restrained with duct tape around his hands, feet and mouth while three intruders ransacked his residence. The men allegedly escaped with $30,000 in cash, two gold chains valued at $12,000, two cellphones, a television, a surveillance system and a burgundy 2017 Toyota Rush valued at $45,000. The total value of the stolen property was reported at $89,900.

Police subsequently located the stolen SUV in Santa Familia Village, Cayo District, on October 15. Investigators allege that Reynolds was inside the vehicle when officers approached, but sped away before crashing and abandoning it.

Usher later positively identified the recovered vehicle as his property.

During an October 16 police briefing, Assistant Superintendent Stacy Smith confirmed that two persons of interest had been detained and that investigators were seeking another individual in connection with the burglary.

Reynolds reportedly surrendered to police on Monday, October 19, in the presence of an attorney. During Tuesday’s court appearance, he requested additional time for his attorney to arrive, but the arraignment proceeded after approximately two hours without counsel.

The charge remains an allegation, and Reynolds has not been convicted. Investigations into the involvement of the other alleged intruders continue.

World.title: International News: World Food Programme to cut food assistance for 500,000 people in Gaza
World.content:
International News: World Food Programme to cut food assistance for 500,000 people in Gaza

By Zoila Palma: The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) will suspend monthly assistance to approximately 500,000 people in Gaza because of a funding shortfall, the agency announced on Monday.

The reduction means that about 1.1 million Palestinians, roughly half of Gaza’s population, will continue receiving monthly food or cash assistance, down from the 1.5 million to 1.8 million people reached each month since the October 2025 ceasefire.

Shaun Hughes, the WFP’s country director, told AFP in East Jerusalem that the assistance had been a lifeline for families struggling to survive. He stressed that the cuts were not caused by a lack of humanitarian access to deliver food, but by insufficient funding. The agency’s decision comes as many Palestinians continue to face displacement, insecurity and difficult living conditions, with the United Nations estimating that 1.2 million people have lost their homes.

Under the revised assistance programme, families receiving food will get one parcel instead of two, along with a smaller bag of wheat flour.

Meanwhile, approximately 75,000 families receiving cash assistance will see their monthly payments reduced from 1,250 shekels, about US$400, to 750 shekels, or roughly US$240.

Hughes said conditions in Gaza remained severe, with daily airstrikes, continued displacement and widespread homelessness.

Recent assessments indicate that 1.4 million people, or about two-thirds of the population, remain acutely food insecure and require assistance to survive.

World.title: Belize City student reported missing
World.content:
Belize City student reported missing

By Zoila Palma: The family and friends of Belize City student, Cheryl Castro,14, is seeking the public’s assistance in locating her.
