World.title: Saudi finance minister promises to review delayed US$77 million solar energy loan for Belize
World.content:
Saudi finance minister promises to review delayed US$77 million solar energy loan for Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño says he personally raised Belize’s long-delayed solar energy financing arrangement with Saudi Arabia’s finance minister during meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.

Briceño explained that he attended a small gathering involving several high-level participants, including the Saudi finance minister, where he took the opportunity to raise concerns over the delayed project.

According to the Prime Minister, the Saudi official was not fully familiar with the details but assured him that he would examine the matter.

Briceño expressed optimism that the discussion could help move the project forward.

Belize signed a US$77 million financing agreement with the Saudi Fund for Development in August 2023 to support the construction of a 60-megawatt solar energy project.

However, as Breaking Belize News reported in August, Minister of Public Utilities Michel Chebat confirmed that no funds had been disbursed three years after the agreement was signed.

Chebat previously attributed the delays to procurement requirements, engineering consultations and procedures imposed under the Saudi financing arrangement.

The government has also discussed restructuring the project to combine solar generation with battery storage.

While Briceño described his conversation with the Saudi finance minister as encouraging, he did not announce a specific date for disbursement or the start of construction.

World.title: PM blames two-year delay in battery storage project on disputed iguana sanctuary claim
World.content:
PM blames two-year delay in battery storage project on disputed iguana sanctuary claim

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño has again criticized bureaucratic delays at the World Bank, claiming that a dispute involving an alleged iguana sanctuary in San Pedro held up a major electricity storage project for approximately two years.

Speaking after returning from international financial meetings in Bangkok, Briceño said the government had been pursuing World Bank financing for battery storage facilities capable of supplying approximately 40 megawatts of electricity.

According to the Prime Minister, the project was delayed after concerns were raised that land earmarked for the development was being used as an iguana sanctuary.

Briceño disputed the claim, describing the person occupying the property as a squatter, and said World Bank officials were embarrassed when he explained the circumstances during their meeting.

He argued that the delay had serious consequences for Belize’s energy security.

The Prime Minister explained that battery storage would allow Belize to purchase cheaper electricity from Mexico during periods of low demand, particularly in the early morning hours, store the power and use it during peak consumption periods.

He suggested that the project could have helped Belize avoid some of the electricity supply problems it has experienced.

The World Bank announced the US$58.4 million Belize Energy Resilience and Sustainability Project in February 2025. The initiative includes battery energy storage systems at four strategic locations to improve electricity reliability and reduce dependence on imported power.

Briceño said the government is continuing discussions to resolve the outstanding issues while pursuing greater energy independence through solar and other renewable sources.

World.title: PM seeks extension of World Bank agriculture project as March 2027 deadline approaches
World.content:
PM seeks extension of World Bank agriculture project as March 2027 deadline approaches

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño says Belize is requesting an extension of a World Bank-funded agricultural development project, warning that complicated administrative requirements have delayed its implementation.

Speaking following his return from Bangkok, Briceño explained that the project is intended to assist small farmers in adapting to climate change through improved agricultural practices and technology.

However, he complained that the World Bank’s requirements and approval procedures have made it difficult for Belize to complete the necessary work within the prescribed timeframe.

The Prime Minister said he raised the matter directly with two World Bank vice presidents during his overseas meetings.

The project is scheduled to conclude in March 2027, but Briceño said the government has made the case for additional time to ensure that farmers benefit from the initiative.

According to the Prime Minister, a World Bank technical team is expected to visit Belize shortly to review implementation, assess the project’s successes and consider the government’s request for an extension.

The Climate Resilient and Sustainable Agriculture Project, approved in March 2022, aims to improve agricultural productivity and encourage the adoption of climate-smart farming practices. World Bank records identify March 31, 2027, as its scheduled closing date.

Briceño expressed optimism that the government’s discussions would help secure more time for the project, although no extension has yet been confirmed.

World.title: NWC seeks 51% hike
World.content:
Acting president of National Water Commission Kevin Kerr (left) speaks during Tuesday’s sitting of the Public Accounts Committee as permanent secretary in the Ministry of Water, Environment and Climate Change Wayne Robertson listens. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

The Office of Utilities Regulation (OUR) will decide within 10 days whether to accept a National Water Commission (NWC) application for a tariff review which could pave the way for higher water and sewerage rates.

The OUR confirmed Tuesday in a release that it received the application on Friday, October 16, covering the five-year period from 2026/27 to 2030/31.

The regulator said it would first assess whether the application meets its requirements and may request additional information from the NWC before deciding whether to formally accept it for review.

The development comes as the NWC seeks a 51 per cent increase in water and sewerage rates amid worsening revenue collection and rising expenses.

The utility wants to raise its annual revenue from about $40 billion to $60 billion to cover operating costs and critical investments over the next five years, while noting it owes the Government approximately $21 billion in General Consumption Tax (GCT).

The disclosures were made by NWC officials on Tuesday during a sitting of the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), where the utility’s unpaid bills and financial difficulties came under scrutiny.

Acting NWC President Kevin Kerr told the committee that the proposed increase was included in a tariff application submitted to the OUR last Friday and noted that the commission is awaiting approval from the regulator.

“So what our submission includes is a 51 per cent increase, and there are some scenarios involved if that is not provided; we will have to revise our investment plan, adjust with the determination made at the end of the process and, as usual, the public will be required to participate in a more consultative process by the OUR over the review period,” Kerr said.

Chief financial officer at the NWC Fabian Christie told the committee that the request reflected the utility’s financial challenges.

“The fact is that our revenues have worsened in terms of paying from our customers, and also the fact that we would require a tariff increase, because our expenses have been increasing dramatically,” Christie told the committee.

He also pointed to the impact of natural disasters and worsening droughts on the commission’s finances. Christie said these events could reduce the utility’s revenue by between 10 and 15 per cent in a given year, depending on their severity.

The proposed increase comes against the background of a sharp rise in the NWC’s unpaid bills.

PAC Chairman Julian Robinson, referring to the Auditor General’s findings, said the commission’s payables rose from $10.6 billion in the 2016/17 financial year to $33.2 billion in 2025/26.

The report also found that the NWC’s net receivables — money owed to the utility — stood at $4.6 billion as at March 2026.

Christie told the committee that the $21-billion owed in GCT accounted for the largest share of the NWC’s $33.2 billion in payables. He explained that the commission withholds GCT when it is billed by suppliers and is expected to pass that tax on to the Government.

Christie also confirmed that the money was being used to support the utility’s day-to-day cash needs.

He revealed that the remaining approximately $12 billion in payables includes approximately $6 billion owed to Central Wastewater Treatment Company, which treats much of the sewage from Kingston and parts of St Catherine at the Soapberry facility. The other roughly $6 billion is owed to contractors and suppliers.

Christie acknowledged that the outstanding payments were affecting the commission’s ability to carry out work.

He gave an approximate breakdown of some payments owed to contractors and suppliers, saying about $1.3 billion was between zero and 30 days overdue, $400 million between 30 and 60 days, $500 million between 60 and 90 days, and $1.6 billion outstanding for more than 90 days.

The proposed tariff increase is not the only measure being pursued to improve the NWC’s finances. Kerr said reducing non-revenue water was a priority.

He said the commission had previously undertaken reduction projects in Kingston, St Andrew and Portmore, and was in the final stage of procurement for an islandwide programme, adding that the NWC hopes to select a bidder or bidders by the end of the current financial period.

The planned programme would be rolled out in stages, beginning in areas including Spanish Town, Old Harbour, May Pen, Mandeville, Montego Bay, Negril, Lucea, Ocho Rios, and Port Antonio, before further work in Kingston and Portmore.

Kerr said the long-term target was to reduce non-revenue water to 30 per cent islandwide within 11 years as the current level averages between 70 and 73 per cent.

The NWC’s financial position was also a concern for Robinson, who questioned how the utility would improve its cash flow beyond seeking higher tariffs. He pointed to the growth in payables and the amount owed to suppliers, while raising the need to reduce losses and improve the collection of money owed to the commission.

Christie said the NWC was working on a plan to improve its working capital management, which he expects to submit to the board at the start of next year. He said the effort would need to improve the amount of cash available to meet the utility’s obligations.

Furthermore, Kerr said, the tariff application was tied to an investment plan designed to ensure that financing could be secured for priority projects. He noted that the NWC received an interim tariff in 2019, before the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 eroded its cash flow.

World.title: Twinkle Brothers honoured on home turf
World.content:
Councillor for the Falmouth Division Garth Wilkinson (left) shares a light moment with Twinkle Brothers band member Ralston Grant and his wife Della following the Trelawny Municipal Corporation, in collaboration with the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission, National Heroes’ Day Civic and Awards Ceremony in Falmouth on Monday.

FALMOUTH, Trelawny — There was a flood of emotions as reggae musicians Ralston and Norman Grant, of the Twinkle Brothers, Falmouth natives, were recognised for their contribution to Jamaican music at a National Heroes’ Day awards ceremony in historic Water Square in the parish.

Norman is currently on tour, but for Ralston, the occasion held special significance, as decades ago the siblings operated a record shop almost on the exact spot where the awards ceremony was held, long before their music took them to audiences around the globe.

The recognition came through the Trelawny Municipal Corporation, in collaboration with the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission (JCDC), during its 2026 National Heroes’ Day Civic and Awards Ceremony.

Reflecting on the moment, Ralston said the honour was particularly meaningful because it was his first award in their native Trelawny, despite receiving international recognition for the band’s musical achievements since they started out in 1962.

“It means everything, you know, because I’ve never got one from Trelawny before,” he said.

The musician recalled the brothers’ early accomplishments in the Jamaica Festival Song Competition in 1970, where they placed third behind winner Hopeton Lewis and the Jamaicans.

Their musical journey also includes performances before former Governor General Sir Clifford Campbell during an era when their talent was gaining recognition at home.

The citation accompanying the award praised Norman and Ralston for their outstanding contribution to Jamaican music, cultural heritage, and the country’s representation on the international stage.

It also traced their beginnings on how they fashioned their own musical instruments, demonstrating the ingenuity and determination that would underpin their careers that have spanned more than six decades, with an extensive catalogue of albums and singles.

Through their commitment to independent music production, conscious reggae and roots culture, the brothers helped preserve the tradition of live-band reggae while introducing Jamaican sounds to audiences beyond the island.

Their collaboration with Polish group Trebunie-Tutki was also highlighted as an example of their ability to bridge cultural divides through music.

Despite spending more than four decades living largely overseas, Ralston maintains ties to Jamaica, travelling between the island and California, with his wife Della.

The Twinkle Brothers boast an extensive catalogue of songs which include

Faith Can Move Mountains, Never Get Burn, Jahoviah, Since I Threw the Comb Away, Give Rasta Praise, Rasta Pon Top, Enter Zion, among many others.

World.title: A CLASS ABOVE
World.content:
Calabar’s Christopher Taylor, seen here competing in the Class 2 boys’ 400m at the ISSA Boys’ and Girls’ Athletics Championships in 2016, is one of several athletes, who started their Champs careers in Class 3 despite being young enough to compete in Class 4 at regional championships. ISSA is reportedly contemplating adding a Class 4 age category for next year’s staging of the championships.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Inter-secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) Boys’ Championships-winning Coach Neil Harrison has thrown his support behind reported plans for the high school sports administrative body to introduce Class 4 boys’ competition at the annual track and field championships, although questions remain about the potential long-term developmental implications for younger athletes.

There have been persistent whispers that ISSA plans to introduce Class 4 boys at next year’s staging of the five-day championships, along with other changes.

Presently, there are three age classes for boys — Classes 1, 2 and 3 — unlike the girls, who compete across four age groups: Classes 1, 2, 3, and 4. For years, ISSA has resisted requests to add an age group for younger boys. The lowest class currently for boys, Class 3, includes athletes under the age of 13.

Earlier this week, ISSA President Keith Wellington said the organisation had discussed a number of changes but was awaiting feedback from principals and coaches.

Two proposals he mentioned were allowing first-year Class 3 boys to compete in more than one individual event and adding the 400m to the Class 4 girls’ events.

While David Riley, head coach at Excelsior High and a member of the coaching staff when Wolmer’s Boys’ won Champs in 2010, declined to comment, saying, “I cannot comment at this time until the details are released for us as coaches to digest.” Harrison is among those who are leaning towards the change.

Harrison, who is currently the head boys’ coach at St Elizabeth Technical (STETHS), having previously held the position at Jamaica College, Kingston College and Munro College, said that, given Class 4 boys have been competing at regional championships, the proposed inclusion at the national high school championships would not be that big of a jump.

“Yes, I think so,” Harrison told the Jamaica Observer. “Class 4 boys compete in our regional championship, so why not the ultimate? It’s a good motivation for them because when they are not allowed to compete, not only the interest in the sport is lost, but sometimes they get lost in the school system as well.”

Meanwhile, Machel Woolery, head coach at Petersfield High, pointed out that Class 4-aged boys have in fact been competing at Champs, but against generally older boys.

“It is just that they will now be separating them and having them run independently and in their own class,” said Woolery before weighing up the pros and cons of their potential inclusion at Champs.

“It can be a plus as well as can be a negative.”

Woolery noted that Class 4 girls have been competing at Champs for a long time, but raised concerns that younger boys, who are good enough to qualify for the championships and compete in an age group above their own, may already be facing excessive demands on their developing bodies.

From a physiological perspective, the doubts linger.

Supporters of the potential move have argued that the introduction of a separate Class 4 boys’ category could provide younger athletes with a more appropriate competitive environment, reducing the need for some to compete against older and potentially more physically developed opponents.

However, such a move would not come without some opposition.

Detractors have raised questions about training loads, recovery, injury risk and the demands placed on boys who are still undergoing significant physical growth and maturation.

There is also a broader question about whether introducing another competitive category would improve long-term athlete development or place additional pressure on schools and young competitors to achieve results at an earlier age.

The challenge for ISSA, the coaches note, would be to ensure that any new category serves as a developmental pathway rather than simply creating another level at which young athletes are expected to produce results.

Woolery suggested that ISSA introduce restrictions for Class 4 boys, similar to those already in place for the girls.

“Maybe they can be limited to one event and a relay,” he added.

World.title: Former CMU worker details university’s accounting, banking systems
World.content:
Campus of Caribbean Maritime University in Kingston (Photo: CMU)

A former senior member of staff of the Caribbean Maritime University (CMU) is expected to continue testimony regarding the school’s finances on Wednesday, with information on the now-defunct CAP-YES programme, in the fraud trial of former CMU boss Fritz Pinnock along with former education minister Ruel Reid and their co-accused.

The witness, appearing before Senior Parish Judge Sanchia Burrell at the Kingston and St Andrew Parish Court on Tuesday, testified how money came into and left certain bank accounts controlled by the university between 2016 and 2019, including accounts for payroll, CAP (Career Advancement Programme) and CAPYES (Career Advancement Programme – Youth Empowerment Services) programme, among others.

The department in which they worked was guided by the FAA (Financial Administration and Audit Act) and PBMA ( The Public Bodies Management and Accountability Act), the witness said, adding that it oversaw payroll, including salary deductions for CMU employees; accounts receivable, which dealt with collecting money owed to the school; and accounts payable, which dealt with any money the school owed to vendors or debt obligations.

While testifying, the witness indicated that the weekly accounts payable process included the submission of documentation verifying the debt obligation, which would be entered on CMUs system and included in an aged payables report. Any vendors to be paid by the school would then be selected from that report.

When pressed on what type of vendors this included, the witness listed utility entities, suppliers of goods to the school’s tuck shop and others undertaking special projects.

The witness also told the court that the school received a monthly subvention from the Ministry of Finance through the Ministry of Education that was deposited to a specific bank account.

When asked where that subvention was funded from, to their understanding, the witness said “from taxes”.

That account, the witness said, was used as a flow-through to other bank accounts, including payroll accounts.

The witness also touched on the operations of the school’s canteen or tuck shop, which had multiple accounts associated with it. The witness testified that cash proceeds would be deposited into the accounts and canteen vendors paid from it, adding that when enough cash was not in the account to pay vendors, the canteen would be provided with an advance by CMU, which would also go to the account.

The school also received money from the government for the operation of the CAP and CAP-YES programmes, deposited directly into accounts set up by CMU, the witness told the court. The witness said accounts were used for expenses associated with CAP and CAP-YES, including paying some salaries as well as stipends for students in need and other initiatives.

CAP, which is carried out at institutions across the island, was intended to provide technical, vocational, and academic training to youth, and CAP-YES was a programme offshoot attached specifically to the Caribbean Maritime University (CMU).

CAP and CAPYES were shuttered at the Caribbean Maritime University in 2020 with instructions to complete the course for those already in training and take in no further applicants.

During testimony, the witness identified Pinnock as the former head of the university, pointing out his striped shirt and orange tie. Pinnock, who has sought leave to take notes during the trial, did not react visibly at being identified. He was represented by a junior of his attorney in the matter, Hugh Wildman.

Pinnock, Reid and their co-accused, Reid’s daughter Sharelle Reid and wife Sharen Reid and Councillor Kim Brown Lawrence’s are before the court on a 35-count indictment, accused of participating in a scheme with others unknown that siphoned off more than $25 million from the Ministry of Education and CMU.

They have pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Issues with disclosure were also put before Burrell in the courtroom on Tuesday with defence attorney Linda Wright, who represents Reid, Carolyn Chuck, who represents Sharelle and Kevon Johnson, who holds for Brown Lawrence’s attorney Oswest Senior Smith, all rising to express concern.

Wright maintained that more documents relating to certain witnesses, including the witness scheduled to be called that day, had been shared by the prosecution at a late hour, thus creating challenges for the defence to go through the documents and take instructions from their clients.

Wright maintained that this was not a “trial by ambush”, describing the disclosure as untidy.

The prosecution maintained that the documents in relation to Tuesday’s witness were not new and that any late disclosure of new documents was not a deliberate effort on its part.

Burrell, who reminded counsel to exercise care around disclosure, is expected to grant a brief adjournment in relation to the issue.

World.title: NWC seeks 51 per cent tariff increase
World.content:
Acting NWC President Kevin Kerr

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The National Water Commission (NWC) has applied to the Office of Utilities Regulation (OUR) for a 51 per cent tariff increase, a move that could affect its approximately 500,000 customers.

Acting NWC President Kevin Kerr told the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) on Tuesday that the application was submitted to the OUR last Friday, adding that the regulator is expected to make an announcement shortly.

Kerr said the proposed increase is tied to an investment plan designed to secure funding for the company’s priority projects.

He warned that if the OUR does not approve the full 51 per cent increase, the NWC would have to revise its investment plan.

Kerr also noted that members of the public would have an opportunity to provide feedback through a consultation process before the OUR makes a determination on the application.

The NWC has argued that the increase is necessary to bring its revenues in line with its expenses. The commission last received a tariff increase in 2019.

NWC Chief Financial Officer Fabian Christie told the committee that the company’s revenue position had deteriorated over time, particularly in relation to customer payments.

He said the proposed increase was needed to keep pace with rising operating costs, including energy expenses.

World.title: 11 things only a Queen’s girl would know
World.content:
In this file photo, Miss Jamaica World 2010 Chantal Raymond strikes a pose with a group of students from the Queen's School.

From the famous ‘Holy Ground’ to the lizards roaming the school grounds, The Queen’s School had its own quirks, traditions and unwritten rules, according to the St Andrew-based institution’s alumni community.

Based on Observer Online’s discussions with past students, here are 11 things that will have any Queen’s girl reminiscing about life at the institution.

1. Holy Ground

Holy Ground never looked or felt particularly holy, so why was it called that in the first place? That remains a question worth asking. One thing was certain: students know the spot well, as it was reserved for devotions and, on occasion, punishment. It was hardly the place anyone wanted to visit for the wrong reasons!

2. Big Tree

Big Tree was one of the most recognisable landmarks on the school grounds. Towering over the area, it served as an outdoor lunchroom, complete with concrete tables and chairs where students gathered to eat, chat and socialise. And when all the seats were taken, the tables became seats, too. Rules or no rules, a girl had to find somewhere to sit!

3. The Hall

The Hall was the designated space for music and drama classes, but it doubled as a favourite hangout for several cliques. Getting students to leave was sometimes a task in itself, particularly for Mr Heriage, who old girls remember having had his hands full trying to get everyone out. For some, it was a classroom; for others, it was the place to catch up with friends.

4. Etheline Aiken

Legendary former principal who served as headmistress from 1976 to 1992. It was under her stewardship that The Queen’s School won the 1978 Girls’ Athletic Championship. Former students remember her as being strict, holding students accountable and requiring them to behave as proper young ladies. But, at the same time, she was well-loved.

5. The ‘iguanas’

Queen’s had lizards in every shape, size and colour imaginable. They were so plentiful that it sometimes seemed there were more lizards than students on the grounds. Whether perched somewhere in plain sight or scurrying across the grounds, these reptiles were a familiar part of the school environment.

6. The ‘Chiney’ shop across the road

The wholesale across the road was a popular stop before and after school. From bag juice and cake soap to rags and socks, it supplied students with a range of essentials. Despite repeated warnings not to cross the road to visit the shop, students somehow found themselves making the trip day after day.

7. Smithy, aka Mr Smith

When it came to Mr Smith, there were two sets of students: those who were lucky enough to be in his class and those who wished they were. Affectionately known as Smithy, he brought a distinctive personality and energy to Mathematics and Accounts lessons, making the subjects enjoyable. His famous Mathematics marathons were another highlight, giving students plenty to remember long after the lessons ended.

8. Reverend Pointsette’s prayers

Reverend Pointsette’s devotions could feel especially long when students had to stand in the blazing sun. Some would deliberately arrive late in the hope of missing part of the session, while her voice coming over the speaker in the afternoon was often met with collective sighs across the school. Those prayers may not have been everyone’s favourite part of the day then, but their value is something many have come to appreciate with time.

9. The in-school vendors

Every form seemed to have its own go-to vendor, making it easy to find a snack or treat after lunch. But the offerings went well beyond food. From haberdashery items and CDs to clothing, these enterprising young women catered to a variety of student needs. Even better, some have since registered their businesses and are thriving in their entrepreneurial ventures, showing that the hustle extended well beyond the school gates.

10. Mrs Keane-Dawes

Another long-serving principal, Mrs Keane-Dawes made it her duty to monitor the school gates in the mornings, earning her reputation as the school’s very own gate police. Strict but understanding, she commanded respect while ensuring students remained disciplined and focused. Her firm approach, balanced with compassion, helped create an environment in which students were encouraged to excel.

11. The standpipe

The standpipe, originally used to water the school grounds, often became a busy wash-up station shortly before the morning bell. Girls would gather to wash their faces and freshen up, with cake soap and soap dishes in abundance. With just 15 minutes to go before classes, the area could become quite crowded as everyone tried to get ready in time for the school day.

– Carlysia Ramdeen

World.title: Where is the outrage?
World.content:
Minister of religion Lisean Gordon delivering the sermon during the Heritage Week Thanksgiving Service at the Greater Highway Church of Christ Apostolic in Caterwood, Trelawny, on Sunday. Looking on are Mayor of Falmouth C Junior Gager (left) and moderator Leisa Dawson. (Photo: Horace Hines)

CARTERWOOD, Trelawny — Minister of religion Lisean Gordon has criticised what she described as the public’s readiness to demand justice when police officers use force, but silence following the killing of two members of the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) last Friday.



Preaching under the theme ‘Let the Children Know’ during a Heritage Week Thanksgiving Service at the Greater Highway Church of Christ Apostolic in Caterwood, Trelawny, on Sunday, Gordon said the lack of comparable demonstrations demanding justice for the slain cops reflects a troubling imbalance.

“They may be somebody’s father, somebody’s son. Nobody came out because we have placed in the heart of ungodly people that we are allowing them to take over this country, all in the name of politics,” said Gordon as she addressed the service hosted by the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission (JCDC) in Trelawny and the Trelawny Municipal Corporation.

Two members of the JCF’s Special Operations Branch, Corporal Trevoy Shaw and Constable Devoney Rose, sustained fatal gunshot wounds during a firefight with men who had barricaded themselves inside a house in the Five Miles area of St Catherine on Friday.

Three civilians, Errol Hussey, his son Malique Hussey, and nephew Javoun Cogle, also died in the incident while a 10-year-old girl was left nursing a gunshot wound.

Delivering the sermon, Gordon condemned the tendency to vilify members of the police force without knowing the circumstances surrounding an encounter, and charged that media coverage and circulating recordings often fuel premature judgements.

Gordon linked the hostility towards law enforcement personnel to a broader erosion of respect for authority, and contended that political allegiance is encouraging Jamaicans to excuse behaviour they might otherwise condemn.

“There is something called the hidden curriculum, which we sometimes forget about. The hidden curriculum: What they see us do is what they will do,” said Gordon, who is also an educator.

She also took issue with verbal attacks against political leaders, including Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness and Opposition Leader Mark Golding, warning that adults risk normalising disrespect among children who observe and absorb their behaviour.

“This disrespect that we put up with…because we are affiliated to a party, and to politics, it must stop. Disrespect is disrespect, and everybody who leads us needs to be respected, whether they are on the Opposition side or they are on the ruling side,” declared Gordon.

She argued that while children are taught to assert their rights, adults are neglecting the importance of responsibility and accountability.

“But we teach them about their rights, but no longer teach them about their responsibility,” Gordon said as she insisted that parents and other adults must uphold discipline, principles, and respect rather than retreat from the challenges of raising the younger generation.

She warned that Jamaica faces a dangerous escalation of disorder if the erosion of these values continues, describing the threat as a storm more severe than Hurricane Melissa.

“I am afraid of what is coming to Jamaica. There is a storm coming that is worse than Melissa… It’s called a storm of lawlessness, it’s called the storm of disorder, and it’s coming towards us. It’s worse than a Category 5,” said Gordon.

The minister of religion urged Jamaicans to reflect on the values they are passing on to their children as she argued that a meaningful inheritance extends beyond material possessions.

Meanwhile, mayor of Falmouth C Junior Gager, in his remarks, called on Jamaicans to preserve the legacy of the national heroes through their everyday actions rather than limiting remembrance to speeches and ceremonies.

“Our national heroes stood firm in the face of adversity, injustices, challenges, and paved the way for the freedom and opportunities we enjoy today,” Gager said.

He urged citizens to serve their communities, stand up for what is right, invest in young people, and work together to build a better Jamaica.

Gager also underscored the Church’s role in strengthening families and communities through prayer, mentorship, compassion and outreach, helping young people embrace their heritage and recognise their potential.

World.title: Nigeria confirms Ebola case, as Congo outbreak spreads
World.content:
The case underscores the difficulty in stopping the spread of the highly-infectious disease. The Democratic Republic of the Congo, the epicenter of the outbreak, is currently grappling with the fastest-growing and deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country’s history, caused by the Bundibugyo strain for which there are no approved vaccines or treatments. As of Oct. 19, Congo reported 9,552 confirmed cases, including 4,602 related deaths.

In Nigeria, where there is a more established private health care market and less reliance on international aid for services, health authorities are working to track down and monitor people who may have been exposed, with 44 close contacts already identified.

“There is no need for panic,” the health ministry wrote on social media. “What matters is staying informed, practising good hand hygiene, knowing the symptoms and seeking guidance from public health authorities if you suspect exposure.”

The disease has also recently spread to Kenya, in Eastern Africa, with nine confirmed cases all linked to a man who traveled from Congo to Uganda before taking a flight to Kenya. He died at a hospital in Nairobi after testing positive for Ebola on Oct. 5.

Jean Kaseya, director-general of Africa CDC, told Devex last week this case illustrated the difficulties in contact tracing. Health authorities were still trying to ascertain who was on his flight, and if they had made onward travel, he said.

The WHO has urged “all countries in the region to sustain a high level of readiness as the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to evolve.”

The U.N. health agency, which first declared the outbreak in Congo on May 15, also advised against any restriction of travel to, or trade with, affected countries.

Von der Leyen also addressed the trade imbalance with China.

She confirmed that the European Commission would present a new deterrent tool as soon as December. This tool is expected to be based on the one proposed by Berlin and Paris earlier this month and would empower the EU executive to restrict or even ban imports from countries seen as distorting the single market. It would require minimal consultation from member states, allowing faster action from Brussels.

This instrument would come alongside a diversification instrument and a solidarity mechanism which are already in the works.

"We see jobs lost in our industrial heartlands," von der Leyen said, adding that the EU will continue to seek deals with Beijing after an agreement to cap Chinese hybrid imports. As POLITICO reported last week, the EU is expected to prioritize chemicals and industrial machinery in its efforts to protect European industry from Chinese competition.

Camille Gijs contributed to this article.

World.title: Burnham’s gas gamble: Why he’s approved Jackdaw
World.content:
The government has approved the Jackdaw gas field.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh says the decision will support the country’s energy security and that it is compatible with legally binding climate commitments.

Critics say the move breaks the spirit of the 2024 Labour manifesto – and makes Andy Burnham look like he’s living in a “parallel universe” after the hottest summer on record.

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy discuss how the prime minister goes about squaring the circle of gas drilling with potential budget cuts to green projects.

World.title: Brussels goes looking for billions to fund Ukraine
World.content:
With Washington’s support for Kyiv increasingly uncertain, Brussels is looking to its allies to help keep Ukraine afloat. The price tag: €70 billion.

On today’s show, Zoya Sheftalovich and Kathryn Carlson discuss how the EU hopes to persuade Canada, Britain and Japan to help foot the bill — and whether closer trade and defense ties could be part of the bargain.

Then, Germany’s far-right AfD leader Alice Weidel is in Strasbourg to present her vision for a radically different European Union.

And who owns your face and voice in the age of AI? As deepfakes become increasingly convincing, MEPs are pushing for new protections.

If you have a question or comment, don’t hesitate! Message us on our WhatsApp here or at +32 491 05 06 29.

Articles mentioned in this episode:

World.title: EU to press Canada and UK for more Ukraine funding
World.content:
European Council President António Costa told the European Parliament on Wednesday morning that “international partners have to intensify and step up financial support to Ukraine.”

The EU has committed to a €90 billion loan for 2026 and 2027, intended to cover about two-thirds of Ukraine’s needs. Brussels had expected other partners — including Canada, Japan, South Korea, Australia and Norway — to provide another €45 billion, but much of that money has been slow to arrive as other governments have yet to firm up or disburse the support Brussels expected.

While calls to help Ukraine defend itself are not new, the projected 2027 bill has grown as Russia intensifies its assault, the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran drives up costs and Washington shifts toward positions more favorable to Moscow — leaving Europe and other allies to shoulder more of the cost of keeping Kyiv afloat.

Brussels is heading into negotiations about closer economic and defense ties with London and Ottawa. Diplomats and EU officials said they do not expect a formal bargain, but that support for Kyiv from the EU’s partners is likely to shape the political climate around the talks. Like others in this article, they were granted anonymity to speak about the sensitive diplomacy.

European Council President Antonio Costa, Ukraine president Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the European Council Summit in Brussels on Oct. 16. | Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga/AFP via Getty Images

The EU has also raised Ukraine’s 2027 financing needs at meetings of the International Monetary Fund, the G7 and the G20, as well as with Gulf Cooperation Council countries.

“During my meetings in Bangkok, the need to secure financial support for Ukraine in 2027 was a prominent topic,” European Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis told POLITICO, referencing last week’s IMF and World Bank Group meetings. He said he called for “broad burden sharing and stressed the importance of international partners each doing their part as Ukraine continues fighting Russian aggression.”

World.title: Maybe it’s personal: Europeans worry Trump just likes Putin more than Zelenskyy
World.content:
As they scratch their heads for explanations for Trump’s latest turn against Ukraine, some European officials and diplomats think it comes down to the president’s personal preferences, as much as his country’s political aims.

“I do think it’s a personal thing,” said former British Cabinet minister David Lidington, now distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a leading security think tank in London. “Trump is self-centered — his personal predilections for dictators and autocrats, his desire to give opportunities to U.S. businesses … are very important parts of his motivation.”

In private, EU officials agree. “Trump doesn’t like [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy. He just doesn’t like him,” said one government official who has observed both men closely. “That makes it harder to get the U.S. to help on peace. Everything is a rational business deal with Trump, until it’s not.”

A diplomat from an EU country — granted anonymity, like others in this report, to discuss sensitive matters — said the inconsistent Trump could change his mind again and reverse recent moves against Ukraine. The U.S. president has chopped and changed on many issues, “except one thing,” the diplomat said. “He seems to be supportive of the Russians.”

“He’s been critical of Ukraine, the EU, NATO, but hardly ever said anything critical about Putin. It is striking. We have to deal with an administration that seems to be more pro-Russian than anything else,” the diplomat said.

The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Poland’s government votes to ease abortion laws in challenge to conservative president
World.content:
Still, neither bill would allow abortion on request up to 12 weeks of pregnancy, as Tusk's Civic Coalition promised during the 2023 election campaign. The multi-party coalition includes many conservatives and lacks agreement on the liberalization going this far.

Both bills now move from the lower chamber, or the Sejm, to the Senate, where they seem poised to pass, but their eventual fate remains uncertain. President Karol Nawrocki, an ally of the nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) party, said before his election in 2025 that he would not sign legislation easing abortion rules.

“By refusing to sign [the abortion] legislation, the president is hurting people," Włodzimierz Czarzasty, speaker of the Sejm, said Tuesday before the votes. "If he wants to hurt women, he will hurt them. I think women will see that and hear that.”

Tusk's coalition government will likely keep turning up the heat on the president and PiS if Nawrocki blocks the liberalization, as he has said he would.

Overriding a presidential veto requires a three-fifths majority in the Sejm that the Tusk-led coalition doesn’t have. The proposals that passed Tuesday lingered in a parliamentary committee for two years before surfacing, spurred by the campaign heating up 12 months before the next general election, slated for late 2027.

Overturning restrictions

At the parliamentary level, ending criminal penalties for helping women with abortion passed with 217 votes in favor, 213 against and three abstentions. The other bill won a slightly clearer majority of 233 for, 203 against and a single abstention.

World.title: Europe’s conservatives have 2 new targets in their campaign to weaken EU climate laws
World.content:
Both policies are central pillars in the EU’s effort to reduce its planet-warming emissions. A successful repeal of ETS2 in particular would be a blow to EU climate goals, as it covers around 40% of the bloc’s greenhouse gas emissions.

But it would also be a major victory for conservative and pro-business lawmakers and national governments that have been campaigning for less stringent EU climate laws in the name of industrial competitiveness.

Ax the tax

The EU Emissions Trading System, launched in 2005, requires power plants and factories in sectors like steel, chemicals and cement to acquire carbon allowances for every ton of carbon they emit. The total number of allowances is reduced each year, eventually reaching zero.

ETS2 applies the same idea to suppliers of fuel for transport and heating from 2028.

The cap-and-trade scheme will be a powerful tool for reducing emissions from these highly polluting activities. But many policymakers worry it will raise the cost of gasoline, diesel and natural gas and add to voters' cost-of-living pressures.

Nine national delegations of the EPP — the Polish, Spanish, Italian, French, Romanian, Croatian, Slovenian, Slovak and Estonian — are now calling for ETS2 to be repealed, according to draft amendments obtained by POLITICO. “ETS2 should be deleted,” the amendment, sponsored by Polish EPP lawmaker Adam Jarubas, argues.

World.title: Trump tells companies to pay 'dividend' to communities to make data centres popular
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has suggested that companies building data centres should pay a “dividend” to the communities where they are based to make them more appealing to local residents.

 

With companies around the world racing to deploy AI infrastructure, there has been a widespread backlash against new projects due to the substantial water and energy requirements of these sites and the impact they have on the local environment, energy prices and water scarcity.

The US President said that he had been “watching data centers very closely” and that he had “come to a very strong conclusion” over the matter, namely that highly unpopular data center projects become “extremely popular” once a financial deal is struck to address locals’ concerns.

On energy, Trump stated that he had personally mandated that data centres must "make their own electricity and give or sell any excess back to the local community, or grid” to offset energy price increases, believing that if they do so, there “could be a substantial decrease”.

In 2026 alone, at least 47 large-scale projects have been delayed and more than 1000 local communities across the US have formally proposed or sought moratoria, zoning caps or strict environmental limits on incoming AI infrastructure, according to financial site Investing Live.

Yet there are no signs of developments slowing down. Investing Live’s analysts say US AI infrastructure spending is projected to exceed $10 trillion (€8.9tn) between 2025 and 2032, around 3.6% of the country’s GDP per year.

While some data centre projects have gone ahead once agreements, now referred to as “Community Benefits Agreements” or CBAs, have been struck with local authorities, this hasn’t necessarily resulted in shifting public opinion.

Earlier this summer, Meta struck a deal with Texas governor Greg Abbott over a controversial data centre project in El Paso, Texas, funded by investment giant BlackRock.

What started as a $1.5 billion (€1.3bn) investment in 2023 and blew up to a $14 billion (€12.5bn) mega-campus project, resulting in widespread public backlash and prompting authorities to consider scrapping the project. In June, the local council voted 5-3 against cancelling the deal.

The governor then reached a deal establishing a number of guardrails to protect the local community, including paying making Meta pay for their electrical infrastructure, reuse their own water and promise to “eliminate reliance on outdated taxpayer-funded incentives”.

Meta has since commented on the deal, but not on the specifics set out by the governor, with critics including Democratic nominee for governor of Texas Gina Hinojosa, who argues that the agreement does not set out any binding conditions on the tech company. Meta expects construction to finish in two years.

In September, the first fully executed CBA for a data centre project in the US was signed by the Lancaster City Council in Pennsylvania for a $6-10 billion (€5.3-€8.9bn) cloud computing and AI complex — the Lancaster AI Hub.Emilia.

It included a number of measures aimed at supporting the local community such as a $10 million (€8.9 mn) economic development fund, another $10 million (€8.9 mn) fund for sustainable development and clean energy, $250,000 (€222,500) planning fund and $10 million (€8.9 mn) worth of credit to protect the city should the default on its environmental and financial promises.

And this October, developer Digital Realty won initial public approval for a project in De Soto, Kansas, for a new 280-acre data centre campus by bypassing local rules and paying citizens directly.

The company is offering locals $1000 (€890) in utility and property tax credits for 10 years, as part of an overall $20 million (€17.8mn) investment that they argue will provide recurring tax revenue, create jobs and deliver other economics benefits to residents.

Close to home in Europe, so-called "Cash for Communities” approaches have taken off.

In Ireland this October, one of Europe’s largest data centre clusters, OpenAI has said future data centres could come with cash for local communities to address citizen concerns over their impact.

The country, however, already has strict requirements for data centres including a mandate that they must provide electricity into the grid.

Germany also has strict reciprocity requirements, especially in relation to energy use. In major hubs such as Dietzenbach, where Google is building a multi-billion euro campus, developers must first secure energy infrastructure deals to feed excess heat generated by data centres back into the grid to lower local residents’ utility bills.

World.title: Trump is taking Russia's side against Ukraine, former US general tells Euronews
World.content:
Retired US Army Lieutenant General Ben Hodges has accused President Donald Trump of deliberately undermining Ukraine's ability to defend itself against Russia, saying the administration's actions were "entirely predictable".

 

"He was never going to support Ukraine, and was going to take the Russian side, the signs were all there," Hodges tells Euronews.

"I do not trust this administration to be honest about what they are doing with Russia for or against Ukraine," he said an interview from his home in Frankfurt. "What he has done to Ukraine was entirely predictable."

Hodges believes recent US decisions restricting Ukraine's defences and its ability to respond to Russian bombardments are designed to pressure Kyiv into surrendering territory in exchange for an end to the war.

"This has been the goal of the Administration from the beginning, when US Secretary of State Rubio said in the first weeks of being in Office that Ukraine was going to have to give up some land in order to end the war, as if this was a Manhattan real estate deal," he said.

In recent days, US President Trump has demanded Ukraine stop targeting Russian diesel refineries as part of its military response to the Kremlin's full-scale invasion.

The Ukrainian government said they would agree to it if Russia likewise stopped targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The Kremlin refused.

Trump has also waived new bipartisan sanctions on Russia just days before they were due to take effect. The measures, part of the so-called Lindsey Graham Act, named after the late Republican senator, included tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil.

Since then, Ukraine have been unable to access the Starlink satellite system owned by Elon Musk but controlled by the US. The Ukrainian military use it to intercept jet-powered drones, often Iranian origin Shahed drones.

Ukrainian President Zelenskyy says the army's access is restricted after speeds exceeding 161 km/h meaning the can no longer intercept these deadly drones.

Speaking to journalists in Brussels last week, Zelenskyy described the situation as "painful", pointing to the lives lost as a result of the restrictions.

Trump has also called for elections in Ukraine, and for Zelenskyy to be replaced.

He has blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries for rising diesel prices, despite a surge in energy prices following US and Israeli attacks on Iran in February.

The resulting disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway through which roughly a fifth of global oil supplies normally pass, has added to pressure on energy markets.

Washington has also come under scrutiny over the delivery of Patriot air defence interceptors to Ukraine which have been funded by European countries.

Under NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), European allies and Canada purchase US-made weapons and interceptors for Ukraine.

However, global shortages of Patriot systems have complicated efforts to replenish Kyiv’s defences, with US stockpiles under pressure from as a result of military operations in Iran.

A NATO official told Euronews that PURL deliveries were continuing but declined to comment specifically on Patriot shipments.

Hodges is pessimistic about the prospect of a breakthrough between Washington and Kyiv, arguing that the impasse reflects a deliberate policy choice.

“There isn't a hope in hell the administration is providing Patriot [defence systems],” he added.

“They're even preventing other countries from delivering such systems to Kyiv,” Hodges told Euronews.

Zelenskyy has also said that the delivery of Patriot interceptors is being delayed, despite the systems’ importance in defending against certain Russian missile attacks.

“Right now, a new missile package is still awaiting Mr Hegseth's signature,” Zelenskyy said on Tuesday.

European partners are also awaiting US approval to transfer Patriot interceptors from their own stocks to Ukraine, Zelenskyy said in an interview with an Italian newspaper.

"The Administration's actions with Patriot interceptors and intelligence are all intended to pressure Ukraine into accepting a terrible outcome by which Ukraine would have to agree to allowing Russia to keep what it has taken and perhaps even more," said Hodges.

“The horrific thing about what Trump is doing is that it's got real-world life-and-death impact for Ukrainians,” said Kurt Volker, a former US ambassador to NATO who served during Trump's first administration.

Europe urged to take tougher line on Russia

Both Hodges and Volker argue that European countries must respond more decisively to Russia’s hybrid aggression.

They warn that if Russian President Vladimir Putin believes Washington is on Moscow’s side, the Kremlin could be emboldened to intensify its attacks.

NATO countries have faced a range of so-called grey-zone incidents, including drone incursions, sabotage and arson. However, European governments have been reticent in formally attributing responsibility to Moscow. Germany and Estonia are among the countries that have only recently blamed Russia for specific incidents.

Hodges argues that European governments must each time recognise Russia as the aggressor and impose consequences for attacks.

He suggested European countries seize Russian shadow-fleet vessels operating in the Black Sea in response to such incidents. He also called for an end to issuing visas to Russian citizens entering the EU and urged European governments to reconsider the use of frozen Russian assets to support Ukraine.

Europe needs to tell Russia "every time we have an incident, we will seize a shadow fleet vessel out on the Black Sea," said Hodges.

"And how in the hell are Russians still getting visas to move around Europe," he asked.

While several EU governments agree Russian frozen assets could serve both as compensation for damage caused by the war, and as a penalty for Russian war crimes and aggression, the Belgian government continues to oppose moves to use the assets without sufficient guarantees against the financial and legal risks.

Around €180 billion is kept in Euroclear, a Belgian repository, which amounts to the vast majority of the approximately €220 billion.

Hodges says Belgium's refusal to budge on the issue is "unacceptable."

"It's unacceptable the country that hosts NATO and the EU is so unwilling to unlock the door to one of the best things we can do to support Ukraine," he said.

Volker, who also served as the US special envoy for Ukraine during Trump's first administration, said Europe needed to develop a “Plan B” for its security as Washington's relationship with Moscow shifts.

For decades, Europe's security architecture has relied heavily on the United States. Volker said a new agreement involving European countries and other allies, modelled on the Coalition of the Willing, might be needed to defend the continent.

Europe must “start pushing back on hybrid attacks otherwise one of these will lead to major escalation”, Volker said, warning that Putin could be emboldened by his relationship with Trump.

European governments should also make clear that any aircraft or drone entering NATO airspace unlawfully would be intercepted, Volker said.

He added that Russia should be held responsible if civilian casualties result from such incidents.

World.title: No kids invited: A new travel package offers a child-free flight and adults-only cruise
World.content:
Anyone who has had a relaxing pool day disturbed by screaming kids will have dreamt of a completely child-free holiday.

 

And while there are many adults-only resorts out there, you can’t escape young ones on the journey – or you couldn’t until now.

That’s because JetBlue Vacations and Virgin Voyages have teamed up for “Do Not Disturb”, an adults-only holiday that includes a dedicated kid-free JetBlue flight and a Virgin Voyages sailing.

Taking place from 4-8 March 2027, the four-night package includes round-trip flights from New York's JFK to Fort Lauderdale/Hollywood International in Florida.

The itinerary includes stops in Key West as well as Virgin Voyages' Beach Club at Bimini in the Bahamas.

“We love creating vacations for all kinds of travellers, including families, but we also know there are moments when adults are looking for a different kind of getaway,” Jamie Perry, president of Paisly, JetBlue’s travel website, said.

“With Do Not Disturb, we wanted that feeling of truly switching off to start well before you step onto the ship.

“From the flight to the transfer to the cruise itself, we’ve thought about the entire journey so our customers can simply show up, settle in and enjoy some uninterrupted time away.”

What to expect on board

Guests will be sailing on the relatively new vessel, Brilliant Lady, which has just 60 cabins on board.

First launched in 2025, there are more than 20 restaurants and bars on board, including Spanish eatery Rojo by Razzle Dazzle, Mexican spot Pink Agave and Korean barbecue Gunbae.

Aside from making your way through the food options, guests can head to the spa, relax by the rooftop pool, or enjoy live entertainment across the cruise ships’ various venues.

World.title: Restorers work to preserve frescoes in one of Pompeii’s grandest Roman houses
World.content:
Nearly 2,000 years after Mount Vesuvius buried Pompeii in volcanic ash, one of the ancient Roman city's grandest homes is getting a new lease of life.

 

The House of Marcus Fabius Rufus, a lavish four-storey residence believed to have belonged to a wealthy Roman magistrate, is undergoing a €1.46 million restoration to preserve its elaborate frescoes and decorated interiors.

The work follows structural stabilisation and excavation efforts completed between 2021 and 2023.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | October 21st, 2026 – Midday
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: French government 10-year bond yield tops 5% for first time since 2002
World.content:
French yields have been rising for weeks as lawmakers wrangle over a 2027 budget that calls for billions of euros in spending cuts to reduce a debt pile that now stands at around 120% of France's GDP - one of the highest levels in the eurozone and well above the EU limit of 60%.

 

The French Treasury's OAT bond is also used to set interest rates across a wide swath of the economy, meaning borrowing costs could begin rising for businesses and households.

The last time it was that high was during the dot-com financial crisis.

The spread between the 10-year yield and the German 10-year bond, considered the European benchmark of creditworthiness, also surged to nearly 160 basis points.

The bond selloff puts further pressure on the government ahead of a decision Friday by the ratings agency Moody's on France's sovereign credit rating, with most economists expecting a downgrade that would automatically raise the government's borrowing costs.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is trying to get a 2027 budget approved in parliament despite not having a political majority for the €43 billion ($48bn) in spending cuts he seeks.

Even if approved, the budget would bring France's deficit down to only 5% of GDP next year, well above the 3% limit for EU members.

Meanwhile, protests over the weekend calling in part for more spending on schools and other public services, degenerated into the worst street violence seen in years.

World.title: Former Hungarian central bank chief György Matolcsy detained in financial fraud probe
World.content:
Former Hungarian central bank governor György Matolcsy was detained on Wednesday morning and taken to the Central Chief Prosecution Office for Investigations.

 

A longtime associate of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, Matolcsy led the National Bank of Hungary (MNB) for 12 years until 2025.

"My client is suspected of the felony of financial fraud causing significant financial loss and the misdemeanour of using a forged private document," Matolcsy's lawyer, Pál Bátki, told Hungarian newspaper Telex.

Bátki said his client's questioning had not yet begun but was expected to take place later that morning.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, the prosecution office said it was conducting coordinated operations at several locations as part of an investigation into suspected breach of trust causing particularly significant financial loss.

Prosecutors said they expected to release further details early in the evening, once the initial investigative steps had been completed.

Being detained for questioning does not mean Matolcsy has been remanded in pre-trial custody. It remains unclear whether he will be allowed to leave after questioning. If he is formally named as a suspect, a court may decide whether to order his pre-trial detention.

Matolcsy was questioned as a suspect in a separate case in September over alleged abuse of office involving pressure on Erste Bank Hungary, part of Austria's Erste Group. He denied the allegations and was allowed to leave after questioning.

Investigation into central bank foundations

The current leadership of the MNB and Hungary's State Audit Office have both filed criminal complaints concerning the central bank's foundations.

Optima Investment, the asset manager of the Pallas Athéné foundations established by the MNB under Matolcsy in 2014 and merged in 2019, managed almost 500 billion forints (more than €1 billion) in public funds.

The State Audit Office identified an opaque network of companies and investments, serious management failings and suspected criminal offences.

The merged foundation, PADME, and Optima subsequently faced severe financial difficulties. Hungarian media have also reported links between the investment network and associates of Matolcsy's son, Ádám.

Matolcsy has previously denied allegations concerning the management of the central bank foundations' funds.

On 26 May 2026, Hungary's parliament adopted a resolution to establish an inquiry committee into alleged abuses at the central bank.

Investigators have also been examining suspected breach of trust involving the foundations and the renovation of the MNB's headquarters, alongside a separate money laundering investigation.

In May 2026, authorities said they had seized cash and securities worth 91.8 billion forints.

World.title: More Russians are settling in the EU with each year of war in Ukraine
World.content:
The number of Russian citizens legally residing in the EU has grown by 105,000 since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, reaching 876,600 by the end of 2025, an analysis of Eurostat data shows.

 

The figure represents a 13.6% rise from the 771,800 Russians holding valid temporary or permanent residence permits across EU member states in 2021. Germany hosts the largest community, with 218,000 residents, followed by Spain (116,800) and Estonia (78,400).

Southern Europe has seen the sharpest growth: Spain issued residence permits to 44,400 Russian nationals over the period, France 13,700, while Cyprus and Portugal saw their Russian-born populations increase 2.5 and 3.5 times, respectively.

Several EU states have moved in the opposite direction. Latvia, Estonia and the Czech Republic have recorded the largest drops in Russian residents, driven by tough migration policies and, in the Baltic states, security concerns over large Russian-speaking communities.

Significant communities have also formed outside the EU. In Serbia the Russian population rose from roughly 5,000 before the invasion to 61,900 by the end of 2025. By spring of this year, Kazakhstan had absorbed more than 107,000 Russian migrants, while Armenia and Georgia hosted 43,500 and 70,000, respectively.

Turkey drew large numbers in the immediate post-invasion period but later tightened residency rules. By June, valid Russian permits there had fallen to 75,900, half the 2023 peak.

Researchers tracking emigration patterns have identified at least four distinct waves since February 2022. The most recent, running from this spring, has been sparked by renewed claims of impending mobilisation for Moscow's all-out war in Ukraine.

"Everyone now understands that they have no future in Russia. There is no image of the future, no understanding of what will happen in six months or a year," said Anastasia Burakova, a lawyer and founder of Kovcheg, a legal assistance project for Russians abroad. "What is more, there are risks linked to mobilisation and conscription, which people feel very personally."

'Now I have nothing and I feel free'

Ivan, 19, left Russia this spring to avoid conscription and now works in construction in Yerevan, posting videos on YouTube. A year earlier he had been a mobile phone store manager.

"I thought: this is it, this is life, everything is going the way it should," he said in a YouTube video. "Now I'm sitting on a bench in Yerevan, with no title and no steady job. My wife is next to me. Back then I was a manager and felt trapped. Now I have nothing, and I feel free."

Surveys by independent researchers show the Russian emigrees include predominantly young couples, often without children, with both partners under 36.

They tend to have high levels of education and are concentrated in professions either vulnerable to political repression — journalists, human rights workers, political analysts — or in high international demand, particularly IT, engineering and academia. Around 20% of those who left do not hold university degrees. Some 18% are studying or plan to study abroad.

They fall into three broad groups: those who have settled and expect to remain abroad long-term, those who have already moved once and are preparing to relocate again, and those still in Russia who intend to leave within six months.

The economic impact on host countries has been visible yet uneven. In Armenia and Georgia, the sudden influx of people and capital contributed to GDP growth of between 9% and 9.4% at its peak between 2022 and 2024, according to analysis published by the CASE Center research institute.

Average Russian household incomes in Serbia ran to around €3,500 per month against a local average of €900. In Georgia the figures were €3,300 against €650. The effect has since moderated as host economies adapted, with growth settling back to 5–7% annually.

Rather than competing for local jobs, most Russian migrants have worked remotely or set up their own businesses.

In IT, up to 41% have maintained income from foreign clients, while in the media sector around 21% have done so, channelling money into host economies through taxes and everyday spending.

Meanwhile, Russian authorities and independent researchers have documented some returns, but the scale remains disputed.

The independent OutRush sociological project estimated that no more than 8% of emigrants had returned to Russia by summer 2024, with around 5% more intending to do so.

The Institute of Applied Economic Research at RANEPA, a state-linked academic institution, put the overall return rate from the 2022–2023 wave at roughly 10%.

Estimates from consulting firms and recruitment agencies are considerably higher, ranging from 16% among IT workers to 40–45% of those who left at the peak.

Commonly cited reasons for returning include difficulty finding work, legal status problems and the closure of relocated Russian businesses.

Russia's own official resettlement programme recorded a historic low in 2025, drawing only 26,700 people into the country.

Euronews could not independently verify Russian government data.

World.title: Russia frees jailed American Stephen Hubbard, US envoy says
World.content:
After the meeting, Putin announced the release of Stephen Hubbard, an American taken captive by Russian forces years ago in Ukraine.

Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the release of US captive Stephen Hubbard during talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday.

Hubbard had been taken captive by Russian forces on charges of being a mercenary, which he denies. He was sentenced to seven years in prison at a closed trial in 2024.

Putin said Hubbard was at the airport and Witkoff said he was now "going home to his family."

A Russian court convicted Stephen Hubbard of being a mercenary in 2024, which he denies Image: Moscow City Court press service/AFP

Putin, Witkoff to discuss Ukraine peace deal

The release of Hubbard was seen as a goodwill gesture to the Trump administreation as the two sides discuss a peace deal in Ukraine.

"We've brought some papers. It's really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you'll read that at your leisure," Witkoff told Putin.

Putin proposed that Witkoff discuss the restoration of bilateral ties between Washington and Moscow, and the possibility of meeting with Trump in Beijing.

The meeting — the ninth such talks between Witkoff and Putin —comes a day after Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway, which US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described as "positive."

"He will now, armed with those ideas, be able to ‌go to St. Petersburg and share them with the Russian side, and ‌let's ​see if we can make some progress," he said ahead of the talks.

Witkoff to return to Oslo

Witkoff's meeting with Zelenskyy and other European leaders in Oslo has brought fresh momentum to peace efforts, more than 4 years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Ukrainian leader remained in Oslo on Wednesday where met with lawmakers in the Norwegian parliament.

Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said that Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for further consultations after his trip to St. Petersburg.

"I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy," he told Norway's public broadcaster NRK on Wednesday morning.

Nevertheless, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow was willing to listen but that he didn't expect any "miracle." US President Donald Trump on Tuesday reiterated that he wants Zelenskyy "to make a deal."

World.title: UK approves Jackdaw gas field after years in limbo
World.content:
Drilling is set to begin in the controversial North Sea plot as the government seeks to tackle high energy costs. Environmental groups have criticized the move and called for more clean energy.

The UK government gave its approval for drilling to begin in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea on Wednesday following years of legal and political problems that had blocked the controversial fossil fuel venture.

The Labour government justified the move saying it would strengthen the UK's energy security amid rising energy costs due to the US-Israeli war against Iran.

The gas field had previously been approved by the previous Conservative government, but wes held up by a Scottish court that said the approval had failed to consider carbon emissions.

The field lies about 150 miles (240 kilometres) east of Aberdeen in Scotland.

What did the UK government say about the Jackdaw approval?

Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has been under pressure from US President Donald Trump to increase drilling in the North Sea, said the new gas field would "protect hundreds of jobs and help keep millions of homes warm this winter."

"At a time when people are really struggling, it's right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help," he said.

"We're committed to moving towards renewable energy and reaching net zero by 2050. But even on our ambitious climate path, we'll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come. That's why we're taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea," Burnham added.

Energy Minister Miatta Fahnbulleh said gas could start flowing to British houses and businesses by the end of the month. It is expected that Jackdaw will increase domestic gas production by 6% and run for 11 years.

What has been the reaction to the UK's new gas project?

Shell, which is part of the Adura joint venture along with Norway's Equinor, welcomed the decision.

"Long-term energy projects depend on a competitive and stable investment environment, alongside timely and predictable regulatory decisions," Shell said.

However, the move has also been met with strong criticism. The Green Party called it "climate vandalism," while Greenpeace said the approval showed "the toxic grip fossil fuel lobbyists still hold over our energy policy."

"True pragmatism means severing our reliance on expensive oil and gas that leaves British households broke, supercharges extreme weather, and leaves our energy security at the mercy of petrostates," said the environmental group's Ami McCarthy.

Critics have also questioned whether the new project would indeed have an impact on British gas bills since prices are determined by global energy markets.

Protesters had called on Burnham to block approval for the Jackdaw gas field Image: Henry Nicholls/AFP

In an attempt to show the government's commitment to its climate targets, alongside the Jackdaw approval, it announced the set up of a new Energy Wealth Fund, with an initial £2 billion ($2.7 billion), aimed at channeling oil and gas revenues into funding the transition to cleaner energy.

The UK is targeting net zero emissions by 2050, although this target must be examined under the realities already facing the planet, with a new UN report saying the world is heading for 2.8 degrees of warming, way beyond the 1.5 degrees target set in the Paris Climate Agreement.

It also comes after the UK experienced its hottest ever summer on record, with temperatures hitting previously unheard of 38 degrees in some areas in June, according to the Met Office.

Edited by: Kieran Burke
