World.title: Lauri Läänemets: Estonia must be among the shapers of European foreign policy
World.content:
Estonia must do more to influence decisions shaping Europe's security and Ukraine's future rather than risk having its own future decided by others, argues the author.

On October 9, U.S. presidential special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, senior Ukrainian security officials and national security advisers from France, Germany and the United Kingdom gathered at a golf club near Miami. Representatives of the European Commission and NATO were also at the table. For six hours, they discussed how to end the war in Ukraine, what security guarantees Ukraine should receive and what the security architecture of Ukraine and Europe should look like after the war.

At the same time, President Donald Trump held a phone call with Vladimir Putin, after which Trump announced a decision to allow Russia to resume selling large quantities of diesel fuel on the global market and expressed a willingness to ease sanctions on Russian fuel.

These developments should give us serious pause. We are living in extremely dangerous times, with the United States and Russia seeking a way to end the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to themselves. For us, there is a real danger that an agreement will be reached over our heads and that Europe's new security order will be decided by a small group of people somewhere at a Miami golf club.

Putin's objectives have not changed. He wants a Europe where great powers decide the fate of individual countries and where empires and spheres of influence prevail over free cooperation. Subjugating Ukraine would be an important step toward realizing that vision, but not the ultimate goal. There is no reason to believe Moscow has scaled back its demands. Instead, Russia is seeking to achieve through negotiations what it has failed to accomplish by military force.

All the fundamental questions remain unresolved. How will the war end? On what terms will peace be achieved? Will that peace guarantee Ukraine's security, freedom and opportunities for economic development, as well as our own? The answers to these questions will determine Europe's future for decades to come. That is why having a seat at the table where these decisions are made and being able to influence them is the single most important issue for Estonia's security and prosperity.

Even in Brussels, where we have a seat and a voice, we must know how to make ourselves heard. But the situation is even more complicated. As the Miami meeting demonstrated, decisions shaping Europe's future are not always made within common institutions. Crucial discussions may take place among a small group, without us, even when our own future is directly at stake.

Estonia cannot limit itself to commenting on decisions made by others after the fact. We must be able to secure a place in discussions to which we are not automatically invited and we must do so in a way that gives our positions real weight.

This requires political leadership, persuasiveness and courage. The prime minister must be capable of shaping international opinion, not merely attending meetings. When the great powers begin discussing Europe's future among themselves, is Estonia's prime minister capable of influencing Washington, Paris or Berlin on such matters?

Under Kaja Kallas, Estonia wielded more influence than its population or economic size would suggest. Kallas built personal relationships with European leaders, called them directly and actively participated in discussions that shaped Europe's policy toward Ukraine. She did not simply present Estonia's positions but also sought to influence other countries' decisions.

Under Prime Minister Kristen Michal, that ambition has disappeared. It is difficult to name a single major European security policy discussion in which Michal has convincingly taken a leadership role. Michal's government has voluntarily placed itself outside the circle of those shaping European foreign policy.

It is an open secret that Michal confines himself to reading out Estonia's official talking points at European Council meetings instead of actively trying to shape other countries' positions. While Kaja Kallas exchanged messages with Emmanuel Macron, Michal has shown no comparable active network of personal relationships or influence on the international stage. Yet this is precisely the kind of capability Estonia desperately needs right now. We do not need a prime minister who comments on decisions. We need a leader who helps shape them.

Actions, above all, are what give words weight. Estonia was a leading advocate of military assistance to Ukraine and had the moral authority to demand more from others because we were doing our part. Now, our efforts to organize that assistance have been overshadowed by confusion, scandals and questions about transparency. This is no way to build international trust and influence. Instead of setting an example for others, we now find ourselves embarrassed in front of them.

Estonia's future will not be secured by social media comments in Estonian or forceful statements aimed at domestic audiences. Securing it requires knowledge, relationships, well-considered proposals and the courage to speak uncomfortable truths. Above all, however, it requires the ability to persuade others and the willingness to back up words with actions.

Neither the Center Party nor Isamaa has a plan to increase Estonia's influence in the world. Mihhail Kõlvart has said that America will decide Ukraine's future and that Europe has no influence over it. Estonia cannot accept such apathy. Isamaa and Urmas Reinsalu offer forceful slogans, but slogans alone are not enough to stand up for Estonia's interests.

Estonia cannot simply wait for one of the major powers to invite us to the decision-making table. Europe's small and medium-sized countries must work more closely together, forge new alliances and identify common interests they can pursue collectively. This applies to both security and the economy. The more effectively we can align our interests with those of other countries, the greater our chances of making ourselves heard.

To achieve this, Estonia must be represented by people with the necessary preparation, knowledge, skills and international networks, as well as the determination and courage to shape Europe's future. People who know the decision-makers and understand how decisions are made and who attend meetings not to read out talking points but to shape the discussion.

Estonia's future depends on whether we are present when important decisions are made or only hear about them afterward. What is at stake is not Estonia's international prestige, but our security, prosperity and freedom. We cannot afford to have our future decided without us. Estonia must have a seat at the decision-making table.

World.title: MP: Russian satellite's shadowing of Finnish satellite a 'deliberate provocation'
World.content:
The recent maneuvering of a Russian military satellite dangerously close to a Finnish radar satellite was a deliberate provocation and could have resulted in a major accident, physicist and Riigikogu member Mario Kadastik (Reform) said.

Earlier this month, a Russian-made satellite may have come within less than a mile of a commercial Earth-observation satellite that may be used to provide national security services to countries such as Ukraine, CNN reported.

"The observation satellite, called Iceye-X36, is operated by Iceye, a multinational company with offices in the United States, Finland and several other countries across Europe and Asia," the outlet wrote.

"The fact that the Russians simply came and parked their satellite a few dozen meters away is unprecedented. And it is also extremely dangerous," Kadastik said Wednesday to ERR's morning radio show "Vikerhommik".

He explained that because satellites travel at very high speeds, a collision can occur very easily at such a short distance: "When you are that close, if you make a small correction maneuver, a difference of less than 0.1 seconds in thruster firing time can be enough to change the orbit by a couple of dozen meters. And that means a collision occurs. So this is extremely risky activity in any case, and it was definitely a provocation."

Kadastik said the radar satellite built by Finnish space company Iceye that was targeted was designed for Earth observation. Because it uses radar, its advantage is that it can measure and monitor what is happening on the ground both in darkness and through clouds, providing an overview of activity on the ground in almost any weather.

"Because its resolution is quite good, around 20 centimeters, it can identify vehicles and various objects quite well. And the Russians' main interest is that Iceye is one of those whose data is regularly provided to Ukraine about what is happening in the border areas. In other words, it is capable of imaging that area several times an hour and showing where various objects are moving," he explained.

'Not accidental activity'

According to Kadastik, Russia sent its Kosmos 2612 satellite close to Iceye, and according to some sources, every time the Finnish radar satellite tried to move away, the Russian satellite maneuvered back into its vicinity.

"So in that sense, this was not accidental activity in any way. Because accidental close encounters happen all the time, especially now that there are so many satellites up there. But deliberately adjusting orbits to get progressively closer and then parking alongside it at almost zero relative velocity. Well, what exactly was the purpose of that?" Kadastik said.

He believes one possible motive could be espionage, but thinks this is unlikely as it is fairly well known how radar satellites work.

"Rather, it was probably because a metallic object near a radar interferes with its operation, meaning that it is impossible to operate in certain frequency bands because it scatters [the radar signal] so strongly and creates so much noise. /---/ Perhaps it stayed near Iceye for a certain period precisely to conceal, for example, the movements of certain Russian units," Kadastik speculated.

"And the other possibility is simply a show of force, the Russians' classic big-stick approach – I come up behind you with a big stick and see whether you react! I would consider this a hybrid attack in any case. The only question is at what level we classify it," he said.

NATO response

The MP said this is another escalation by Russia, but in a new domain, and a response should come from NATO. Especially as the satellite was developed by a Finnish company and licensed and launched by its U.S. subsidiary.

"Such a strong escalation in the space domain is, I would say, a very significant escalation, precisely because of its potential impact. I certainly hope there will be some kind of reaction from NATO. Because the Russians are doing what they usually do — trying to provoke without causing enormous consequences," he said. "The classic NATO handbook still provides for responses based on the consequences. And if there were essentially no consequences, then the question is what the response should be," he said.

Kadastik explained that activities in space are relatively well regulated by the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, because what happens in space affects all parties. There are no borders there, as virtually all satellites that are not geostationary travel over the entire Earth, and therefore rules must be followed so that everyone can coexist.

"Traditionally, any approach within a few kilometers is considered something that must be closely coordinated with all parties to avoid a collision. Because a collision in space is not like a collision between two cars. A space collision has quite dramatic consequences, and that is why [traffic] is very tightly coordinated — corrective maneuvers are made tens or hundreds of kilometers in advance," he said.

"Because the worst thing is the collision effect, the Kessler syndrome, that can result from it," Kadastik said.

He recalled the Hollywood film Gravity, which illustrates well what a large number of fast-moving objects in space means: "This is what can happen when two spacecraft collide: two objects suddenly become a couple of thousand objects. They spread out across the orbit, their orbital speeds are 27,000 kilometers per hour, and if you approach at even a slightly intersecting angle, it is like a serious burst of machine-gun fire tearing through you."

World.title: National Audit Office to analyze Financial Intelligence Unit data requests
World.content:
The National Audit Office has launched an audit to assess whether the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) has implemented sufficient and effective controls over queries made to government databases.

Ines Metsalu-Nurminen, chief auditor at the National Audit Office, added that the audit will also assess whether the types of data requested correspond to those specified in the regulations governing the Financial Intelligence Unit's (FIU) database.

The audit will also assess whether FIU users' access rights are properly managed within the FIU and government databases, whether queries made by the FIU can be reviewed retrospectively and whether effective oversight of these queries is in place.

The National Audit Office will provide details of the audit's specific focus and key questions once the audit plan is finalized. The audit report is scheduled for completion in the third quarter of 2027.

In recent years, the Estonian Financial Intelligence Unit (Rahapesu Andmebüroo or RAB) has faced mounting criticism over privacy and fundamental rights regarding its extensive data-gathering practices. Concerns peaked following legal controversies and proposed legislative updates that expanded the agency's authority to make broad, real-time data queries across financial institutions.

World.title: 3,000 liters of paint: Estonia's largest spray-painted mural completed in Tallinn
World.content:
Estonia's largest spray-painted mural has been completed after 2,000 hours on old factory walls in the Ülemiste City district of Tallinn and depicts a local legend.

The Old Man of Ülemiste is one of the best-known figures of Estonian folklore who, according to legend, lives in Lake Ülemiste and watches over the fate of Tallinn.

The Old Man rises from the lake from time to time and asks if the capital has been completed. If someone answers "yes," he floods the city. Therefore, the answer must always be no, and that there is still work to do.

The mural shows the Old Man sitting on a rock in the lake while working on a laptop. A plane flies above and animals can be seen around the water's edge. The painting is located next to the older mural depicting a girl holding a red umbrella.

The image was designed and painted by artist Silver "SBoy" Seeblum and sprayed onto a huge gray factory wall. It took more than 2,000 working hours, or just over half a year, to complete and approximately 3,000 liters of paint.

"When painting with spray cans, the most important thing is to do the upper sections first, because paint and dust fall downward. I spent a total of two months painting the background, and another month on the character, the stones and the box," he told ERR.

The image will also be visible to travelers flying in and out of Tallinn Airport, with the best view available to those taking off in the direction of Lake Ülemiste.

Covering nearly 5,000 square meters, the mural is the largest in Estonia, and Seeblum already has thoughts of setting a new European record.

"I can understand very well why such a large work has never been done in Estonia and has only been done once before in Europe. This work falls just a couple of hundred square meters short of Europe's largest. We still have room on the roof, so perhaps we'll do that section too," Seeblum said.

World.title: PPA: Nothing extraordinary about right to confiscate electric scooters
World.content:
Police should be allowed to confiscate electric scooters that are banned from public roads without court approval, as similar powers already exist for other prohibited items, a senior police official said.

Confiscating electric scooters that are banned from public roads is nothing unusual, as police and various government agencies already have the right to confiscate items whose possession or use is prohibited by law, Sirle Loigo, head of the Police and Border Guard Board's traffic enforcement unit, told ERR.

"For example, the Weapons Act allows us to confiscate bladed weapons and firearms that are prohibited for civilian use. But we're also talking about smuggled cigarettes, radar detectors and devices used to manipulate tachographs. We also confiscate illegal drugs. This [confiscation] power is nothing unusual, but it's important to understand that it applies to items whose use is illegal under Estonian law."

Loigo clarified that the proposal does not concern all electric scooters or small mopeds, but only vehicles whose use is prohibited.

"In other words, vehicles that do not qualify as either light electric vehicles or small mopeds based on their technical specifications. They do not meet the requirements and cannot be registered as mopeds or motorcycles because they do not meet the technical standards. These are vehicles that are prohibited from being used on public roads."

She explained that the ban applies to vehicles capable of reaching speeds of 85 kilometers per hour or more, for example. "At that point, we're no longer talking about a light electric vehicle. A light electric vehicle has a power output of one kilowatt, a manufacturer-specified maximum speed of 25 kilometers per hour, no seat and is designed to carry one person."

Loigo said there are many prohibited vehicles on the roads and that the legislative amendment is needed to curb their growing numbers.

"The biggest problem today is that a large number of minors are riding these prohibited vehicles. They have been involved in very serious traffic accidents, including fatal ones. To prevent this trend from growing, the state has taken the position that just as we do not allow firearms prohibited for civilian use, we should take the same approach to vehicles whose use is prohibited."

Asked why confiscation decisions should be made by the police rather than a judge, Loigo said there was no need to burden the court system with decisions concerning items whose possession or use is illegal in Estonia.

An electric scooter. Source: LSM/Freepik stock images

"Judicial discretion is needed in situations where confiscation is decided based on the individual or the offense they have committed. For example, when it comes to drunk drivers, courts can confiscate their vehicles today and will continue to do so in the future. But that is a matter of judicial discretion because the motor vehicle is registered and permitted on public roads. The judge must weigh whether or not to confiscate the vehicle used to commit the offense. And if it is confiscated, the purpose is to prevent that person from committing further offenses with that particular vehicle. But the expansion of confiscation powers currently being proposed concerns vehicles that are not permitted on public roads in the first place."

ERR reported Monday that a proposed amendment to the Traffic Act would give police the authority to confiscate electric scooters that do not meet legal requirements. Currently, such vehicles can only be confiscated with court approval, but courts have not granted a single confiscation request to date. Since the proposal became public, it has drawn criticism from lawyers as well as former Prosecutor General Andres Parmas. Parmas argued that such a significant infringement on property rights should remain a matter for the courts to decide.

World.title: Tartu plans new pedestrian bridge between Kvissentali and Supilinn
World.content:
A new bridge for pedestrians and cyclists over Tartu's Emajõgi River largely depends on state support, but population growth in new residential developments is forcing the city to act.

More than 20 apartment buildings are being built in Tartu's Kvissentali area, between Raadi and Tähtvere. Once the buildings are completed, several thousand new residents are expected to move into the area.

However, large-scale developments are placing new pressure on people's daily transportation needs.

"Parents naturally want to be as independent as possible so they do not have to act as taxi drivers. This means children need to be able to get to extracurricular activities, sports practices and schools on their own as safely as possible," said Diana Hein, a real estate agent at Domus Kinnisvara.

To avoid traffic congestion on Narva maantee, Tartu is planning to build the nearly 100-meter-long Tuglase pedestrian and bicycle bridge by 2030. No buildings will be constructed immediately next to the bridge, and the green riverside area will be preserved.

"Back when the comprehensive plan was being drawn up many years ago, there was also an idea to design the bridge for car traffic. This met with very strong criticism from both the Supilinn and Tähtvere communities," said Tartu Deputy Mayor Kertu Vuks.

The new bridge, connecting university buildings and a sports park on the opposite bank, is already affecting the real estate market.

"This has been quite a significant selling point, for example, for students and rental property investors looking to buy apartments to rent out, because many university teaching buildings are located in Tähtvere and Veeriku," Hein said.

The construction of the bridge and the extension of Ujula Street are estimated to cost a total of €13 million. Tartu is applying for funding to cover 70 percent of the cost through the Ministry of Climate's sustainable mobility program.

"It all depends on how we fare in this funding round, but the need for more bridges in Tartu has already been agreed upon during the comprehensive planning process. If we don't secure funding this time, we will certainly keep an eye on future opportunities. At present, it is rather difficult to finance investments as large as bridge construction solely from the city's budget," Vuks said.

A decision on the funding is expected early next year, and if the application is approved, the bridge must be completed by 2030.

World.title: Tallinn wins Estonian Christian Orthodox Church rental dispute
World.content:
A yearslong rent dispute between the City of Tallinn and the Estonian Christian Orthodox Church came to an end Tuesday after the Supreme Court declined to hear the church's appeal.

The dispute between the City of Tallinn and the Estonian Christian Orthodox Church (formerly known as the Estonian Orthodox Church of the Moscow Patriarchate) concerned commercial premises at Pikk tänav 64 in Tallinn, which the church occupied under an open-ended lease. The Tallinn City Center District Administration terminated the lease on April 17, 2024.

Tallinn Mayor Peeter Raudsepp (Isamaa) said the protracted dispute had finally been resolved.

"The city acted lawfully in terminating the lease and the city-owned premises will be vacated. We are now looking to the future and the district administration will do everything it can to put the premises back into use as quickly as possible," Raudsepp said.

The church challenged the termination in court, seeking a ruling that the termination was invalid and that the lease remained in effect.

On August 29, 2025, Harju County Court dismissed the church's lawsuit, finding that the Tallinn City Center District Administration had the right to terminate the lease. The church appealed, but Tallinn Circuit Court upheld the lower court's ruling on June 12, 2026.

On October 19, 2026, the Supreme Court's Civil Chamber declined to hear the appeal because it did not meet the legal requirements for review. The Supreme Court's decision cannot be appealed.

The ruling confirming that the Tallinn City Center District Administration had lawfully terminated the lease has therefore entered into force.

The City of Tallinn has been negotiating with church representatives over vacating the premises at Pikk tänav 64. The parties have reached a verbal agreement to vacate the premises and are currently working to finalize the deadline.

World.title: DNO’s oil sales in northern Iraq double in Q3 2026
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Norway-based oil and gas operator DNO reported that its crude oil sales in Iraqi Kurdistan nearly doubled on an annual basis, reaching an average of 28,058 barrels per day in the third quarter of 2026.

The increase in oil sales comes after the corporation proactively halted its regional activities in response to the military escalations between the United States, Israel, and Iran in late February 2026, which resulted in a total collapse in revenues in the second quarter of 2026.

During the third quarter of 2026, gross operating production from the Tawke and Peshkabir oilfields rose significantly to 73,219 barrels per day, a substantial increase from just 363 barrels per day in the second quarter of the year.

All payments for DNO’s share of the oil during the third quarter were made in advance and deposited into the company’s foreign bank accounts before delivery began, aiming to mitigate previous regional payment risks.

Compared to oil sales of 14,449 barrels per day during the third quarter of 2025, the company’s supplies in the third quarter of 2026 represent an increase of about 94 percent.

World.title: Iraq offers mediation between Iran, Gulf States
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein stated on Sunday that Baghdad is attempting to arrange a meeting between Iran and the Gulf States as part of diplomatic efforts to reduce tensions and advance regional stability.

Hussein’s remarks took place during his speech at the conclusion of the 52nd session of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), where he confirmed that Iraq was maintaining contacts with both sides to facilitate dialogue, according to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA).

There are ongoing discussions between Iraq, the Gulf countries, and Iran aimed at bringing their viewpoints closer together, according to Hussein.

“We are trying to organize a meeting in Baghdad between Iran and the Gulf States,” Hussein said, without specifying a date or the degree of representation expected.

The proposal comes amid regional tensions that severely impacted maritime shipping and security in the Arabian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.

The goal of the diplomatic framework is to bring together Iran and the six Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) members—Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Oman—to address common security issues.

Hussein stressed that the region cannot purchase security from elsewhere and that internal collaboration is the only way to establish stability.

Although Hussein and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met in Baghdad on the sidelines of the summit to reaffirm a commitment to communication, the date of the joint meeting has not yet been disclosed.

World.title: Iraq holds funeral for 47 security personnel executed by ISIS years ago
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi authorities held a mass funeral on Tuesday in the northern city of Mosul for 47 victims, including security personnel and civilians, who were executed by the terrorist group of ISIS ten years ago.

Teams from Iraq’s Martyrs Foundation recently unearthed the remains from a mass burial south of Mosul. The Department of Forensic Medicine used DNA testing to positively identify the victims.

During ISIS’s brutal rule between 2014 and 2017, people from places south of Mosul, such as Hammam al-Alil, al-Shura, and al-Qayyarah, were kidnaped and executed. The victims included soldiers, police officers, religious figures, and local civilians.

Under the direction of Nineveh Governor Abdul Qader al-Dakhil, security personnel carried coffins covered in the Iraqi flag during an official ceremony. A public funeral procession headed toward the Qayyarah district for final burial after the central ceremony in Mosul.

In 2014, the terrorist group ISIS took control of large areas in Iraq and Syria before being defeated in 2017.

Over five million Iraqis had to flee the governorates of Nineveh, Salah al-Din, parts of Kirkuk, Diyala, and Anbar because of ISIS control over these areas in 2014.

Although Iraq declared in late 2017 that all of its regions were free of ISIS, the government continues to conduct security operations to hunt out any remaining members of the terrorist group.

World.title: Iraq’s oil exports to China hit 1.18 million bpd in September
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s oil supplies to China during September totaled 4.84 million tons, or about 1.18 million barrels per day, a 19 percent decline compared to the previous year and a 248 percent increase compared to August.

The General Administration of Customs of the People’s Republic of China revealed that the country’s imports of crude oil from Russia, its largest supplier, reached 9.94 million tons (approximately 2.42 million barrels per day) in September, according to Reuters.

China oil imports from Russia in September are 20 percent more than the volumes it received during the same period in 2025, though it marks an 11 percent decline compared to the previous month.

During the first nine months of 2026, Brazil was the second-largest crude oil supplier to China, with imports reaching 44.29 million tons (approximately 324.65 million barrels) from Brazil, compared to 43.12 million tons (around 316.07 million barrels) from Saudi Arabia.

Brazil’s oil supplies to China increased by 18 percent on an annual basis to 5.15 million tons in September alone, or almost 1.25 million barrels per day.

China’s crude oil imports from Saudi Arabia stood at 2.70 million tons, or about 660,000 barrels per day, marking a 62 percent decline compared to the previous year.

Chinese independent refiners increased recently their imports of Iraqi and Qatari crude to compensate for a sharp decline in Iranian oil supplies.

As their stockpiles near depletion, private refineries in China are paying considerable premiums to acquire alternatives, according to Reuters.

Experts see that the step represents a desperate search for alternatives due to logistical obstacles, rather than a true rebound in Chinese domestic crude demand.

World.title: Two oilfield operators in northern Iraq merge in $600 million deal
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Gulf Keystone Petroleum and ShaMaran Petroleum have reached a merger agreement, becoming one of the top private oil producers in Iraqi Kurdistan.

According to a statement from the corporation, the all-share acquisition is worth $601 million, Reuters reported.

As of October 19, shareholders of ShaMaran, who are listed on Euronext, will receive 0.075 shares of Gulf Keystone for each share of ShaMaran they own, reflecting a premium of 23 percent.

Each company’s stockholders will own roughly half of the merged business when the merger is complete.

According to the announcement, Gulf Keystone intends to cease its London listing and transfer its principal listing to Euronext Oslo Bors’ main list.

Following the completion of the deal, the listing of ShaMaran shares will end.

The proposed combination has received unanimous approval from the boards of Gulf Keystone and ShaMaran. December will see special meetings to complete approval.

With combined estimated reserves of 323 million barrels and daily production of 53,000 barrels of oil, the merged business is expected to profit from greater size and diversity.

As part of its ambitions to increase its oil production capacity, Iraq has given many contracts to businesses from the United States, China, France, and other countries.

As Baghdad looks to boost natural gas supply and oil output, British Petroleum (BP) and its US and Turkish partners took over operations at four oilfields in the northern Iraqi province of Kirkuk this week.

World.title: Iraq Stock Exchange records 2.5 billion IQD in weekly trading turnover
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraq Stock Exchange (ISX) reported weekly trading turnover exceeding 2.5 billion Iraqi dinars ($1.68 million) for the previous trading week, according to an official market report published on Tuesday, October 20, 2026.

Across the five trading sessions, shares of 57 joint-stock companies were actively traded out of 103 listed entities. Equities of 36 firms saw zero transactions due to pricing bid-ask disparities between buy and sell orders, while 11 companies remained suspended from trading for failing to meet mandatory corporate financial disclosure and regulatory reporting deadlines.

Trading volume expanded by 6.8% compared to the prior week, reaching 1.852 billion traded shares. However, total trading value contracted by 67% to 2.560 billion dinars, executed across 3,676 transactions. The main price benchmark, the ISX60 index, closed at 943.57 points, shedding 1.54% from its previous session close.

Foreign investment activity posted net inflows into domestic equities. Non-Iraqi investors bought 158 million shares valued at 331 million dinars over 55 contracts, while foreign selling remained muted, tallying 5 million shares worth 10 million dinars across 38 transactions.

The exchange convenes trading across five weekly sessions from Sunday through Thursday, listing 103 joint-stock enterprises spanning banking, telecommunications, industry, agriculture, insurance, financial investment, tourism, and services.

World.title: US dollar edges down across Baghdad, Basra, and Erbil Exchanges
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The exchange rate of the U.S. dollar against the Iraqi dinar edged down across exchange shops in Baghdad, Basra, and Erbil on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, slightly paring back gains recorded earlier in the week.

In Baghdad, foreign exchange counters registered a dip of 500 dinars per $100 compared to Monday’s trading, setting the retail selling rate at 169,000 dinars against buying bids of 168,000 dinars.

In Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan Region, trading displayed a similar softening, with selling desks quoting 168,200 dinars per $100 and buying transactions settling at 168,000 dinars.

In the southern commercial port hub of Basra, rates slipped by 250 dinars per $100 compared to yesterday’s levels. Exchange bureaus posted retail selling rates at 168,500 dinars against purchase bids of 168,000 dinars per $100.

Parallel market activity continues to reflect a sustained premium above the Central Bank of Iraq’s official statutory peg of 152,000 dinars per $100, driven by commercial merchant demand for physical liquidity outside the central electronic clearance platform.

World.title: Rubio lands in India for ‘trade diplomacy’
World.content:
Mumbai – US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in India on Tuesday, his second official visit to the country this year, as he pursues an Asian tour blending diplomacy and trade.

Rubio visited Uzbekistan, where he called for stronger partnerships with Central Asian countries, before landing in Mumbai for talks with Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar and meetings with business leaders.

He visited New Delhi and Kolkata in May, when he also toured the Taj Mahal and met Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Modi is not scheduled to meet Rubio this time.

The top US diplomat will visit Jamnagar, in the western state of Gujarat, a port and stronghold of billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance conglomerate and its flagship refinery, the world’s largest.

He is also due to lay a wreath in memory of the 2008 Mumbai attacks that killed 166 people.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday he had also spoken to Rubio and raised issues with the US military satellite system that Ukraine uses, as well as missile delays.

Zelensky, expected in Oslo for talks with US envoys, said he told Rubio that “Starlink/Starshield needs to be restored” and that ballistic missile interceptors “are needed to protect lives”.

– ‘Energy supplies’ –

Rubio’s visit comes as India and the United States struggle to finalise a trade deal, a persistent source of friction between the two countries.

Speaking in Samarkand, Rubio said Washington and New Delhi were “very close” to an agreement.

However, a deal during his visit appears unlikely.

US President Donald Trump’s tariff war launched in April last year has added to friction over India’s imports of Russian oil and warming ties between Washington and Pakistan, India’s arch-rival.

Asked about temporary US sanctions waivers for Russian oil, of which India is a major importer, Rubio said Washington had to juggle multiple factors “including our bilateral relationships with other countries and what they realistically are capable of being able to do in terms of their own energy supplies”.

“You also can’t unravel the economy of other countries because of one central issue,” he said.

The two countries reached an interim trade agreement in February aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian goods.

But days later, the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s sweeping tariffs, fuelling uncertainty over when the agreement would take effect.

The two sides have been negotiating ever since.

Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said this month the talks had reached “a plateau, beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult”.

Jaishankar met with his United Arab Emirates counterpart in Mumbai earlier on Tuesday. The UAE is a key supplier of Indian energy, especially liquefied natural gas (LNG).

“The situation in the Gulf remains a matter of deep concern,” Jaishankar told UAE Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, in public comments broadcast before their meeting started.

He said India continues to support “free, safe and unimpeded flow of trade, energy and fertiliser”.

World.title: 'Forces working to destabilise India, have 3 core agendas': BJP blames oppn, draws Ravana comparison
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

Sudhanshu Trivedi on Wednesday accused certain opposition forces of attempting to destabilise India under the guise of legitimate public demands, alleging that their ultimate objective was âregime changeâ through violence and conspiracy.

Referring to the Prime Ministerâs Vijayadashami address, Trivedi said certain forces were driven by three agendas: exploiting power for personal gain, creating divisions within society, and harbouring hatred towards Indian culture and religion.

âThese are the forces that seek to divide society, plunder state resources, and harbor animosity toward Indian culture and the Hindu faith. They organize conferences calling for the 'eradication of Sanatan Dharma,' spearhead global campaigns to 'dismantle Hindutva,' and propagate misleading narratives about Indiaâs institutions.

These are the very forces that do not wish to see India progress,â he said.

Trivedi questioned the recurring demands and allegations concerning institutions such as LIC, HAL, SBI and SEBI, as well as vaccines, electronic voting machines (EVMs) and electoral rolls.

Comparing the repeated demands to Ravanaâs ten heads, he said, âIn reality, much like Ravana, who possessed ten heads, if one head were severed, another would immediately emerge.





Their demands are similar: satisfy one demand, and another will promptly take its place.â

He argued that the common language used across various movements could help identify what he described as their underlying agenda. Drawing a parallel with Ravana disguising himself as an ascetic before abducting Sita, Trivedi alleged that certain forces were concealing their intentions behind seemingly legitimate demands.

âIn the Ramayana, when Ravana arrived to abduct Mata Sita, he did not appear in his true, demonic form, but rather disguised himself as an ascetic. Today, various forces are operating under such disguises, cloaked in deception. Their true objective is not the specific demands they present... their singular goal is 'regime change' through violent conflict and calculated conspiracy,â he said.

Trivedi criticised those claiming the legacy of Shiv Sena founder Balasaheb Thackeray for allegedly aligning with forces that seek to undermine Indian religion and culture.

âIt is truly bizarre that those who claim to be the rightful heirs to the legacy of the highly revered Balasaheb Thackeray have now aligned themselves with the very forces that seek to destroy our religion and culture, and they state this with great conviction that 'Let him come from Vietnam, then 'regime change' will happen',â he said.

Trivedi also questioned what Sanjay Raut knew about Rahul Gandhi that even Congress leaders were allegedly unaware of.

âWhat is this 'lead,' this 'secret,' or this 'information' that Sanjay Raut possesses regarding Rahul Gandhi, something that even the Congress party's own leaders are unaware of? What kind of conspiratorial threads are these?â he asked.

He further questioned the significance of references to developments following overseas visits, citing remarks about dropping a âhydrogen bombâ, predicting a âtsunamiâ and Rautâs comments.

Trivedi alleged that such statements pointed to the involvement of unidentified and suspicious entities seeking to destabilise India.

âWhether it is talk of dropping a 'hydrogen bomb' upon returning from abroad, or predicting a 'tsunami' after such a visit, and now these remarks by Sanjay Raut, all of this suggests that these actions are being orchestrated by unknown, suspicious entities, forces from across the border that seek to incite unrest within our nation,â he said.

Expressing confidence in the government's position, Trivedi said the alleged attempt at âregime changeâ would fail under Prime Minister Narendra Modiâs leadership, backed by public trust and a commitment to the country.

The remarks come amid a political row over calls for âregime changeâ by opposition leaders and student activists during ongoing protests in Delhi against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

Senior advocate Prashant Bhushan, All India Students Association (AISA) president Neha Bora and Congress spokesperson Pawan Khera have used or discussed the phrase at conferences and press briefings linked to the protests.

Earlier, Shiv Sena (UBT) chief Uddhav Thackeray backed the calls, arguing that denying people the right to express their views through elections and protests would leave them with no option but to seek a change of government.

World.title: 'Human rights shouldn't be used for political pressure': India amid UN criticism over handling of protests
World.content:
A protestor is detained by the police during a youth demonstration demanding the resignation of the country's election chief Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India

Remarks come amid UN expertsâ concerns over protests

UN experts flag mass detentions, alleged ill-treatment

An independent investigation Fair and unbiased reporting Protecting the right to peaceful assembly Cooperation between governments and international bodies 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday asserted that human rights should not be used as an instrument of political pressure or selective targeting of countries, opposing attempts to turn allegations and incomplete statistics into a ânegative characterisationâ of the world's largest democracy.While speaking at UNGA Third Committee, deputy secretary in the ministry of external affairs Barkha Tamrakar said, "Human rights not to be used as an instrument of political pressure or selective country targeting.""India engages with international human rights mechanisms, but such engagement must be based on dialogue, consultation, cooperation with non-selectivity and transparency as guiding principle," she added."We call on delegations to cite the report faithfully, not to inflate a humanitarian communication into a verdict."She also opposed any "attempt to convert unverified allegations, incomplete statistics or a report that contains no India country observation into a negative characterisation of the world's largest democracy".Tamrakar's remarks came amid concerns raised by UN human rights experts over recent youth-led protests in New Delhi.On Tuesday, more than 20 UN human rights experts in Geneva expressed alarm over what they described as a ârepeatedly heavy-handed police responseâ to peaceful youth-led demonstrations in the national capital.In a statement shared by UN special procedures, the experts alleged that law enforcement agencies had used force against unarmed students, detained protesters arbitrarily and imposed broad restrictions on public gatherings. They called on Indian authorities to respect the right to peaceful assembly and ensure accountability for alleged abuses.âDespite the non-violent nature of the assemblies, law enforcement has deployed force against unarmed students,â the experts said.The experts said hundreds of thousands of students and their supporters had gathered peacefully across the country to protest government decisions concerning the education system and, more recently, voter-roll deletions.They referred to reports that the deletions affected 130 million individuals, reportedly belonging to Muslim, Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe communities.According to the statement, more than 7,000 young people, journalists, human rights defenders, lawyers and political party members were recently detained in New Delhi and taken to detention centres farther away. Their phones were allegedly seized and protest-related material deleted. Most were released after 24 hours, including protest leaders, the experts said.The statement also cited reports of injuries and ill-treatment among protesters, expressing particular concern over allegations of sexual violence and other forms of gender-based abuse during demonstrations and related detentions.The experts also raised concerns over the reported use of Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) to impose broad restrictions on public gatherings, suspend public transportation and enforce internet shutdowns.They said restrictions on peaceful assembly must be lawful, pursue a legitimate objective and be necessary and proportionate.They urged Indian authorities to immediately stop the excessive use of force, lift blanket restrictions on assemblies and refrain from the misuse of digital surveillance, including biometric monitoring and internet disruptions.The UN experts called for an independent, impartial and thorough investigation into the conduct of law enforcement personnel and affiliated forces, urging authorities to ensure accountability, justice and reparations for victims.

World.title: Kochi’s waste management facilities under scanner after Perumbavoor yard fire
World.content:
A safety audit of waste management facilities in Ernakulam district seems to be on the cards with a major fire at such a facility near Perumbavoor raising serious concerns.

The incident, in which tonnes of plastic waste stored at a 20,000-odd sqft material recovery facility of a private Kochi-based waste management company at Arackappady was gutted, has highlighted the need for a timely safety audit of other similar facilities, according to senior officials of the Fire and Rescue Services Department.

“There maybe similar sites in other parts of the district also. They need to be identified and it has to be ensured that fire safety measures are in place,” a senior fire officer said.

Firefighters involved in the dousing operation at Arackappady said the facility lacked key fire safety mechanisms. “Garbage should be ideally stored compartmentalised in such facilities so that spread of fire could be prevented. Such large facilities should also have water curtains — specialised open nozzles to spray a continuous sheet of water. No-objection certificate from Fire and Rescue Department must be made mandatory for issuing licence to such facilities,” another officer said.

There are around 15 non-biodegradable waste management companies empanelled by the Suchitwa Mission in Ernakulam district, including the one which was gutted in fire, while several unauthorised firms also operate in the sector. The inorganic waste collected by Haritha Karma Sena volunteers are delivered to the material collection facilities in different parts of the district. From there, the waste is sorted and sent to the resource recovery facility. They are then handed over for reuse or recycling.

“Many new players keep entering the sector, but often they don’t comply with safety norms. Proper sorting of garbage doesn’t take place in some facilities, and also there is a tendency to stock up beyond the capacity,” the founder of a waste management company engaged by several local bodies said.

He also called for a periodic safety audit of the facilities by the local bodies concerned.

World.title: GRAP-1 curbs imposed in Delhi-NCR as air quality slips into ‘poor’ category
World.content:
As the air quality in Delhi worsened to the ‘poor’ category, the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) in the NCR and adjoining areas announced Stage 1 of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) on Wednesday (October 21, 2026).

The GRAP is a set of short-term emergency measures aimed at reducing air pollution and is divided into four stages, depending on the level of air pollution that exists at a particular time or is predicted for the near future.

“The Air Quality Index (AQI) of Delhi, which was observed to be 179 (moderate category) on October 20, has exhibited a sharp rise with an AQI of 244 at 2 pm on October 21 (poor category),” said the CAQM in a statement.

It added that the forecast by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) and the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology had predicted AQI to remain in the ‘poor’ category in the coming days.

“Do not permit inter-city/inter-state buses from any city/town of the states of Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, and Rajasthan, and also from the adjoining states of Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand and J&K, other than EV/CNG/BS-VI Diesel, to ply in Delhi-NCR,” read one of the measures under Stage 1 of the GRAP.

The first stage, GRAP-1, kicks in when the AQI is between 201 and 300; the second stage, GRAP-2, is invoked when the AQI is between 301 and 400; GRAP-3 kicks in between 401 and 500; and GRAP-4 is invoked when the AQI is more than 450.

(With PTI inputs)

World.title: Godavari-Cauvery link project turning into controversy as BRS senses major conspiracy
World.content:
The Godavari-Krishna-Pennar-Cauvery link project proposed by the Central Government is turning out to be a political controversy with the main Opposition Bharat Rashtra Samiti (BRS) sensing a major conspiracy behind the plan.

The issue figured in the recent Southern Zonal Council meeting wherein Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chadrababu Naidu termed the project as a south India link, envisaging water from Godavari (Polavaram) to Krishna, from Krishna to Banakacherla and from Banakacherla to Cauvery. If this link was established, there would be flexibility for all the four States, he said.

Mr. Naidu reportedly addressed a letter to the Central Government to suggest the Godavari–Cauvery link from Polavaram.

He wanted the issue to be included in the agenda of the next meeting of the National Water Development Agency (NWDA) and the agenda of the NWDA meeting on November 3 was drafted on the basis of the letter.

BRS senior leader T. Harish Rao, however, alleged that the plan was yet another attempt by the Andhra Pradesh government against the interests of Telangana. Mr. Naidu had been trying one route after another to take away Godavari water. The Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister initially brought up Polavaram–Banakacherla to take 200 tmc ft water, which was renamed as Nallamalasagar subsequently.

Mr. Naidu had convinced the Centre and was clearing the way to Banakacherla in the name of the Godavari–Cauvery link. It was his third proposal to carry water directly from Polavaram through Bollapalli, Nagarjunasagar and Somasila to Cauvery, Mr. Harish Rao said.

He appealed to Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy to stop the injustice being scripted against Telangana in the name of Godavari-Cauvery link and if allowed to go ahead, it would be a death warrant for Telangana’s water rights.

Telangana Deputy Chief Minister Mallu Bhatti Vikramarka said at the southern zonal council meeting that the State was not against river linking in principle, but it should not be at the cost of its benefits. Though water is available in Godavari, the State had still to tap the water as per its share.

He said instead of 43 TMC of water proposed to be utilised for the State, Telangana had proposed 74 TMC of water from the water passing through it — through the diverted Godavari-Cauvery link waters — and also 200 TMC of Godavari flood waters for irrigation and drinking water, while protecting existing approved projects.

The State Irrigation department explained that several meetings were held on the issue and an in-principle approval for the source — for Godavari-Cauvery link — to be at Icchampally/Sammakka Sagar Project had been given.

Union Jal Shakti department explained at the meeting that alternative studies to divert surplus water available in Godavari basin and unutilized waters in Indravati sub-basin of Godavari basin through Godavari-Cauvery link project were carried out by the NWDA. The Godavari (Inchampalli)-Cauvery (Grand Anicut) link comprises three links Godavari (Inchampalli)-Krishna (Nagarjunasagar) link, Krishna (Nagarjunasagar)–Pennar (Somasila) link and Pennar (Somasila)-Cauvery (Grand Anicut) link.

World.title: Several houses torched in abandoned Manipur village amid ethnic tensions
World.content:
Several houses were set on fire in an abandoned village in Manipur’s Kamjong district on Wednesday (October 21, 2026) morning, triggering fresh tensions.

Khoikai Kuki village, located near Chassad village, was set ablaze by suspected militants around 5.30 a.m., police said.

The village had been deserted after residents fled amid escalating clashes between the Kuki and Naga communities, they said.

The extent of the damage and the identity of those involved were yet to be ascertained, they added.

More than 50 people have been killed and dozens of houses burnt in ethnic clashes between the two tribal communities in the state since early this year. Tamenglong, Noney, Kangpokpi, Ukhrul and Kamjong are among the districts affected by the violence.

World.title: NHAI turns to AI and open source to preserve institutional knowledge lost to officer transfers
World.content:
The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) is using artificial intelligence (AI) to help officials navigate the organisation’s policies, contracts and highway project data, while working to preserve institutional knowledge that can be lost when officers are transferred.

Mayank Kumawat, an AI engineer at NHAI, and Deep Saikia, Deputy Manager (Information Technology) at the authority, outlined the initiative at the recent IndiaFOSS 2026, the annual conference organised by FOSS United. Their presentation described how NHAI’s internal AI team is using open-source software to build tools for everyday administrative and technical work, and how it is exploring ways to make employees’ knowledge reusable across the organisation.

Mr. Kumawat is part of NHAI’s AI Cell, where he helps build internal AI tools, including the authority’s assistant ‘Marg Sarthi’. According to his IndiaFOSS, he has worked on applied AI, education technology and public-sector systems, was a lead contributor to the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation’s MCP initiative, and built an adaptive AI learning system called SMART in 2023 in collaboration with XLRI and Harvard faculty.

Mr. Saikia, a Computer Science and Engineering graduate from the National Institute of Technology (nit), Silchar, works on AI-based tools, digital transformation and workflow automation at NHAI. His work focuses on applying technology to public infrastructure and large-scale institutional processes.

Mr. Kumawat said that when he joined NHAI, he found that officials had to consult multiple sources to carry out routine tasks. These included laws, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways circulars, more than 1,800 internal NHAI policy circulars, and standards issued by the Indian Roads Congress. More complex tasks, such as approving contractor bills, drafting notices, handling land acquisition and obtaining environmental clearances, required officials to navigate several rules and documents.

He said officials often maintained their own folders of relevant circulars and guidelines, updating them as new documents were issued. But frequent transfers and deputations meant that incoming officers had to rebuild this knowledge base.

Mr. Saikia said the problem was not a lack of expertise within NHAI, but the difficulty of making that expertise reusable across the organisation. “The problem is that the knowledge is not always reusable,” he said during the presentation, adding that when officers move or are transferred, some of the context they have accumulated moves with them.

The team is experimenting with converting recurring administrative and technical processes into reusable workflows. Mr. Saikia said experienced officers could explain how particular processes work, identify the documents and approvals required, and have other experts review those procedures before they are incorporated into the system.

He said this could allow a workflow understood in one office to be used in another, and help prevent mistakes identified by one officer from being repeated elsewhere.

An assistant for everyday work

Mr. Kumawat demonstrated how ‘Marg Sarthi’, NHAI’s internal AI assistant, allows officers to query project data and policy documents through a conversational interface.

In one demonstration, Mr. Kumawat showed how an officer overseeing highway projects in Bengaluru could use the AI assistant to identify unresolved problems across projects. The system searched monthly progress reports, grouped the problems by category and displayed them on a dashboard. It could also generate a PDF report that the officer could send to contractors to seek explanations and follow up on the issues.

In another demonstration, the assistant was asked whether an additional work proposal worth ₹50 crore could be approved for a highway project originally valued at ₹250 crore. Rather than immediately answering yes or no, the system asked for more details about the contract and the officer’s authority to approve the proposal. It then provided an answer with references to the relevant rules, allowing the officer to check the original documents and verify the basis for its response.

The team said the system was designed to make answers auditable. During the question-and-answer session, the speakers distinguished between errors arising from retrieving incomplete or irrelevant information and errors in the answer generated from the retrieved material. They said citations and feedback from officers helped them identify and address gaps.

The speakers also said the assistant used role-based access controls linked to NHAI’s existing project-management system. An officer’s access through the assistant was intended to correspond to the projects and information that the officer was authorised to access in the underlying system.

NHAI to deploy 3D sensors to identify potholes, road cracks across 23 States

Open-source software

Mr. Kumawat said the team had built the assistant using existing open-source software rather than developing every component from scratch. LibreChat provides the conversational interface, while the Model Context Protocol (MCP) connects it to tools and data sources. The team also uses PostHog and Langfuse for AI observability, and Forgejo for code hosting.

Mr. Saikia said open-source software allowed the team to experiment with different solutions, adapt existing tools to NHAI’s requirements and obtain feedback from officers without having to begin a lengthy development process for every new idea.

He said the team could test a proposed tool with users, continue developing it if it proved useful, or abandon it if it did not address the problem. Conventional software development could be time-consuming, involving requirements gathering, procurement, vendor onboarding and development. Open-source software allowed the team to experiment with solutions more quickly.

The team said officers had begun suggesting new applications and reporting gaps in the assistant’s responses. Mr. Saikia said this interaction had also changed the relationship between the technology team and the engineers using the system, with officers contributing knowledge of their own workflows rather than remaining only users of the tools.

‘Marg Sarthi’ had reportedly crossed 15,000 conversations and 50,000 questions from more than 1,000 NHAI employees, with two in three users returning at least once a week. Mr. Kumawat separately said the system had answered more than two lakh queries since its launch on April 18, 2026.

The team also described developing specialised tools for tasks such as analysing technical schedules and geotechnical and road-safety reports. Mr. Saikia said not every problem needed to be solved by adding a workflow to the assistant; some required dedicated tools for repetitive technical checks before an expert exercised judgment.

World.title: Tamil Nadu government sanctions ₹71 crore to enhance contingency funds for police stations
World.content:
The Tamil Nadu government, on Wednesday (October 21, 2026), issued an order sanctioning ₹71.01 crore to enhance the contingency funds provided to all police stations in the State to meet routine administrative and operational expenses.

According to an official press release, Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay had announced the enhancement of contingency funds to all police stations during the demand for grants for the Home Department for 2026-27 in the Legislative Assembly. Accordingly, the State government has issued an order allocating the amount with the objective meet unforeseen expenses and eliminate corruption, the release said.

Police stations are classified into three categories based on the number of crimes reported. The monthly contingency fund for Light category police stations has been increased from ₹3,750 to ₹30,000, for Medium police stations from ₹6,000 to ₹40,000, and for heavy police stations from ₹8,250 to ₹50,000, the release added.

World.title: TDP gets 48 of 62 divisions in Vizianagaram NDA deal, says MLA Aditi Vijaya Lakshmi
World.content:
Telugu Desam Party (TDP) MLA Aditi Vijaya Lakshmi on Wednesday (October 21, 2026) said the combined strength of the NDA parties, the TDP, the Jana Sena Party (JSP) and the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), would ensure a massive victory for the alliance in the Vizianagaram mayoral election. She expressed happiness over the peaceful completion of the seat-sharing agreement. Of the 62 divisions, the TDP got 48, the JSP 10 and the BJP four.

She thanked JSP Parliament coordinator Avanpu Vikram, JSP senior leader Palavalasa Yeshaswi and others for cooperating with the TDP in finalising the seat-sharing agreement. Speaking to the media, she said the TDP won the Vizianagaram seat with a majority of 60,000 votes in the 2024 elections. She expressed confidence that the TDP’s mayoral candidate, Avanapu Bhargavi, would get a huge majority in the ensuing election.

Ms. Bhargavi said her father-in-law, Avanapu Suribabu, had developed Vizianagaram city as municipal chairperson a decade ago. She promised to improve civic infrastructure in all 62 wards of the district headquarters.

Ms. Bhargavi’s husband and senior TDP leader Avanapu Vijay said the YSRCP had failed to develop the Fort City, although the party won 48 divisions in the previous local body elections held in 2019. He said Ms. Aditi’s development works in the last two years would help his wife win an absolute majority in the mayoral election.

World.title: How Hyderabad artist Priti Samyukta turns fabric scraps into art
World.content:
Hyderabad-based artist Priti Samyukta has won third prize at the XI Tashkent International Art Biennale, held in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, from October 12 to 16. An associate professor and head of the painting department at Jawaharlal Nehru Architecture and Fine Arts University (JNAFAU), Priti presented three works from her series Stitching Memories. Two used cloth appliqué, while the third drew inspiration from quilts.

Her exploration of textile art deepened during her Fulbright-Nehru postdoctoral fellowship in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, where she researched the quilt-making traditions of the Gee’s Bend quilters, a small African American community. The experience encouraged her to experiment with materials and incorporate a new approach into her practice. “When I say ‘new’, I mean the newness in the use of material,” she explains.

The other Indian artist to participate in the biennale was Bengaluru-based Ajitvar Kumar, known as Douglas.

Platform for dialogue Curated by Zaynutdinova Zukhra Bakhtiyor Qizi, the XI Tashkent International Art Biennale brought 70 international participants from 33 countries, along with 70 participants from Uzbekistan on a platform. Among the 500 works displayed in eight venues, Marina Borodina, Academician of the Academy of Arts of Uzbekistan, won a grand prix. While the ‘Scole’ group from the Republic of Sakha, Russia won the first prize, the second prize went to Nuriddin Rasulov, representing the ‘5+1’ group of Uzbekistan.

Having never worked with cloth or scraps from worn-out clothes before, Priti found the practice both challenging and engaging. She has been exploring this new medium of image-making for three years, learning patience through the slow, continuous process of hand-stitching each piece.

The fabric comes from clothes gifted by friends and family, each carrying its own history and memories. By bringing these fragments together, Priti draws on their personal associations to tell a story of her own. “I am stitching their memories of their ‘outfits’ together in order to narrate my own story,” she says.

Abstract artworks

A quilt typically has three layers: a base, padding or batting, and the top layer, which carries the main work. While Priti’s earlier works used all three, she now intends to work with just two, much like a painting on canvas. Using denim or corduroy as a base, she builds her narratives with different fabrics, leaving the knots and threads visible. “I like viewers to see what is behind the base. These colourful knots of thread appear like an abstract artwork in themselves,” she says.

Instead of brushstrokes and paint, Priti uses plain, embroidered, textured and shimmering fabrics to tell stories. She enjoys the process more than the outcome, preferring hand-stitching to carefully planned outlines. “I like the unannounced, childlike stitches that aren’t purposeful but emerge during needlework. My soul thrives when I stitch these pieces together to create a composition,” she says.

The process is laborious, sometimes taking a month to complete a three-by-four-foot work. Unexpected turns during stitching are part of the process, which she embraces. Once the narrative is complete, she adds running stitches, or kantha work, to give the piece a fuller, more textured appearance.

The XI Tashkent International Art Biennale opened up new possibilities for Priti. Interacting with artists from other countries and experiencing their work was overwhelming. “The prize is an encouragement to do better and also contribute to the next generation of artists,” she says.

World.title: PM Shehbaz vows to strengthen Maldives ties for 'all time to come'; 20 MoUs signed
World.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday vowed to strengthen bilateral relations with the Maldives, as the two countries signed 20 memorandums of understanding (MoUs) during the visit of President Dr Mohamed Muizzu.

Muizzu arrived in Islamabad on Tuesday on a three-day visit at the invitation of PM Shehbaz Sharif. The visit marks the first by a Maldivian president to Pakistan in 11 years, and comes as the two countries celebrate the 60th anniversary of their diplomatic relations, established in 1966.

Addressing a joint press stakeout following the signing of 20 wide-ranging MoUs, PM Shehbaz said, “There is no doubt that the two countries [will] keep on strengthening these relations for all time to come.”

The premier extended a “very warm welcome” to the visiting dignitary and his delegation.

PM Shehbaz expressed his “warmest greetings and heartfelt affection to the people of Dhivehi Raajje, the land of islands, a nation whose spirit is as vast as the ocean that surrounds it,” hailing 60 years of diplomatic ties between the two countries.

The prime minister noted that he and Muizzu, in their bilateral and delegation-level talks, discussed “all important issues which have direct bearing between our two brotherly countries and of course, regional and international issues”.

“I am very happy to announce that we had a wonderful session, very productive and very fruitful discussions,” he remarked.

PM Shehbaz noted that the conversations encompassed “economic and trade relations, our strategic defence cooperation, our support for training of our brothers and sisters from Maldives in Pakistan in various walks of life; police, defence, education, health and many other” fields.

The prime minister went on to announce that both sides had agreed to raise their bilateral trade from $13.9 million — “just a fraction of our potential” — to $200m in the next two years.

While highlighting that the two South Asian countries had “very strong” relations, coupled with a “long list of mutual achievements”, PM Shehbaz said both sides noted that their ties “do not reflect the true strength of our economic cooperation”.

Thanking Muizzu for his “personal support in this behalf”, the premier went on to announce that Islamabad would support Malé in promoting the plantation of 5m trees in the Maldives by providing 100,000 olive cuttings and 100,000 seeds of various plant species within a mutually decided timeframe.

Referring to the MoUs signed, he affirmed that he “will be very happy to personally work with [Muizzu] to translate these written MoUs into action with prompt decision-making and speedy implementation”.

The prime minister declared that Pakistan was “absolutely ready to provide technical expertise to various segments of our mutual cooperation and, above all, Pakistan is very happy to learn that Maldives is moving forward speedily to establish data centres in other places”.

“This is great news, and as a matter of good luck, Pakistan has also attained a reasonable level of expertise and professional capability in this field,” he added, noting that the country had set up data centres in various locations. He offered Pakistan’s “experience and our professional capabilities in this behalf” to the Maldives.

PM Shehbaz noted that a large number of Maldivian students were receiving education in Pakistani universities and colleges, particularly in the field of healthcare, and that 250 Pakistani doctors and other paramedics were serving in the Maldives.

“This shall continue in future with bigger numbers so that whatever requirements you have, we as a brotherly country would be more than happy to fulfil those requirements willingly and with utmost sincerity of purpose,” the prime minister assured Muizzu.

Speaking on international developments, PM Shehbaz commended the Maldives’ “unwavering” support for the Palestinian cause, adding that Islamabad remains fully committed to the Palestinians’ right of self-determination and the establishment of an independent state of Palestine.

The premier further said he briefed Muizzu on Pakistan’s principled position on occupied Jammu and Kashmir, declaring Islamabad’s support for a peaceful resolution of the dispute in accordance with the relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions.

“Till they have won their struggle and gotten the right of self-determination, Pakistan shall continue to support them diplomatically and, of course, support them at all international forums till they become an independent sovereign country as per UNSC resolutions, and their sacrifice will not go to waste at all,” he said.

The prime minister also expressed Pakistan’s “serious concern” over India’s decision to place the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in abeyance in April 2025, pointing out that it was a violation of an international binding treaty.

“Pakistan’s position is loud and clear and beyond an array of doubt; legally binding treaties must be respected and shared water resources must never be weaponised or used as an instrument of political pressure or blackmailing,” he stated.

PM Shehbaz said Pakistan has made it “abundantly clear at various forums”, including the UN General Assembly last month, that water was a “red line” for the country.

“Waterflows in any canal or ocean, sea or straits, carries trade, commerce, message of prosperity and progress, and not threats, confrontations and conflicts,” he said.

“Water is a lifeline for humanity […] so this should be known to all and sundry that any violation in this behalf will be regarded by Pakistan as an act of war,” the prime minister warned.

Concluding his remarks, PM Shehbaz said Muizzu’s visit had given Pakistan-Maldives relations “new purpose and new momentum”.

He remarked, “The same ocean that touches the shores of Karachi and Gwadar embraces the islands of the Maldives.

“For centuries, its waves have carried traders, scholars and travellers between our lands. Today, they carry the renewed promise of our wonderful friendship whose finest chapters are yet to be written.”

In his comments, Muizzu appreciated PM Shehbaz, the government and people of Pakistan for “their exceptional warmth and gracious hospitality”.

He added that his visit coming on the 60-year mark of Pakistan-Maldives diplomatic relations made it “particularly significant”. The 60 years have been marked by warmth, friendship and shared perspectives, he said.

“This visit takes place after a decade-long interval. It offers us an important opportunity not simply to celebrate the friendship of the past but to define the partnership of the future,” Muizzu said.

Stressing on the close relations between the two countries, he said, “Only two such longstanding friends could have talked so widely and agreed on so much about our future together”.

Muizzu said, for him, the talks represented a “clear shared ambition to move the Maldives-Pakistan partnership into a new era”.

He said the discussions encompassed several sectors including trade and investment; health and education; environment, fisheries and agriculture; youth and sports; policing and defence; training and capacity-building; and tourism.

He said he was pleased about the signing of 20 MOUs. “These memoranda will open new avenues for cooperation among multiple sectors, but agreements are meaningful only when they produce results.

“Our next step, of course, is to translate these understandings into tangible opportunities and meaningful benefits for the people of both nations.”

Muizzu said he endorsed the goal to take the two countries’ bilateral trade quantum from $13m to $200m in two years.

“The Maldives and Pakistan are worlds of untapped potential for each other,” the Maldivian president said.

He reaffirmed that the two countries would take a “firm step in the right direction”, adding that Thursday’s business forum would provide an opportunity to bring together business leaders, inventors and innovators from both countries to turn the friendship into mutually beneficial investments.

He said he was encouraged by the discussions to establish direct flights between Pakistan and the Maldives, adding that direct flights would help support tourism as well.

He further said that the two countries’ leaders saw “considerable potential in halal and Muslim-friendly tourism”.

Muizzu appreciated Pakistan’s scholarships and placements for Maldivian students, adding that the leaders would broaden the opportunities further, especially in artificial intelligence, digitisation and future technologies as well as health.

“We want our next generation to be prepared for the future and be prepared to shape that future.”

Muizzu stressed that climate change was “not an abstract environmental concern” for the Maldives. Instead, he said, “it is a direct challenge to our security, our development and our future”.

He welcomed cooperation with Pakistan in areas of climate resilience, conservation, sustainable waste management and renewable energy. He thanked PM Shehbaz for his announcement of donations to help the Maldives plant 5m trees in five years.

“Our nations share a commitment to advancing common interests through constructive engagements.”

He said the Maldives remained committed to revitalising the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, adding that “rebuilding trust, encouraging meaningful dialogue and strengthening mutual understanding are essential to unlocking the full potential of regional cooperation”.

He further expressed the Maldives’ “unequivocal and steadfast solidarity” with Palestinians and their “legitimate right to self-determination”.

Muizzu also commended Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts “to promote dialogue, de-escalation, humanitarian assistance and a just and lasting peace” in the Middle East.

Concluding his remarks, he said, “For 60 years, Pakistan has stood as a trusted friend of the Maldives.” The two countries have now agreed to “build a new era of partnership on the foundations of our six decades of friendship”, he said.

The Maldivian president was later conferred with an honorary doctorate in politics by the International Islamic University Islamabad.

PM Shehbaz had noted that the degree recognised Muizzu’s “sagacious and wise leadership and your great public service to your people in the Maldives”.

20 MoUs signed

Pakistan and the Maldives on Wednesday signed a series of MoUs aimed at deepening bilateral relations in multiple sectors, including defence, IT, cybersecurity, health, education, social protection, agriculture and tourism, among others.

PM Shehbaz and Muizzu witnessed the ceremony as the representatives from both sides exchanged the pre-signed documents.

The two countries signed an MoU on cooperation in the fields of information technology, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, digital skills, and technology and innovation. An MoU was inked to strengthen cooperation in combating illicit trafficking and abuse of narcotic drugs.

The two sides also signed an MoU on social protection as well as on health cooperation and between Maldives Food and Drug Authority and the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan.

Both nations signed MoUs focused on the recruitment of health professionals, strengthening defence ties and maritime security cooperation.
