Hello, new neighbor

Nana was just a pup in the summer of 2024, when fishermen first spotted him resting on a buoy in waters off Beihai, in the southern Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. Noticing he was thin and had wounds on his body, likely caused by boat propellers, they alerted the authorities, who transported him to the Beihai Aquatic Rescue and Rehabilitation Center.

The spot where Nana was discovered lies just off a migration route for spotted seals between the western Pacific Ocean and Dalian’s Liaodong Bay. Experts suspect he drifted from his colony and was stranded alone.

In November 2025, after being nursed back to health, Nana was transferred to a wild species rehabilitation center in Dalian operated by the Liaoning Ocean and Fisheries Science and Research Institute. There, he quickly went from 50 to 70 kilograms and grew a new coat of glossy fur. “You could see him looking better every day,” says Chai Yuqiao, a researcher at the base.

By this spring, Nana was deemed well enough to return to the wild. On April 16, the institute released him and two other rescued seals roughly 10 kilometers from shore in the Yellow Sea, thinking they would naturally head for the migration route and find a new colony.

Nana’s two companions did exactly that, but data from his satellite tag shows he never left the Yellow Sea. Two months later, he popped up at Dachangshan Island.

Locals first spotted the seal relaxing in a rocky tide pool on June 19.

“Back then he was wary and rarely came close,” recalls Feng Zhi, who runs a guesthouse on the island. “He’d just hang around, and if someone walked over, he’d swim away.”

But that changed the more he interacted with tourists. “Wherever the crowd was thickest, that’s where he’d be,” says Li Ai, who also works in the hospitality industry. “But he can be picky about people,” she adds, explaining that Nana appeared especially fond of a wetsuit-wearing livestreamer known as “Man in Black,” who has 24,000 followers on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok. Nana often chased him and snuggled up to him.

Zhou Long, another guesthouse manager, says Nana once squeezed in between him and several friends as they stood in the shallows. The seal was warm, slippery, and plump, “like a balloon that’s about to pop,” he says.

People soon began feeding Nana fish and petting him when he got close. A local boat captain says he often tried stopping tourists from doing this, but few listened. He worried Nana might accidentally be fed a fish containing a fishhook, “the consequences of which don’t bear thinking about.”

Some people were even captured on surveillance cameras throwing Nana barbecued meat, bread, and potato chips, foods that could seriously upset his digestive system, while others kicked him, and thoughtless children threw stones at him.

“I couldn’t bear to watch and couldn’t do anything about it. I could only turn around and walk away,” says Li.

Many locals breathed a sigh of relief on Sept. 7 when the authorities finally arrived to take Nana away.

Gone, but not forgotten

To protect and “re-wild” Nana, the Changhai County government, which administers Dachangshan Island, decided to again transport the seal out to the Yellow Sea, this time to a spot about 140 kilometers away by boat.

Nana was back on the island just six days later. His tracking tag had fallen off a month earlier, but Tian Jiashen, director of marine rare animal conservation research at the Liaoning institute, estimates the seal’s return journey must have covered at least 200 kilometers.

Zhou had an inkling he’d not seen the last of Nana. Social media users had been eagerly sharing news of sightings, and the seal was getting closer all the time. On the evening of Sept. 13, Zhou went to the shore, opened a livestream, and lay in wait, with nearly 200 followers logging on to watch.

As night fell, Zhou heard a splash, like “a huge creature leaping into the water.” When he ran over, Nana was beside the blue pontoon bridge that he’d frequented all summer.

Within hours, Lin Gao, an employee at a beachside water sports center, had reinstalled the giant inflatable yellow duck Nana had liked to sleep on. “We couldn’t let him come back and find it gone,” he says, adding that work had felt “hollow” without Nana around.

Tian admits he never expected the seal to return but now believes Nana’s interactions with tourists might have reawakened his memories of being rescued and fed by humans.

Staff at the Liaoning institute recall that Nana was initially more curious than cautious. Marine researcher Chen Yanyu says he was once scrubbing the rearing pool when Nana surprisingly pushed a long-handled brush toward his hand. He badly wanted to pat the seal’s head, but that would be against the rules of “rehab and release.”

In wildlife conservation, keeping a safe distance is paramount. Rescued seals are fed by pouring live fish into the pool, while researchers deliberately approach the animals with nets to condition them to avoid people. By the time of his release, Nana had begun watching the staff from afar.

On that first release day, Chen watched Nana slide down the boat’s ramp into the sea with tears in his eyes.

However, when the seal became a celebrity, the institute came under attack from netizens who felt it had failed in its responsibilities to rehabilitate Nana.

Tian, who has worked there since 2010, believes the criticism was unfair. He explained that the institute is manned year-round by researchers who volunteer their time for free, and that in the past two decades it has helped rescue 244 spotted seals, releasing 223.

“The sea is his home, and he should go home,” he adds, talking about Nana. “Keeping him here, in a human environment — that would be cruelty.”

The risks human behaviors pose to wildlife are obvious. Ah Nong, a spotted seal rescued late last year after spending 15 months in waters off Wenchang, in the southern island province of Hainan, was found to have diarrhea, elevated liver function, and ultraviolet skin burns from being fed, touched, and photographed by tourists.

When Nana returned a second time, Chai and some colleagues wanted to go see him, “to find out whether he still remembered us.” Others, like researcher Shi Hongyue, held another wish: that one day they would come across Nana naturally during a survey of a wild colony.

Sealing his fate?

Nana became even more famous after returning to Dachangshan Island last month. By 7 a.m., at least 10 livestreamers would already be set up on shore, waiting for the seal to wake up. These channels quickly became a key marketing tool for guesthouses and other local businesses.

In August, Chinese media quoted an unnamed local official as saying that authorities “would not use (Nana) for cultural tourism promotions.” However, that attitude appeared to shift after the seal’s return in September.

The Changhai Culture and Tourism Bureau opened the “Nana Line” on Sept. 25, and beachside stalls hawking Nana-themed merch began popping up this month.

More warning signs and loudspeakers have been placed along the beach, reminding tourists that feeding protected species is forbidden, while enforcement officers and volunteers now regularly patrol the area. The local government has announced it will not attempt to move Nana again and is planning to build him a shelter on the pontoon bridge, away from the crowds.

Residents say the feeding and touching has declined, but it still happens.

This will naturally trail off as the tourist and fishing seasons wind down ahead of the coldest months, leading some to worry that Nana could starve. Despite the rules, in October, Sun Zongjun, the owner of the water sports center, pledged on a livestream that “we’ll definitely keep feeding him when it gets cold.” The county government has yet to confirm whether live fish stocks will be provided for the seal over winter.

Tian says it’s hard to predict whether Nana will ever leave and fully return to nature; it depends on diverse factors like water temperature, his physiological state, and whether he meets any companions and joins a new colony.

Scientific studies using tracking data show that spotted seals tend to rest or breed in the same place, year after year. Tian believes this behavior, and his memories of human interaction, could be what led Nana back to Dachangshan Island.

While most locals were happy to welcome Nana “home,” his presence has also brought pressure. “Our island lives off tourism. If anything happens to him, the criticism of millions of people could crash down on us in an instant,” says Lin, who regularly volunteers to patrol the pontoon bridge in the early hours.

On most nights, Nana can be found sleeping soundly on his giant yellow duck as it rocks gently in the waves. Soon, he will be joined in these waters by other spotted seals. No one knows what will come next.

“It’s fine if Nana stays,” says Liu Yi, a guesthouse owner on the island. “But I still hope he leaves.”

(Due to privacy concerns, Lin Gao, Feng Zhi, Li Ai, Zhou Long, and Liu Yi are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Qin Bing and Feng Haoni.

A version of this article originally appeared in The Beijing News. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: PaperBuddy; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Nana comes ashore at Dachangshan Island, Liaoning, Sept. 27, 2026. From Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019137/Over 150 Chinese Apps Deny AI Assistant’s Use on Smartphone
World.title: Over 150 Chinese Apps Deny AI Assistant’s Use on Smartphone
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019137/Over 150 Chinese Apps Deny AI Assistant’s Use on Smartphone
World.content:
More than 150 Chinese apps have forbidden ByteDance’s mobile AI assistant Doubao from operating them on smartphone manufacturer Nubia Technology’s newly released agentic AI smartphone.

In a list published Oct. 14 on Doubao’s official account on messaging app WeChat, its developers identified dozens of apps that prohibit its graphical user interface (GUI) automation. The technology interprets a user’s spoken command, reads what is displayed on their smartphone’s screen, and navigates across and operates apps to complete the task.

Doubao had released its Smart Assistant Execution Protocol on Sept. 14, giving developers one month to decide whether to let the assistant operate their apps.

Apps owned by ByteDance’s rival technology companies Tencent and Alibaba make up nearly 60% of the list, including WeChat from the former and digital payment system Alipay from the latter, according to domestic media outlet Cailian Press. Others include those from e-commerce giant Meituan, ride-hailing platform Didi, lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, e-commerce platform Pinduoduo, China’s three state-run telecommunications carriers, several banks, and rival AI apps DeepSeek and Kimi. The listed apps can still be installed and used manually.

Absent from the list are e-commerce giant JD.com and most apps from internet service company Baidu, with the exception of Baidu Maps. A Baidu employee told domestic media outlet Caijing magazine that the phone’s shipment volume remains too small to pose a meaningful concern for the company.

Nubia bills the NaviX Ultra as “the world’s first AI-powered smartphone,” bringing agentic AI to consumers. The company, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, said that within seconds of the smartphone’s Sept. 16 launch, it generated 100 million yuan ($15 million) in sales. The phone’s price starts at 5,999 yuan.

Nubia released a prototype of the current AI phone, the M153, for 3,499 yuan in December last year. Though it quickly sold out, users soon reported that whenever the assistant attempted to operate WeChat, they were automatically logged out of the app. Doubao’s developers later disabled the assistant’s ability to operate the super app.

On the same day Doubao published the list of restricted apps, Nubia announced a software update — including improved localized data search, call-recording summaries, and call screening functions — and offered users six months of free Doubao membership, worth roughly 400 yuan.

As of Monday, none of the included app developers have commented publicly on the news.

Liu Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University’s Institute for National Strategic Studies, told Cailian Press that China has no regulations relating to how AI agents operate third-party applications.

Given the lack of oversight, Liu said, it is understandable that developers would deny such access over data security and user privacy concerns. He added that their resistance may also reflect a desire to protect their own AI ecosystems, particularly given Doubao’s already vast user base.

In its post, Doubao’s developers stated that other apps can opt out of its GUI technology at any time, and its list of cooperating companies would be updated every Wednesday.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019133/Duolingo Launches Shanghainese Lessons, Its 2nd Chinese Dialect
World.title: Duolingo Launches Shanghainese Lessons, Its 2nd Chinese Dialect
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019133/Duolingo Launches Shanghainese Lessons, Its 2nd Chinese Dialect
World.content:
SHANGHAI – Popular language-learning app Duolingo has released a Shanghainese course featuring lessons on modern culture and life in old Shanghai as well as offline activities in the city.

The course, launched Thursday, features roughly 50 lessons drawn from everyday life in Shanghai, from ordering street food and taking public transit to exchanging greetings and navigating the city’s landmarks. To access the Shanghainese course, users must first set Chinese as their display language.

Founded in the U.S. in 2011, Duolingo offers courses in over 40 languages. The launch of the company’s Shanghainese course marks its second Chinese dialect offering, following Cantonese released in 2022. China is the company’s fastest-growing and second-largest market.

The course revolves around aspects of modern life in Shanghai like workplace dynamics and coffee culture, while also featuring old Shanghai themes, such as life in the city’s longtang lane houses and local phrases for traditional games, Tan Xiuting, a senior course designer of Duolingo, told Sixth Tone at the launch event in Shanghai on Friday.

Lessons also extend beyond the screen, with offline check-in spots around Shanghai, as well as themed activities on buses and in subway stations. Duolingo has also partnered with local shops; for example, if a user orders a coffee in Shanghainese at a partner café, they will receive a gift.

Wang Chen, an official with Duolingo, said that the course underscores the company’s “long-term commitment” to the Chinese market and its linguistic diversity.

“We want to make dialects cool and help local language and culture stay alive in contemporary life through products that are digital, engaging, and easy to access,” Wang said.

Shanghainese, or the Hu dialect, is a Wu Chinese variety spoken by roughly 10 million people, primarily in Shanghai and the surrounding Yangtze River Delta region. Difficult for native Mandarin speakers to understand, it features more tones and numerous English and French loanwords due to the city’s opening as a treaty port in the mid-19th century. It also preserves many classical Chinese words and structures.

The dialect has declined in recent decades, as national policies have pushed Mandarin use in schools, workplaces, and the media. In the last decade, Shanghai has reintroduced Shanghainese in some kindergartens and on public transportation, and has held speech competitions to inspire younger generations to learn it. TV programs, films, music, and standup comedy shows in Shanghainese have also emerged in recent years.

Zhou Yuwen, a 30-year-old branding manager born and raised in Shanghai, told Sixth Tone that her generation was expected to speak Mandarin both inside and outside the classroom, but over time, Shanghainese-speaking environments decreased.

“I can understand Shanghainese, but when I try to speak it, it comes out so ‘Yangjingbang’ that I feel too embarrassed to keep going,” she said, referencing the colloquial name for the pidgin English used between European and local merchants in Shanghai in the 19th century.

Zhou said she felt “excited” by the release of Duolingo’s Shanghainese course, and shared news of the course’s launch on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, hoping to encourage others to learn. “It’s a pity that someone like me, who was born, grew up, and worked my whole life in Shanghai, can’t speak proper Shanghainese,” she said. “I absolutely love the dialect, and I hope to see it not just preserved, but truly flourish.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Xiaohongshu, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019128/In China, an AI Idol’s ‘Maternity Leave’ Backfires on Her Creators
World.title: In China, an AI Idol’s ‘Maternity Leave’ Backfires on Her Creators
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019128/In China, an AI Idol’s ‘Maternity Leave’ Backfires on Her Creators
World.content:
“I’m pregnant. After much consideration and thorough discussions with the company and my bandmates, I have decided to temporarily leave the group to focus on rest and recovery,” reads a statement signed by Mity, one of five members of the new girl group BABYQUEEN, alongside a selfie of her wearing pink pajamas in bed.

At first glance, nothing seems out of the ordinary, except that she and the entire BABYQUEEN pop group are AI-generated.

The announcement, published Tuesday on the group’s official Xiaohongshu account, also known as RedNote, has drawn criticism for turning women’s reproductive health into entertainment, as well as jokes and incredulity about the situation’s perceived absurdity.

AI girl group accounts have proliferated on Chinese social media in recent months, with virtual idols often maintaining social media accounts where they share glimpses of their daily lives and even secure and promote brand endorsements.

BABYQUEEN, styled as a South Korean girl group, launched its Xiaohongshu account on Sept. 7. As of Friday, the account, whose IP address is located in China’s northeastern Liaoning province, has roughly 1,000 followers.

Mity’s pregnancy was initially announced on the group’s account the day before, reading, “To prioritize her health during pregnancy and prepare for childbirth, she will temporarily suspend all group and individual variety show appearances and stage performances after thorough discussions with the team.” It also urged followers not to “over-speculate about her private life.”

Since it went viral on social media, the topic has attracted more than 6 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Friday.

Many users have expressed astonishment. “AI group members can get pregnant now? I don’t understand the virtual world anymore,” one highly upvoted comment reads. Others joked that the group’s creators might be running short on tokens, implying they had to let one member go because they lacked the computing power.

Users also accused the band’s makers of using the story for views while showing little respect for women. “Using ‘pregnant and preparing for childbirth’ as a marketing hook and a sensationalized narrative trivializes real women’s reproductive experiences by turning them into entertainment,” one comment reads.

The day of the announcement, the account also released a teaser post for a new song performed by the group’s four remaining members.

In a since-deleted Tuesday post on the BABYQUEEN account, the group’s creators cited pressures of running the group as the reason for the pregnancy announcement.

“We’re just a few girls who like K-Pop, and we’re still students,” they wrote, adding that they had “not earned a single cent” from the endeavor. They also said they had experienced personal attacks and online harassment.

On the group’s official parent account, BABYPVSSY Entertainment, the creators said Mity might next “explore two possible career paths: acting or becoming a maternity and infant content creator.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Xiaohongshu, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019132/The Northeast Chinese Meme That Found a Second Life as a Video Game
World.title: The Northeast Chinese Meme That Found a Second Life as a Video Game
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019132/The Northeast Chinese Meme That Found a Second Life as a Video Game
World.content:
In 2016, two groups of Chinese livestreamers began feuding on Kuaishou, a short-video platform popular in China’s countryside and lower-tier cities. Their leaders, Brother Hu and Captain Shamate, were both grassroots streamers from Northeast China, or Dongbei. Video after video, they traded insults, accusations, and challenges. These gang-style exchanges were loud, theatrical, and unmistakably regional, full of Northeastern Chinese dialects, bravado, and the kind of chaos that early Chinese livestreaming platforms thrived on.

The feud was widely believed to be staged, a scripted collaboration designed for dramatic effect. But that did little to diminish its appeal. Audiences couldn’t stop watching, and clips of the confrontations soon took on a life of their own. Over time, they spawned an influential body of memes that spread across various media, even video games, one of which has now become an unlikely hit on Steam.

The phenomenon emerged against the backdrop of Dongbei’s changing cultural identity. Once the heartland of China’s heavy industry, the region is often referred to as the country’s Rust Belt after decades of industrial decline. Locals have turned that history into both tragedy and comedy. TV dramas such as “The Long Season” have tapped into nostalgia for the region’s industrial heyday, helping make the “Dongbei Renaissance” a cultural buzzword. Northeasterners have long played an outsized role in Chinese comedy. On television, Zhao Benshan’s sketches made the Northeastern accent familiar to audiences nationwide; on Kuaishou, Northeastern dialects and slang became a rich source of humor and memes.

It was in this context that the feud between Brother Hu and Captain Shamate gained traction. Fans recorded and reposted clips to streaming site Bilibili, where they were remixed, quoted, and jokingly treated as “classics.” The saga became known as “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei.”

Seven years later, those memes were turned into a video game. A Summer in Northeast China (DongBeiZhiXia), released for free on Steam on Jan. 9, 2023, was developed and published by Zhuangbuchun Studio, led by Zhuangbuchun, a Bilibili content creator with over 2 million followers. Up till today, the game has since accumulated more than 12,000 positive reviews on Steam, earning an “Overwhelmingly Positive” rating despite being available only in Simplified and Traditional Chinese. Its success shows just how far a regional internet joke can travel when platform dynamics, an existing fan community, and a developer’s instincts align at the right moment.

A Summer in Northeast China is a “gal game,” a genre typically centered on interactions with female characters. Set years after the original Kuaishou incidents, the game follows Xiaoliang, who must recover her memories with the help of a cast of female companions, each loosely inspired by figures from the “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei” phenomenon. The game’s most conspicuous adaptation is its gender-swapping: the male roles at the center of the original memes are reimagined as women, retaining their names, signature visual traits, and personalities while being reshaped to fit the conventions of the gal game and ACGN (anime, comics, games, and novels) aesthetics.

In effect, the game translates its source material across cultural registers. “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei” ran on masculine confrontation, local bravado, and the rough-edged authenticity of Kuaishou livestreaming. A Summer in Northeast China recasts that material through the softer, character-driven lens of the gal game, while keeping enough recognizable references to reward those who remember the source. Events from the original memes return as callbacks for longtime fans, while the first-person linear narrative gives newcomers an accessible way into Xiaoliang’s story.

The game also draws on subcultures Zhuangbuchun knows well, including shamate — a Chinese youth subculture known for its flamboyant hairstyles and fashion — and otaku — intense fandom of anime, manga, games, and related media, originating in Japan — while its use of Northeastern dialect keeps it rooted in Dongbei. Together, these influences reflect the game’s broader approach: combining distinctly Northeastern humor and internet culture with the appeal of manga and anime.

Zhuangbuchun made the game the way many Chinese indie developers do: on a limited budget and in public. The project was self-funded, with a crowdfunding campaign on domestic creator-sponsorship platform Afdian covering part of the cost. He handled much of the design and direction himself, outsourced some work, and recruited voice actors for the female cast.

But developing the game in public was not simply a funding strategy. It also became central to how Zhuangbuchun built an audience around the project. Nearly a year before the game’s launch, in April 2022, he posted a video announcing his gender-swapped take on “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei.” The video received over 1.5 million views, 71,000 likes, 23,000 saves, and 11,000 reposts.

From there, Zhuangbuchun kept followers closely involved in development. He posted early character designs, solicited feedback on voice acting, and explained delays. When viewers complained about an accent or suggested a different look, he listened and sometimes changed the game accordingly. In that sense, the project was not simply marketed to its eventual players. It was partly shaped by them.

Zhuangbuchun also visited Shenyang, the capital of the northeastern Liaoning province, several times to document where the original Kuaishou events took place. On one return trip after the game’s release, he even ran into some of its fans. These travel vlogs reinforced the sense that the game was being made by someone invested not only in the memes but also in the places and culture from which they emerged.

The steady updates kept the project visible on Bilibili and positioned Zhuangbuchun as part of the internet culture that turned the original Kuaishou videos into “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei.” His existing followers helped attract attention, while the project’s local roots kept audiences engaged. The original Kuaishou streamers added another layer to this relationship, posting reaction videos and engaging with Zhuangbuchun’s posts, further blurring the line between the game and the people who inspired it.

A Summer in Northeast China is neither the first game to adapt internet memes nor the first to blend Chinese regional culture with global subcultural aesthetics. What makes it unusual is the particular combination: a free gal game with a gender-swapped cast, a distinctly Northeastern setting, a developer who was already a prominent Bilibili creator, and source material rooted in the unruly world of early Kuaishou livestreaming.

For indie developers working with limited resources, A Summer in Northeast China offers a distinctive example of how online culture can move across platforms and media. The same platforms that provided the game with its source material also supplied an audience, feedback, publicity, and a community willing to participate in its development. Rather than simply adapting an existing meme, Zhuangbuchun used the participatory culture surrounding it to carry the material far beyond its origins.

That process creates tensions between local authenticity and internet marketability, and between the crude energy of the original memes and the game’s polished presentation. Yet, A Summer in Northeast China never loses sight of its regional origins. Zhuangbuchun, who has told me he loves Dongbei despite not being from the region, is part of that story: an outsider drawn into its culture who now helps reshape it for new audiences. The game has traveled from Kuaishou to Bilibili to Steam, changing along the way. But for all the distance it has traveled, it has never really left Northeast China.

Zhu Siheng, a Ph.D. candidate at the University of Rochester, and Han Yisong, a postdoctoral researcher at the City University of Hong Kong, also made contributions to this research.

(Header image: Promotional art for the video game “A Summer in Northeast China” on Steam.)

World.title: [DECODED] You no longer have to click anything to be targeted. But you can fight back.
World.content:
With today's technological advances, malicious actors have found a way to get consumer data without you clicking on anything

Remember when the Cambridge Analytica scandal blew up in 2018? It’s the data harvesting scandal that took place around 2014, where Cambridge Analytica had improperly accessed — and sold — the data of Facebook users to target them for political campaigns. Cambridge Analytica was a British political consultancy that worked for Donald Trump’s 2016 election campaign.

Facebook later reported that Cambridge Analytica had harvested personal data of over 87 million users, over 1.1 million of which were Filipinos. The data obtained included users’ phone numbers and contact lists, which allowed them to target not just the users who fell prey to the operations, but also their contacts who weren’t necessarily on their Facebook network.

How did they do it? Well, they had to be creative. They used those viral personality quizzes that tricked users into sharing details about themselves, perhaps convincing them that it was all in good fun. In reality, the firm used these details to profile, segment, and micro-target them for political campaigns.

Targeted advertising has been found to create isolation and division among consumers by limiting their exposure to diverse viewpoints and feedback — hence reinforcing what we now call “echo chambers.”

That happened over a decade ago. So much has changed in our information landscape since then, and malicious actors have gained other tools beyond social media platforms.

What if I told you that, with today’s technological advances, malicious actors have found a way to get consumer data without you clicking on anything?

READ: Israeli firm used online ads to run vast spy operation, researchers say

Just last week, reports said that an Israeli digital advertising agency called Discover-Tech gave access to Candiru, a spyware company blacklisted by the US government, to advertising platforms run by Google, Comcast, and Russia’s Yandex. By doing so, Candiru was able to spy on internet users through a wide network of online ads, which only needed to load on the user’s side for the spying to occur. No clicks needed!

Two research groups, Citizen Lab and Confiant, separately investigated Discover-Tech and said that it utilized its data-sharing arrangements called cookie matching to track people. The researchers also said that some of its ads were used to help “plant spyware” on users’ devices.

Granted, the researchers said that the ads they found to be tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of Discover-Tech’s overall volume. But the point stays the same: unlike the Cambridge Analytica scandal where users had to be coaxed into taking quizzes, there is now evidence that users don’t even have to do anything to be targeted by malicious actors. Simply being served an ad could be enough to compromise their personal details.

You might think that this is a problem for other countries, not for the Philippines. But recall that Cambridge Analytica had used the Philippines as a “petri dish” to test out its strategies before rolling it out to Western countries, thanks to our high social media usage and lack of regulation.

If you find this scary or at least alarming (like I do), Nobel Peace Prize laureate and Rappler CEO Maria Ressa’s new book, The Fight Back: A Citizen’s Guide to Standing Up to Dictators, is a good place to start.

READ: From Duterte to Big Tech: Maria Ressa’s blueprint on fighting back

In The Fight Back, Maria draws on her years on the frontlines against disinformation and Big Tech overreach and discusses in detail what citizens and institutions can do to understand, defend, and rebuild democracy in the age of AI.

She lays out 10 strategic goals across 10 chapters, each broken down into 10 concrete actions, to help people reclaim control over the technologies now shaping our lives — from mapping the battlefield and defending our communities to building a world where technology works for the people, not against us.

Maria discussed these and more in a conversation with WNYC’s Brian Lehrer for the second edition of Democracy Dialogues on October 16. You can watch Maria’s full interview here.

I hope this newsletter spooked you enough to take a more active role in protecting your own data and digital life. October, after all, is not only about Halloween. October is also cybersecurity awareness month. – Rappler.com

World.title: Theater veteran Enchang Kaimo dies at 77
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – Theater veteran Enchang Kaimo died on Monday, October 19, her husband, Mari Kaimo confirmed. She was 77.

“On this month 45 years ago, God brought me the helper who would be suitable for me. Today, He took her back unto Himself,” the actor and journalist wrote in a Facebook post.



“She rests now in His embrace and is fully free of the chains that bind us all. I look forward to the day that we are reunited once again when our Christ returns!” he added.

Enchang, whose full name is Maria Lorenza Dominguez Agudo-Kaimo, co-founded the Christian theater company Trumpets alongside Mari, Audie Gemora, Freddie Santos, and Luna Inocian in 1991. The group has produced plays and musicals like Joseph the Dreamer, The Lion, The Witch, and The Wardrobe, and The Little Mermaid, to name a few.

The theater great spent most of her theater career as an actress and a director. She helped bring to life the children’s musical Kings, Dreams & Schemes, and also performed in several musicals like Hairspray as the Female Authority Figure, The Wedding Singer as Rosie, and First Name Anew as Amy.

“Our dear Achi Enchang is now resting in perfect peace and rejoicing in the arms of her Lord & Savior. Chancel Rep has one less light, but heaven is rejoicing today,” Chancel Repertory Theatre wrote in its tribute to her.

Enchang is survived by her husband and their son, Khalil.

Her wake will be held on October 21 and 22 from 2 pm to 9 pm at the Lighthouse Christian Community, Buencamino Street, Barangay Cupang, Muntinlupa City. – Rappler.com

World.title: Cyber agency warns websites may go dark as PHP prepares critical fix
World.content:
EU CYEBRSECURITY. A hand is seen on a laptop with binary codes displayed in front of the EU flag in this illustration taken, August 19, 2022.

(1st UPDATE) PHP is used across large parts of the internet, and speculation has circulated over the past day that websites running the software could be exposed to serious cyber intrusions

The developers of the widely used PHP programming language said on Wednesday, October 21, they would release patches for two critical vulnerabilities, as EU cybersecurity officials warned organisations unable to apply the fixes should take affected websites offline.

PHP is used across large parts of the internet, and speculation has circulated over the past day that websites running the software could be exposed to serious cyber intrusions.

“PHP is everywhere. It quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful lot of software that doesn’t even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood,” cybersecurity company Huntress said in a blog post.

In a security update, PHP said both vulnerabilities were rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 severity scale and urged users to “upgrade as soon as the release is available”.

It said a patch for both vulnerabilities was scheduled for 1400 GMT (10:00 pm, Philippine time) on Wednesday.

Dane Knecht, the chief technology officer of Web and cloud security firm Cloudflare, said that attacks were emerging and Cloudflare was updating its firewall rules as a stopgap measure.

“We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up. This is a STOPGAP only. Patch as soon as PHP releases the update,” he said on X.

The European Union Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said on Tuesday in an advisory that the 9.2 rating indicated a risk of unauthenticated remote code execution, a type of flaw that can allow attackers to run malicious code on vulnerable systems without logging in.

CERT-EU urged organisations to prepare for the immediate patching of affected assets and said those unable to do so should consider taking affected sites offline.

The Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC) issued similar guidance, urging organisations to identify PHP systems in their environments, prepare to apply patches and monitor applications for signs of malicious activity.

“ACSC is currently not aware of active exploitation related to these vulnerabilities,” the agency said.

Web hosting provider GoDaddy said the flaws could allow attackers to execute code on affected servers over the internet, potentially leading to data theft, website defacement or full system compromise.

PHP’s security team said details of the vulnerabilities, affected versions and the fixed releases would be published when patches are issued.

CERT-EU and the ACSC said all PHP versions from PHP 5 onward could be affected, although PHP has not disclosed which versions are vulnerable. – Rappler.com

World.title: #ScamAlert chat room launched as digital and financial scams evolve
World.content:
LAGUNA, Philippines – Iza Estinopo, a local resident of San Pedro, recalled a 5 am call from her mother, a senior citizen. Her mother said a friend had sent P3,000 and immediately got P25,000 back. She was sure it was real because she had been chatting with that friend on Facebook.

Her mother pressed Estinopo to send funds through GCash, which Estinopo did not have in her account. An hour later, her mother called again. The friend’s Facebook account had been hacked.

“Buti na lang napigilan siya at saka hindi pa siya marunong mag-GCash that time,” Estinopo said.

(Good thing we stopped her, and she didn’t know how to use GCash yet back then.)

Stories like hers took center stage on Monday, October 19, at #ScamAlert Laguna, a forum that drew nearly 200 people, from senior citizens and students to barangay workers, to the Pacita Astrodome in San Pedro. The event called attention to a rise in digital and financial scams, and gave attendees tactics and resources to stay vigilant and protected.

The afternoon was hallmarked by attendees joining and engaging in Rappler’s new chat room, #ScamAlert, housed in Muni, a community-building platform found on Rappler’s free app.

During the forum, participants and organizers used the chat room to swap personal scam stories, takeaways and resources to become scam-proof.

LAUNCH. Rappler’s head of civiv engagement Jene Pangue introduced “ScamAlert Chat Room”on Muni in San Pedro City, Laguna on October 19, 2026. The launch is supported by DILG Laguna, the City Government of San Pedro and SmartCT as the platform enables community members to report scams and receive guidance on handling incidents. Photo by Jake GomezRappler

Although the chat room was initially launched on-ground in San Pedro, Laguna, the space allows users to connect directly with authorities and fact-checkers, sharing screenshots to verify scam threats or learn about scammers’ latest methods to enforce community vigilance. It can be used by other individuals and groups in other areas as well.

A multi-sector response

The afternoon brought together partners across sectors to raise awareness around digital safety. Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH joined SmartCT, the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) Laguna, and the City Government of San Pedro in organizing the event.

The convening was also part of Scam Ready ASEAN, a regional program implemented by the ASEAN Foundation with support from Google.org to build resilience and awareness among communities against online scams and fraud.

It also builds on MovePH’s ongoing #ScamAlert campaign launched in 2025, which has brought digital safety and scam prevention roadshows to various communities across the Philippines, including previous stops in Laguna and Manila.

“Events like this serve as the starting point for bringing together these types of stakeholders,” said Jay Beltran, Laguna Provincial Director of DILG.

AUDIENCE. Participants download and play SmartCT’s ‘Be Scam Ready’ gameplay experience, which walks through real-life digital scams citizens may face today. Photo by Jake Gomez/Rappler.

New landscape, new threats

When SmartCT executive director Kris Libunao asked the room whether anyone had been scammed, dozens of attendees raised their hands.

Stories like Estinopo’s are why Libunao warns that no one is immune.

“Even if you are a tech person, even if you are an educated person, you can still be scammed dahil hindi ito naaayon sa inyong kaalaman, but sa emotions niyo,” Libunao said. (Even if you are a tech person, even if you are an educated person, you can still be scammed because it doesn’t depend on your knowledge, but on your emotions.)

Gemma Mendoza, Rappler’s head of strategic programs, walked attendees through how integrated the internet is in Filipinos’ daily lives, and how the current-day digital landscape allows scams to thrive.

“Hindi lang important na masaya tayo sa digital. Napaka-importante na maingat din tayo sa digital,” she said. (It’s not enough that we enjoy being online. It’s very important that we’re also careful online.)

During her presentation, Mendoza showed a deepfake video of Rappler CEO Maria Ressa spreading fraudulent claims about cures for diabetes, then broke down the digital forensics of the video. While her mouth, which did not match her speech, gave away the doctored video – the voice actually sounded like Ressa’s.

Digital scams, from phishing attempts to identity fraud, are already a mainstay of modern life, but artificial intelligence tools, like voice cloning, are rapidly scaling the number of scams, and the variety.

“Hindi lang nagbibigay ng impormasyon ang AI sa atin kundi, kumukuha rin ito ng impormasyon sa atin,” Mendoza said. “Kailangan maging maingat tayo sa pagshare ng impormasyon online.”

(“AI doesn’t just provide us with information, it also collects information from us,” Mendoza said. “We need to be careful when sharing information online.”)

CONTEXT. Rappler’s head of strategic programs Gemma Mendoza walks attendees through today’s modern scam landscape, and AI’s role in creating and spreading false information. Photo by Jake Gomez/Rappler



But some threats seek to make everyday Filipinos complicit in crimes, warned lawyer Marco Mendoza of the Consumer Account Protection Office under the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP).

Scammers are now recruiting money mules – people who let criminals use their bank or e-wallet accounts to receive and move illicit funds – often for as little as P400 to P500, he said.

“Ang nagiging ano kasi nila approach nila ngayon is nag-re-recruit sila on a massive scale…. Tapos ‘yung mga nagbebenta, nagpahiram na ‘yon, hindi nila alam most of the time kung saan gagamitin ‘yung financial accounts nila,” Marco Mendoza said.

(Their approach now is to recruit on a massive scale…. And those who sold or lent [their accounts], most of the time, don’t know where their financial accounts will be used.)

Once a victim’s money lands in a mule account, scammers rarely leave it there. They “layer” the funds, splitting them and moving them across sprawling networks of accounts to make them harder for law enforcement to trace.

Under the Anti-Financial Account Scamming Act (AFSA), acting as a money mule is punishable by law.

Simulating the scam landscape

Clarence dela Cruz, project officer at SmartCT, led participants through the organization’s Be Scam Ready gameplay, which simulated some of the scams Filipinos may face in their everyday lives.

Testing the audience, Dela Cruz displayed fake texts and emails from claimed legitimate entities like government agencies and banks, breaking down the tell-tale signs of a scam message.

Libunao said the game is backed by behavioral science, and that training that simulates scams is key to understanding and preparing for the real thing.

“In the event of a fire drill, not an actual fire, we go over what we should do during an emergency,” she said. “If you play [the game] from your own perspective, you will actually see how you can become scam-ready.”

Knowing how to protect yourself

Mendoza of the BSP shared with the crowd how Filipinos can protect themselves, especially as consumers.

“Whenever you are conducting financial transactions or managing your financial accounts, take a second or two, pause for a moment… Use those two seconds to consider: what is the right course of action? Should I really click this? Do I need to provide this information, or should I verify it with my bank first?” Mendoza said in a mix of English and Filipino.

He stressed that one-time passwords or PINs (OTPs) and other sensitive personal information should never be shared with anyone.

Scam victims can dial 1326 to reach the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center, where they can report the incident and get assistance.

Individuals and institutions committed in fighting digital fraud can also join the #ScamAlert chat room for free. – Rappler.com

World.title: Malaysia bans civil servants from using mapping app Waze, citing links to Israel
World.content:
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim recommends the use of TuJu, a domestic mapping app developed by the Malaysian Highway Authority, as an alternative

KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia – Malaysia has banned civil servants from using Alphabet’s navigation app Waze after Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said its origins in Israel raised security concerns.

Muslim-majority Malaysia is a staunch supporter of the Palestinian ​cause and does not maintain diplomatic relations with Israel.

Anwar said on Tuesday, October 20, that the government was looking into potential security risks arising from the use of Waze, which he said “was bound to Israeli laws.”

“We cannot compromise on the security of people’s data and identities,” he said in a Facebook post after chairing a national cybersecurity committee meeting.

Anwar did not provide any details of the risks but recommended the use of TuJu, a domestic mapping app developed by the Malaysian Highway Authority, as an alternative.

Malaysia’s Chief Secretary to the Government Shamsul Azri Abu Bakar said all civil servants would now be barred from using Waze, according to a letter dated Tuesday and addressed to the heads of government agencies.

The letter, reviewed by Reuters, said the directive followed a decision taken at the meeting chaired by Anwar, with the prohibition to take effect immediately.

An official with the Prime Minister’s Department confirmed the letter’s authenticity.

Waze, which was founded in Israel, uses satellite signals and crowd-sourced data from drivers to offer real-time traffic information. It was acquired by Alphabet-owned Google in 2013 for about $1 billion. – Rappler.com

World.title: De Lima, Diokno, 8 other House lawmakers want China envoy recalled
World.content:
The lawmakers say the President must 'take decisive action in response to statements and conduct that undermine national sovereignty and threaten the country's security'

MANILA, Philippines – Ten House lawmakers filed a proposed resolution urging President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to either declare Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata or ask Beijing to recall him.

House Senior Deputy Minority Leader Leila de Lima (Mamamayang Liberal) and House Assistant Minority Leader Chel Diokno (Akbayan) joined eight other lawmakers in authoring House Resolution No. 1562, filed on Wednesday, October 21.

Their move followed similar resolutions filed in the upper chamber by senators Erwin Tulfo and Risa Hontiveros.

Other lawmakers who signed the House resolution are:

House Assistant Majority Leader and Lanao del Sur 1st District Representative Zia Adiong

House Assistant Majority Leader and Las Pinas Representative Mark Santos

Zamboanga del Norte 3rd District Representative Adrian Michael Amatong

Pinoy Workers Representative Karl Legazpi

House Deputy Minority Leader and Akbayan Representative Perci Cendana

House Deputy Minority Leader and Dinagat Islands Representative Kaka Bag-ao

House Deputy Minority Leader and Albay 1st District Representative Krisel Lagman

Akbayan Representative Dadah Ismula

“Under the Constitution, the President, being vested with foreign power, holds primary authority to conduct foreign relations and to represent the nation in its dealings with other states, and must therefore take decisive action in response to statements and conduct that undermine national sovereignty and threaten the country’s security,” the proposed resolution read.

The lawmakers cite a number of incidents that led to the filing of the resolution, starting with Jing’s October 15 statement saying that if China wants to use force, “we may easily win.” Philippine government officials, including the President, later said the statement sounded like a threat.

The Chinese Embassy dared the Senate and the House to just declare Jing as persona non grata and “stop bluffing.” It also threatened to block Philippine officials from entering China if Jing were to be declared persona non grata.

Before the group of House lawmakers filed the resolution, they sounded the alarm over Jing’s seeming threat against the Philippines, and the Chinese embassy’s subsequent language that seemed dismissive of Filipinos’ sentiments.

“The embassy’s undiplomatic language taunting our government to declare the Chinese ambassador as persona non grata does little to encourage serious dialogue between two sovereign nations. Instead it reflects their position that our country should simply accept China’s threats and submit to its demands,” they said.

“The Philippines must not be cowed into silence in the face of such arrogance,” the lawmakers added. – Rappler.com

World.title: Musk says SpaceX-Tesla merger is ‘a good idea’ as companies form deal committees
World.content:
MUSK'S SPACEX. SpaceX's logo and an Elon Musk photo are seen in this illustration created on December 19, 2022.

'I think it would be a good idea, but it's really up to the special committees of both companies,' Elon Musk says in the first official confirmation that the companies were formally talking

Elon Musk said on Tuesday, October 20, that a merger of his two companies SpaceX and Tesla would be “a good idea” and that they had formed special committees to discuss a union, sending shares of the space and technology company up 8% in extended trading.

The company earlier posted its first profit as a public company and Musk said he expected annual recurring revenue of between $500 billion and $1 trillion by the end of 2027, as demand for its data-center space surges thanks to the AI boom.

Musk has in the past tantalized shareholders with the idea of combining SpaceX and Tesla, citing growing overlap between them. Speculation about the space company buying the EV maker has gained traction recently, with Barclays suggesting last week that a deal could be announced before Tesla’s annual meeting in December.

“I think it would be a good idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies,” Musk said in the first official confirmation that the companies were formally talking. “Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees,” which comprised independent directors, he told investors on a conference call.

The companies had formed the special committees at the request of shareholders, who ultimately would need to approve a deal, he added.

“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation, connectivity,” he said.

Terafab, the chip manufacturing joint venture between the two companies, should produce its first test chip around May or June of next year and aims to reach volume production by the third quarter of 2028, Musk said on the call.

Musk added that it would be premature to assume a SpaceX-Tesla merger would happen, noting that the special committees had not agreed on transaction terms and may never do so. Tesla shares rose 1.8% in extended trading.

The world’s richest person, Musk owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and just under half of SpaceX, and analysts have said a merger would give him control of the combined entity.

The talks started in recent weeks and could result in SpaceX acquiring Tesla, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters, who declined to be named because they were not authorized to talk to media. Tesla has been working with an investment bank to advise on the discussions, the person said.

AI revenue drives SpaceX transformation

SpaceX’s revenue climbed 161% to $14.58 billion for the three months ended September 30 from a year earlier. AI revenue surged by almost 10 times to $7.56 billion, mostly from renting out data-center capacity to developers such as Anthropic, Alphabet’s Google, and Reflection AI rather than from its own models.

The third quarter offered the clearest evidence yet that SpaceX’s heavy investment in AI is translating into revenue, even as spending on compute infrastructure remains enormous — capital expenses nearly tripled to $19.6 billion.

The shift is reshaping a company whose financial engine has long been its Starlink internet services business and whose longer-term ambitions still hinge on getting Starship rockets into regular service. For now, though, its main business looks closer to a cloud provider’s than an AI lab’s.

SpaceX’s chief financial officer, Bret Johnsen, said the company expects $35 billion to $40 billion in capital expenditure in the fourth quarter.

“SpaceX delivered the quarter the bulls wanted, at least on the top line,” said Will Rhind, CEO of asset manager GraniteShares. “The story now is all about AI. The compute contracts signed earlier this year are turning into revenue faster than a lot of people thought.”

The company’s AI business spans Grok, social media platform X, and a fast-growing data-center operation. The business also turned a profit in the third quarter, compared with a year-ago loss.

SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion versus a net loss of $1.1 billion a year earlier and analysts’ expectation for a profit of $1.57 billion. On a per-share, adjusted basis, it earned 45 cents according to IBES calculations, outstripping a 13-cent average estimate.

The satellite-internet unit has continued to expand its subscriber base, aided by additional satellite launches and a growing range of consumer, enterprise, aviation, maritime and government services.

Starlink reached 13.6 million subscribers in the third quarter, above the 12.19 million analysts expected, but growth is coming at a price: average monthly revenue per subscriber has fallen from $99 in 2023 to $69 in the third quarter as it expands abroad with cheaper plans.

The company has said geographic expansion beyond the wealthiest countries could push average revenue per user lower over time.

Starship, SpaceX’s next-generation reusable rocket system, has yet to enter commercial service. It is expected to enable deployment of higher-bandwidth Starlink satellites and orbital AI-computing infrastructure. The company’s ability to turn Starship into a reliably reusable vehicle is central to its longer-term strategy.

The space segment includes commercial launches, government missions and Starship development and remains a significant source of costs and uncertainty. – Rappler.com

World.title: Taiwan security agency flags rise in Chinese disinformation ahead of elections
World.content:
The report says Beijing seeds narratives through state media before amplifying them via troll networks and PR firms, using content farms, AI-generated videos, fake accounts and coordinated comments to sow discord among Taiwanese

TAIPEI, Taiwan – China spread more than 2.5 million pieces of disputed or false online information targeting Taiwan in the first nine months of this year, the island’s top intelligence agency said, accusing Beijing of stepping up operations ahead of local elections.

In a report to lawmakers this week, Taiwan’s National Security Bureau said such information rose by about 48% in the first nine months of 2026 to more than 2.5 million items, from more than 1.69 million a year earlier.

It said the China-originated content focused on energy, food security and defense policy, as well as the platforms and images of specific candidates, in an effort to influence Taiwan’s elections for city mayors and county magistrates in November.

China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Beijing, which views Taiwan as its own territory over the island’s objections, has previously denied interfering in Taiwanese elections or spreading disinformation.

Taiwan has repeatedly complained about what it sees as China’s “gray-zone” tactics — from daily military drills to cyberattacks — at a time when Beijing is ramping up military and political pressure to force Taipei to accept its sovereignty claims.

The report said Beijing often created narratives through official media outlets before amplifying them through “online troll armies” and public relations firms to sow discord among Taiwanese people. It said the tactics included content farms, AI-generated videos, fake accounts and coordinated comment flooding.

“China has expanded the use of AI technology to manipulate information, seeking to influence voter support and election results,” the report said.

China was using AI technology to gather information on Taiwanese current affairs, candidates’ policies and polling data to shape influence operations and expand AI-driven information manipulation aimed at “affecting voter preferences and election outcomes,” the bureau said.

It said the messages were mainly distributed on social media platforms including Facebook, Threads, YouTube and online forums.

Chinese state media have increasingly amplified Taiwanese critics of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party in an information war, including influencers and politicians linked to the opposition Kuomintang, a Reuters investigation conducted with Taipei-based research group IORG found.

Chinese cyberattacks on Taiwanese government agencies averaged 2.58 million a day in the first nine months of 2026, with detected threats surging from June and reaching 185.6 million in July and 106.4 million in August, data from the National Security Bureau showed.

“It cannot be ruled out that this was advance intelligence-gathering and harassment preparation aimed at interfering in Taiwan’s year-end ‘nine-in-one’ elections,” the report said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Thousands Flee as Regime Troops Push Into Myanmar’s Oil Hub
World.content:
Regime troops backed by airstrikes are pouring into Magwe Region’s Myaing Township as the battle for Myanmar’s oilfields escalates, forcing thousands of residents to flee.

Reinforcements from the Light Infantry Division in Pakokku, an hour to the south, are bolstering the offensive to seize territory — nicknamed “Anyar Dubai” for its oil wealth — from resistance groups.

Resistance forces have controlled the area since 2022, repelling repeated efforts to choke off their crucial revenue stream. However, a regime offensive backed by 1,000 troops gained a foothold on May 24, seizing the Well-2 oil field in Tae Gyi village.

The latest push began on October 18, when regime reinforcements arrived in Kamma town, Pakokku Township while gyrocopters bombed the nearby village of Ohntaw, killing five people, including children, and injuring four others.

On Monday, the troops arrived in Myaing’s Twinma village, controlled by regime-aligned militia, and set up camp there. According to Sayar Htwe from the Anyar Myay Civil Society Organization, up to 5,000 residents fled neighboring villages as airstrikes and troops advanced.

“We have no information on where the troops are heading, but we can assume they are reinforcements for Tae Gyi village,” Sayar Htwe told The Irrawaddy.

Regime troops suffered heavy losses in the three-month battle for Tae Gyi, where they are now encircled and entirely reliant on airdrops for ammunition and supplies.

On September 28, the regime reported that troops had seized 131 small-scale oil rigs in the area, torching some to prevent them from falling back into resistance hands.

On Monday, the Magwe resistance’s Anyar Myay Coalition urged the public to remain on high alert for airstrikes and attacks, as regime troops were mobilizing in Pakokku, Myaing and Pauk townships. It warned that regime troops camped in Tae Gyi had killed around 50 civilians and torched 600 houses since May.

World.title: Regional Body Expels Myanmar Regime’s Human Rights Fig Leaf
World.content:
The South East Asia National Human Rights Institutions Forum (SEANF), a regional umbrella group, has expelled a fig-leaf human rights body controlled by Myanmar’s military regime after it refused to cooperate with a compliance review.

SEANF on Monday said it has terminated the membership of the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission (MNHRC) because it is not an independent institution promoting and protecting human rights.

Established in 2007, SEANF now consist of just five national human rights commissions aiming to strengthen regional cooperation, from Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, the Philippines and Timor-Leste.

The decision, made on Oct. 1 and put into effect immediately, came at the 11th hour before Myanmar was to assume the umbrella group’s rotating chairmanship in 2027.

It follows a review of whether the MNHRC still met the Paris Principles standards for independence, effectiveness, and integrity, which SEANF uses to define a national human rights institution.

SEANF told the MNHRC in early September to respond, but the MNHRC refused, saying the review “did not comply with” the network’s procedural rules—a frequent fallback by the putschist regime in dealing with regional organizations of which it has fallen foul.

SEANF then decided unilaterally that the MNHRC “no longer satisfies the definition of a national human rights institution under amended Article 1 of the SEANF Rules of Procedure,” namely being independent to promote and protect human rights, it said in Monday’s statement. The decision was made in “a fair, transparent and evidence-based manner,” it added.”

The MNHRC was also kicked out of the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI) and the Asia-Pacific Forum (AFP) in 2025.

SEANF added the MNHRC can reapply for membership if it can demonstrate efforts to comply with the Paris Principles.

Established under the quasi-civilian Thein Sein administration in 2011 and once recognized as a “partially independent” body, the MNHRC went rapidly downhill when its leadership was replaced with regime loyalists after the 2021 coup.

It has since remained conspicuously silent about the regime’s glaring human rights violations while offering it a veneer of respectability and protection from scrutiny. Anecdotal evidence suggests that anyone coming to the MNHRC with a complaint could expect a knock on the door from the regime’s enforcers soon after.

Rights groups in Myanmar and beyond have long called its removal from global networks.

Prominent activist Khin Ohmar of Progressive Voice told the Irrawaddy that SEANF’s decision was “a long-awaited principled action” and “strips the criminal military junta-controlled MNHRC of regional legitimacy.”

“This decision sends a clear message that this body can no longer hide behind a SEANF membership card,” she added.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Bombs Civilians While Claiming Military Operations Serve Peace
World.content:
Framing its aerial bombardment of civilians as a peace initiative, the Myanmar regime continued aerial attacks across five regions and states over the weekend, killing over two dozen civilians.

Addressing humanitarian concerns raised in the media over the targeting of civilians, newly appointed Defense Minister Lieutenant General Yar Pyae, who is also chair of the National Solidarity and Peacemaking Negotiation Committee (NSPNC), claimed that the current military operations—a reference to the bombing of civilians in resistance-held territories—were conducted in the pursuit of peace.

He made the remark at the closing ceremony of an event marking the 11th anniversary of the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) in Naypyitaw on October 16.

At the event, the regime again called on ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) to join its purported peace talks while encouraging the People’s Defense Force (PDF), the armed wing of the civilian National Unity Government (NUG), to surrender.

Meanwhile, from October 16-18, the regime bombed civilian targets in Magwe, Sagaing and Mandalay regions and Rakhine and Chin states, killing at least 27 people and injuring 11, according to media reports.

On Friday evening, regime aircraft bombed a Starlink-based WiFi shop in Thitgyitaw Village in Yesagyo, Magwe Region. The attack on the shop, which locals rely on to bypass the regime’s restrictions and access the internet, killed at least 12, including two children aged 1 and 10, and injured two, the NUG said on Sunday.

The number of casualties was likely to increase as bomb damage was making it difficult to determine the number and identities of the dead, the NUG’s Human Rights Department said.

“This is a blatant violation of international humanitarian law and a war crime,” it said.

The operation was carried out by two Russian-made Mi-35 attack helicopters, two fighter jets from Magwe and Nyaung Oo, and two drones from the Pakokku-based No. 101 Light Infantry Division, the NUG said.

However, local media reported that at least 15 civilians were killed in the incident.

On the same day, the regime bombed Magyikan Village in Sagaing’s Myaung, injuring one.

The regime’s airstrikes continued on Sunday, as Y-12 utility aircraft bombed Arakan Army (AA)-controlled ethnic Rakhine villages in Rathedaung. Wai Hun Aung, a prominent ethnic Rakhine writer and aid worker, said five people were killed.

The regime also bombed a jetty in AA-controlled Paletwa, Chin State, on the same day, resulting in 20 casualties according to media reports, though there has been no official statement yet.

A regime drone attacked Shwebayet Village in Mandalay’s Singu Township on October 18, killing three people and injuring four women and girls, including a 5-year-old, the Singu People’s Defense Force reported on Monday.

Three regime gyrocopters bombed Ohntaw Village in Magwe’s Pakokku Township on Sunday, killing five including children and senior citizens. Local media reported that four were injured, including a 2-year-old.

At the NCA anniversary event, regime leader Min Aung Hlaing invited 2015 signatories that have been fighting the Myanmar military since the 2021 coup—the Karen National Union, Chin National Front and All Burma Students’ Democratic Front—to join his peace process. The regime demands that the PDFs surrender.

Lt-Gen Yar Pyae insisted the aerial bombing was conducted for peaceful purposes. “Some parts are military actions, while others are steps to achieve peace,” Yar Pyae said.

World.title: Detained Aung San Suu Kyi Receives UK Royal Package: Regime
World.content:
YANGON—Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi received a package from Britain’s King Charles III on Monday, authorities said, releasing the first pictures of the detained Nobel laureate in two months and describing her as a “special female prisoner.”

It is the first time Myanmar authorities have used the term to describe Aung San Suu Kyi, who was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to monitor ACLED.

The coup leader and former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April following elections that did not include Aung San Suu Kyi’s party, and she was moved to house arrest soon afterwards.

Home Ministry officials met her on Monday to deliver a package of two books about soil, “one sealed envelope, and a sealed diplomatic communication sent by King Charles III of the United Kingdom to the special female detainee,” Myanmar’s presidential spokeswoman said on her Facebook page.

Britain is Myanmar’s former colonial power and the monarch is known to have a keen interest in gardening and the environment.

Accompanying the statement were two images of Aung San Suu Kyi meeting two men with their backs to the camera.

The pictures appeared to be in a similar room to the last released images of her, when she met a Red Cross representative in August, her first publicized meeting with a foreign official since her ouster.

Fact-checkers from AFP examined the latest photos and found no evidence of manipulation using Meta Generative AI or OpenAI tools.

Aung San Suu Kyi remains detained on charges rights groups say were concocted to return power to the military, which has historically ruled Myanmar since independence.

“I have been extremely lenient toward her,” Min Aung Hlaing said in an interview with Time magazine published last month.

In response to questions from AFP, the Foreign Office in London did not say whether British diplomats had sought to deliver the package in person, or been refused permission to do so.

Britain condemns what it describes as Aung San Suu Kyi’s “arbitrary detention” and calls for her immediate and unconditional release.

World.title: Myanmar Regime’s Sittwe Counteroffensive Hits the Rocks on Nga Pyi Island
World.content:
The Myanmar military’s push to land troops on Nga Pyi Island in Rakhine State’s Pauktaw Township has suffered fresh setbacks as the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) strikes regime vessels and tightens its siege on the state capital Sittwe.

Frontline sources said AA artillery hit another navy vessel off the island on Sunday, the third to be damaged in recent days. “The boat was struck and caught fire,” a local source close to the AA confirmed. Intense clashes are raging both on and around Nga Pyi Island as regime forces continue efforts to secure a beachhead despite mounting casualties.

Sources said commanders are driving conscripts forward in near‑suicidal assaults, but few have managed to reach land.

Since Oct. 7, the military has deployed more than a dozen gunboats and landing craft backed by airstrikes and artillery from encircled Sittwe, in an effort to seize the island. The move aims to break the AA’s blockade of the Kaladan River corridor and shield the navy’s Shwe Mingan base in Sittwe, which sits on a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides.

Nga Pyi Island is a key AA stronghold, blocking regime access upriver to AA-controlled Pauktaw and Ponnagyun townships.

“Junta soldiers keep coming despite heavy casualties, but few have made it to shore,” said a source close to the AA.

Meanwhile, AA columns have seized several regime outposts elsewhere in Sittwe and are pressing toward Shwe Mingan naval base and the Sittwe Regional Operations Command.

The assault on Nga Pyi was launched as advancing AA troops threatened to encircle the military’s Sittwe stronghold. Fighting has also intensified just down the coast in Kyaukphyu Township, where AA forces are attacking outposts near Taung Maw Oo naval base.

The AA controls 14 of Rakhine State’s 17 townships along with Paletwa Township in neighboring Chin State, with the regime maintaining a foothold in Sittwe, Kyaukphyu, and the sparsely populated Manaung island.

A regime counteroffensive launched from neighboring Magwe, Bago, and Ayeyarwady regions is bogged down amid fierce resistance and heavy losses.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Defense Minister Claims Airstrikes Are Aimed at Achieving Peace
World.content:
Despite widespread domestic and international condemnation of the military junta’s airstrikes on civilian targets, newly appointed regime Defense Minister Lieutenant General Yar Pyae said the bombing operations were intended to achieve peace.

“Mainly, they [questions raised in the media] are based on human rights and humanitarian concerns regarding the bombings. From our perspective, the current military operations are actually steps taken to obtain peace,” Lt-Gen Yar Pyae, who also serves as chairman of the National Solidarity and Peacemaking Negotiation Committee (NSPNC), said during his closing address to a workshop marking the 11th Anniversary of the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) on October 16.

The military regime routinely bombs civilian targets in resistance-held territories in an effort to undermine anti-regime groups’ administration and to coerce them into joining its purported peace talks. The tactic worked well in northern Shan State and Mandalay Region, where it managed to force the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and its ally, the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA), to stop fighting, agree to China-brokered ceasefires and hand over some seized towns.

The regime continues to use the tactic in other regions and states including Rakhine State, which is almost entirely controlled by the Arakan Army (AA), an ally of MNDAA and TNLA.

On September 28, the regime conducted an airstrike targeting the busy Indian Market in the AA-controlled town of Kyauktaw, killing at least 50 people. The attack drew fierce condemnation from the UN, the UK, ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights and various human rights organizations.

Since the 2021 military coup, the Myanmar military has consistently launched airstrikes across revolutionary strongholds, including the Anyar region (also known as the Dry Zone) and ethnic minority regions—targeting not only military sites, but also schools, hospitals, religious buildings and civilian homes.

Even as it makes peace overtures, the regime continues to engage in heavy fighting with the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) in Bhamo, and clashes are ongoing with the AA in Rakhine State. Airstrikes also continue to target civilians in the Anyar region, where People’s Defense Forces (PDFs) maintain a strong presence.

Amid the ongoing air raids on resistance-held areas, junta leader Min Aung Hlaing made what he called an unconditional peace invitation during the 11th NCA anniversary event in Naypyitaw on October 15. The regime nonetheless continues to pressure the PDFs—the main armed resistance groups across the country—to lay down their arms and surrender.

According to statements made during a press conference at the close of the NCA anniversary workshop, invitations to peace talks were extended to the KIA, but not to the AA.

Furthermore, Min Aung Hlaing stated on October 15 that if ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) wish to engage in politics, they must disarm and form political parties; if they wish to conduct business, they must do so legally; and if they wish to serve in defense, they must join the Border Guard Forces (BGF).

In 2009, the military heavily pressured EAOs to transform into Border Guard Forces. With few exceptions, however, the initiative largely failed.

The KIA, which is currently engaged in intense fighting with the military, was one of the major ethnic armed groups that refused to transform into a BGF at that time. During the Spring Revolution that erupted in response to the coup, the KIA earned the Myanmar military’s ire by providing military training, weapons and combat support to anti-junta PDF forces.

Similarly, following Operation 1027, the AA seized control of most towns in Rakhine State, including a regional military command center. Since then, the regime has launched several offensives to retake lost territory in the state.

While urging PDFs to surrender and asking EAOs to join the BGF, Min Aung Hlaing also told ethnic representatives attending the NCA ceremony that he would cooperate with those willing to work together on peace, while actively finding methods to handle those who refuse to cooperate.

World.title: Solar Mandate Crushes Myanmar Builders as Regime Chief’s Son Profits
World.content:
Contractors warn that a new regime mandate requiring installation of solar power systems in all high-rises and commercial buildings will send construction costs soaring in Myanmar. The directive further squeezes construction companies already pinched by a shortage of materials, import restrictions, and severe currency volatility.

The Yangon City Development Committee’s Engineering Department issued the order on October 1 as part of a nationwide push for solar amid deepening power blackouts.

From November 1, all commercial projects and high-rise buildings must install solar panels sufficient to power elevators and emergency lighting. For commercial buildings, solar systems must be integrated with power supplied by the Yangon Electricity Supply Corporation (YESC).

The order applies to existing projects, buildings under construction, and those awaiting Building Completion Certificates required for habitation.

“We have been handed the order at a time when prices of solar panels and related equipment are rising daily,” complained a Mandalay‑based builder. “Steel and cement prices are already soaring, so this adds yet another burden.”

Meanwhile, industry insiders warn of a scarcity of skilled technicians capable of installing large solar systems, creating technical and financial hurdles. “Household systems won’t power elevators, which require commercial‑grade solar systems,” the manager of a solar dealership explained. “Installation takes at least two months and costs around 100 million kyat.”

Solar imports to feed surging demand created by the new mandate are controlled by Aung Pyae Sone, son of regime chief Min Aung Hlaing.

Aung Pyae Sone swiftly cornered the lucrative market after his father’s regime waived tax on solar imports in April 2023 under the pretext of boosting the energy grid. His Venus Essential company also holds licenses to supply solar equipment for projects in Naypyitaw and planned 40-megawatt solar power plants in Taungdwingyi, Salin, Pakokku, Pauk, Chauk and Kyunchaung.

The solar mandate comes as regime energy rationing intensifies with more frequent rolling blackouts this year.

“They cut electricity during extreme heat, then order solar systems to be installed,” said a former political prisoner from Mandalay. “But only one company — belonging to the coup leader son — is allowed to import and sell the equipment nationwide. This is not aimed at solving the power crisis, but exploiting authority for personal profit.”
