A man has been arrested for making threats and swinging nun-chunks outside the electorate office of state MP Hannah Beazley this afternoon, just days after West Australian politicians voiced their concerns about their safety following the attack on Helen Haines. WA Local Government Minister Hannah Beazley. Holly Thompson Police said they received reports about the man with the alleged weapon around 1.15pm this afternoon, after he entered Beazley’s Victoria Park office. Police attended quickly and found the man nearby in Bentley, arresting him. He is currently helping police with their inquiries, and has not been charged.



Hannah Beazley, who is WA’s Minister for Local Government and represents the electorate of Victoria Park, said in a statement she was aware of what had unfolded. “This afternoon, staff within my electorate office were faced with a confronting situation when a member of the public entered the office armed with a weapon,” she said. “I have spoken to my staff, who are understandably shaken and upset by what took place. Fortunately, no one was injured during the incident. “Right now, my focus is on the welfare of those staff members.” The incident comes just days after federal member for Indi Helen Haines was attacked outside her office in Wangaratta on Monday, after a man allegedly repeatedly hit her with a white Toyota four-wheel-drive.





“I thank the police officers who responded quickly and soon had a person in custody. Their response to this incident and the support they have provided my staff is greatly appreciated. “At this time, I do not know the motivation behind what occurred today, and as the matter is now subject of a police investigation I won’t comment further.” Earlier on Wednesday, One Nation WA leader Rod Caddies claimed a man threatened to kill him while he was driving home from parliament on Tuesday night. WA One Nation leader Rod Caddies. Hamish Hastie Caddies revealed he was about a minute away from Parliament House in the Perth CBD and stopped at traffic lights when a man pulled up next to him and gestured him to wind his window down.



Caddies did and said the man started yelling profanities at him and threatened to kill him. “I just said to him, ‘mate, there’s no need to get angry’ and he just kept yelling quite an amount of abuse, and said he was going to bash me and he was going to do different things, and then he said he’d follow me home,” he said. “He said I don’t care about the police, I’ll follow you home and kill you.” When Caddies said he was going to alert police, the man said he didn’t care. Caddies took a photo of the driver’s number plate and alerted the dignitary protection unit which is investigating the incident.



Related Article Haines attack Security briefing for anxious MPs as Helen Haines loses leg, remains in critical condition Caddies said he didn’t feel unsafe and wouldn’t consider removing his One Nation decals from his vehicle. A WA Police spokeswoman confirmed police were investigating the incident. “WA Police has established capabilities to assess and respond to threats against elected representatives, and those arrangements remain in place,” she said. “We will continue to assess emerging information and respond as required.”

World.title: Our five favourite luxury homes for sale within walking distance of the beach
World.content:
PropertyNewsLuxury property Our five favourite luxury homes for sale within walking distance of the beach Shona Hendley October 21, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Whether it’s water views, the sound of crashing waves, or the fresh sea air, living near the beach has definite perks. Beyond the sensory treat, living near the beach can lower stress, improve mood and sleep, and promote an active lifestyle, plus provide financial benefits: coastal homes often appreciate faster and command high resale prices. Here are five of our favourite luxury homes within walking distance of the beach. 71 Nimmo Street, Middle Park VIC



“Glenhaven” is a c. 1910 Edwardian home only blocks away from Middle Park beach. In addition to its beachside location, the property is close to MSAC, Armstrong Street village and public transport. The home features period details including a tuck-pointed facade, art nouveau leadlight windows, an L-shaped entrance hall, high ceilings, an open fireplace and solid timber floors. With five bedrooms, open-plan and formal living areas, and a rear deck with a lap pool, this property has plenty to offer. 4 Adina Road, Curl Curl NSW



Showcasing coastal living, this Curl Curl home is about 150 metres from the beach. The property offers resort-style living, including a covered, north-facing entertainers’ deck, a mosaic-tiled pool and a near-level lawn framed by landscaped tropical gardens. The home features natural stone and timber, including a sandstone facade and, inside, a sparrow-pecked sandstone feature wall that conceals a Jetmaster gas log fireplace, a marble kitchen, engineered oak floors, plantation shutters, bespoke light fittings, timber cabinetry and shelving. 8 Seacombe Grove, Brighton VIC



Located on a tree-lined street within Brighton’s Golden Mile, this home is only a short walk to the foreshore, the dog beach and the Bay Trail. Designed by Stephen Akehurst, the single-level home features high ceilings, American oak floors and a marble kitchen. The basement is accessible by lift or stairs and includes a fully equipped cinema, gymnasium, and powder room, plus a wine cellar with integrated refrigeration and an ice maker, plus parking for six cars. Paul Bangay’s landscaping is a standout, with formal gardens at the front and rear, plus an al fresco area featuring an outdoor gas fireplace and a plumbed barbecue. 42 Bay Street, Mosman NSW



With harbour views and a foreshore canopy, this Mosman home sits in a unique position, embracing the surrounding rockery and offering a pathway to a private tidal beach and tidal landing in Quakers Hat Bay. The same family has owned the property for more than 40 years. It sits on an approximately 1378-square-metre landholding and includes a swimming pool, deck and a spa and sauna on the home’s lower level. The home is an example of modernist architecture, with an indoor-outdoor connection through floor-to-ceiling windows and wraparound terracing. 1/161 Hedges Avenue, Mermaid Beach QLD



Spread over five levels, this beachfront residence sits on the highly sought-after Hedges Avenue in Mermaid Beach. Ocean views extend from nearly every room, plus a rooftop entertaining terrace with a secondary kitchen, commercial glass washer, double fridge-freezer and a heat pump-heated lap pool with resistance jets. The home features high ceilings, a gourmet kitchen, a high-speed lift, four bedrooms including a main suite with a wraparound robe, an opulent en suite with a freestanding bath and a secluded balcony overlooking the coastline.

Executive chef Alejandro Saravia has crafted a flavour-packed itinerary across Latin America, right in the heart of Martin Place. First stop: Mexico. Slices of raw swordfish and crisp cucumber are rested in a cold, citrusy broth that hints of winter melon. The bluefin tuna belly tostada is a smoky and spicy affair with fiery salsa macha tempered by roasted avocado cream.

Next up is Argentina, with a well-charred and attentively seasoned Black Market Denver steak, melting gracefully on the palate and paired with tangy chimichurri.

A quick journey to Brazil calls for hearty, coconut-scented moqueca, the stew loaded with cod, prawn, scallop and squid, paired with steamed rice and toasted cassava flour.

The elegant dining room may be inside the heritage-listed former Sydney General Post Office, but with such a roving menu, and a wine list that follows the brief, you could well be in Buenos Aires.

Must-order dish: Black Market Denver steak with chimichurri.

World.content:

Judging by the flocks of locals loading up with Ciro’s takeaway boxes, Thirroul residents are quite aware their town has some of the best pizza in the state. The base is thin, blistered and subtly sour, and you can also have it in flatbread form to run through stracciatella with pistachio vinaigrette, or whipped ricotta underneath charred butternut pumpkin.

A pizzeria is only as good as its margherita, of course, and this one has the ideal balance of San Marzano tomato sweetness and creamy dollops of fior di latte. The white-sauced pizzas are just as good, including the garlicky, earthy “Shroom” number, which goes great guns with a house orange wine made by co-owner Joel Mucci’s label Benson and Mooch.

House-made limoncello also feels essential, and if you’re in the market for something more protein-heavy, ask about the wood-fired rice with confit chicken.

Good to know: On Mondays, only pizzas are available, but all of them are $20.

World.content:

David Prest of Thrumster writes: “When I started my Mechanical Engineering Certificate in 1975, I was forced to get a calculator as the rest of the class were worried that my use of logarithm tables and slide-rule (C8) wouldn’t be fast enough during the exam. I still have that calculator but the logarithm table book and the slide-rule have since gone.”

Perhaps Valerie Bray of East Killara can help: “I still have my old slide-rule and book of logarithm tables. The problem is, I’ve forgotten how to use them.”

“I once sat for an exam with an array of jelly beans (for sugar),” says Pasquale Vartuli of Pennant Hills. “I noticed an examiner looking at them to see if I had inscribed any messages on them. ”

Ian Nicholls of Baulkham Hills makes a good point “Years ago, during an engineering lecture, the topic of exam nerves came up. Our stern old school professor said self-control was important and went on to tell us that when he had a panic attack during an exam, he had to stab his hand with his pair of compasses to regain control.”

Edward Loong of Milsons Point (C8) has a fair bit to unpack regarding his new-found fame: “No, Graham Lum, I ain’t Edmund – he’s my older brother! Loong story. But, yes, Maureen Lysaght, Nancy is my older sister. Small world, indeed.”

World.title: The ripple effects of political behaviour

NationalVictoriaLetters Editorial The ripple effects of political behaviour

October 21, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. If the behaviour we walk past is the behaviour we accept then the behaviour we engage in must be the behaviour we promote. The only thing politicians have total control over is their own behaviour. Aspects of social media and the extreme behaviours of some groups should be considered in the light of the alleged attack on Helen Haines. The more powerful tool politicians have is to change their own behaviours. The behaviour of politicians in question time and public commentary surely must contribute to the way members of the public behave towards them. It would only take one party to ensure their behaviour adheres to what it spouts about respectful conversations in the context of question time for a significant increase in the safety of all of them and us.

Dianne Wilson, Wantirna South Waves of being desensitised

I applaud all the letters (21/10), written in relation to Helen Haines. Yes, we need to change our speech, our online posts, our hateful thoughts. But part of the reason these events are becoming more common lies on TV. The most popular shows seem to be crime shows where bodies are strewn galore and in graphic detail sometimes. Plus video games that depict sword-wielding heroes blithely chopping down enemies. We are desensitised to pain and violence. Not to mention the promotion of war, the misogyny, the inequality, drugs, domestic violence and more. The answer to all this disillusionment and anger is hard to work out and implement, but mouthing phrases like ″⁣we must do better″⁣ are meaningless banalities.

Margaret Collings, Anglesea Will the vitriol in parliament stop?

What are the chances that the vitriol in parliament such as MP Angie Bell’s statement a week ago that Anthony Albanese and Anne Aly should be ″⁣shamed and stoned in the square″⁣ might now cease? A number of our elected representatives need to have a good look at themselves and reflect on the language and example they set. Are they really working in the best interest of this country?

Bruce McQualter, Richmond



Following the path of a leader

Crossbench MPs have a saying, “What would Helen do?” Helen Haines would undoubtedly have expressed her extreme sadness at the terrible incident. However, Haines would not speculate about the motive. Instead, she would wait for evidence before attributing motive, show consideration for all involved and be opposed to inflammatory dialogue. Most importantly, she would show leadership by opening her door to all those in her community who feel traumatised by the event.

Sarah Russell, Mt Martha Abuse within the chamber cause for concern

The alleged attack on Helen Haines, has shocked the community and highlighted the vulnerability of MPs to harm while working in their constituencies. It should also be of concern that abuse occurs within the chambers of parliament, where some MPs use uncivil and violent language against their political colleagues. A lack of civility among the political class does not augur well for change of negative attitudes within the community.

Ellen Ryan, Soldiers Hill Behavioural norms need to be elevated

The alleged attack on Helen Haines illustrates the descent in behaviour norms in society. For politics, it is now an attack dog chamber that has descended into nastiness and vitriol mirroring the tactics of the US president. Julia Gillard’s misogyny speech was a response to a decaying calibre of conduct. Things have only got worse in the past 14 years. Parliament used to have robust and respectful debate. This is no longer. We need to get back to this as exemplar behaviour norms. If society sees the government and its elected members behaving badly, it legitimises this behaviour.

Julian Druce, Balaclava THE FORUM State of the nation

We’re all shocked at what happened to Helen Haines. We tell ourselves this isn’t who we are as Australians.

In the next breath, we say the government should do more to prevent incidents like this. What exactly? Of course, it would be better if politicians didn’t use ugly rhetoric to get their point across, but the overwhelming source of ugliness in our lives comes through the social media to which so many are addicted. A platform where misinformation, disinformation, outright lies and outrage crowd out kindness, tolerance and facts.

The grim reality is that social media is a failed experiment. Whatever good might have come from it has been swamped by the negative consequences of a business model that relies on outrage to drive engagement.

“Turning down the temperature” isn’t a government responsibility. It’s on all of us. If we’re serious about it, we should all get off any platform that makes use of algorithm-driven feeds. Instead of scrolling on our devices, try talking to the people around you, watching the evening news to see what’s happening in the world and finding ways to contribute positively to the country we claim we want to live in.

Donna Cohen, Southbank



For shame

The two major parties do not engage in ″⁣robust debate″⁣ in parliament as Anthony Albanese would have us believe. They yell, bully, hurl abuse and insults and belittle their opposition in a way that would not be tolerated in any workplace or around a family dinner table. The contrast in behaviour with community independents like Helen Haines is stark. Do better. Show respect.

Belinda Burke, Hawthorn Reduce house size

In all of the debates about how to solve the housing crisis, scant attention has been paid to the size of new homes. In my area, a house that fills the entire block is becoming the norm.

This week, I walked past one for sale – five bedrooms, five bathrooms and five lounges. At a time when family size is shrinking, who needs these homes?

And all the materials needed to build such homes, would probably build two or three smaller ones.

Why not put a moratorium on house size until we are able to house all who need a home? It was done after the Second World War when building materials were scarce.

Margaret O’Connor, Balwyn Dig deeper on sale

At face value, the state Opposition’s announced plan to follow other states and sell off the Melbourne Wholesale Fruit & Vegetable Market seems like a reasonable policy (″⁣Coalition’s fresh plan to sell fruit market, pay off $578m debt″⁣, 21/10).

However, a final decision should be made only after extensive consultation, detailed modelling and big picture planning.

Victorians with long memories will remember past sales of government assets with promises to reduce government debt, be better run by the private sector and lead to lower prices for consumers. These commitments were made when large-scale privatisation occurred in the 1990s. In real terms, Victorians are now paying more than ever for electricity, gas and water and, of course, the replacement of VicRoads day labour gangs by private contractors who repair our roads has been a great success, hasn’t it?

Paying $578 million off state debt and allowing traders to take control of the market seems to make sense. However, if owner traders are profit driven, what will be the impact on prices that consumers pay for fruit and vegetables?

James Young, Mt Eliza High-rise future

Former New York mayor Bill de Blasio’s comment that urban sprawl is a ″⁣massive failure″⁣ of the Western world should be uppermost in the minds of all people, not just governments, town planners and developers.

Cars are a major factor in allowing cities to sprawl. Cities have been grappling with the problem of how to reduce their dependency on cars for transport in urban settings. Victoria is a slow learner.

Unfortunately, if Melbourne is to develop using the most sensible ideas available, and for the future predicted populations, high-rise is inevitable. Social justice arguments require it also. Real consultation is a key essential.

Howard Tankey, Box Hill North Mapping the reality

Cutting migration could be a disaster for many areas of employment. My husband has been in aged care for 18 months. I have mounted a map of the world on his wall where we record the names and country of birth of all the exceptionally wonderful people who look after him.

The staff enjoy having their names recorded and we all laugh about the fact that only one carer was born in Australia. Most are from Nepal. Even my husband was born in another country.

Long may immigration continue. This aged care facility and others, hospitals, outback roadhouses and your local restaurant would have staffing problems without migrants.

Ann Kriegler, Brunswick



Listen to needs

Instead of recycling middle-class welfare (″⁣Labor’s $30 weekly transport cap″⁣, 19/10), the state government could be really tough on crime and use tax dollars to properly fund key social services such as child protection and family services, housing and homelessness, community support, and public education to prevent crime before it happens. True social equality comes from genuinely listening to and providing for people’s needs. Doing so is also the most effective way to minimise the relevance of One Nation and other extremist groups.

Jennie Epstein, Little River We are not the US

Politicians talk about our shared values with the United States. It is difficult to see what these shared values are, if you move past a common language and a democratic system.

Australia does not have capital punishment. Twenty-three American states actively retain the death penalty.

We do not have ill-trained, heavily armed men roaming the streets and occasionally shooting innocent citizens while looking for illegal migrants. Australia has gun control legislation. In 2024 in America, 44,447 people died from gun-related injuries.

With an increasingly erratic president and his supporters attacking the various pillars that sustain a strong democracy such as an independent judicial system, public accountability and free and fair elections, it is becoming clear we share very few values with them.

Carolyn Worth, Brighton East PM, act on gambling

Perhaps now after the results of the inquest into the suicide of young gambling addict, Kyle Hudson, Anthony Albanese will, at last, take some action against the pernicious gambling industry (″⁣Coroner slams Sportsbet over man’s suicide″⁣, 21/10).

Reg Murray, Glen Iris Grist for her mill

I would think Pauline Hanson does not really care who she insults and upsets. These attacks on whatever target she feels will generate publicity is all grist for her mill. And publicity is the ultimate goal. An unenthusiastic apology is the price she is willing to pay.

Marie Nash, Balwyn How to reach surplus

Columnist Ross Gittins writes that the Grattan Institute proposal to raise the GST to 15 per cent will do nothing to balance the federal budget (Comment, 21/10).

The reason is that under the Grattan plan, all the additional revenue is put back into economy, mainly to compensate low-income earners for the regressive effects of the increased GST.

Gittins states that Australia actually needs to run a budget surplus at present. However, apart from a brief mention of increased tax on gas exports, there is little indication of how it might be achieved. Not a word about the other side of the budget: government spending.

Rod Wise, Surrey Hills



Tax by another name

It is disappointing to see Ross Gittins arguing that the GST rate should be increased, and doubly disappointing to see him claim this would be taxation ″⁣fairness″⁣, between younger and older Australians.

Given that older Australians often spend money from their superannuation, and Gittins and The Grattan Institute want that spending taxed through GST – this tax reform proposal is a superannuation tax by another name.

It is also important to note that the Grattan Institute presents its proposal for a higher rate of GST as a solution to our ballooning public debt. That debt would be far less of a problem if Jim Chalmers and the PM had been more disciplined with their spending.

When Wayne Swan in 2013 brought down the final budget of the Gillard government, Commonwealth spending was 24.9 per cent of GDP. The Commonwealth Budget this past May showed it at 26.8 per cent. Add the $65 billion of hidden ″⁣off budget″⁣ spending that economist Chris Richardson has pinpointed and it’s arguably 29.1 per cent. There’s your ″⁣problem″⁣.

The economic theoreticians should also note that not all older Australians are wealthy.

Think again please Ross Gittins.

Alun Breward, Malvern East It’s not a joke

As a retired teacher, I often have cause to reflect on the effort I, and many of my colleagues, made to help teenagers understand the importance of behaving respectfully towards others. Many times their pranks and “satirical” comments were justified with “but it was just a joke ... they can’t take it”. A joke? But at whose expense? Thinking about some of today’s adult politicians.

Ken Fisher, Warragul Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING



Haines

The issue of male violence against women is increasingly recognised but more needs to be done from an early age to understand and eliminate misogyny and its highly damaging impact across society.

Tony Delaney, Warrnambool I am so, so sad for Australia.

Robyn Carey, North Fitzroy The mass media must accept some responsibility for routinely denigrating politicians, helping turn political disagreement into hostility and making them easier targets for hate.

Steve Melzer, Hughesdale After the devastating attack on Helen Haines, my heart is slightly lifted by the sight of a mother and father duck and their seven fluffy ducklings swimming in our pool.

Susan Munday, Bentleigh East Job cuts

NAB boss Andrew Irvine should lead from the front and take a 6 per cent pay cut to keep in line with the bank’s efficiency push (″⁣Fears banks to follow NAB’s jobs layoff lead″⁣, 21/10).

Peter Baddeley, Portland



Hopefully, the sacked NAB workers are qualified to work in aged care.

Tim Durbridge, Brunswick Furthermore

Employers will need to be dragged screaming and kicking before being forced to share increased productivity (″⁣Former NY mayor warns of AI impact″⁣, 19/10).

Malcolm McDonald, Burwood Among a slew of terrible news it was good to read that Albertans have voted to stay a part of Canada.

John Walsh, Watsonia Yes, in maths two negatives can make a positive, when the numbers are multiplied or divided (Letters, 21/10). But adding two negatives just makes it more negative.

Mark Herrmann, Bentleigh East Finally

Grumpy after being woken early from a nap, my two-year-old grandson declared he was ″⁣crosstrated″⁣ with everyone. Clear favourite for Word of the Year.

Dale Crisp, Brighton

World.title: Man arrested after entering WA MP’s electorate office with ‘nunchucks’
World.content:
NationalWACrime Man arrested after entering WA MP’s electorate office with ‘nunchucks’ Hannah Murphy and Hamish Hastie October 21, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A man has been arrested for making threats and swinging nun-chunks outside the electorate office of state MP Hannah Beazley this afternoon, just days after West Australian politicians voiced their concerns about their safety following the attack on Helen Haines. WA Local Government Minister Hannah Beazley. Holly Thompson Police said they received reports about the man with the alleged weapon around 1.15pm this afternoon, after he entered Beazley’s Victoria Park office. Police attended quickly and found the man nearby in Bentley, arresting him. He is currently helping police with their inquiries, and has not been charged.



Hannah Beazley, who is WA’s Minister for Local Government and represents the electorate of Victoria Park, said in a statement she was aware of what had unfolded. “This afternoon, staff within my electorate office were faced with a confronting situation when a member of the public entered the office armed with a weapon,” she said. “I have spoken to my staff, who are understandably shaken and upset by what took place. Fortunately, no one was injured during the incident. “Right now, my focus is on the welfare of those staff members.” The incident comes just days after federal member for Indi Helen Haines was attacked outside her office in Wangaratta on Monday, after a man allegedly repeatedly hit her with a white Toyota four-wheel-drive.





“I thank the police officers who responded quickly and soon had a person in custody. Their response to this incident and the support they have provided my staff is greatly appreciated. “At this time, I do not know the motivation behind what occurred today, and as the matter is now subject of a police investigation I won’t comment further.” Earlier on Wednesday, One Nation WA leader Rod Caddies claimed a man threatened to kill him while he was driving home from parliament on Tuesday night. WA One Nation leader Rod Caddies. Hamish Hastie Caddies revealed he was about a minute away from Parliament House in the Perth CBD and stopped at traffic lights when a man pulled up next to him and gestured him to wind his window down.



Caddies did and said the man started yelling profanities at him and threatened to kill him. “I just said to him, ‘mate, there’s no need to get angry’ and he just kept yelling quite an amount of abuse, and said he was going to bash me and he was going to do different things, and then he said he’d follow me home,” he said. “He said I don’t care about the police, I’ll follow you home and kill you.” When Caddies said he was going to alert police, the man said he didn’t care. Caddies took a photo of the driver’s number plate and alerted the dignitary protection unit which is investigating the incident.



Related Article Haines attack Security briefing for anxious MPs as Helen Haines loses leg, remains in critical condition Caddies said he didn’t feel unsafe and wouldn’t consider removing his One Nation decals from his vehicle. A WA Police spokeswoman confirmed police were investigating the incident. “WA Police has established capabilities to assess and respond to threats against elected representatives, and those arrangements remain in place,” she said. “We will continue to assess emerging information and respond as required.”

World.title: Armed Offenders Squad storm Massey property after man reported with firearm
World.content:
The Armed Offenders Squad have stormed a property in the west Auckland suburb of Massey following reports of a man with a firearm.

An RNZ reporter at the scene said police used a battering ram to enter the house and several loud bangs were then heard, accompanied by bright flashes.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407175242112

An ambulance was then seen driving through a cordon towards the property.

Another ambulance arrived later, and a man sitting up on a stretcher was brought out of the house and loaded into the back of a waiting ambulance.

Do you know more? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz

Earlier, about 10pm, police said they were at a property in Massey following reports of a male with a firearm.

"Specialist Police staff are at the scene and are working to speak with the male to bring the situation to a safe conclusion.

"The scene is currently contained to the property on Manutewhau Road, and people are asked to avoid the area."

They said no one was believed to be injured at that time.

Police are in the west Auckland suburb of Massey following reports of a man with a firearm. RNZ / Calvin Samuel

The police Eagle helicopter began circling the area before 9pm.

Hate Hone St John confirmed it was called at 7.49pm and had an ambulance, rapid response and manager on standby.

It said the operations manager and ambulance were stood down by 10.15pm, but the rapid response was still on standby.

An online aviation tracker shows a Police helicopter circling above Massey. Screenshot / adsbexchange.com

An RNZ reporter at the scene said several armed police were blocking Manutewhau Road at the intersection of George McWhirter Avenue.

Armed Offenders Squad (AOS) and police vehicles could be seen further down Manutewhau Road where they were focusing attention on a property near Orowaru Avenue.

They reported members of the AOS were coming and going up the front steps of a block of units.

What looked like a communications or negotiation unit, where several police staff were located, had also been set up on George McWhirter Avenue, they said.

About 10.30pm, another police vehicle arrived and officers were seen removing and prepping rifles from the boot.

World.title: Blindspott cancels Auckland show after singer lands in hospital
World.content:
Blindspott's one-off show in Auckland has been cancelled after vocalist Damian Alexander landed in hospital.



The alternative metal band was due to host a release party for its new single Stitches on 7 November at The Powerstation.



In a post on social media, the band announced the event's cancellation.



"Last week, Damian experienced a serious vascular health issue that will require some time to heal and ongoing specialist follow-up," it said.



"He's doing well and is in good hands, and is incredibly grateful to the team at Auckland Hospital for the care he's received.



"Unfortunately, this means our November 7 show at Auckland's Powerstation has been cancelled, not postponed. All ticket holders will be advised of the refund process."



The release of Blindspott's upcoming album would also be put on hold until Alexander was medically cleared "to return to the studio and stage to put the finishing touches on the record".



"Damian wants to thank everyone who has reached out and checked in on him. He's incredibly grateful for the support and is focused on getting well," the band said.



"As a band and a family, Damian's health and wellbeing are our absolute priority. We're all behind him and wishing our brother a full and speedy recovery.



"Thank you all for your understanding, love and continued support."



Blindspott was formed in the late nineties in West Auckland.

World.title: Silver Ferns beat Australia again to take commanding Constellation Cup position
World.content:
The Silver Ferns have put themselves in the best possible position to win the Constellation Cup for just the fourth time after beating Australia 62-50 in Christchurch.

After losing the first Test in Auckland by six goals, the Diamonds came out stronger but the Silver Ferns managed to weather the storm to go 2-nil up before the series heads to Australia for the final two Tests.

The Silver Ferns have now beaten Australia four times in a row, going back to last year's annual series, while the Diamonds surprising losing streak on New Zealand soil now sits at 12.

Peta Toeava returned to the black dress for the first time in a year, starting at wing attack, where she quickly resumed her telepathic connection with her former Mystics team-mate Grace Nweke.

The Diamonds welcomed vice-captain Kate Moloney back, after a finger injury and the more traditional Australian shooting line-up of Sophie Garbin and Kiera Austin provided good structure for the visitors.

New Zealand led 17-14 at the end of the first quarter, where a few turnovers were the difference.

Diamonds coach Stacey Marinkovich made several changes throughout the game, particularly in her defensive end.

The Silver Ferns patiently absorbed the pressure of a more clinical Australian side, and were able to bide their time before finding opportunities to bomb it into Nweke.

The circle defensive pairing of Kelly Jackson and Karin Burger built across the game and the Ferns extended their lead 33-26 at half-time.

Mila Reuelu-Buchanan came on at wing defence at half-time, which saw Kate Heffernan and Maddy Gordon shift one position up the court.

Grace Nweke of the Silver Ferns and Courtney Bruce tussle for the ball. John Davidson / www.photosport.nz

The Silver Ferns went out to an 11 goal lead in the early stages of the third quarter before the visitors launched a fightback.

Jessie Grenvold, who made her Diamonds' debut in the first test, was able to make some inroads at goal keep.

The Diamonds managed to cut New Zealand's lead to just three heading into the final turn but the home side held their nerve.

Te Paea Selby-Rickit entered at goal attack for the final quarter and Toeava returned, which saw Gordon shift back to centre, and Kate Heffernan went to the bench.

Silver Ferns coach Dame Noeline Taurua told Sky Sport some changes needed to be made as "tired errors" came into the game.

Shooter Donnell Wallam made a long-awaited return for Australia and faced the Silver Ferns for the first time in her career, when she came on during the final quarter.

Toeava had an impressive 45 minutes on court. Nweke had a brilliant game finishing with 49 from 55.

Gordon, who maintained a high work rate in the midcourt, came away with MVP honours.

The Diamonds penalty count of 84 was significantly higher than the Silver Ferns.

Despite the bigger score line, the Diamonds posed more challenges for the Silver Ferns in the second Test.

The Silver Ferns have found playing in Australian a challenge, winning just one of their last nine tests across the Tasman.

If the series ends with two wins each, the winner will be decided by goal percentage.

World.title: Puberty blocker restrictions for gender-diverse youth overturned by High Court
World.content:
The High Court has ruled regulations banning new prescriptions of puberty blockers for young people with gender dysphoria were unlawful.

In 2025, the Government sought to introduce regulations stopping doctors from making new prescriptions of puberty blockers for children and adolescents with gender dysphoria or gender incongruence.

The Ministry of Health undertook public consultation in 2024 on whether there should be additional safety measures for the prescribing of puberty blockers in young people with gender-related health needs.

The majority of public submissions opposed further restrictions on the prescribing of puberty blockers.

In November 2025, the minister recommended the regulations be made in light of the potential harm caused by puberty blockers. The regulations prohibited new prescriptions to treat gender dysphoria or gender incongruence in children and adolescents.

However, the prescription of puberty blockers remained available to pause puberty for young people with other medical conditions, and for use in gender-affirming care for those who had been prescribed them prior to the regulations.

The following month, the Professional Association for Transgender Health Aotearoa (PATHA) applied for judicial review of the regulations. Court orders were granted preventing enforcement of the regulations pending final resolution of the proceedings.

In a decision released today, the court found the Government failed to adequately consult those affected by failing to consult on the substance of the regulations and failing to directly consult with gender diverse young people.

It also found the restrictions unlawfully discriminated against gender-diverse young people, breaching the Bill of Rights.

It found there was differential treatment between young people with gender-related health needs and those who could access puberty blockers for other health conditions.

"This differential treatment imposed a material disadvantage on young people with gender-related health needs, as they are at high risk of seriously poor health outcomes, particularly self-harm and suicide."

It found while there was a rational basis to impose restrictions on access to puberty blockers for some, a complete prohibition on prescriptions for new patients was a disproportionate response to the potential harm caused by puberty blockers.

The court did not accept that the Minister abdicated his decision-making power to Cabinet and acted for an improper purpose of advancing New Zealand First's "anti-woke" agenda.

It ruled that the regulations were unlawful and invalid, and made an order setting them aside.

PATHA president Jennifer Shields said the organisation was "incredibly relieved" with the court's findings.

"Moves to restrict transgender people's right to access healthcare are rooted in disinformation and have massively significant impacts on the health and wellbeing of transgender people in Aotearoa. I'm pleased that the court agreed that this ban was an act of unjustified

discrimination.

PATHA vice-president and GP Dr Elizabeth McElrea said clinicians saw the benefits of puberty blockers and the significant impact they had on the lives of young transgender people.

"Decisions about this healthcare are best made by patients and their doctors. The removal of this regulation is crucial and puts that decision back in the consult room."

McElrea said clinicians could continue to prescribe puberty blocking medication in line with best practice and without fear of retribution for doing the right thing.

PATHA secretary Avery Zavoda said the announcement of the regulations and the year-long wait for the findings of the judicial review had caused harm to trans young people, their families and their doctors.

"Such an act of discrimination is something no young person should have to experience. It's now a matter of law that restricting trans

young people's access to puberty blockers is discriminatory."

Family First NZ said it was "shocked" by the decision, and that the High Court was siding with activists instead of vulnerable children.

Chief executive Bob McCoskrie said there was no settled scientific consensus supporting gender-affirming care for minors.

"The stakes could not be higher. These treatments can have life-altering consequences for young people. The Government has a responsibility to ensure that policies are guided by the strongest available evidence and not by pressure from advocacy groups."

A spokesperson for the Health Minister said the government was committed to introducing new safeguards for prescribing puberty blockers, while ensuring patients with medical needs could continue to access care.

They said there was a lack of high-quality evidence demonstrating the benefits or risks of the medication for treating gender dysphoria or incongruence.

"While this uncertainty persists, the government is taking a precautionary approach.

"The government will continue to take an evidence-based approach to this matter and is seeking advice on next steps."

World.title: Photos only a part of 'overwhelming' case against Scott Watson, Crown says
World.content:
Crown lawyers in the Supreme Court today say a photo montage at the heart of Scott Watson's appeal is only one piece of evidence in an "overwhelming" case against him.

Watson is appealing his conviction for the murders of Ben Smart and Olivia Hope in Marlborough Sounds on New Years' Day in 1998.

His lawyers argue the evidence of water taxi driver Guy Wallace - used in the original trial - who picked out Watson in "Photo Montage B" as the man seen boarding a boat with the young pair, is inadmissible.

Crown lawyer Madeleine Laracy said the Crown always relied on a "large volume of evidence" - not just a photo montage.

"This was and is an overwhelming case."

Laracy referred to the Court of Appeal's judgment in 2024 - which rejected a previous bid by Watson to quash his convictions.

The Court of Appeal had found there were just too many factors pointing to Watson, Laracy said.

"If Mr Watson was not the man on the Naiad, then the lone man, like Mr Watson, happened to be alone, happened to have a yacht, happened to have moored his yacht out from the jetty, happened to be in the same age range, late twenties or early thirties, happened to have an appearance that was so like Mr Watson's as to mislead Mr Wallace into thinking it was the same man."

Crown lawyer Stuart Baker said Wallace's evidence did not solely rely on picking him out of a photo montage.

"This was not a case of a fleeting glance by Mr Wallace, rather Mr Wallace observed the male at the lodge for some time throughout the evening, both in the main bar and the garden bar."

Baker said Wallace gave descriptions of the "lone man", prior to going to the wharf, including who was on the naiad, where exactly they went, what was said, and a description of rafted boats in the bay, where the three people disembarked.

The justices questioned Baker on Watson's lawyers' argument that police pressured Wallace to identify Watson in an interview in early January, 1998.

"It was inappropriate wasn't it?" Justice Joe Williams asked.

"I've never in all the trials I did read an interview like that," Williams said.

Baker replied: "I accept that the officer...that the questioning was challenging, and was at a level that quite clearly wouldn't be dealt with at the present day."

Baker said Wallace didn't succumb to pressure at the time to identify Watson, and ended up identifying him due to other reliable factors.

Another key issue that came up in the hearing was the photo police used of Watson in Montage B.

Watson had his eyes half-closed in this photograph, and his lawyers said yesterday it unfairly stood out and led to Wallace and others identifying him.

Chief Justice Helen Winkelmann put to Baker that this was "quite an extraordinary photograph", and asked him whether it was acceptable for police to choose a photo that most closely matches witness descriptions.

Baker replied that he thought it was acceptable, but the other photos in the montage needed to have other similar characteristics.

He said it didn't have the effect of substantially leading people to choose Watson, because about half of the 53 people shown the photo in montage b chose Watson.

Laracy said a major point in the Crown's case at the original trial was motive.

"The motive is a long-harboured intention to kill a woman," she said, and in her address she referred to witnesses who had pointed to such comments expressed in different words and different places.

"It [That motive] is suffused throughout this Crown case, and the way it is held together, it's a very important aspect of the Crown's case for identity."

Watson's Court of Appeal bid sought to overturn his convictions on the question of reliability of DNA evidence of two blonde hairs found on Watson's boat, as well as the photo montage evidence.

The Supreme Court is only considering the question of whether a miscarriage of justice arose from the decision of the original trial judge to admit Wallace's photo ID evidence.

World.title: Hundreds of critically endangered NZ weevils released back into the wild
World.content:
Hundreds of the critically-endangered Canterbury knobbled weevils have been released at a secret location.

The tiny creatures - which are protected under the Wildlife Act - were thought be extinct, but were rediscovered in the early 2000s.

Six of them became 260, after mating in a laboratory in Mosgiel.

Audio player for " Hundreds of endangered weevils released into the wild " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/environment/2059882%2Fhundreds-of-critically-endangered-nz-weevils-released-back-into-the-wild

Hundreds of endangered weevils released into the wild Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Department of Conservation entomologist Tara Murray - who set the weevils free today - told Checkpoint the weevils were "one of the most threatened insects in the country", but they did not expect them to be quite so easy to rear.

"We didn't think we'd get so many of them. So we're pretty chuffed that they've produced so many offspring and they've survived."

The Canterbury knobbled weevil on speargrass. Supplied / Department of Conservation

Murray said the weevils were a native species that would historically have been through a lot of the Canterbury lowlands, and humans had destroyed almost all of their natural habitat, so it was only fair that humans should help them out.

She said today's release had gone well, with about 215 of the tiny insects placed in special areas.

While she could not reveal where the weevils had been released, Murray said the insects were very particular about what they ate, and the spiky plants they favoured were found in the low foothills of Canterbury.

While owls would have been their main predator in the past, introduced species like hedgehogs and rodents were now the greatest threats to the weevils.

Releasing the knobbled weevils in Canterbury. Supplied / Department of Conservation

Murray said they had carried out a "soft release" to give the insects their best shot at survival.

"That means we've put little cages over the plants that they feed on and then we put the weevils into the middle of the plant and they just hunker down. Straight away they were scurrying right down into the base of the plant, which is exactly what we wanted them to do. And that just gives them the greatest chance of settling in instead of just running away straight away in a panic.

"They settle in, and after a week or two we'll take cages away and hopefully they'll stay exactly where they are on those plants."

Murray said the weevils were charming little creatures.

World.title: Hawke's Bay vet nurse challenges politicians to live on her income for a month
World.content:
Audio player for " Hawke's Bay mother challenges politicians to live on her income " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2057953%2Fhawke-s-bay-vet-nurse-challenges-politicians-to-live-on-her-income-for-a-month

Hawke's Bay mother challenges politicians to live on her income Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

A Hawke's Bay vet nurse and mother of two has challenged politicians to live on her income for a month.

Kayla Knibb wrote in to RNZ's Checkpoint saying she was sick of politicians arguing while families struggled to get by.

"I am angry, I am exhausted and quite frankly, I am sick of watching politicians argue over election polls while families like mine are drowning," she wrote.

Knibb spoke to the programme on Wednesday and said her family were struggling to make ends meet.

"You shouldn't be having to make these choices, you're meant to be working people, full-time jobs, we should be in a better place than where we are."

Knibb and her husband both work, earning about $100,000 to $130,000 a year before tax.

They've been making decisions on what they can go without in order to manage bills, she said.

"I can't really remember the last time I really bought packets of meat at the supermarket, we've gone to lentils, and chickpeas, and things because they're really cheap.

"There's just so many things that we have to try and juggle to make things a little bit better, and I don't really know what else there is."

Knibb was also fundraising for her son who has a chronic lung condition and was on IV antibiotics.

They've been declined additional financial help from anywhere else, she said.

"We work too much and we've been told we earn too much money to have any help from any external means," she said.

She said they've been trying to upgrade there home, so it can be a healthy home for her son.

"I had no idea that working hard, and kind of being put in this position, that it's not something that we're going to ever be able to do."

It was especially tough for families with children, she said.

"You've got to juggle daycare, food, working, sick leave, annual leave, it just all adds up and there's nothing left to give at the end."

Knibb wanted to see a politician try and survive on her income.

"I don't think they've ever had to be in that position, I don't think they've ever had to choose, or if it was, it was a very, very, very long time ago" she said.

World.title: Live: Aussies slump to 6-65 as Proteas quicks strike back
World.content:
Before we get underway today, just a quick word from David Warner, South Africa's favourite Australian, who has laid into the poor attendances at the cricket so far in the Republic.

In a social media post, Warner asked where the fans are, critiquing the empty stands and lack of atmosphere.

"We keep hearing how important Test cricket is, but where are the fans in South Africa?" he wrote. "Empty stands, no atmosphere, and we’re supposed to believe the format is thriving?"

I don't know if anyone in the T20 age believes the format is "thriving" David, but by all means continue...

"You can’t keep calling Test cricket the pinnacle of the game if no one turns up to watch it. "Harsh reality, but someone has to say it. Pathetic."

Harsh from Warner? Probably.

Fair? Probably.

As previously mentioned, it's no secret that outside of England and Australia, Test cricket is woefully supported.

The reasons are legion and far too many to talk about here with the cricket about to start, but there is a sense of a vicious circle of neglect when it comes to the format outside of the big three.

The first Test in Durban was the first home Test for South Africa in 641 days, the best part of TWO YEARS without a home Test?

Why? Because India, Australia and England take the bulk of the profits from cricket and the smaller nations simply cannot afford to host them any more.

South Africa doesn't get the high profile series during the height of their summer any more and, without a pattern of Tests at that time, how does one create a culture of going to the Tests?

This, as it happens, could be something Cricket Australia might want to think about given the lack of internationals the women are playing over the summer this year...

Additionally, it's not even summer in South Africa at the moment! October is the earliest South Africa have played a Test match at home in their history.

So before Mr Warner gets all high and mighty, maybe he might want to think about WHY nobody outside of Australia or England is turning up to Test cricket anymore and offer solutions, instead of just criticism.

World.title: Diamonds go down again as Ferns take control of Constellation Cup
World.content:
The Diamonds trail the four-game Constellation Cup series 2-0 after a 62-50 loss to New Zealand in Christchurch, continuing a five-year losing run across the ditch.

The series moves back to Australia for the final two matches — in Sydney on Sunday and Melbourne next Wednesday — as the Diamonds try to hang on to the trophy they reclaimed last year.

If the Silver Ferns win all four matches of the series they are expected to dethrone Australia from its number one world ranking for the first time since 2013.

After the six-goal loss in the opening match in Auckland, the Diamonds made a better start in game two but once again let the lead blow out to double digits by the third quarter.

The Diamonds regained the momentum and cut it to a two-goal difference just before three-quarter-time, but again the Silver Ferns responded and started the final term with a 10-3 run.

New Zealand captain Karin Burger praised her team for maintaining their focus even as the Aussies closed in.

The Silver Ferns were up and about as they took a 2-0 lead. (Getty Images: Joe Allison)

"Our training has been focused on staying really composed," she told Sky.

"In the past we've been guilty of letting that lead slip and then not being able to fight back."

The Diamonds shot just 82 per cent compared to New Zealand's 93, did not nab any intercepts, committed 18 turnovers to the Ferns' 11, lost the rebound battle 6-4 and, crucially, were penalised 31 more times in the game.

Captain Liz Watson credited the World Cup and Commonwealth Games champions, but suggested the Diamonds shot themselves in the foot more than a few times.

"Critical moments, turnovers, basic errors, those sort of things. Disappointing, really disappointing," she said.

"Sometimes it is perceived pressure rather than actual pressure. It could be the crowd, it could be [umpires'] calls, it could be what the Ferns are doing as well.

"They're a great team and when go hard they go really hard, so that can force errors, but we've got to be able to stay calm in those moments and read the game for what it is and not get caught up in what's happening around us."

Look back at how game two in Christchurch unfolded in our live blog below.

World.title: How Antonelli can become F1's youngest world champion this weekend
World.content:
Italian F1 driver Kimi Antonelli has his first chance to win the world championship this weekend, as the 20-year-old closes in on a maiden title in just his second season.

The Mercedes driver has been a class above the rest in 2026, with eight grand prix wins and a further six podium places across 17 rounds.

This Monday's (AEDT) United States Grand Prix will be Antonelli's first match point where he can officially seal a championship that has felt like his for many months.

The equation for Kimi Antonelli is very simple: win and hope for other results.

Antonelli enters this weekend's grand prix on 340 points, 102 more than teammate George Russell and 111 ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton.

The Italian needs to have a lead of 125 points or more to seal the drivers' championship at the United States Grand Prix.

That will happen if Antonelli wins the race, Russell finishes ninth or worse, and Hamilton finishes fifth or worse.

Antonelli Russell Hamilton Championship result Win 9th or lower 5th or lower Antonelli becomes champion Win 8th or better 5th or lower Hamilton eliminated Win 9th or lower 4th or better Russell eliminated Win 8th or better 5th or lower Championship remains alive 2nd or lower Any Any Championship remains alive

After this weekend, there will be five grands prix left in the season — Mexico, Brazil, Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

There will be a maximum of 125 points left to win.

If Antonelli finishes exactly 125 points ahead of either Russell or Hamilton in Texas, mathematically either of those drivers could end the season level on points — if they won every race and Antonelli failed to score another point.

Even in that unlikely scenario, Antonelli would still become champion through a tie-break, having won more grands prix than the others.

6:30am: ACDT: South Australia
